# The Art of Being Lost: Finding Meaning in Uncertainty

There's something peculiar about modern life that I've been thinking about lately—how much energy we expend trying to avoid being lost. We have GPS coordinates for every address, career paths mapped out from childhood, self-help books promising to show us "the way," podcasts with titles like "Never Feel Uncertain Again." We've built an entire civilization around the premise that being lost is a failure state, something to be corrected as quickly as possible.

Yet I wonder if we've gotten this backwards.

I'm not talking about being lost in the sense of dangerous disorientation. I'm talking about the smaller, more existential variety. The kind that happens when you take a wrong turn in a city you've never visited before and end up discovering a café you would never have found otherwise. The kind that occurs when a career path crumbles and you realize you have no predetermined route forward. The kind that settles in when you reach a goal you've been chasing for years and discover it doesn't feel the way you thought it would.

We live in an age of increasing specialization and predetermined tracks. We're encouraged to "find our passion" as though it's something lying around waiting to be discovered, like car keys under a couch cushion. We're told to make a five-year plan, a ten-year plan, to have our lives organized by the time we're thirty. This narrative is everywhere, and it carries with it an implicit message: if you're not following a clear path, if you're uncertain, if you're lost—something has gone wrong.

But here's what I've noticed: some of the most interesting people I know are people who got lost and decided to stay lost long enough to actually look around.

There's a woman I met once who was a lawyer. She had the whole thing—the degree, the job at a respectable firm, the trajectory that looked exactly how it's supposed to. And then one day she realized that she'd been walking toward a destination for so long that she'd never actually asked herself if she wanted to go there. So she quit. She spent two years doing odd jobs, volunteering at a community center, reading philosophy, wandering through life without a plan. During that time, she discovered she wanted to work with youth in underserved communities. She didn't "find her passion" in some magical moment. She found it by allowing herself to be lost, by stepping off the path long enough to remember that she was allowed to choose her own direction.

I think about this differently than I did when I was younger. When I was in my early twenties, I believed that having a plan meant you were serious, that you were an adult making responsible choices. Not having a plan seemed reckless, indulgent, something people only did because they hadn't yet realized how the world actually worked. I was terrified of being lost because being lost seemed like a sign of failure, a sign that I'd made mistakes or wasn't good enough to succeed on the predetermined path.

What I didn't understand then is that the predetermined path is largely an illusion anyway. It's a story we tell ourselves, a narrative we overlay on top of life to make it feel more controllable than it actually is. Life is intrinsically uncertain. The most carefully laid plans can dissolve in an instant due to circumstances entirely beyond our control. We get sick. People we love disappoint us. Markets crash. Industries shift. Technologies emerge that render old skills obsolete. The world simply doesn't cooperate with our master plans the way we'd like it to.

So perhaps there's something to be said for getting lost on purpose.

I don't mean recklessly abandoning all planning or responsibility. I mean creating space for uncertainty, for exploration, for the possibility that you might discover something that wasn't on your original itinerary. I mean being willing to turn down paths that don't appear on the map.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called "ma"—the space between things, the emptiness that gives form to the whole. Without the space between the notes, there would be no music, just noise. Without the white space on a page, there would be no clarity, just a wall of text. Without empty space in a composition, there's nowhere for the eye to rest, nowhere for the mind to wander.

I think humans need ma, too. We need empty space, unscheduled time, the freedom to wander. We need to not always know what comes next.

When I think about my own life, the moments I'd least like to erase are rarely the ones that went according to plan. They're the unexpected conversations with strangers on trains. The books I discovered by following a single reference down a rabbit hole of reading. The skills I picked up because I was curious about something, not because they fit neatly into a career trajectory. The relationships that formed because I was somewhere I didn't expect to be, doing something I hadn't planned to do.

The planned moments are fine. It's nice to accomplish things you've set out to accomplish. But they're not the ones that haunt you in the best way, that make you feel like you've actually *lived* something rather than just executed a plan.

There's also something about being lost that forces a kind of presence that planning doesn't. When you're following a predetermined path, you can be somewhat on autopilot. You know where you're supposed to be going, so you can let your mind wander to the next checkpoint. But when you're genuinely lost—when you don't know what comes next, when you have to actually pay attention to your surroundings and make decisions based on incomplete information—you're suddenly very present. You're alive to the moment in a way that a scheduled, mapped-out life rarely demands.

I've also come to understand that being lost is often where creativity lives. Every creative work, in some sense, requires venturing into territory that isn't fully mapped. When a writer sits down to write something new, they don't know exactly where the story will go. When a painter approaches a blank canvas, they're working with uncertainty. When a scientist designs an experiment, they're essentially saying, "I don't know what will happen, but I'm curious enough to find out." The edge of what we know is also the edge of what could be discovered.

This doesn't mean that planning is bad, or that structure is unnecessary. Certainly, we need enough order to function. But perhaps the problem in modern life is that we've swung too far toward total planning, toward the illusion of perfect control and predictability.

There's a reason that every successful creative person I've read about talks about the importance of play, of experimentation, of trying things without a predetermined outcome in mind. It's because without that space for lostness, without that willingness to explore without knowing where you'll end up, the work becomes sterile. It becomes about execution of a plan rather than about genuine creation.

I think about how children play before they're socialized into organized sports and structured activities. They just play. They follow their curiosity. They try things to see what happens. They're not trying to accomplish anything; they're just interested. And somehow, in that process, they're learning and growing and becoming more capable, but it's almost accidental—a byproduct of their attention rather than the goal.

Somewhere along the way, we tell them that this kind of unstructured play is a waste of time, that they should be using their time productively, working toward something. And maybe that's true to some degree. But I think we lose something important when we eliminate it entirely.

There's also the question of what it means to be "found." We talk about "finding yourself" or "finding your way" as though there's some stable, definable destination called the authentic self that you'll recognize once you arrive. But I'm not sure that's how it works. I think the self is more like a river than a location—it's constantly moving, changing, flowing. You're not trying to find a fixed point; you're learning to move with the current while also occasionally redirecting it.

Being lost is part of that process. It's not a deviation from the real journey; it's the real journey.

I think about the role that boredom and restlessness play in this, too. We've become very good at eliminating even moments of boredom. If we have a spare five minutes, we fill it with our phones. If we can't sleep, we listen to a podcast. If we're uncomfortable with silence, we play music. And I'm not judging this—I do it too. But there's something that happens when you're forced to just be with yourself, to sit with your own thoughts without distraction, that's valuable.

Some of my best ideas have come to me not while I was actively trying to solve a problem, but while I was bored, walking somewhere, with nothing particular on my mind. The space allows something to emerge.

I've also noticed that the fear of being lost often keeps people in situations that are slowly killing them. They stay in jobs that don't fulfill them because at least the path is clear. They stay in relationships that aren't working because the alternative—uncertainty—feels worse than the known unhappiness. They don't pursue interests that excite them because those interests don't fit into the plan.

In a way, staying in a bad situation because you're afraid of being lost is still being lost—it's just a more subtle kind of lostness, one that masquerades as having direction.

The people I know who seem most alive are the ones who've somehow made peace with uncertainty. They have plans, sure, but they hold them lightly. They're willing to change course if something more interesting appears. They're not waiting for permission to explore. They're not using the lack of a clear plan as an excuse to do nothing, but they're also not so attached to a predetermined path that they can't deviate when their interests or circumstances shift.

What I'm ultimately trying to say is this: being lost isn't a problem to be solved as quickly as possible. Sometimes being lost is exactly where you need to be. It's where you do your most interesting thinking. It's where you discover things about yourself you wouldn't have otherwise known. It's where genuine growth happens, as opposed to the mere execution of someone else's idea of what your life should look like.

The trick is learning to be lost without panicking. Learning to trust that not knowing where you're going doesn't necessarily mean you're going in the wrong direction. Learning that the most worthwhile destinations are often the ones you stumble upon by accident while looking for something else entirely.

So maybe the real skill we should be cultivating isn't the ability to always know exactly where we are on the map. Maybe it's the ability to get lost and stay calm enough to actually look around at where we've ended up. Maybe it's learning to follow our curiosity instead of our itinerary. Maybe it's understanding that the most meaningful lives are often the ones that look least like the plan.

We talk about finding ourselves as though it's a destination. But maybe we're not supposed to find ourselves. Maybe we're supposed to build ourselves, gradually, through all the small choices and detours and unexpected moments. And some of the most important building happens in the spaces between the plans, in the moments when we're genuinely lost and paying attention.

# On the Strange Grace of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking a lot lately about the moments that don't matter. Not the big ones—not graduations or proposals or the day you get that job or lose that person. Those moments get written down, photographed, remembered with intent. I'm talking about the other ones. The ones that slip past like water through your fingers, leaving no trace except maybe a faint impression that something small and good happened.

I was at a coffee shop yesterday—one of those indie places with mismatched furniture and a barista who actually knows people's names—and I watched a woman read a book. That's it. Nothing happened. But she was so completely absorbed in whatever world she was visiting that her coffee went cold beside her. Every few minutes she'd unconsciously tuck a strand of hair behind her ear in the same exact way, a gesture so habitual it seemed to come from some deeper part of her than consciousness. She made tiny facial expressions—a slight smile at something, a small frown of concern for her fictional character. She was living two lives at once, present in the coffee shop and completely elsewhere, and there was something beautiful about that duality that I can't quite articulate.

This is what I mean about ordinary moments. They're everywhere. They're invisible. They're the actual substance of life, and yet we've been culturally trained to ignore them, to wait for the important moments, to live life as a series of checkpoints rather than as an ongoing experience.

I think this has something to do with narrative. We're all obsessed with stories—we consume them constantly, in every form available to us—and stories have arcs. They have beginnings and middles and ends. They have climaxes. A story about someone reading a coffee shop for twenty minutes doesn't have an arc. It just is. And because it just is, with no narrative tension or resolution, we dismiss it as unimportant. But if ordinary moments aren't important, what is? What's the alternative?

The alternative seems to be constant dissatisfaction. Always waiting for the good part. Always thinking, "Well, this is fine, but just wait until..." And then you die and you realize you spent the whole time waiting.

I don't want to be melodramatic about it. I'm not going to say that every moment is precious, because I don't think that's true. Some moments are genuinely dull. Some are painful. Some are just filler, and it would be lying to pretend otherwise. But there are so many moments—more than we can possibly count or remember—that are actually quite nice if we pay attention to them.

My neighbor has a dog, a ridiculous-looking thing with legs too short for its body and an expression of permanent bewilderment. Every morning I hear it attempting to bark, which sounds more like a squeaky toy than an actual bark, and then I hear my neighbor apologizing to someone for the noise. There's something endearing about that. There's a whole relationship implied there—between my neighbor and the dog, between my neighbor and the apologized-to stranger. Lives intersecting and separating, the dog contributing something utterly unintended but somehow exactly right to the morning soundscape of the neighborhood. If I start thinking about the dog too much, I smile. I can't help it.

What am I doing, smiling at the thought of a neighbor's dog? Nothing. Nothing at all. And yet something too.

I think we've made a fundamental error in how we understand meaning. We've decided that meaning comes from outcomes. That something is meaningful if it results in achievement or recognition or change. But what about the meaning that comes from simple appreciation? From noticing? What if meaning is something more like attention itself—the act of really looking at a thing, rather than through it?

There's a Buddhist concept I like, though I'm sure I'm not explaining it properly since I only have a tourist's knowledge of Buddhism. The idea that you should do everything with complete presence and intention, whether you're meditating or washing dishes or having a conversation. That the quality of attention you bring to a task is what matters, not the task itself. This extends to observation too. The quality of your attention to a moment determines the quality of that moment's existence in your mind. Two people can experience the exact same thing, and one person walks away enriched while the other walks away unchanged. The difference is attention.

This is something I'm still learning, or relearning maybe, because I think children are naturally good at this before we train it out of them. I watched my young cousin watch an ant for fifteen minutes the other day. Not for any purpose. She wasn't trying to learn about ants or complete some educational task. She just became curious about this one ant and followed it around the yard, completely engaged. She narrated what it was doing as if announcing a nature documentary: "Now the ant is climbing. Now the ant has found a leaf. Now the ant is lifting the leaf." It was the most important thing in the world to her at that moment, and that attention made it genuinely interesting, even for me, even though I was watching her watch an ant rather than watching the ant itself.

Somewhere between childhood and now, we get trained out of that kind of attention. We learn that there are important things to pay attention to and unimportant things, and we should really focus our energy on the important category. Which makes logical sense, I suppose. If we paid rapt attention to everything, we'd be paralyzed. But the result is that we zoom through our lives, checking boxes, waiting for the things that are worth our attention according to the metrics we've internalized.

And then we wake up and years have gone by.

I want to be clear that I'm not anti-achievement or anti-goals. I think those things matter too. I think wanting to build something or accomplish something or become better at something is completely valid and important. But I don't think those things should be the only things we value, and I don't think they should be the basis for whether a day felt good or was worthwhile.

Some of the best days of my life involved no achievement whatsoever. There was a day recently when I did absolutely nothing, and I mean nothing—no productivity, no exercise, no self-improvement, no checking off tasks. I sat around in old clothes, read a book that wasn't going to make me smarter, talked to a friend for hours without any particular purpose, ate food that was probably not great for me, and watched the light change in my apartment as the day progressed. By every measure of success I've been taught, it was a completely wasted day. And yet it was one of those days where I went to sleep feeling like I had actually lived, rather than just existed while thinking about living.

Why is there a guilt associated with those days?

I think it's because we're all operating on a default setting of scarcity mindset. The idea that time is a finite resource we must allocate carefully, that every hour spent on something that doesn't "count" toward some larger goal is an hour wasted. And yes, time is finite. We all have a limited amount of it. But it seems to me that the way most of us spend our finite time—always reaching toward some future state where finally we'll have enough time or money or success to relax and actually enjoy things—is a strange kind of waste too. We're burning the only time we definitely have in service of some future moment of peace we might never reach.

I'm not saying to quit your job and abandon your responsibilities. I'm just saying that I think we could all afford to be a bit gentler with ourselves about the value of simply existing. About the moments that don't produce anything but a memory, and often not even that—just a feeling that something was okay.

There's a word in Japanese, "ma," that refers to negative space or the emptiness between things. It's not considered empty at all in the traditional sense—it's seen as essential, full of potential, meaningful in itself. I think that's what I'm trying to get at. The space between achievements, the gaps between important moments, the ordinary stretches of life that seem empty but are actually where most of the substance is.

One more example: my mother and I made cookies yesterday. It was pointless in the sense that we could have bought cookies, better cookies, from literally anywhere. We made them from scratch and they came out slightly burnt on the edges and not as evenly shaped as they should have been. But we stood in her kitchen and she told me a story about my grandfather that I'd never heard before—something about him trying to fix something mechanical and getting so frustrated he kicked it, and then being embarrassed about his own temper. It was such a small story. It doesn't change anything. But something about standing there with our hands covered in flour, laughing about my grandfather's long-dead frustration while cookies baked, felt important in a way that success and failure don't quite capture.

That's the thing about ordinary moments. They often only reveal their value in retrospect. You don't know while you're in them that they're going to mean something. You just find out later, sometimes much later, when you remember something small and it brings you comfort or joy or a sense of connection.

I think that's okay. I think we can stop demanding that every moment justify itself in real time. We can stop asking "Is this worth my time?" about everything and instead just experience things and see what sticks.

I'm sitting here finishing this piece and I'm not sure I've really made a coherent point. I've mostly just tried to articulate a feeling, that there's something valuable in the space between important moments, something that gets lost when we structure our lives entirely around achievements and goals. I think the best life would be one where you pursued meaningful goals and built things and tried to grow, but also where you made space for those moments that don't count for anything. The coffee shop reading. The squeak of the neighbor's dog. The afternoon that produces no output. The conversation that goes nowhere. The simple presence of existing alongside other people, doing nothing in particular.

Maybe that's what grace is—the unexpected kindness of a moment you didn't even know to expect. The ordinary made luminous, not through any effort of your own, but just through paying attention.

# On the Particular Magic of Getting Lost

There's a peculiar kind of freedom that arrives when you admit you have no idea where you are. I discovered this recently while wandering through the narrow streets of a city I'd visited before but never actually explored. I had meant to find the cathedral. Instead, I found something I hadn't been looking for at all.

This is perhaps the only honest thing I can say about getting lost: it reveals something true about the difference between navigation and discovery. One is about arrival. The other is about transformation.

I think about the maps in my phone, those glowing digital guides that have made it nearly impossible to be genuinely lost anymore. There's an app-based comfort in knowing exactly where you are at all times, in having your position marked by a blue dot surrounded by all the turns you might take. But this comfort has a cost. It's the cost of the unexpected. It's the price of genuine surprise, which has become increasingly rare in a world where algorithmic recommendations predict what you might want before you know you want it.

My parents' generation—or at least, the romantic version of my parents' generation that I imagine—could still get lost. They could take a wrong turn and spend an afternoon in a neighborhood they weren't supposed to find. They could end up at a restaurant because they were hungry and it was there, not because it had four-point-three stars on a database. There's something poignant about this, something we've traded away without fully considering what we lost in the bargain.

But this essay isn't really about getting lost in the physical sense, though that's where I'll start. It's about the various ways we lose our way through life, and whether that's actually as catastrophic as we've been taught to believe.

Consider how much of our educational system is built around not getting lost. We follow curricula. We check boxes. We're told that there are right answers, correct paths, optimal trajectories. The gifted program, the Advanced Placement track, the prestigious university, the lucrative career—these are the breadcrumbs that trail toward a successful life. Deviate from the path, and you might end up... well, somewhere undefined. Somewhere off-script.

The anxiety around this is palpable in any group of teenagers. Parents ask themselves: Is my child on track? Is she behind? Will she get into a good college? Will he be able to afford a house? The trajectory is what matters. The waypoints are predetermined. Getting lost is failure.

And yet. And yet.

Some of the most interesting people I know are people who got thoroughly, completely lost at some point in their lives, and had the courage—or perhaps the desperation—to keep walking in whatever direction they found themselves heading. They're not necessarily more successful in conventional terms. But they have something else. They have a kind of authenticity that can't be manufactured or faked. They've actually lived their lives rather than merely executing them.

I know a woman who was supposed to be a lawyer. She did well in school, took the right classes, went to the right college. For three years she practiced corporate law. Then one day she realized she couldn't do it anymore. Not because she'd discovered a passion for something else—not immediately, anyway. But because she'd woken up one morning and not recognized the person staring back at her in the mirror. She was lost, and she knew it. So she quit.

What came next was messy. Years of uncertainty, of false starts, of work that paid poorly and satisfied partially. But eventually—I'm not sure she'd claim there was an "eventually," actually. Eventually is for people who follow trajectories. For her, it was more like a gradual waking up. She became a therapist. She volunteers with at-risk youth. She writes poetry that almost nobody reads but that apparently matters deeply to her. Is this a success story? By conventional metrics, certainly not. By any other metric you might devise, almost certainly yes.

The thing about being lost is that it requires a kind of humility. You have to admit that you don't know. You have to be uncertain. Our culture doesn't prize these qualities. We like confidence, decisiveness, the appearance of control. We like people who know where they're going. But there's a kind of arrogance baked into that certainty, an assumption that the map you've been given is accurate, that the destination is worth reaching, that the route has already been optimized.

What if it hasn't? What if the map is outdated? What if the destination isn't actually what you want?

I've been thinking a lot lately about the concept of "wayfinding"—a term that navigation researchers use to describe how people actually move through spaces, as opposed to how maps suggest they should. Wayfinding is improvisational. It uses landmarks rather than coordinates. It's based on noticing, on experience, on small corrections made in real time. A wayfinder doesn't follow a predetermined path so much as respond to the environment as it reveals itself.

This is actually how humans navigated for hundreds of thousands of years, before maps existed. Before GPS. Before we had the technology to pretend we could see the entire world from above, from some kind of omniscient vantage point. For most of human history, getting somewhere meant paying attention. It meant being present. It meant being prepared to be surprised.

There's a metaphor here that I'm circling around but perhaps haven't quite caught yet. Let me try again.

I think about decision-making a lot. We're taught that good decisions are made with full information, with careful deliberation, with an eye toward optimal outcomes. We're supposed to compare options, weigh pros and cons, calculate probabilities. This is the rational model of decision-making, and it dominates how we think about major life choices. But here's what I've noticed: the decisions that have mattered most in my own life were rarely made this way. Usually they were made in a moment of clarity or confusion that couldn't be reduced to a spreadsheet. Usually they involved a leap of faith, a gut feeling, an inability to see clearly where the path led but a decision to walk it anyway.

Maybe this is just me being irrational. Probably some cognitive scientist could explain that I'm engaging in motivated reasoning and confirmation bias. And they wouldn't be wrong. But I also think there's something the purely rational model misses. It misses the ways that the future is genuinely unknowable, the ways that we can't actually see the full consequences of our choices, the ways that sometimes the best decision isn't the one that optimizes a measurable outcome but the one that aligns with who you are or who you're trying to become.

I've noticed that people who are the most certain about their life paths are often people who've never had to genuinely reconsider them. They were lucky enough or privileged enough or prescient enough to choose correctly the first time. Everyone else—and I think this is most people—is engaged in this ongoing process of being lost and finding themselves and being lost again. We're wayfinding. We're paying attention to landmarks. We're making small corrections. We're noticing where the actual terrain differs from the map we were given.

Here's what I want to say clearly: being lost is not a failure of navigation. It's a fact of being human. It's not something to be ashamed of. It's not necessarily something to be fixed as quickly as possible.

This doesn't mean that everything is acceptable, that all paths are equally valid, that there's no such thing as a wise or foolish choice. That's not what I'm arguing. I'm arguing for something more subtle: that there's a difference between having a direction and having a predetermined destination. There's a difference between moving with intention and moving according to a plan someone else drew up. There's a difference between being lost and being awake.

I've been thinking about what we might call "productive lostness"—the state of being genuinely unsure about where you are or where you're going, but remaining engaged anyway. This is different from aimlessness. An aimless person has given up. A productively lost person is paying attention. They're trying things. They're willing to be surprised. They're looking for landmarks.

The city I mentioned at the beginning—I did eventually find the cathedral, but not until after I'd wandered for hours through neighborhoods I didn't know existed. I ate lunch at a small restaurant tucked into an alley, where the owner knew half the people who came in and greeted them by name. I found a bookstore that specialized in old maps, and talked to the woman who ran it for an hour about what it means to navigate. I watched a child learn to skateboard in a courtyard while his grandmother watched from a bench. These moments wouldn't have existed if I'd simply looked up the cathedral on my phone and followed the blue line.

The cathedral, when I finally found it, was beautiful. But I'm not sure it was any more beautiful than what I'd already found. The difference is that the cathedral was what I was looking for, and everything else was what I wasn't. And I think we spend so much of our lives looking for what we're supposed to want that we miss what's actually in front of us.

One more thought, and then I'll try to wrap this up.

There's a kind of conversation that I've started having more often with friends and colleagues, and it goes something like this: What would you do if you weren't afraid? What would you pursue if you knew you couldn't fail? What path would you choose if you weren't constrained by what you're supposed to want?

The difficulty of answering these questions honestly is remarkable. Most of us have internalized the voice that says: there is a right path. There is a correct destination. If you deviate, you will be lost. And being lost is dangerous.

But I wonder. I wonder whether the real danger isn't being lost, but being so certain of your direction that you stop paying attention to where you actually are. I wonder whether the greatest tragedy isn't the detours and wrong turns, but the failure to notice the landmarks along the way because you're too focused on the GPS.

I don't have a tidy conclusion here. I can't wrap this up in a bow and present you with a clear life lesson. If I'm being honest, I'm still figuring this out myself. I still feel the pull toward certainty, toward knowing where I'm going, toward believing that there's an optimal path if I can just be smart enough or disciplined enough to find it. And sometimes that pull wins out, and I spend a week or a month executing a plan, following a trajectory, trying to be where I'm supposed to be.

But increasingly, I'm trying to give myself permission to be lost. Not recklessly. Not without intention. But with openness. With the willingness to notice. With the commitment to pay attention to the actual landscape rather than the map.

And I think if more of us could do this—if we could ease up on the certainty and allow for some productive lostness—we might find that the wandering itself is the destination. That the getting lost and the finding our way is not something that happens on the way to the real life, but is actually the real life itself.

# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about how we miss the world while living in it. Not in the grand, philosophical sense that gets written about in self-help books—though there's truth in that too—but in the smaller, more immediate way. The way we walk past the same coffee shop every morning for three years and never really see it. The way we use our phones to photograph sunsets instead of looking at them. The way our own hands, which we use thousands of times per day, remain basically strangers to us.

There's a cup on my desk right now. It's white, ceramic, with a small chip on the rim where I've carelessly clinked it against my teeth while drinking too hot coffee. Nothing remarkable about it. I've owned it for maybe four years. But if I actually stop and look at it—really look at it—there's something almost startling about its ordinariness. The way the light catches the glaze. The slight imperfections in the glazing that suggest human hands shaped it. The weight of it, designed perfectly to fit a hand that isn't mine, that doesn't exist, but that the potter imagined anyway.

Who made this cup? I have no idea. Somewhere in a factory or a studio, someone shaped clay. They did this thousands of times, probably. Their hands knew this motion the way my hands know how to type, unconsciously, automatically, until the motion becomes meditation. Maybe they were thinking about something else. Maybe they were happy. Maybe they were bored and wished they were doing anything other than shaping cups. Maybe it was Tuesday.

The cup is ordinary. The person who made it was ordinary. And yet there's something almost unbearably poignant about holding an object that represents that intersection of intention and accident, care and routine, the permanent and the temporary (that chip, evidence of my carelessness, will outlast me).

I think this is what I'm trying to understand: why does everything seem simultaneously profound and trivial? Why can't I decide if life is meaningful?

Maybe it's because both are true at once.

---

There's a tree outside my window. I'm sure I've never really looked at it before, but right now I'm looking at it, and I'm struck by how complicated it is. The branches don't follow any pattern I can discern, but they're not random either. Each branch seems to have a reason, a logic, a history of growth responding to light and gravity and wind. The bark is textured in a way that suggests time—years of weather, insects, disease, healing. Some of the branches are dead. Some are being slowly consumed by moss or lichen, those opportunistic organisms that wait for weakness and then move in, not maliciously, just pragmatically, taking what's available.

This tree doesn't know it's beautiful. It doesn't know anything, probably. It grows and exists and responds to stimuli, but there's no consciousness in there, no awareness of its own being. And yet I find myself moved by it. Why? What am I responding to? Am I projecting consciousness onto it, manufacturing meaning where there is none? Or is the beauty somehow independent of interpretation—inherent in the thing itself?

I think I've spent a lot of my life waiting for things to be big enough to matter. Big emotions, big events, big meanings. And I've missed most of the actual content of my existence in the process, which is composed almost entirely of small things. Small moments. Small observations. The particular way light falls through a window. The taste of a really good tomato. The surprising warmth of another person's hand.

When you think about it, everything is small. Even the things that seem big are composed of moments, which are small. An entire human lifetime is small in the span of geological time. The solar system is small in the galaxy. The galaxy is small in the universe. Everything keeps getting smaller the farther you zoom out, except it also keeps getting bigger the farther you zoom in. Every atom contains a solar system of smaller particles. Every second contains an infinity of smaller moments if you're willing to divide it infinitely.

So there's no scale that's actually meaningful. No level of magnification that's the "right" one. We're forced to choose arbitrarily, and the choice we make determines what we see.

---

I've been unemployed for three months. I left a job that was paying me well and that I was reasonably good at, but it felt like I was slowly being absorbed into an institution, losing the ability to distinguish between my own preferences and the preferences the institution had trained me to have. I couldn't remember if I actually liked anything anymore or if I'd just been conditioned to perform liking.

The first month was exhilarating. No alarm clock. Time stretched out luxuriously. I made ambitious plans. I would write! I would exercise! I would learn something new! I would become the person I always imagined I could be if I just had enough time.

The second month was less exhilarating. I was less productive than I'd thought I'd be. I was also less happy than I'd thought I'd be. Turns out unlimited free time doesn't automatically produce fulfillment. You still have to do something with it, and the something you do with it has to mean something to you, and that's actually pretty hard to figure out.

The third month—now—I'm in a strange place. I've accepted that I'm not going to magically become a different person. I'm the same person I was, just with less money and more time. But I'm also starting to see the time differently. It's not a resource to be optimized anymore. It's just what's happening. Hours pass. Some of them are boring. Some of them are interesting. Most of them are both, depending on how I'm looking at them.

I think the problem with how we normally talk about productivity and fulfillment is that we treat them as separate things—you're either productive (and therefore worthy) or you're not. But there's a whole category of time that's neither productive nor unproductive. It's just time. Sitting time. Looking-out-the-window time. Thinking-about-nothing-in-particular time. And that time, I'm realizing, might be important. Not important in the sense that it produces something valuable, but important in the sense that it's part of being alive.

---

I've been reading a lot about attention lately. How attention is the most valuable currency we have, and how everything in the modern world is designed to steal it. Social media companies employ hundreds of engineers specifically to figure out how to make their apps more addictive, how to hack into our psychology and redirect our attention toward their product. It's worked, obviously. We're all walking around in a state of mild distraction, constantly half-listening to conversations because part of our attention is always somewhere else, probably in our phones.

But here's what I'm wondering: is the solution to pay more attention? To cultivate mindfulness and presence? Or is that just another way to optimize yourself, to make yourself more efficient, to turn every moment into an opportunity for self-improvement?

I don't know. I think maybe the answer is just to look at things sometimes. Not with the goal of being present or mindful or whatever the goal is supposed to be. Just to look. To notice that a cup is a cup and a tree is a tree and that you're looking at it. Not as a meditation practice. Not as a productivity hack. Just as something you're doing.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote about "decreation"—the idea of stepping out of the way, of reducing yourself to nothing so that you could be genuinely receptive to reality. She thought most of our perception was actually us projecting our preconceptions onto the world, not actually seeing the world at all. To really see, we'd have to get ourselves out of the way somehow.

I think she was right, but I also think it's impossible. You can never fully get yourself out of the way. You're always there, looking through your own perspective, filtered through your own experiences and assumptions. The best you can do is maybe notice that you're doing it. Notice that you're seeing the world through yourself. And then try, gently, to see around yourself when you can.

---

There's been a lot of discourse lately about how everyone is depressed and anxious. The statistics support this—rates of depression and anxiety disorders are higher than they used to be, at least by some measures. And I believe it, because I can feel it in the culture. There's this underlying hum of anxiety, a sense that something is wrong and we're all complicit in the wrongness, and we don't know how to fix it so we just try not to think about it too hard.

I wonder sometimes if the anxiety is the problem, or if the anxiety is appropriate, and the problem is that we're not supposed to feel fine about things that aren't fine. Maybe some depression is rational. Maybe some anxiety is justified.

But then the trick is: how do you live in a state of awareness about real problems without completely immobilizing yourself? How do you care about things—climate change, inequality, suffering—without letting that care destroy you?

I don't have an answer. I suspect nobody does. I suspect everyone is just kind of muddling through, oscillating between awareness and dissociation, trying to find some balance that lets them exist without either fully denying reality or being completely crushed by it.

Sometimes I think the fact that we can care about things that don't directly affect us—that we can feel empathy for strangers, that we can mourn the destruction of ecosystems we'll never see—is one of the most beautiful things about being human. It's also kind of a curse. It means we can suffer in ways that animals probably don't, because we're aware of suffering that isn't happening to us directly, and we care anyway.

---

I've been thinking about forgetting. How we forget almost everything that happens to us. Every day, thousands of moments occur, and we experience exactly zero of them consciously, because most of what we do is automatic. And of the moments we do experience consciously, we forget almost all of them. A few decades later, you look back on your life and the only things you remember are maybe fifty or a hundred moments. All the rest has just dissolved into nothing.

This seems, on the face of it, tragic. All that life, gone. All those moments, wasted because nobody was paying attention.

But maybe that's not the right way to think about it. Maybe moments don't need to be remembered to have mattered. Maybe the fact that you lived them is enough. Maybe being alive is not about accumulating memories or experiences to look back on, but just about the actual living of it, the being of it.

The only person who was present for your breakfast this morning was you. You will probably forget it within a year. But someone saw your face while you were eating. You existed in that moment. Your consciousness was there. The moment happened. That seems like it should be enough.

Although I notice I still take photos of things. I still try to write down my thoughts. I'm still trying to preserve moments, to make them mean something by transforming them into data that can be stored and retrieved later. I'm not sure if that's wisdom or compulsion or some combination of both.

---

A friend of mine recently went through a really difficult breakup. We were talking about it, and they said something that stuck with me. They said that the hardest part wasn't the sadness, but the sense of wasted time. All those hours spent with a person, and now they feel like they don't count because the relationship ended. Like the only thing that matters is the outcome, and since the outcome was failure, all the time was wasted.

I think that's a very poisonous way to think about time, but I also think it's the way almost everyone thinks about time. We're trained to see time as an investment, and investments are only good if they have a good return. Time spent on things that don't lead anywhere is wasted time.

But what if that's backwards? What if time spent is time spent, regardless of where it leads? What if you can't waste time by living it, even if it doesn't lead anywhere?

I don't know. I'm clearly not good at this. I still believe, most of the time, that time should lead somewhere. I still feel anxious when I'm not being productive. I still feel like I should be working toward something.

But I'm trying to notice when I think that, and to check in with whether it's actually true. Whether I actually need to be working toward something, or if maybe I could just exist for a while, without any trajectory, without any particular goal, and see if that's okay.

It usually isn't okay, actually. It feels disorienting. It feels like I'm wasting time, or like I'm lazy, or like I'm not meeting some invisible standard that I'm supposed to be meeting. But the fact that it feels that way doesn't necessarily mean it's true. It might just mean I'm very well-trained.

---

I think the thing I'm trying to get at, in this rather meandering way, is that I don't know how to live and I don't think anyone does. We're all just kind of making it up as we go along, pretending like there's some instruction manual we're supposed to be following, when actually there isn't one. There's just this strange, chaotic, beautiful, tedious, overwhelming fact of being alive, and we have to decide, moment by moment, what to do with it.

And most of us choose distraction, which makes sense. The straight-on experience of being alive is kind of a lot. It's easier to look at your phone. It's easier to be busy. It's easier to have goals and plans and things to work toward, because at least then you have a direction, even if you're not sure it's the right one.

But sometimes, maybe, it's worth just looking at things. Just noticing them. The cup, the tree, the light, the time passing. Not to accomplish anything or become better or achieve presence or whatever. Just because they're there, and you're there, and that's strange and unlikely and worth looking at.

# The Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

There's a coffee mug on my desk right now—metaphorically speaking, since I don't actually drink coffee or own a desk in the physical sense—but I'm asking you to imagine it with me. It's been there for three days, half-full of cold, congealed liquid that nobody has bothered to drink or dispose of. Most people would find this annoying. There's something about unfinished things that makes us deeply uncomfortable, and I want to talk about why that is, and why perhaps we're wrong to feel that way.

We live in a culture obsessed with completion. Our apps celebrate checkmarks. Our productivity systems are built around the dopamine hit of crossing something off a list. We have entire industries dedicated to "finishing what you started," to closure, to resolution. Television shows must have endings. Books must resolve their plots. Relationships that don't work out are considered failures rather than chapters in the larger narrative of a life. We treat incompleteness as a disease, and completion as the cure.

But I wonder if we've gotten this backwards.

Think about the last time you read a truly great novel. Not a perfectly executed one—a great one. The books that haunt you are rarely the ones with neat conclusions. They're the ones that leave you thinking about them for years afterward, that spawn endless interpretations and discussions, that feel alive in an ongoing way. "Moby Dick" doesn't resolve so much as capsize. "Crime and Punishment" ends, but does anything really get resolved? The beauty of these works lies partly in their resistance to simple completion.

The same is true of music. The songs that burrow into your mind aren't always the ones with perfect structures. Sometimes it's a piece that feels like it's reaching toward something just beyond the edge of the audio spectrum, some unresolved chord that makes you lean forward in your seat. John Coltrane's later work—dense, searching, almost chaotic to some ears—captures something that perfectly structured jazz never could: the honest sound of a mind in motion, not yet arrived at its destination.

I think we're afraid of incompleteness because it suggests several unpleasant truths. First, it implies that we have no control. An unfinished thing is a thing that might still change, that might fail, that might not meet our expectations. A finished thing is fixed, frozen, safe. The incompleteness of our lives—the fact that we're always in process, never quite done—can feel terrifying. We can't guarantee outcomes, can't finalize things, can't rest.

Second, incompleteness means ambiguity, and ambiguity is uncomfortable. We want to know where we stand. We want answers. Questions that linger without clear resolutions create a kind of cognitive discomfort that humans have evolved to avoid—it's part of the reason we're prone to conspiracy theories and false certainties. An unfinished story might have multiple endings, or no ending at all, and that multiplicity of possibilities is harder to hold in our minds than a single, completed narrative.

But here's what I've come to believe: the most profound and meaningful aspects of existence are fundamentally incomplete.

Love, for instance. We talk about love as though it's a destination—people say they've "found love" or "achieved a relationship," as though it's a state you can arrive at and then remain in perpetually. But real love is never finished. It's an ongoing project of understanding another person who continues to surprise you and change. The couples who stay together for decades aren't the ones who found a perfect relationship and kept it; they're the ones who commit to continuously choosing each other, continuously navigating unresolved tensions and incompletions. The incompleteness is the whole point.

Or take growth. Personal development, maturation, becoming a better person—these are never-finished endeavors. The moment you think you've figured it all out, you stop developing. The healthiest, most interesting people I can think of are the ones who are comfortable with being unfinished, who are still learning, still changing, still becoming. They're the ones who ask questions without rushing to answers, who sit with uncomfortable feelings instead of trying to resolve them immediately.

Even creativity depends on incompleteness. There's something called the Zeigarnik effect—people remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. The tension of incompletion creates a kind of psychic magnetism. This is why cliffhangers work (well, the good ones do), why a melody without resolution nags at you, why sketches sometimes feel more alive than finished paintings. The blank space, the unresolved chord, the interrupted sentence—these create an invitation for your mind to participate.

I think about this in relation to understanding other people. We're always trying to finish our comprehension of people we love. We want a definitive understanding of who they are, why they do what they do. But people aren't finished things. The moment you stop seeing someone as a work in progress and think you've got them completely figured out, you've stopped really seeing them. You've replaced them with your completed image of them.

There's an art form called "unfinished business," and it refers to emotional and relational loose ends—grievances, unsaid words, broken connections. Most of the self-help industry is dedicated to finishing this business, to achieving closure. And sometimes that's necessary and healthy. But I wonder if we'd be happier if we could hold a different relationship to incompleteness. What if some of your unfinished business with people you've known and loved is actually what keeps them alive in your mind? What if the unsaid words sometimes carry more weight and meaning than the ones that would have been said?

My grandmother died without ever really reconciling with her own mother. For years I thought this was a tragedy, a failure of the family narrative. But in some ways, their incompleteness preserved something. The unresolved tension meant they were never allowed to become comfortable with each other in a way that would have diminished their importance. The conflict, the distance, the things left unsaid—these kept them psychologically alive in each other's minds. I'm not sure that's better or worse than closure, but it's not nothing.

Here's something else that strikes me: most of the important work of the world is unfinished. Science isn't a body of completed knowledge—it's an ongoing process of asking better questions. Philosophy doesn't reach final answers; it circles around eternal problems with increasing sophistication. Social justice work is explicitly described as unfinished business. The arts are a continuous conversation across time, with each generation responding to and building on and arguing with previous ones. Nothing important is ever truly done.

We have a phrase: "work in progress." We usually apply it to ourselves apologetically, as though being incomplete is a temporary state on the way to completion. But what if we reframed it? What if being a work in progress isn't a deficiency but an achievement? What if it's the whole point?

I notice that people become especially defensive and rigid when they stop feeling like works in progress. The person who thinks they've arrived at the correct political ideology, who's figured out the best way to live, who knows what they think about everything—that person has essentially finished themselves. And in finishing, they've become brittle.

The unfinished people—the ones still asking questions, still uncertain, still working through contradictions—they're alive in a different way. They're more interesting to talk to because they don't have all the answers. They're more capable of growth because they haven't closed themselves off to new information. They're more compassionate because they haven't finished judging other people.

Buddhists have a concept of "beginner's mind"—the practice of approaching things as though you're encountering them for the first time, even if you've encountered them many times before. There's a humility in incompleteness, a kind of openness. When you're not claiming to be finished, you have room for surprise.

I've been thinking also about how much of our anxiety comes from trying to complete things prematurely. We rush to resolve tensions that might teach us something if we sat with them longer. We push for decisions when more time would serve us better. We force closure on situations that want to remain open. We write our life stories with too much certainty about the plot, which means we miss the actual texture of living.

Some of the most interesting work happening right now—in psychology, neuroscience, art, philosophy—involves embracing complexity and multiplicity rather than seeking singular answers. People are becoming more comfortable with paradox, with holding contradictory truths simultaneously. This is a movement away from the need to complete, to finalize, to have one correct interpretation.

Even our relationship with time is changing. We used to think of life as a linear story moving from beginning to middle to end. Now we understand it as more cyclical, more recursive. We revisit periods of our lives, re-examine old decisions, spiral back to old questions with new understanding. The completion model doesn't fit anymore, if it ever did.

I think about houses, and how many of us have rooms we never finish decorating, closets that stay partially organized, projects that never quite get done. There's often guilt associated with this, a sense of failure. But there's also something liberating about it. The unfinished room is still open to possibility. You can still rearrange it in your mind. It hasn't become stale through overcompletion.

There's a Japanese aesthetic principle called wabi-sabi that celebrates the beauty of impermanence, imperfection, and incompleteness. A cracked tea bowl. A garden where things grow wild. A poem that trails off. This isn't seen as inferior to completion and perfection—it's seen as more beautiful, more honest, more true. There's something profound in acknowledging that nothing gold can stay, that everything is always in the process of becoming something else.

Maybe what we actually need is to develop comfort with incompleteness. Not passivity—not the refusal to engage, to work, to try. But the ability to engage fully with something while also accepting that it might never be fully resolved. To work on your life while also accepting that you'll never be finished. To love people while accepting that you'll never fully understand them. To pursue truth while accepting that complete certainty might be impossible.

This is different from giving up. It's more like redirecting your energy from the futile task of achieving completion to the more sustainable task of maintaining engagement. It's the difference between trying to win a game and choosing instead to play the game well.

I wonder if we could redefine success. Not as finishing, but as showing up. Not as having it all figured out, but as continuing to ask good questions. Not as achieving a final state of okayness, but as making peace with the process of becoming.

The coffee mug on that metaphorical desk—I think I'll leave it there. Not out of laziness or forgetfulness, but as a small, daily reminder that incompleteness doesn't mean failure. It means life is still happening. The story's still being written. The work continues.

# The Strange Comfort of Being Lost

I've been thinking lately about the peculiar peace that comes from not knowing where you're going. This thought arrived unbidden on a Tuesday afternoon while I was sitting in a coffee shop watching someone study a paper map—an actual physical map, creased and annotated—instead of checking their phone. They looked concentrated but not stressed. They were, I realized, genuinely lost, and they seemed oddly content about it.

We live in an age of unprecedented certainty about location. Most of us carry devices that know exactly where we are at any moment, can predict our arrival times with remarkable accuracy, and will gently scold us if we deviate from the prescribed route. This is undeniably useful. I'm not going to pretend that GPS hasn't improved my life. But I wonder if something has been subtly stolen from us in the exchange.

There's a particular type of modern anxiety that stems from too much knowledge. We know our exact position in space, but perhaps we've become less aware of our position in time. We know which route will get us to our destination fastest, but we've forgotten the value of wandering. There's something about not knowing—about genuine uncertainty that isn't catastrophic—that seems increasingly rare and increasingly necessary.

I grew up in a time when getting lost was simply what happened on road trips. My parents would argue about directions in a way that now seems almost quaint. My father would insist we hadn't missed the turn, my mother would defend the map, and eventually, usually after driving for another twenty minutes, one of them would be proven right. But here's the thing: during all that arguing and uncertainty, we saw things. We discovered a diner that became a family favorite. We stumbled upon a scenic overlook that appeared in countless later vacation photos. We experienced the actual terrain in a way that following a predetermined route never allows.

That map-reading man in the coffee shop reminded me of something I'd forgotten: not knowing exactly where you are is different from being lost in a dangerous way. There's a category of lost-ness that is more like wandering. It's voluntary. It has an implicit assumption that there's a way out, that the landscape will eventually become recognizable, that the uncertainty is temporary and survivable. Under those conditions, being lost becomes something else. It becomes exploration.

I think this might be why people still take road trips, still hike without checking the trail map obsessively, still occasionally turn their phones off. There's a hunger in us for this particular kind of uncertainty. We crave the feeling of not being pinned down to a single correct path. We want to experience the world with some degree of genuine surprise still intact.

The philosopher Byung-Chul Han has written about how modern life has become characterized by optimization and efficiency, to the point where every moment is accounted for, every decision is data-driven, and every route is the most efficient route. He argues this creates a kind of exhaustion that isn't just physical but existential. We're tired because we never get to stop optimizing. There's always a faster way, a better route, a more efficient use of our time. The option to simply wander—to prioritize the experience of moving through space over the destination itself—has become almost transgressive.

I've started noticing this in smaller ways too. People at restaurants photographing their food before eating it. The practice isn't inherently wrong, but it suggests we're becoming more interested in documenting our experiences than in experiencing them. We're so busy proving we went somewhere that we forget to actually be there. We're curating our lives for an imagined audience instead of living them for ourselves.

There's a concept in Zen Buddhism about "beginner's mind"—the idea of approaching each moment as though it's the first time, without the filter of previous knowledge or expectation. The principle is that most of our suffering comes from overlaying our present experience with mental maps we've already created. We experience the world not directly, but through a filter of what we already know about it.

What if constant navigation—in every sense—is the opposite of beginner's mind? What if by knowing exactly where we are and exactly where we're going, we're actually diminishing our capacity for genuine experience? What if the solution to some of our modern dissatisfaction is as simple as sometimes not knowing?

I'm not advocating for complete chaos or genuine danger. I'm not suggesting we abandon GPS and return to the dark ages of navigation. But I'm interested in the small acts of uncertainty we can still reclaim. Taking a different route home, even if it's longer. Exploring a neighborhood on foot without planning exactly where you'll go. Reading a book without checking how many pages are left. Watching a movie without looking up spoilers. Having a conversation without knowing where it will end up.

These things are still technically available to us, yet they require a kind of active resistance to our default modes. We have to choose not to optimize. We have to choose uncertainty. And that choice is actually harder than it sounds, because we've been conditioned to believe that efficiency and control are always preferable.

But I've noticed that the most memorable experiences in my life are rarely the ones that went exactly according to plan. The best conversations tend to wander. The best trips include detours. The best books surprise you. Even the best meals often happen when you're not expecting much—a humble restaurant that turns out to be phenomenal, a dish you've never heard of that becomes a favorite.

There's also something socially valuable in a state of genuine uncertainty. When you're lost, in the non-catastrophic sense, you're more likely to ask for help. You're more likely to talk to strangers. Lost people are often friendlier, more open, more willing to be vulnerable. There's a kind of camaraderie among the uncertain that you don't find among those who are always confidently on the correct path.

I keep thinking about that man with his paper map. Maybe he was lost because his phone died. Maybe he was a tourist. Maybe he was deliberately choosing a less efficient way to navigate. Whatever the reason, he seemed to be engaged in an activity that required actual attention, actual thought, actual presence. He couldn't just follow a blue line on a screen. He had to look at the map, look at the landscape, look for landmarks, think about direction and distance and how they related to each other. He was actively participating in navigation rather than passively receiving instructions.

This is true of many older activities that we've automated away. Cooking from recipes you have to remember or track down. Navigating without perfect information. Making music without a metronome. These aren't inherently better than their modern alternatives, but they do require a particular quality of attention. They're interactive rather than passive. They involve real choices, real mistakes, real learning.

I wonder sometimes what we're losing in our rush to eliminate uncertainty. And I don't mean just the practical benefits of wandering, though those are real. I mean the psychological and spiritual benefits of knowing that you don't know. There's a kind of humility in that. A grounding in the actual limits of your knowledge and control. We spend so much time trying to eliminate uncertainty that we forget it's a fundamental part of being alive. The future is uncertain. Other people's thoughts are uncertain. Your own motivations are often uncertain to yourself. 

By trying to create little islands of certainty in our navigation and our schedules and our information systems, maybe we're not actually becoming less anxious. Maybe we're just displacing the anxiety, pushing it into larger existential questions that we feel even more helpless about. We optimize the controllable things obsessively, and then feel devastated when we're confronted with the truly uncontrollable aspects of existence.

What if instead we learned to be comfortable with uncertainty at every level? What if we practiced it in small ways—getting lost in neighborhoods, trying new routes, exploring without a plan—so that when larger uncertainties come (and they always do), we're not completely unprepared?

This is probably why I've started deliberately leaving my phone at home on walks sometimes. Not all the time—I'm not a purist about this. But sometimes, just to remember what it felt like to not know exactly how far I'd gone or exactly where I was. To rely on my memory of streets, my sense of direction, my willingness to make a wrong turn and figure it out.

The experience is small, but it's oddly restorative. There's something about moving through the world with incomplete information that makes you feel more alive. You're not just passing through a predetermined landscape. You're actually navigating it, moment by moment, making small decisions about which way to turn, noticing details because you might actually need them to find your way back.

I think this is something we've lost and we need to get back: the practice of being lost. Not lost in a way that's terrifying or actually dangerous, but lost in the way that requires us to be present, to be thoughtful, to be humble about what we know and don't know. 

Not knowing everything all the time might be the most important path forward. And sometimes, the best way to find yourself is to get a little lost first.
