# The Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

There's a mug in my kitchen that's been half-full of cold coffee for three days. Not because I forgot it—I see it every morning when I reach for the orange juice. I simply haven't decided whether to drink it, pour it out, or wash it. This small indecision has become oddly comforting, a tiny pocket of incompleteness in a life that desperately wants everything resolved.

We live in an age of completion. Finish the project, close the loop, achieve closure, reach your goals, check the boxes. Every productivity guru, self-help book, and motivational podcast insists that the uncompleted is the unresolved, and the unresolved is the problematic. There's a reason we call them "loose ends." They feel chaotic, like a thread hanging from a sweater that might unravel everything if we pull it.

But I wonder if we've gotten something fundamentally wrong about what matters in life.

Last week, I was talking to my friend Marcus about a novel he's been writing for six years. He has about eighty thousand words written, multiple character arcs developed, a clear ending in mind. And yet he hasn't touched it in months. When I asked why, expecting to hear about some creative block or practical obstacle, he said something unexpected: "I think I'm afraid to finish it because then I'd have to accept that it's not perfect, and I'd have to let it go into the world as it actually is, not as I imagined it could be."

This hit me harder than it probably should have. Because what he was describing wasn't really about writing—it was about the fundamental human experience of living in possibility. As long as the novel is unfinished, it exists in potential. It could be the best thing he's ever written. It could change everything. The moment he completes it, submits it, publishes it, he has to accept its actual limitations. He has to live with the reality rather than the promise.

I think about my own life constantly through this lens now. How much of my anxiety comes not from actual failures but from the gap between what I could potentially accomplish and what I've actually accomplished? The gap is where the shame lives. The gap is where we tell ourselves we're not trying hard enough, being good enough, doing enough. The gap is uncomfortable, yes, but it's also where hope lives. And maybe those are the same place.

Consider the way we treat relationships. We speak about "closure" as though it's a destination we need to reach with every person who passes through our lives. We agonize over unanswered questions, unresolved conflicts, words we didn't say. Some of this is legitimate—there are things that genuinely need to be addressed, conversations that need to happen. But I've noticed how often we torture ourselves over the fact that we can never fully explain ourselves to another person, never make sure they understand us completely, never know if we left a good final impression.

What if that incompleteness is actually the basis of all human connection?

I have a theory that we fall in love not with people as they are, but with people as they are *becoming*. We fall in love with possibility. The person your partner might become, the depths you haven't yet discovered in them, the ways they might surprise you ten years in. The moment you think you've fully understood someone, you've already stopped really seeing them. Real people are always unfinished. Real people are always essays in progress, not final submissions.

My parents have been married for forty-three years, and when I asked my mother recently if she feels like she knows my father completely, she laughed in a way that was both sad and joyful. "God, no," she said. "I'm constantly discovering things about him that contradict things I thought I knew. It drives me crazy sometimes. But I think that's the whole point. The day you think you've figured someone out is the day you stop being curious about them."

This applies to ourselves as well. We're so focused on finding our "authentic self," our final form, the real version of us that we'll be when we get everything together. But what if there is no final version? What if the point isn't to reach some stable endpoint where we've figured everything out, but rather to learn to be okay with the fact that we're always going to be confusing, contradictory, and incomplete?

I've been thinking about this a lot in the context of aging. We're encouraged to see aging as a process of decline, a slow completion of our lives in the worst possible direction. But I notice that older people—the ones who seem genuinely content—rarely talk about their lives as though they're winding down. They talk about them as though they're still being written. My grandmother, at eighty-seven, still debates with my grandfather about things, still changes her mind about decisions she made years ago, still surprises herself with reactions she didn't expect to have.

"I thought I'd be done learning by now," she said to me once. "Isn't that funny? I've lived most of my life, and I'm still regularly confused about what things mean."

There's something liberating about that admission. Something that makes me want to stop rushing toward completion and instead develop a tolerance for unfinished business.

I think about the projects I've abandoned. Stories I started but never finished. Skills I began learning and then set aside. I used to feel shame about these abandoned things, seeing them as evidence of my inconstancy, my lack of follow-through. But I've recently started thinking about them differently. What if they weren't failures? What if they were just experiences that changed me and then naturally concluded? What if the point of starting something isn't always to finish it?

This was the hardest lesson to learn because it flies directly in the face of how I was raised. I was raised to finish what you start, to see projects through, to not be a quitter. These aren't bad values, exactly, but they can become tyrannical. They can transform life into one long to-do list, where peace is only possible when every item is crossed off—which, of course, it never is, because there are always more items.

I read somewhere that the Japanese have a word—*ma*—that refers to the space between things, the pause, the emptiness. And that this emptiness isn't negative; it's actually essential to the meaning of the things around it. Without silence, there would be no music. Without space, there would be no room. Without the pause between heartbeats, the heart wouldn't work.

I wonder if the same applies to our lives. Without the unfinished, without the pause, without the gaps—maybe there would be no meaning. Maybe we need the ongoing projects, the perpetual questions, the relationships that never quite become fully knowable, the growth that never quite completes.

This doesn't mean we shouldn't try to accomplish things. It doesn't mean we shouldn't set goals and work toward them. It's not an argument for laziness or complacency. It's just an argument for being less violent about our relationship to completion. For understanding that some of the most important things in life are by definition unfinishable.

Take parenting, for instance. You never finish being a parent. Your children become adults and you're still figuring it out, still wondering if you did it right, still discovering new ways you've affected them. There's no graduation ceremony where you turn in a complete project. And this should be terrifying, probably, but instead I find it oddly beautiful. The incompleteness isn't a flaw in the system—it's the entire point.

Or consider something like learning a language, or learning to play music. The common wisdom is that you should aim to achieve fluency or mastery, as though these are destinations you can reach and then be done. But musicians and linguists who genuinely love what they do don't talk about it that way. They talk about the endless discovery, the way that learning to play a new piece always teaches you something about the instrument you didn't know before, the way a language is always revealing new depths and nuances.

The best students I've ever encountered are people who became genuinely comfortable with not knowing. Not because they didn't care about learning, but because they understood that absolute mastery would mean the end of the interesting part. The growth would stop. The discovery would end. And that would be terrible.

I have a friend who practices yoga, and she told me something her teacher said that stuck with me: "The posture is never complete. There's always a deeper level, a better alignment, a subtler awareness you can bring to it. And that's not discouraging—it's the whole point. It means you'll never be bored. It means there's always more to discover about your own body, your own being."

This seems like the opposite of how we usually think about skill acquisition. We want to reach competence and then move on to the next thing. But there's something to be said for the practice of deepening, for the willingness to spend years in the same space, discovering new dimensions of it.

I've been trying to apply this to my own anxiety about productivity. I'm a person who has internalized the cultural narrative about constant improvement and self-optimization to an almost pathological degree. I have spreadsheets tracking my habits. I have systems for organizing my time. I measure my worth somewhat unconsciously against how much I accomplish. This has gotten me some things—some real achievements, some genuine successes. But it's also kept me in a state of low-level anxiety that I'm not doing enough, being enough, becoming enough.

What if, instead of trying to optimize my way to peace, I just... stopped? Not in the sense of giving up, but in the sense of being willing to have an afternoon where I don't accomplish anything and simply exist. An evening where I don't learn anything. A day where I'm not becoming a better version of myself.

This feels radical because we've been taught that time is a scarce resource we need to maximize. Every moment not spent improving ourselves is, by this logic, wasted. But what if the wasted moments are the most important ones? What if doing nothing is sometimes the most powerful thing you can do?

I'm thinking about this partly because I've been spending more time outside lately, just sitting and watching things. Not meditating in the purposeful, self-improving sense, but just being present without agenda. And I've noticed that these are often the times when something shifts in me. When I suddenly understand something I've been struggling with. When a problem that seemed urgent suddenly loses its urgency. When I feel more like myself than I do when I'm actively trying to be better.

Maybe the trick is that you have to let go of trying to improve in order to actually change. Maybe all the pushing and striving is actually counterproductive. Maybe we're supposed to unfold gradually, without constant intervention, like a flower.

I don't have answers to any of this. I'm sitting with questions. And increasingly, I'm okay with that. The questions feel more interesting to me now than the answers would be. An answered question is a dead question. A living question is one you can keep asking in different ways, getting slightly different answers each time, discovering that the question itself changes as you change.

So my coffee is still sitting there, half-full, and I think I'm going to leave it. Not forever—eventually I'll throw it out or drink it or wash the mug. But for now, it sits there as a small monument to incompleteness, a reminder that it's okay to not know what happens next. That some decisions don't need to be made immediately. That some things can exist in a state of pleasant suspension.

And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's everything.

# On the Quiet Art of Paying Attention

There's a moment that happens almost every day, usually in the afternoon when the light slants through windows at that particular angle that makes everything look like it's made of amber and memory. I'll be doing something mundane—washing dishes, walking to the mailbox, sitting in traffic—and suddenly I'll notice something I've seen a hundred times before as if for the first time. The way water beads on a ceramic plate. The specific geometry of shadows under a mailbox door. The particular shade of frustration on someone's face in the car ahead of me.

These moments feel like small gifts, though I'm not entirely sure who's giving them to me, or whether I'm giving them to myself by finally pausing long enough to receive them.

I've been thinking a lot lately about attention, which is to say I've been thinking about presence, and presence is really just another word for love, though we don't usually admit that. We talk about attention as if it's a resource we manage, the same way we manage time or money. We speak of "paying" attention, which is interesting because it implies both a cost and a transaction. But I think attention is less like currency and more like oxygen—it's everywhere, we need it constantly, and we barely notice it until we're gasping for lack of it.

The pandemic did something to how I experience attention. I think it did this to a lot of people, though we don't always talk about it in these terms. We talk about it being "weird" or "surreal," but what we're really talking about is how it stripped away so many of the automatic, unconscious patterns of paying attention that we'd developed. Suddenly, there were fewer places to direct our focus. The world got smaller, squeezed into a few rooms, a few daily routines.

And in that smaller world, things became vivid.

I found myself noticing the way light moved across my kitchen table throughout the day. I could track time by it, almost. And I started to understand, in a way I never had before, that this is what monks were doing. That's what meditation is—a deliberate practice of directing attention inward, or toward the present moment, or toward whatever chosen object of focus. It's not mystical, though it can feel that way. It's just attentiveness made practice.

But here's what troubles me about our current moment, and what I've been wanting to write about: we're living in a time of radical attention fragmentation. Our devices don't just compete for our attention; they're designed specifically to hack it, to break it into smaller and smaller pieces. There's an entire industry built on the science of keeping our minds fractured, scattered, reaching for the next notification like a pigeon pecking at seeds on a floor.

This has a cost. I don't just mean the obvious costs—the mental health impacts, the loneliness despite constant connection, the anxiety, the sense of time slipping away. Though those are real. I mean something deeper. I mean the cost to our capacity for intimacy. Because intimacy, real intimacy, requires a kind of complete attention that has become genuinely rare.

When you give someone your complete attention—not just your eyes, but your mind, your nervous system, your presence—you're doing something radical. You're saying, through your actions rather than your words, that they matter more right now than anything else in the world. You're saying that this moment, this conversation, this person is worthy of your full self. In our current age, this has become nearly an act of resistance.

I think about this when I'm with friends, and I notice how hard it is to be fully present. Even when my phone is in another room, there's a kind of mental residue left behind. Fragments of attention still catching on the emails I didn't send, the messages I haven't read, the way the internet constantly hums in the background of consciousness. It's like trying to hear someone speak while music plays faintly in the distance—you can do it, but it takes effort that shouldn't be required.

There's a practice called "deep reading" that's supposed to be disappearing. I think what's actually disappearing is the capacity for sustained attention more generally. The research suggests that reading long-form prose, in particular, requires a kind of attention muscle that atrophies if you don't use it. But I think the same is true for listening, observing, being present in conversation. These are all skills, and like any skill, they require practice and can be lost through disuse.

What worries me is that we're raising a generation with underdeveloped attention muscles. I'm not being alarmist—the research is pretty clear on this. Rates of anxiety, depression, and ADHD diagnoses have risen dramatically, particularly among young people. Now, correlation isn't causation, and there are many factors at play. But I can't help but think that when your basic neurological wiring is trained from infancy to expect novelty every few seconds, to respond to interruptions as if they might be urgent, to understand that attention itself is a commodity to be sold to the highest bidder—that has to do something to you.

And yet. And yet, I'm not interested in writing some preachy jeremiad about phones and technology. That's been done, and honestly, it misses the point. The problem isn't the technology itself, any more than the problem with alcohol is the existence of wine. The problem is how we've chosen to use these tools, and the incentive structures that have been built around them.

What I'm interested in is the other side of this: what attention practices might look like for people living in this fractured age. Not "go sit in a monastery," but something more practical. Something that acknowledges that we live in the world as it is, not as we wish it were.

One thing I've started doing is taking what I call "attention walks." It's not exercise, though I'm walking. It's not meditation, though it shares some qualities with meditation. It's simply a deliberate walk through a familiar place—my neighborhood, usually—with the specific intention of really looking. Not looking at my phone, not thinking about where I need to be or what I need to do. Just noticing.

I notice the way a particular fence has weathered. The different colors of green in the plants along a single street. The small signs of people's lives—a child's drawing in a window, a garden gnome that's fallen over, the way someone has arranged rocks in a garden, presumably for beauty or to prevent erosion or both. These are not profound observations. But the act of making them feels profound. It feels like I'm practicing presence. Like I'm building the capacity to be here, really here, in my own life.

Another thing I've noticed: writing this way, by hand, feels different than typing. The pace is slower. There's less editing happening in real-time. Your thoughts come out more roughly, more truly. There's a kind of attention required in handwriting that typing has made optional. You have to commit to the word by putting it down. It creates a different relationship with your own thoughts.

I think this is why people are increasingly drawn to "analog" practices—journaling by hand, reading physical books, cooking from scratch. It's not really about the analog-ness, I don't think. It's about the pace. It's about the kind of attention that these practices require and cultivate.

Here's something I've been wanting to say for a while: I think the fundamental spiritual or philosophical question of our time is not "what is the meaning of life?" but rather "where do I place my attention?" Because where you place your attention is literally where your life happens. Your attention is your life, in a very real sense. Every moment that passes—and they are all passing—is a moment of your attention placed somewhere. Spent on something. Given to someone or something or somewhere.

This is why the current attention economy bothers me so much. It's not just that it's making us anxious or distracted. It's that it's training us to give our attention—which is to say, our lives—to people and things and causes that we don't actually care about. We're being literally harvested for our attention by companies whose business model depends on us not being present to our own lives.

And the weird part is, I don't think even the people designing these systems are necessarily trying to be evil. I think they're caught in the same system, the same incentive structures. But the system itself is structured in a way that's deeply at odds with human flourishing.

So what do you do with that knowledge? You can't opt out entirely. You can't go live in a cabin in the woods and pretend the world works differently now. Well, you could, but most of us won't, and maybe that's not even the right answer anyway.

I think what you do is you start small. You notice. You practice. You develop what might be called "attention hygiene"—small, deliberate choices about where you place your focus. You read a book without your phone in the room. You have a conversation without checking the time obsessively. You take a walk and actually look at things. You sit with a cup of tea and just sit with it, for a few minutes, without doing anything else.

These sound small because they are. But small practices become habits, and habits shape the underlying architecture of your mind and your life.

I've been thinking too about how attention relates to gratitude. You can't really feel gratitude for something you're not paying attention to. Gratitude isn't something you can fake or force—it emerges naturally when you actually notice the things you have. The meal in front of you. The person you're talking to. The fact that you got to see another sunset. That you have a body that can walk. That the sky is this particular shade of blue today.

This is why practices of attention and practices of gratitude are so closely linked in contemplative traditions. They're almost the same thing, viewed from different angles. When you attend to something with real focus, with real presence, gratitude naturally follows. You can't really be fully present to something without appreciating it, at least a little.

There's a writer I admire named Annie Dillard who wrote about this. She said something like: how we spend our days is how we spend our lives. The implication being that most of us are not very conscious about how we spend our days, so we're living unconsciously. And that if you want to live differently, to live more meaningfully or more fully, you need to start paying attention to how you actually spend your time. You need to wake up to your own life.

I think that's maybe the deepest thing that attention is about. It's about waking up. Being awake to your own existence while you're having it, rather than sleepwalking through it, reaching the end and wondering where the time went.

The pandemic taught me something about this. When everything stopped, when all the normal ways of staying busy and distracted were unavailable, I had to actually be present to the life I was living. And what I found was that it was enough. The small things were enough. The quiet morning, the afternoon light, the particular texture of a particular day. These were not nothing. They were everything.

I'm trying to hold onto that knowledge now that the world has largely restarted its normal pace. I'm trying to keep remembering that attention is not just a practical thing, not just about being more productive or less stressed (though it might be those things too). It's about being alive. It's about the quality of being alive. It's about the difference between existing and actually living.

And maybe that's what I want to say, in the end. That paying attention is not a productivity hack. It's not about doing more things or doing things better. It's about doing fewer things with more presence. It's about choosing, consciously and repeatedly, to be here now. To put your whole self into whatever you're doing, whoever you're with, whatever moment you're having.

Because this moment, this one, right now—it's the only one you're actually having. The rest are memories or fantasies. This one is real, and it's passing, and there's nothing else there.

# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about the paradox of attention—how the moment we truly look at something, it transforms. A coffee cup becomes a small engineering miracle. The way light falls through a window becomes a meditation on physics and perception. A person's face, really looked at, reveals an entire universe of experience.

There's a painting I saw once, years ago, that I can't stop thinking about. I don't even remember the artist's name, which bothers me in a way that probably says something unflattering about my memory. But the image stayed with me: a simple wooden table, rendered with such care and specificity that you could feel the grain of the wood, could sense its age and the hands that had rested on it. What struck me most wasn't the technical skill—though it was undeniably skillful—but the artist's clear love for this unremarkable object. They had chosen to devote their attention to something that billions of people walk past every day without seeing.

This is what I want to explore, I think: the way that sustained attention is a form of love, and how the most profound experiences often arrive disguised as the most ordinary ones.

We live in an age of unprecedented access to extraordinary things. I can watch a concert performed by musicians I've admired for years. I can read interviews with brilliant minds. I can travel, virtually or otherwise, to places that would have seemed impossibly distant to people a generation ago. And yet, I find myself increasingly drawn to the small and nearby. There's something radical about this in our current moment—something almost rebellious about choosing to really see what's in front of you rather than constantly reaching for what's distant or novel.

I live on a street with about a hundred trees. I've walked down this street probably two thousand times. For the first year or so, I barely noticed them. But last spring, something shifted. Maybe I was in a particular mood, or maybe I was just tired of my own mental chatter and needed something external to focus on. I started really looking at these trees. And suddenly they weren't just "trees"—they were individuals. There was the oak with the peculiar double trunk, the maple that turned a color I'd never seen before, the elm with branches that grew downward before curving up again, as if the tree had changed its mind about where it wanted to go.

I started to notice the seasonal cycles with new depth. The subtle variations week to week—not just spring's arrival, but spring's slow unfolding. The different shades of green as leaves first emerge. The way the light quality changes as the season progresses. I became aware of weather in a new way too, not as an abstraction (sunny vs. rainy) but as something that had visible effects on these organisms. After a particularly dry spell, I could see the stress in the leaf color. After a heavy rain, there was a visible renewal.

This observation took no special equipment or expertise. Just attention. Just the willingness to really look instead of merely glancing. And the reward—and I use that word deliberately, because it was genuinely rewarding—was that I got to know these trees. They became companions in a real sense. I looked forward to walking past them. They gave me a sense of continuity with something older and slower than myself.

I think about how much of our anxiety and dissatisfaction might stem from a kind of attentional poverty. We are rich in access but poor in attention. We have everything available but engage deeply with almost nothing. The result is a kind of background hum of unsatisfaction, a sense that we're missing out on something just beyond our reach. But what if the missing thing isn't out there? What if it's right here, waiting for us to actually look at it?

I've noticed this in my relationships too. The most connecting moments with other people don't happen when we're doing anything particularly special. They happen when I'm actually present. When I'm not mentally rehearsing what I'll say next or thinking about what I should be doing. When I'm genuinely curious about what someone is saying, about who they are. These moments are rare enough that when they happen, they feel almost sacred. But there's no reason they should be rare. The ability to pay attention to someone else is free and unlimited. We just seem to have chosen not to exercise it very much.

There's a Zen concept about chopping wood and carrying water—the idea that enlightenment or deep meaning isn't found in special experiences but in the complete, full-hearted engagement with simple, necessary tasks. The most mundane aspects of life, properly attended to, reveal their profound nature. I think about this when I'm washing dishes. I'm generally not someone who enjoys this task, but I've been experimenting with doing it as a form of meditation. Not in a grim, self-improving way, but with actual interest. The feeling of warm water. The small satisfactions of cleaning something. The geometric simplicity of stacking dishes. When I do this, the task becomes almost pleasant. More importantly, a time that would normally be dead time, time I'm trying to escape or rush through, becomes alive.

What's interesting to me is that this isn't self-deception. I'm not pretending dishes are more interesting than they are. Rather, interest itself is something that can be cultivated. Boredom and engagement aren't fixed properties of activities—they're properties of the relationship between the person and the activity. The same walk can be either tedious or fascinating depending entirely on the quality of attention brought to it.

This has made me wonder about the nature of happiness. We tend to think of happiness as something that comes from special events or special circumstances. If I achieve X, then I'll be happy. If I acquire Y, then I'll be satisfied. And certainly, some circumstances make happiness easier. But I've been increasingly convinced that there's a baseline happiness available all the time, accessible through the simple practice of paying real attention to what already exists. 

Not in a toxic-positivity way. I'm not saying we should be happy about injustice or suffering or real problems. But there's a difference between realistic acknowledgment of difficulty and the kind of chronic low-level dissatisfaction that comes from constant comparison and the sense that actual life is somehow a poor substitute for a better one we should be having.

I think about social media and how it's engineered to exploit and worsen this feeling. We're presented with an endless stream of other people's curated experiences, designed to trigger comparison and inadequacy. And because these are curated highlights, we're comparing our unfiltered reality to everyone else's filtered best. Of course we come up short. Of course we feel like we're missing out. We're comparing our actual life, with its mundane moments and small frustrations, to an imaginary life that no one actually has.

The antidote, I've found, is deliberate cultivation of appreciation for what's here. Not forced gratitude—that often feels like gaslighting yourself. But genuine interest. Genuine attention. When I'm scrolling through photos of other people's lives, I'm not engaging with my own. And my own life, while undramatic, is actually quite interesting if I bother to look.

I've become fascinated by the concept of the uncanny—that strange discomfort we sometimes feel around something that's almost right but slightly off. A doll that looks almost human but not quite. A room that's familiar but slightly rearranged. It's an unsettling feeling, and we tend to avoid it. But I wonder if there's also something valuable in reverse: the practice of finding the almost-miraculous in the familiar. To look at something completely ordinary—your own hand, the texture of concrete, the sound of traffic—and really take in how strange and remarkable it actually is. This isn't mysticism. It's neurology. The more you attend to something, the more details your brain processes, and the more complex the thing reveals itself to be.

There's also something countercultural about insisting on the value of things that can't be monetized or optimized or quantified. A walk with no fitness tracker, no destination, no optimization of route. Reading a book with no educational purpose, just for the experience of it. Having a conversation with no agenda. These things feel almost irresponsible in our current culture. We're supposed to be productive, improving, working toward something. Time spent in simple appreciation feels like laziness.

But is it? What, exactly, is the purpose of productivity if not ultimately to create a good life? And what makes a life good? I'd argue that the texture of lived experience—the small moments of beauty and connection and engaged presence—matters more than the list of accomplishments. And yet we tend to sacrifice the texture for the list, thinking we'll come back to it later, after we've achieved enough. But later never quite comes. There's always another achievement to pursue.

I don't have this figured out. I'm not writing from some enlightened place where I've solved these problems. I'm as susceptible as anyone to the pull of optimization and comparison and future-focused thinking. But I've had enough moments of real presence, of genuine engagement with the ordinary, to know that it's worth cultivating. These moments don't cost anything. They're not rare or hard to achieve. They just require the most difficult thing to give in our culture: genuine attention.

I want to end with something I observed last week. I was sitting outside a coffee shop, and there was a child, maybe four years old, examining a crack in the sidewalk with absolute intensity. His mother kept trying to move him along, but he was completely absorbed. Not in a way that looked like he was learning or developing or optimizing his time. He was just... looking. Marveling. Discovering this small imperfection in the concrete as if it were the most interesting thing in the world. 

From an adult perspective, it was clearly nothing. A crack. Meaningless. And yet, watching him, I saw something I've largely lost: the capacity to be genuinely fascinated by what's right in front of me. We call this quality in children "wonder," as if it's something exclusive to them, something we necessarily outgrow. But I think it might be a trainable skill. Not something we lose but something we neglect until it atrophies.

The good news is that we can start again at any time. Right now. You could look genuinely at your hand. At the words on this screen. At the space around you. You could do it with actual, non-ironic interest. You could ask yourself: what's actually remarkable about this thing I've stopped seeing?

The trees on my street are still there. The dishes still need washing. The people around me are still present, waiting to be genuinely seen. The ordinary is always available. The only question is whether we'll notice it.

# The Strange Beauty of Waiting

There's something I've been thinking about lately, something I can't quite pin down but that feels important enough to spend time with. It's about waiting—not the annoyed, foot-tapping kind of waiting that happens when you're stuck in traffic or on hold with customer service, but the deeper, slower kind of waiting that comprises so much of human life and seems almost invisible because it's so pervasive.

I think we don't talk about waiting enough. We celebrate arrival, achievement, completion. We obsess over productivity and efficiency, as though the goal is always to minimize the time between desire and satisfaction. But I'm becoming convinced that waiting is where actual life happens, and I wonder if learning to wait well might be one of the most underrated skills we could develop.

Consider childhood. Almost all of it is waiting. You wait to be old enough to stay up late, to go to school, to drive, to leave home. You wait for Christmas morning, for summer vacation, for the girl or boy to notice you. When you're a kid, this waiting often feels excruciating. Time moves differently when you're young—a week feels like a year. But there's also something magical about it. The anticipation itself is its own form of experience. The days before something you're excited about can be just as vivid and real as the event itself.

I remember in middle school, my best friend and I would spend entire lunch periods reading the same comic books series we'd discovered, theorizing about what would happen next, constructing elaborate narratives about where the characters would go. The books came out monthly, which meant roughly thirty days of wondering. Those thirty days were precious in a way I didn't understand at the time. We lived in them. We inhabited the space between episodes like it was a real place.

As we get older, our culture increasingly tells us that this is a waste of time. We can watch the next episode immediately on streaming services. We can skip ahead. We can spoil ourselves if we want. And certainly, some of this technology is genuinely wonderful. But I wonder what we've lost in gaining the ability to skip the waiting.

There's a theory in psychology about flow states—that particular experience of being so absorbed in an activity that time seems to disappear and you're completely engaged with the present moment. What if waiting, real waiting, is its own kind of flow state? What if the quality of our lives might be measured not by how efficiently we get through our days, but by how present we can be in the gaps?

I've noticed this particularly in relationships. When I was younger and newly interested in someone, there were all these small waits that structured the experience. You would have a conversation, and then you'd wait—sometimes anxiously, sometimes deliciously—for the next one. You'd think about what they said. You'd construct possible futures in your mind. You'd write and rewrite messages before sending them, or you wouldn't message at all because that was how you did things.

Now, with instant messaging and constant connectivity, that waiting is almost entirely removed. You can reach someone immediately. You can know almost everything about them before you've had a single conversation. And perhaps this makes modern relationships more efficient, but I'm not sure it makes them deeper. There's something about the space between—the not-knowing, the imagining, the anticipatory daydreaming—that seems to be part of what builds real connection.

I find myself thinking about artists too, and how waiting has historically been central to artistic practice. A painter spends months or years on a single piece, watching it emerge slowly, making small decisions that compound over time. A writer might spend years on a novel, inhabiting the world of their characters, letting it deepen. A musician practices the same piece thousands of times, the waiting between today's practice and tomorrow's, between learning it and mastering it and playing it in front of an audience.

But contemporary culture pushes toward speed in creative work too. Overnight success stories dominate the narrative. We celebrate the prodigy who emerges fully formed, the viral sensation that appears from nowhere. Social media rewards constant output and immediate engagement. There's less space in popular discourse for the artist who worked in obscurity for decades before being recognized.

I wonder if this is a loss. Not everyone can be a overnight success, and even those who are often report that it was hollowing in some way. They hadn't finished becoming who they needed to become. The waiting, it turns out, was doing something important—not preventing their success, but building them into the person capable of handling it meaningfully.

This makes me think about aging, too. Our culture despises aging, fights it viciously, which I think is partly because we've lost any sense that the passage of time might be valuable in itself. We treat getting older as a loss of something, without any sense that we might be gaining anything.

But waiting teaches us things. Patience isn't just patience—it's a way of developing trust in time itself, in the idea that good things can't be rushed and that the process matters as much as the destination. Anticipation teaches us to imagine, to construct possible futures, to hope. Long-term projects teach us about follow-through and commitment. Grief—which is a kind of waiting for acceptance—teaches us about depth and meaning.

I think about people I know who seem genuinely content, and I notice that many of them have developed relationships with waiting. They have gardens, so they wait through seasons. They have partners they've been with for decades, so they know that depth takes time. They have creative practices they've maintained for years. They read books that take a long time, reread them, think about them over years. They don't rush.

And I notice too that they are not bored. If anything, the opposite. There's a richness to their experience precisely because they're not constantly trying to optimize it, to get to the next thing. They're present in what is.

There's something else I've been turning over too, and it's harder to articulate. It's the idea that waiting might be connected to meaning itself. That the meaning of something—how much it matters to us—might be partly a function of how much we've waited for it, thought about it, anticipated it. 

Consider holidays. In cultures where holidays were more anticipated—where they were rare, where you had to wait months for them, where the period before them had specific rituals and preparations—they seem to have meant more. Christmas in earlier centuries, before commercialization, must have felt genuinely transcendent to people because the entire year was in some sense structured around anticipating it. The waiting was half the meaning.

Now we have holidays constantly. There's always something to buy, some next special occasion being marketed to us. And I wonder if this is part of why modern life can feel so meaningless despite having so much—if constant access to everything empties things of their significance.

I've been thinking too about hope, which seems like a form of waiting. Hope is not optimism, exactly. Optimism is a belief that things will turn out well. Hope is something more active—it's a way of maintaining belief in possibility while acknowledging difficulty. It's a verb. You hope; you wait; you trust; you work; and hope sustains you through it. Hope is what allows you to be present with the waiting rather than destroyed by it.

There's this passage from a poem I can't quite remember, something about how "the waiting is all there is." And I think there's truth to that. Even if we get what we're waiting for, we'll just start waiting for something else. Even at the end of our lives, we might be waiting—waiting to know what it all meant, waiting for understanding. 

So the question becomes: can we make peace with the waiting? Can we fall in love with the process rather than remaining fixated on the outcome? Can we understand that waiting well is not wasting time, but using it to build the capacity to live deeply?

I find myself wanting to practice this more intentionally. To put my phone away and wait for someone face-to-face without filling the silence with checking messages. To read a physical book over months instead of devouring it on a screen. To plant seeds and wait for them to grow without checking on them obsessively. To commit to small creative projects without expecting immediate results. To have conversations and not know where they'll go, to be comfortable in not-knowing.

There's a courage in this, I think. It's easier to be constantly stimulated and distracted than to be truly present with waiting. There's an anxiety in it too—the fear that we'll wait for the wrong thing, or that while we're waiting, we're missing something else. But I'm starting to think that's okay, that some anxiety is the price of depth.

And maybe the real insight is this: we are all waiting, always, whether we acknowledge it or not. We're waiting for the future to arrive, and the future will never arrive in the way we imagine. By the time it gets here, it will be the present, which is always much more ordinary and complicated and mixed than we anticipated. So the waiting is what we actually have. It's the real thing. Everything else is what we think should be real, but the waiting—the living in anticipation and process and not-knowing—that's where we actually exist.

I want to close by saying something about gratitude, because I think it's connected. When we wait for something, and we're present in the waiting, we often approach what we receive with more gratitude. We notice it more. We appreciate it more. We see it not as inevitable, but as a gift, as something that took time and effort and luck to attain. This seems like another reason that our culture's obsession with speed might be impoverishing us—not just removing the joy of anticipation, but removing the gratitude that comes after.

I don't have a neat conclusion to offer here. I'm still thinking about these things, still learning to wait better. But I wanted to write about waiting because it's on my mind and it seems important and because I think we'd do well to talk about it more. To defend it. To recognize waiting not as wasted time but as the texture of a meaningful life. To remember that sometimes the best things in life are the ones that take the longest, cost the most, demand the most patience. And to somehow find peace and even beauty in that eternal present-tense of anticipation, where we're always moving toward something and never quite arriving, and somehow that's exactly as it should be.

# On the Peculiar Grace of Ordinary Afternoons

There's a particular kind of light that arrives in mid-afternoon, the sort that makes you want to stop whatever you're doing and just sit with it for a while. Not the dramatic golden hour of sunset, which demands your attention and your Instagram stories, but something quieter—the light of 2 PM on a Tuesday, filtering through dusty windows, turning coffee cups into small vessels of amber. I've been thinking about this light a lot lately, and about what it means that we move through thousands of these ordinary afternoons without really seeing them.

We're taught to value the extraordinary. From childhood onward, we're encouraged to reach for the peaks, the milestones, the moments we'll "never forget." The first day of school. Graduation. The proposal. The job offer. The vacation. These moments get capitalized in our minds and in our family histories. We take photos. We tell stories. We mark them in time as the moments that mattered.

But what about the other 364 days? What about the afternoon you made coffee and sat in the window, and the light was just right, and for three minutes you felt completely at peace? Nobody photographs that. Nobody writes essays about it. Yet those moments are the actual substance of our lives. They're the hours we get to inhabit.

I think about my grandmother sometimes—how she spent sixty years living in the same house, creating thousands of ordinary afternoons in that kitchen. The repetition seemed, from the outside, almost tragic. The same meals made over and over, the same routes walked, the same conversations circling back on themselves. I remember thinking as a teenager that she deserved something more, something *special*. I couldn't understand that maybe those afternoons, the reliability of them, the way they accumulated into a kind of love, were the thing. Maybe the special thing was knowing that you had a place where you belonged, and that you would be there again tomorrow.

There's a concept I encountered once called "the sublime," usually applied to grand vistas—mountains, oceans, the night sky. Something so vast and beautiful it makes you feel small, insignificant, but in a way that's supposed to be spiritually elevating. I wonder why we don't apply that to the everyday. What if an afternoon light coming through your kitchen window was a kind of sublime? What if ordinariness itself could be transcendent?

The pandemic taught a lot of us, quite brutally, that we'd been saving up too much for later. We were always going to travel next year, see friends this coming summer, really focus on our hobbies once things settled down. And then the world paused, and we were stuck with our current lives, no intermission, no cut to the next scene. Some of it was genuinely hard—the isolation, the fear, the loss. But there was something else too. For the first time in years, many of us were forced to be present in our own lives. To notice the way afternoon light moved through our homes. To watch how the same street corner changed across seasons. To see the people we lived with, really see them, without the constant motion toward the next thing.

I've been trying to hold onto that forced attentiveness, though it's slipping away. The world is in motion again, pulling us toward the extraordinary, the next big thing, the life we're supposed to be building. It's a constant low hum underneath everything: *more, better, different*.

There's this idea that contentment with what you have is somehow a failure of ambition. That being satisfied with an ordinary afternoon means you lack vision or drive. But I'm not sure that's true. I think maybe the opposite is true—that the ability to find meaning and beauty in the unremarkable is actually the most sophisticated skill we can develop. It's easy to be happy on a vacation. It's harder to be present in your regular Tuesday.

I've been thinking too about how we talk about time differently as we age. As a child, a summer felt infinite. A year was a huge stretch of time. Now I'm in my thirties, and time moves with terrifying speed. Years collapse into each other. It's almost vertiginous, the velocity of it. Which makes the ordinary afternoons matter even more, because there are fewer of them ahead than there are behind. The finite quantity of afternoons you get to sit in good light and drink coffee—that's actually a sobering thought if you pay attention to it.

There's a piece of writing by Annie Dillard that's haunted me for years. She writes about wasting her life, or nearly wasting it, by not paying attention: "How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives." And then later: "The way to live is to live as if it mattered." The simplicity of it is devastating. You get a limited number of afternoons. What are you doing with them?

This isn't a call to productivity, necessarily. I'm not suggesting we all need to optimize our afternoons or squeeze more achievement into them. Actually, I think it's almost the opposite. I think it's about permission. Permission to sit. Permission to watch light move across a wall and consider that a worthwhile use of thirty minutes. Permission to have a conversation that meanders and doesn't accomplish anything but deepens how you understand someone. Permission to let an afternoon unfold without an agenda.

I was in a coffee shop recently—the kind where people sit for hours on their laptops, the kind that's become a kind of secular church for people who need a space that isn't home and isn't work. I watched a man across from me reading a book, and he wasn't taking notes or reading for any obvious professional purpose. He was just reading, occasionally looking out the window, occasionally sipping cold coffee that was definitely cold by then. And I thought: this is it. This is what it looks like. Someone taking an afternoon and choosing how to spend it, not because it would go on his resume or make his Instagram feed more interesting, but because it was what he wanted to do. The radical ordinariness of it made it almost revolutionary.

We talk sometimes about "living in the moment," and it's become such a cliché that it's lost all its power. We say it while scheduling our next vacation, while planning next week's meals, while mentally composing a social media post about how we're "trying to be present." But actually being present is much less photogenic than that. It's boring, often. It's repetitive. It's finding yourself on a Thursday afternoon with nothing particular to do and choosing not to fill that space with something productive or impressive, but just... being.

I think about my phone a lot, how much of my undivided attention it's trained away from actual reality. I don't think I'm alone in this. I think a lot of us are slowly developing a condition where we're never fully present anywhere because we're always capturing it, curating it, preparing it to be seen by someone else. Even right now, even writing this, I'm aware of that pull—the sense that an experience isn't quite real until it's been articulated, shaped into narrative, made shareable.

But the best afternoons I remember aren't the ones I documented. They're the ones where I forgot about documentation entirely. Where I was too engaged in what was happening, or too calm, or too absorbed, to even think about my phone. They're the afternoons that only I know about. They exist nowhere but in my own memory, which is rapidly becoming faulty and strange as I age. When I'm gone, they'll be gone too. No record. No proof. Just... something that happened, that I was there for, and then it was over.

That's either deeply sad or deeply freeing, I haven't decided which. Maybe it's both. Maybe the fact that it all disappears eventually is what makes it matter. Because there's no external value system, no achievement unlocked, no progress toward some larger goal. The afternoon is just the afternoon. You're just a person in a room with light coming through a window. That's your whole life happening right then.

I don't write these words thinking I've solved anything. I'm obviously not living in constant acceptance of the ordinary. I scroll my phone with the same numbing frequency as everyone else. I make plans and anticipate futures that haven't happened yet. I sometimes exist in a state of low-grade dissatisfaction, always aware of what I'm not doing, what I'm missing, where I could be instead.

But there are moments—increasingly more frequent as I get older—when I manage to let that go. When I'm just here, on a Tuesday afternoon, with a cup of something hot, and the light is making everything beautiful, and I'm not wishing I was somewhere else. And in those moments, I understand something that's hard to hold onto: that this is enough. Not as a resigned settling, but as a genuine recognition that this particular afternoon, this ordinary unremarkable afternoon, is actually the whole point. This is the life. Not the version you're building toward, but this one. Right now. With all its mundanity and repetition and lack of narrative arc.

That's what I've been thinking about. The peculiar grace of ordinary afternoons. The radical act of paying attention. The way that most of life is not the moments we celebrate but the ones we move through barely noticing, and how tragic that is, and how we might—if we were brave enough, or quiet enough, or present enough—actually see them.

# On the Peculiar Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about how we move through the world mostly blind to it. Not blind in any literal sense—our eyes work fine, scanning faces and screens and the path ahead. But there's a deeper blindness, a learned incuriosity that makes us see without really *seeing*. I notice this especially in myself when I'm in a hurry, which is almost always. The coffee cup becomes merely a vessel for caffeine. The commute becomes merely time to endure. The person sitting across from me becomes merely someone whose turn it is to talk while I wait to talk.

This seems like a disease of modernity, though I suspect people have always struggled with this problem. The farmer probably looked at the same field for forty years and stopped seeing it around year two. The fisherman's wife probably stopped noticing the smell of the sea. We habituate. We adjust. We stop marveling. This is efficient, I suppose. Useful. But something gets lost.

I've started collecting small observations, trying to rewild my attention a little. Nothing profound—just moments where something ordinary suddenly seems strange and beautiful if you really look at it.

Consider the human hand. I know, I know—artists have been waxing rhapsodic about hands forever. But that's actually my point. They're not waxing rhapsodic to be pretentious. Hands are genuinely, almost offensively perfect in their design. The way the thumb opposes the other fingers, allowing us to grip and manipulate and create. The specific musculature that lets someone play a cello or a video game, type a love letter or a grocery list. The scars and calluses and wrinkles that tell stories. We mostly just use them without thought, moving them through space like we move our eyes, as if they're magic that needs no explanation.

When I actually *look* at a hand—someone else's or my own—I'm struck by how much of human civilization is possible because of this particular configuration of bones and tendons and skin. Not just the physical things we've built, but everything we've created: music, art, writing, cooking, the specific comfort of holding someone's hand. A hand reaching out. A hand held out in greeting. A hand covering a mouth in surprise. The vocabulary of human touch wouldn't exist without this remarkable piece of biological engineering.

Or think about water. This is embarrassing—I'm embarrassed even writing it—but I was struck recently by the fact that water is transparent. Like, I *know* water is transparent. I use it every day, bathe in it, drink it. But sometimes I'll be pouring water into a glass and actually consider what I'm looking at: a liquid that lets light pass through it. It's such a specific and valuable property, and it's *everywhere*, and we barely notice. We notice when something blocks our vision, but perfect clarity? Invisibility? We take it for granted.

My sister sent me a video recently of her daughter—my niece—who is four years old, discovering that she can see her hand through a glass of water. Not that the glass of water was particularly magnifying, just that she was seeing her hand in a completely different medium, and it had that slight warping to it, and she was absolutely astonished. She kept moving her hand and giggling. She must have done it for five minutes straight, and her mother said she came back to it multiple times that day. It was, to her, the most incredible discovery.

I wonder when we lose that. When does watching light refract through water stop being astonishing and become just something water does? First grade? High school? Sometime in adulthood when we've decided that novelty only belongs to genuinely new experiences?

I've been trying to recapture that sometimes. Looking at the way light hits a puddle. Watching the specific way someone's face changes when they're really listening to something that matters to them. Noticing the complex geometry of a tree, the way branches split and split again, each segment following the same mathematical principle but always ending up looking slightly different.

There's a tree outside my window—I've walked past it maybe five thousand times—and last week I really *looked* at it. It's a birch tree. I don't know exactly which species, but it's the kind with papery white bark that peels. The winter had worn it, left bare branches reaching up, and I noticed that each branch has this series of small dark marks on it, like the spots on a leopard. I pulled out my phone to look it up, because I had to know if there was a name for those marks, if there was a reason they were there. (Apparently they're lenticels, pores that let the tree breathe. Of course. Everything has a reason.)

This is the weird thing about really looking: once you start noticing the detail and the reason and the mechanism, it somehow becomes even more interesting rather than less. You'd think that understanding would drain the mystery out of something. But somehow it doesn't. Knowing that those marks are how a tree breathes doesn't make the pattern less beautiful. If anything, it makes the tree seem more alive, more intentional in its design.

I think this is why people develop hobbies and obsessions. Birders don't spend hours in the woods because birds are merely birds. Aquarium enthusiasts aren't just keeping fish alive. Gardeners aren't just growing food. They're all doing the same thing: they're choosing to look closely at something, to let it become complicated and detailed and endlessly interesting. They're choosing not to habituate.

And it strikes me that this might be one of the deepest sources of meaning available to us, if we wanted it. Not in the grand sense—not necessarily in major life achievements or relationships (though those matter too). But the smaller, granular meaning of *actually paying attention*. Of noticing. Of letting the world be strange and detailed and specific rather than blurring it into categories and generalizations.

There's a restaurant I like, a small place run by a woman named Claire who's probably in her sixties. She's been making the same menu items for twenty years, and she makes them impeccably. But what I've noticed is that she seems genuinely interested in each plate of food she prepares, even though she must have made the same dish a thousand times. She's not just assembling ingredients. She's arranging them carefully. She's thinking about how it looks and tastes and sits on the plate. 

I asked her once if she didn't get bored, making the same ten dishes forever. She looked at me like I'd asked if she gets bored by breathing. "Every tomato is different," she said. "Different season, different soil. Every person who comes in is different, so you're making the same dish but for a different person, so it's not the same at all." 

That's stuck with me. Every tomato is different. Which seems obvious once you think about it, but it means that no dish is ever quite repeated. Every moment of cooking is genuinely novel, if you're paying attention.

I think the older I get, the more I realize that this is what separates a life that feels rich from one that feels empty: not what happens to you, but whether you're actually *there* for what happens to you. Whether you're really experiencing it, or whether you're just moving through it on autopilot, checking boxes, waiting for the real part of your life to start.

The real part never starts, by the way. Or rather, it's always already started. It's happening now, in this moment, whatever moment you're reading this in. The light in your room right now will never exist exactly this way again. The specific configuration of things around you is unique. The thoughts in your head are completely your own. This moment will never come back.

This sounds like I'm building toward something inspirational, like "so live each day as if it were your last" or some sort of motivational poster sentiment. But I don't think it needs to be quite so dramatic. I'm not suggesting we should approach every moment with reverent intensity. That would be exhausting. More like: occasionally pause. Notice something small. Become interested in something for its own sake, with no utility involved. Let yourself be surprised by the ordinary.

Because the ordinary is actually extraordinary if you look at it properly. A coffee cup holds hot liquid against gravity, contains temperature through careful material engineering. A morning commute is a journey through space taken by a biological being so complex that scientists still don't fully understand how it works. Someone sitting across from you is a person who experiences the world from completely inside their own head, whose inner life is as real and complex as yours, whom you can never fully know despite living in the same reality. These aren't small things.

I've been trying to write about attention and wonder for a while now, and I keep coming back to the same conclusion: we've got it backwards. We treat ordinary things as boring and commonplace when they're actually endlessly interesting if we just look. And we treat extraordinary things—vacations, accomplishments, rare experiences—as if they're the only things worth paying attention to. But the truth is that everything is extraordinary. A cup of tea. A person's face in different light. The sound of rain. The way a dog's whole body gets involved in wagging its tail, not just the tail. The texture of bread crust. The first moment you realize someone finds you funny, the split second of connection when humor clicks.

I think the greatest tragedy of modern life might not be that bad things happen, but that good things happen all the time and we're too distracted or habituated to notice. We walk through gardens and don't see the flowers. We eat beautiful food without tasting it. We talk to people we love while thinking about our phone. We're surrounded by small miracles and we're too preoccupied to care.

So I'm trying to reverse-engineer the child's attention, to become like that four-year-old with the glass of water. Not in a naive way—I don't need to pretend I don't understand physics to be fascinated by it. But to let myself be astonished by how things work, how things are designed, how someone looks when they're lost in thought, how the light changes through the day, how every single thing is exactly as strange as I'm willing to look at.

The good news is that this doesn't require anything special. No expense, no travel, no achievement. Just a choice to look. To really look. To let yourself be interested. To notice that the ordinary is already extraordinary, if you pay attention.

# The Strange Comfort of Uncertainty

I've been thinking lately about how we're all collectively pretending that certainty is a normal state of being. We're not, and it never was, but we've become remarkably skilled at the pretense.

Walk into any coffee shop in any major city and you'll see people hunched over laptops, phones glowing in the dark, their faces illuminated by carefully curated versions of their lives. Everyone appears to know exactly where they're going, what they're doing, and why it matters. LinkedIn profiles read like résumés for a life well-planned. Social media streams chronicle the highlights of journeys that seem preordained, as though their narrators simply executed a master plan they'd formulated years ago.

But here's what I think: nobody actually knows what they're doing. We're all just figuring it out as we go, and the ones who seem most confident are usually just better at committing to their own narratives.

I find this comforting, actually.

There's a strange freedom in accepting that uncertainty isn't a temporary condition—something you pass through on your way to understanding—but rather the default state of human existence. We're meaning-making creatures adrift in a fundamentally ambiguous universe, and we've invented countless systems to organize that chaos. Religion, science, philosophy, psychology, social structures, routines. These are all magnificent human creations, but they're creations nonetheless. The universe itself doesn't come pre-loaded with meaning or purpose. We pour that in.

What would it mean to actually embrace this? Not in some nihilistic "nothing matters so why bother" way, but in a genuinely liberatory sense?

I think about the people who seem most alive—not the most successful, necessarily, but the most genuinely engaged with their own existence. They tend to be the ones who've made peace with not knowing. They ask better questions than they answer. They're curious in the way children are curious, except they've also accumulated enough experience to recognize patterns and understand context. They're not waiting to feel ready before they do things. They understand that readiness is mostly a myth, that every meaningful thing you do will involve some degree of stepping forward into fog.

The irony is that we build entire industries around the promise of certainty. Self-help books, coaching programs, productivity systems, investment advisors—they all traffic in the fantasy that if you just follow these steps, absorb this knowledge, implement this framework, you can reduce life to something manageable and knowable. And some of it helps! I'm not cynical about all of it. But the underlying pitch is always the same: let me sell you a map to a territory that doesn't actually exist.

What strikes me most is how exhausting the performance of certainty must be. To maintain that facade constantly—in your professional life, your romantic relationships, your friendships, your relationship to yourself—requires an enormous amount of energy. You have to keep editing. You have to pretend that the doubts don't exist, or that you've overcome them, or that you never had them in the first place. You're constantly scanning for inconsistencies in your own narrative, making sure everything aligns.

I wonder what would happen if we all just... stopped.

Not in a reckless way. I'm not advocating for abandoning all planning or responsibility. But what if we could admit uncertainty without shame? What if "I don't know" became an acceptable answer? What if we could hold our plans lightly, understanding them as best guesses based on current information, subject to revision?

One of the strangest developments of modern life is that we've simultaneously become more specialized and more universally expected to have opinions on everything. We're supposed to be experts in our professional domains while also maintaining thoughtful positions on politics, culture, economics, parenting, health, ethics, and probably astrology. The cognitive load is extraordinary. Every topic immediately becomes a minefield of potential contradiction. So we pick tribes, adopt their talking points, and perform consistency.

But inside most of us is a person who, if given permission, would say: "I genuinely don't know about most of this. I have intuitions and partial information and lived experiences that point in certain directions, but I'm aware that all of this could be wrong."

That person is probably much wiser than the one we present publicly.

I've noticed that the moments in my own life when I've actually learned something significant have typically come after I've abandoned the pretense of knowing. It's not pleasant—there's a vulnerability to it, an exposure. But it opens up space for genuine understanding. When you stop defending a position, you can actually consider it. When you admit you don't know something, you become genuinely curious about it instead of just pretending to have it figured out.

This applies to self-knowledge too. How much time do we spend in a kind of self-deception about our own motivations, desires, and capacities? We tell ourselves stories about who we are—stories that usually feel like accurate descriptions when we're living inside them. I'm ambitious, or I'm not. I'm creative, or I'm practical. I'm an introvert, or I'm an extrovert. And sometimes these narratives are useful heuristics. But sometimes they're just convenient prisons. We mistake our current circumstances and habits for our nature, then spend years defending the walls.

What if you didn't know who you were? What if that was okay? What if the point was to keep discovering, keep surprising yourself?

There's something almost sacrilegious about that idea in a culture obsessed with self-optimization and authentic self-expression. We're supposed to find ourselves, develop ourselves, know ourselves. But what if the self is not a thing to be found—some fixed nugget of identity buried inside—but rather something that emerges through the process of living? What if who you are is less important than what you do?

I think about how many conversations would be different if they weren't performances. If I could say to a stranger, "I'm not actually sure what I think about that, but I'm interested in understanding it better. What's your take?" Instead of constructing a position and defending it. If professional environments allowed for actual intellectual humility instead of just the performative kind. If we could admit that we're figuring it out without that being held against us.

The fear, I think, is that admitting uncertainty is the same as admitting weakness. That if you don't have all the answers, people won't take you seriously, won't trust you, won't follow you. Maybe that's sometimes true. But I suspect the opposite is more often the case. I trust people who know what they don't know far more than people who seem to have everything figured out. The ones who claim certainty are either lying or delusional, and neither is particularly reassuring.

There's also something almost transcendent about genuinely not knowing. I've experienced it most clearly in moments of awe—standing in a landscape so vast it exceeds your ability to comprehend it, listening to music that bypasses language and logic, experiencing art that rewires your sense of what's possible. In those moments, there's no room for pretense. You're not thinking about how you appear. You're just present to something that exceeds your understanding.

What if we could access more of that—not in those rare transcendent moments, but in ordinary life?

I suspect it would change everything.

It would change how we relate to others, because we'd spend less energy managing impressions and more energy actually connecting. It would change how we approach problems, because we'd be willing to explore solutions without knowing in advance that they'll work. It would change our relationship to time, because we wouldn't be so fixated on a predetermined destination. It would change how we treat failure, because we'd recognize that learning requires experimentation and experimentation involves mistakes.

One of the most depressing things about modern life, I think, is how prematurely people seem to foreclose possibility. By a certain age—somewhere between twenty-five and thirty-five for many people—their lives have become surprisingly fixed. They've chosen their career, their partner, their geography, their identity, and now they're just executing on those choices. Their daily lives are about optimizing within predetermined parameters rather than questioning whether the parameters themselves are the right ones.

Is this inevitable? Or have we just become very skilled at talking ourselves into it?

I think about what would change if you gave yourself permission to not know what you'll be doing in five years. If you held your current circumstances as a story you're telling right now, not a permanent condition. If you understood that the person you are is still under construction, and that construction might take surprising directions.

The funny thing is, I don't think this would lead to chaos or directionlessness. Actually, the opposite. I think it would lead to better decision-making, because you'd be basing decisions on genuine insight rather than accumulated assumptions. It might lead to more risk-taking, yes, but the kinds of risks that lead to growth rather than the self-destructive kind.

And there's something liberating about not having to be right all the time. About not having to maintain consistency across all domains of your life. About not having to have an opinion on everything. About being able to say "I don't know" and having that be the end of it rather than the beginning of an apology.

Maybe I'm romanticizing this. Maybe unlimited uncertainty would be paralyzing rather than liberating. Maybe we need some structure, some narrative coherence, some sense of direction to function. Probably true.

But I'm wondering if we couldn't find a middle ground. A way of holding our plans lightly enough that we can adjust them when reality presents better options. A way of knowing ourselves flexibly enough that we can grow. A way of engaging with the world that doesn't require performing certainty.

One practical thing that might help: asking better questions. Instead of "What should I do?" maybe "What am I curious about?" Instead of "What's the right answer?" maybe "What happens if I try this?" Instead of "Who am I?" maybe "What can I do? What do I care about? What am I willing to risk for?"

Those questions don't require false certainty. They're compatible with genuine not-knowing.

I think what I'm really trying to say is this: there's a version of your life that's possible if you admit you don't have it figured out. It might not look like the version you were supposed to have. It might not match the narrative you've been telling yourself. But it might be better. More real. More alive. More genuinely yours.

The uncertainty isn't a bug. It's not a temporary condition you need to overcome. It's the fundamental texture of human existence, and the sooner you make peace with it, the sooner you can actually start living.
