# On the Peculiar Comfort of Doing Nothing

There's a particular kind of afternoon—let's say it's a Saturday, though it could be any day when the world hasn't made demands of you yet—when you find yourself suspended in that rare state of having nowhere to be. Not the anxious "nowhere to be yet" of someone waiting for their shift to start, but the genuine, guilt-free nowhere to be. These moments have become increasingly precious, I think, almost archaeological in how rarely we unearth them anymore.

I was thinking about this recently while sitting on my porch, ostensibly reading but mostly watching the way light moves through oak leaves. There's a particular quality to this kind of useless observation that society has somehow made us feel guilty about. We're supposed to be *optimizing* our time, *maximizing* our potential, *hustling* our way toward some undefined better version of ourselves. The language itself is violent—all those hard consonants, the sense of force and conquest. But sitting on a porch, watching leaves, has its own kind of productivity, I think, one that doesn't appear on any spreadsheet.

The thing about doing nothing is that it's much harder than it sounds. I don't mean physically—anyone can sit still. I mean the internal quieting that's required. Our minds are so well-trained now to be restless, to skip between thoughts like a stone across water. When you actually try to do nothing, you realize how full of small urgencies everything is. You should check your phone. You should think about that email. You should really get around to organizing the garage. There's someone you haven't texted back. The guilt about not doing something productive crawls up your spine like a chill.

But if you persist, something shifts. Not immediately, and not completely, but eventually you reach a point where you stop fighting the stillness and simply exist within it. Your mind doesn't go blank—that's rarely what happens in my experience—but it becomes gentler, less insistent. Thoughts arise and pass without grabbing your attention like desperate passengers trying to board a train. You notice things you've walked past a thousand times: the way dust catches light through a window, the specific sound of wind that means rain is coming, the exact shade of blue in the afternoon sky that you've somehow never named before.

I wonder sometimes if this is what people in previous generations had access to without even trying. Not the content of relaxation, necessarily, but the *permission* for it. The understanding that a person might spend an afternoon doing nothing and this was simply a normal part of being alive, not something to feel guilty about or monetize or document for social media. The rhythm of life seemed to have spaces built into it, like the silence in music that makes the notes meaningful.

We talk about mental health and burnout and the importance of balance, but we often miss the actual mechanism of how rest works. It's not that you accumulate rest like you accumulate wealth, pouring it into a container that eventually fills up and solves all your problems. It's more like you're an instrument that's constantly being played, and rest is the tuning of it, the maintenance that allows it to make anything resembling a true sound. You can't tune an instrument while you're playing it.

There's something almost rebellious about it, this commitment to deliberate uselessness. In a world obsessed with productivity metrics and optimization, simply existing without purpose feels like a quiet form of resistance. Not in a dramatic way, not in a way that changes anything structurally, but in the small personal way of saying: I am enough as I am, not as much as I can produce. My value is not measured in output. My time is not a resource to be exploited, even by myself.

This doesn't come naturally to me, I should say. I come from the lineage of people who feel guilty if they're not doing something "productive," who view relaxation as a reward to be earned through suffering rather than a birthright. There's a Calvinist streak in American culture that runs deep, this notion that idleness is the devil's workshop, that being useful is the primary moral good. I've internalized this more than I'd like to admit. But I'm trying to unlearn it.

What's interesting is that some of my best ideas, my most genuine insights, have come from periods of doing nothing. I don't mean the productive kind of nothing, where you're supposedly "giving your subconscious a chance to work," turning relaxation into another productivity hack. I mean the genuine, purposeless kind of nothing, where you're not even aware that you're thinking. You're just sitting with the world as it is, and something about this receptiveness allows novelty to enter, allows your mind to make connections it wouldn't have made if you were forcing it.

The other thing about doing nothing is that it's democratic in a way that so few things are. You don't need money to do it. You don't need talent or intelligence or gym membership or special equipment. You just need permission, and that's the hard part—getting yourself to believe you deserve it. Anyone can sit and watch the world, and in that simple act, there's something leveling, something that reminds you that maybe the most important parts of being alive aren't the parts you can put on a resume.

I'm not arguing that everyone should quit their jobs and sit on porches. That's neither realistic nor entirely desirable—we live in the world as it is, not as we wish it to be. But I do think there's something worth defending about the space for uselessness, the space for simply being without producing. The afternoon with nowhere to be. The walk that has no destination. The conversation that accomplishes nothing except the pleasure of talking. These things are not luxuries that can be deferred until retirement, if we're lucky enough to reach it.

They're essential, in the way that the space between the notes is essential to music, or the white space is essential to a painting. Without them, everything collapses into a flat, exhausting drone.

So here's to the nothing. Here's to porch afternoons and useless observations and the quiet rebellion of doing absolutely nothing at all.

# On the Peculiar Joy of Being Slightly Lost

I've been thinking lately about how we've systematized almost everything. Maps that know where you are down to six feet. Algorithms that predict what you want before you want it. Turn-by-turn directions that don't just show you the way, but scold you if you deviate. It's efficient, certainly. It's safe. It's also, I think, quietly destructive to something we rarely discuss: the productive confusion of being lost.

There's a specific kind of joy that emerges when you're in an unfamiliar place with no immediate way out. Not genuine danger—I'm not romanticizing being trapped in the woods without supplies. I mean something gentler. The kind of lostness that happens when you take a wrong turn in a city and end up on a street you didn't know existed. When your phone dies and you're navigating by memory and landmarks. When you wander off the marked trail and find a meadow nobody else seemed to know about.

That state of gentle disorientation does something to your brain that GPS cannot replicate. It forces you to pay attention. The curve of a building becomes a landmark. The smell coming from a cafe becomes navigation. You notice things—really notice them—because you're actively trying to construct a mental map rather than passively following a blue line. You become a researcher of your immediate environment rather than a follower of directions.

I wonder if we've lost something important by making lostness obsolete.

When I was nine, my father did something that terrified my mother. He took me into the woods near our house and deliberately didn't tell me which way we came. "We're going to get lost," he said, with a grin that suggested this was somehow festive. "And then we're going to find our way back."

For twenty minutes, I was genuinely anxious. Not afraid, exactly, but alert in a way I'd never been before. Every moss-covered log became a potential landmark. I noticed which direction the sun was traveling. I watched which way the stream flowed (everyone knows streams lead somewhere). My father didn't help much—just walked alongside me while I fumbled through the logic of direction-finding like a medieval navigator. Eventually, I got us home by essentially reversing the turns I remembered, confirming them against the landscape.

I was so proud. More than that, I felt *connected* to the physical world in a way I hadn't before. It wasn't my neighborhood anymore—it was *my* forest, mapped by my own cognition rather than handed to me pre-digested.

Now I think about how different that experience is from what we're training our children to do. Swipe, look at the blue dot, go there. The world becomes a series of nodes on a network rather than something you have to actually *know*. And knowing—true knowledge—requires struggle. It requires the productive discomfort of not immediately understanding something.

This extends beyond navigation, I think. We've engineered lostness out of so much of modern life. Streaming services recommend what you watch next. Social media algorithms decide what you read. Amazon suggests what you buy. We're increasingly smoothed into prefabricated paths through information and experience.

There's something to be said for aimlessness. Real aimlessness, not the Instagram-performance of "taking a spontaneous weekend trip." I mean the kind of boredom that forces you to find your own entertainment. The kind of empty afternoon that leads you down a rabbit hole of unexpected thinking. The kind of bookstore browsing where you find something you'd never have searched for.

Some of my best ideas have come from being slightly lost in conversation. Someone says something that doesn't quite make sense, and instead of moving on, I sit with the confusion for a moment. That moment of confusion is where interesting thinking happens. The moment right before everything resolves into understanding is often where genuine insight lives.

We've trained ourselves to minimize that moment. Google it. Look it up. Get the answer. Confusion is an inefficiency to be corrected rather than a space to inhabit. But inefficiency, I'm beginning to suspect, is where the best parts of life happen.

My most meaningful conversations never go as planned. The best vacations always involve at least one misunderstanding. The most interesting people I know are often the ones who've made significant mistakes, gotten lost, and had to figure things out the hard way. There's a kind of depth to someone who has actually *had* to think rather than just consumed pre-processed thinking.

I'm not advocating for rejecting all technology or information systems. That's naive and impossible now anyway. I'm saying that maybe we should be more suspicious of seamlessness. Maybe we should occasionally turn off the GPS just to remember what it feels like to genuinely navigate. Maybe we should sometimes let boredom run its course instead of immediately filling it with content. Maybe we should defend the right to get lost—intellectually, physically, socially.

Because here's what I think is happening: by removing all friction from the process of finding things out, we're potentially removing something that made us more thoughtful, more observant, more fully present in the world. We're trading depth for efficiency. We're choosing the blue dot over the meadow.

The meadow will still be there, theoretically. But if everyone's following the same GPS-optimized path, nobody will ever stumble into it. It'll just be a quiet place that nobody knows about, which is sad for the meadow and sadder for us.

So maybe this is my argument for intentional lostness. For seeking out situations where you don't immediately know what to do. For reading books without first checking what they're about. For taking routes without knowing where they lead. For having conversations that meander instead of arriving at predetermined conclusions.

Not because efficiency is evil. But because the good life—the fully alive life—isn't actually that efficient. It's full of detours and dead ends and unexpected discoveries. It requires the kind of attention that only emerges when you're slightly confused, slightly lost, and forced to pay closer attention to find your way.

And honestly? That state of productive confusion might be the most human thing we have left to protect.

# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

There's a moment that happens most mornings if I'm paying attention—that peculiar instant when you first wake and haven't yet remembered what day it is or what problems are waiting. The world exists in a kind of neutral suspension. The light is just light. The sounds are just sounds. You haven't yet assembled them into meaning.

I've been thinking lately about how much of life consists of this act of assembly—how we take the raw material of existence and constantly organize it into narratives, problems, significance. And I wonder if we're missing something by doing this so automatically, so completely, that we rarely pause to notice the noticing itself.

There's something almost embarrassing about acknowledging wonder. It feels childish or naive, like you haven't yet learned how the world actually works. We're taught that sophistication means moving beyond amazement, that maturity is recognizing the ordinary as ordinary. But I think we've confused familiarity with understanding. A thing can be familiar and still be extraordinary. A sunset doesn't become less remarkable because it happens every day.

I was in a café yesterday—the kind of aggressively ordinary place that exists in every city, designed to be pleasantly forgettable—and I watched a woman tear open a packet of sugar and pour it into her coffee. Nothing remarkable. Except that I really looked at it. The crystalline granules, each one a tiny solid thing, dissolving into liquid and changing it. The small gesture of care embedded in the action: she wanted her coffee a particular way and did a small thing to make it so.

This is what I mean about noticing. Not the sugar and coffee themselves, but the underlying reality beneath: that we're all constantly engaged in this practice of small transformations, of making our immediate world slightly more suited to us. Of wanting things and doing modest things to get them.

Everyone you see is this entire universe. That line gets repeated so often it's become almost meaningless, but it's still true. The person sitting across from you on the train has as much interior life as you do—same density of memory, same quality of concern about whether people like them, the same strange loop of consciousness folded back on itself. And you'll never really know them. You'll share space with them and then you'll never meet again, and they'll continue existing after you've forgotten them, living their life according to their own logic.

I think about this when I'm annoyed with someone—in traffic, in a conversation, in my own family. Because there's always a moment where I catch myself and realize: this person has a specific reason for what they're doing. Not an excuse, necessarily. A reason. They're not being a traffic obstruction; they're being late to something. They're not being obtuse in the conversation; they're understanding it through their own history. We're all operating from inside such specific, particular frameworks that conflict is almost inevitable.

The question is whether you meet that with contempt or curiosity.

I've noticed I'm much happier when I choose curiosity. Not in a performative way—not the false listening where you're just waiting for your turn to talk. But genuine curiosity, which is actually quite rare. It requires setting aside, temporarily, your own framework and actually trying to see through someone else's lens. It's harder than it sounds. It requires a kind of humility.

There's a phrase I've been turning over: "the privilege of noticing." I can't remember where I encountered it. But it stuck because it suggests that attention is a kind of fortune, a gift you give yourself. And it's not evenly distributed. Poverty and exhaustion and pain all make noticing harder—when you're desperate or in crisis, the world contracts to just the immediate problem. So there's something almost guilty in having enough space in your life to notice things.

But I think that's exactly why we should do it. Not to feel guilty, but to actually exercise that capacity. Because I suspect that the people who are happiest, in a deep way that has nothing to do with circumstances, are the ones who've somehow maintained this ability to really see things. To see their own small life with the kind of attention normally reserved for art or nature.

There's a writer I love who talks about the "unlived life"—all the ways we move through time on autopilot, doing things without really being present to them. You eat a meal without tasting it. You have a conversation while checking your phone. You drive home and can't remember the drive. You reach the end of a day and it's vanished. That's not really living, even though it looks like living from the outside.

What would it mean to actually live those moments? Not all of them—that would be exhausting and probably impossible. But some of them. To actually taste the meal sometimes. To be fully present in a conversation. To notice the specific quality of light on a particular afternoon, knowing you'll never see this exact combination again because time is moving in one direction and we're all carried forward in it.

Maybe this is what people mean by mindfulness, though that word has been so commercialized and drained of meaning. What I mean is simpler: looking at things. Actually looking.

There's a poem where Mary Oliver asks: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" And the answer everyone gives is: something great, something meaningful, something important.

But I'm increasingly convinced the real answer might be simpler. Notice things. Really see them. Meet people with curiosity rather than judgment. Taste your food. Feel the weather. Read something that changes how you think. Sit with the fact that you exist, which is genuinely improbable, and that you're aware that you exist, which is even more so.

Do that, and maybe everything else organizes itself around it. Or maybe it doesn't, and your life is ordinary in every way.

But you'll have actually lived it. You'll have been present for it.

And that seems like something.

# The Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about how we're taught to fear incompleteness, yet some of the most beautiful things in life exist in that liminal space—not quite done, not quite begun, suspended in potential.

There's a painting in my mind that I never finished. It was supposed to be a landscape, something with trees and water, but I abandoned it somewhere around the third layer of acrylic. My mother asked why I didn't just complete it, and I realized I couldn't quite explain that finishing it would somehow diminish it. The unfinished painting held infinite possibility. It could become anything. The moment I added that final brushstroke, it would become something specific, something limited, something that could be judged as successful or failed.

This extends to so many things. I think about friendships that fade without explicit endings—you don't have a fight, you just gradually see each other less often, and somehow that feels more honest than many of the friendships that do end with a conversation. There's less pretense in gentle fade-outs. Both people recognize something has shifted without needing to dramatize it.

Or consider conversations that end naturally, mid-thought, when both people understand there's nothing more to say even though the topic isn't technically resolved. Those moments feel richer to me than conversations that are neatly wrapped up with conclusive statements. Reality is rarely conclusive. Our understanding of things remains perpetually incomplete, and I think pretending otherwise is a kind of lie we tell ourselves.

I wonder if this is why I'm drawn to certain books that frustrate other people. The ones where the ending is ambiguous, where character motivations remain somewhat mysterious, where you close the cover and have to sit with uncertainty. Everyone wants to know: Did they end up together? Was the protagonist reliable? What actually happened? But maybe the refusal to answer is the point. Maybe the book is better for it.

This relates to something deeper, I think—the problem with solutions. We're obsessed with them. Every problem needs a solution. Every question needs an answer. Every story needs resolution. But life isn't structured that way. Life is mostly unresolved. Most of our problems don't get solved; they just get slightly better managed, or we adapt to them, or we die with them still unsolved. Most questions don't get answered; we just get tired of asking. Most stories don't have neat endings; they have periods where we stop paying attention.

The grief counselors tell you that you don't "get over" loss; you learn to live with it. That's not completion—that's integration of an unfinished thing into your ongoing life. And somehow that's more honest than the narrative of "closure" that we've convinced ourselves is necessary and possible.

I think about all the projects people abandon. The guitar in the closet, the half-written novel, the course started but not finished, the language app downloaded in January. We treat these as failures, as evidence of our lack of commitment or discipline. But what if they're actually evidence of something else—that we're responsive to what life offers us? That we're willing to try things without needing to be guaranteed we'll finish them?

There's something almost aggressive about the insistence on completion, isn't there? A kind of stubborn assertion of will against the natural entropy and distraction of existence. I admire it sometimes, but I also think it misses something important.

I had a teacher once who said that the difference between a professional and an amateur is that the professional finishes things. She meant well, I think. But I've known professionally finished things that felt soulless, and I've known magnificently unfinished things that felt transcendent. The completion wasn't the difference.

Maybe it's just that the world has enough finished things. Libraries are full of completed sentences. Museums are full of finished paintings. We have thousands of resolved narratives. What we might need more of is the ability to sit with unresolved ones, to find meaning in the incomplete, to understand that a sketch can be more powerful than a detailed rendering, that a suggestion can be more evocative than an explicit statement.

This has practical implications too. I think we're raised to believe that our lives should have a trajectory, a narrative arc, a beginning, middle, and end that makes sense. We should get the job, then move up, then retire happily. We should find the person, fall in love, get married, live ever after. We should discover our passion, pursue it relentlessly, achieve success. But life doesn't work that way. Life is a series of unfinished chapters. New ones start before the old ones end. Sometimes you're living in three different stories simultaneously and they never resolve into one coherent narrative.

And I think if we could make peace with that—if we could stop treating our unfinished lives as failures—we might be happier. We might stop waiting for the moment when everything clicks into place, when we'll finally be ready to be happy, when we'll finally have all the answers. That moment doesn't come. Happiness has to exist in the unfinished spaces, in the questions still being asked, in the projects half-started, in the relationships that are ongoing without clear definition, in the understanding that evolves without ever reaching final form.

The Japanese have a concept, wabi-sabi, that embraces incompleteness and imperfection. There's something wise in that perspective. The cracked tea bowl is more beautiful because of the crack. The garden is more interesting because it's always growing, never finished. The artist is more interesting than the art because the artist is still becoming.

I think I'll keep that painting unfinished. And I'll keep having conversations that trail off. And I'll probably abandon some books before I finish them, and start projects I don't complete, and leave things unsaid that maybe should have been said, and become a person who hasn't figured it all out, probably won't, and is increasingly okay with that.

There's a peace in it, oddly enough. In admitting that you're not going to resolve everything. That some of the best things in life exist in the incompleteness. That becoming is more interesting than being, that potential is more beautiful than manifestation, that an unfinished life honestly lived is better than a perfectly completed life that was never quite real.

And maybe that's a more complete philosophy than I could have articulated if I'd tried to finish it.

# The Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

There's something oddly liberating about being completely, utterly lost. Not the panic-stricken kind where your phone dies and you're genuinely worried about missing an important meeting, but the genuine, wandering-through-an-unfamiliar-city-with-nowhere-to-be kind of lost. The kind that turns into adventure.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, particularly after realizing how rare this feeling has become in modern life. We have GPS satellites following our every movement, Google Maps knowing every street corner, our phones vibrating with reminders about where we're supposed to be next. We've engineered uncertainty almost entirely out of our existence, and in doing so, we've removed something that humans actually need—the surprise, the discovery, the chance encounter.

When I was a kid, getting lost was practically inevitable. My friends and I would set out on our bikes with vague destinations in mind, and inevitably we'd end up in parts of town we'd never seen before. We'd discover weird little gardens tucked behind residential streets, find tiny cafes that seemed to exist in their own pocket dimension, stumble upon used bookstores run by ancient men who knew every volume in their inventory by heart. There was no way to quickly verify if we were heading in the right direction. We just had to follow our intuition, ask strangers, or keep riding until something felt recognizable.

Those discoveries seemed magical because they were genuinely accidental. We could never quite retrace our steps to those places. They existed in memory rather than in GPS coordinates, which made them feel more real somehow, more truly ours.

Now I'm an adult, and I've been thinking about how this relates to bigger things—like how we've systematized most of human experience. We have optimal routes to everything, algorithms that predict what we'll want before we want it, career paths that are well-trodden and mapped out. We're encouraged to be efficient, to minimize wasted time, to know what we're doing and where we're going.

But there's a cost to all this optimization. Somewhere in the process of removing friction from our lives, we've also removed the possibility of genuine surprise. And surprise—that moment when you turn a corner and see something you weren't expecting—is what makes you feel alive.

I wonder if this is why some of the most interesting conversations I have happen with strangers in unexpected places. There's something about the randomness of it that opens people up. You meet someone at a bus stop, and because you'll probably never see them again, they tell you something true. You're not performing for anyone. There's no social media audience. It's just two people, briefly connected by geography and circumstance rather than algorithm.

The internet promised to connect us to everyone, but in practice, it's mostly connected us to people exactly like ourselves. The algorithm learns what you like and shows you more of it. You follow people whose opinions you already agree with. You end up in these bubbles that feel diverse until you realize everyone around you has read the same articles and shares the same references.

Getting lost—real, old-fashioned, analog getting lost—is the opposite of this. It forces you to encounter the world as it actually is, not as a curated collection designed for your consumption. It makes you vulnerable. You have to ask for help, which means talking to actual humans. You have to trust your instincts, which might be wrong. You might end up somewhere weird or uncomfortable, but you might also find something wonderful.

I've started deliberately getting lost in cities I visit. I'll leave my phone at the hotel or ignore it completely and just walk, turning whenever something catches my eye. It sounds like a small thing, but it feels radical. My friends think I'm insane. "Why wouldn't you just use Google Maps?" they ask, genuinely confused.

The answer is harder to articulate than it should be. Because I want to remember this city as something I discovered, not something I navigated. Because the inefficient path is usually more interesting. Because the detour is where the story is.

There's also something about the feeling of being lost that makes you more present. You can't walk on autopilot when you're not sure where you are. You notice things—the architecture of buildings, the smell of a restaurant, the way light hits a street corner at a particular time of day. You're more alert, more alive, because your brain isn't already three steps ahead of where you're going.

I think about teenagers today, and I wonder what they're missing. They have maps but not mysteries. They have connection but not coincidence. Everything is arranged for them, optimized for their preferences, predicted before they even know they want it. Where do they learn to trust their instincts? Where do they experience genuine surprise? How do they develop the kind of confidence that comes from figuring things out on your own?

Maybe this is why people seem so anxious now. We've removed all the small risks from life—the possibility of getting lost, of being late, of showing up somewhere and finding it closed or different than expected—but we haven't made ourselves feel safer. Instead, we've just become more fragile. We've outsourced our navigation to machines, and in doing so, we've forgotten how to navigate ourselves.

So I'm going to keep getting lost. I'm going to turn down streets without knowing where they lead. I'm going to talk to strangers and take detours and show up late because I got distracted by something interesting. I'm going to make mistakes in a world that doesn't require perfection.

Because there's something about confusion and discovery that's essential to being human. Not the anxiety kind of confusion, but the good kind—the kind that precedes learning something, that comes right before you understand something new about the world or yourself.

The future doesn't have to be a place we navigate toward. Sometimes it's better to wander in its direction and see what we find.

# On the Strange Comfort of Incomplete Things

There's a mug on my desk that's missing its handle. It sits there among the functional ceramics, and I've never thrown it away, though I've had plenty of opportunities. Every time I clean, I pick it up, consider it, and then return it to its spot. I think there's something worth examining in that impulse—the strange reluctance we feel to discard imperfect objects.

Most of us are raised with a kind of implicit perfectionism. Things should work. Objects should serve their purposes. A mug without a handle has failed at its primary job, which is to be held comfortably while containing hot liquid. Yet I keep it. Why? Because I find myself drawn to what it represents—a narrative of use, of time passing, of something that was whole once and now isn't, but still exists. It's archaeological in a way. It's a small monument to the fact that nothing lasts unchanged.

I think about this a lot lately—how much of our anxiety comes from the expectation that things should be intact, that we should be intact. We speak about our mental health in terms of being "broken" or needing to be "fixed," as though wholeness is the natural state and fracture is an aberration. But is it? Walk through any old city and you'll see buildings that have been patched and modified countless times, that bear the marks of centuries, and somehow they're more beautiful for it. The kintsugi tradition in Japanese ceramics goes even further—it glorifies the repair, making the breaks visible with gold, transforming damage into decoration.

I wonder what would change if we approached our own incompleteness this way. Not as failures to achieve some imagined perfect state, but as evidence of having been alive, of having weathered something.

There's also something liberating about incomplete things, I think. A finished project can be intimidating. You judge it against some ideal. But an incomplete thing—well, it still has possibilities. That half-written story on your computer could become anything. The half-finished painting leans against the wall, waiting for you to discover what it actually wants to be. There's hope in incompletion that perfection paradoxically destroys. Once something is complete, it can only degrade or be judged. While it remains unfinished, it remains full of potential.

I've noticed this in conversations too. The best ones never feel finished. You leave them still thinking, still turning over what was said, still discovering new implications days later. The conversations that feel complete, that wrap up neatly with satisfying conclusions, often feel hollow in retrospect. We think we connected, but the other person has already moved on, the moment is sealed shut. But the inconclusive conversation, the one where you both hung in the space of uncertainty together—that one stays with you. It keeps working on you, the way that mug keeps working on me.

This might be why I'm suspicious of self-help books and life advice in general, even as I understand why people seek them out. We want someone to tell us the complete truth, the final answer, the way to fix ourselves. But real growth doesn't work that way. It's messier. It's partial knowledge that you have to keep re-examining. It's taking advice that contradicts other advice you've been given, and somehow learning to live in that contradiction. It's becoming more complicated, not less.

The older I get, the more I notice that the people I most admire are not the ones who seem to have it all figured out. They're the ones who are comfortable admitting what they don't know, who can hold conflicting ideas at once, who haven't stopped asking questions. They've made peace with their incompleteness. There's a kind of grace in that—a refusal to perform certainty that they don't feel.

I think about the books I love most, and so many of them have unsatisfying endings. Or rather, endings that satisfy something deeper than plot resolution—they satisfy the need for honesty. They end where the story actually ends, not where convention suggests stories should end. They leave you with questions. They trust you to do the work of interpretation.

There's a line in one of Elena Ferrante's novels where she writes about how we go through life leaving pieces of ourselves everywhere, in the people we meet, in the experiences we have, and we're never fully present anywhere because we're always partially distributed across all our past encounters. We're incomplete creatures by definition, scattered across time. Maybe the only way to survive that is to stop trying to gather ourselves back together into some coherent whole and instead accept the scattering as our fundamental condition.

I think this is what draws me to reading biographies and essays—they're often more honest about incompletion than fiction is. A life doesn't resolve into a narrative arc unless you impose one on it afterward. The actual living of it is contradictory, unresolved, full of threads that lead nowhere and questions that remain open. We're always in the middle of becoming, never arriving at final definitions of ourselves.

So I keep that mug. And I use other complete mugs for my coffee, because pragmatism is also important. But I keep the broken one because it reminds me of something I need to remember regularly: that damage is not the opposite of value, that incompleteness is not a temporary state to be fixed but a permanent condition to be accepted and even cherished. The cracks are where the light gets in, as Leonard Cohen said, though he was quoting Rumi, because nothing is ever original anyway. Everything is a fragment of something else, all of us composed of broken pieces fitted together, and the coherence we feel is an illusion we maintain together through collective agreement.

Maybe that's the most honest thing I can say: we're all walking around with missing handles, and the secret is learning not to mind, and even learning to find that beautiful.

# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

I've been thinking lately about attention—that most ordinary and extraordinary thing we do constantly without thinking about it. We attend to things. We notice. We become aware. And I suspect this capacity might be one of the most underrated gifts we possess.

There's a tree outside my window that I've probably walked past ten thousand times. Maple, I think. Medium-sized, nothing particularly remarkable about it. But the other day I actually *looked* at it—not just with my eyes pointed in that direction, but with actual attention. The way the bark twisted as it grew upward. The particular shade of green in its early spring leaves. The small architectural miracle of how branches split and resplit into smaller and smaller twigs. And I was struck by this thought: I've been living near this tree for years, and I'd never really seen it before.

This sounds like a cliché. I know it does. The kind of thing people write in journals to prove to themselves they're awake and alive and not just sleepwalking through existence. But I think there's something genuine underneath the cliché, something true and worth exploring.

We live in an age of unprecedented distraction. Every moment, we're being asked to divide our attention into smaller and smaller pieces. Your phone buzzes. An advertisement catches your eye. Someone calls your name. A notification pops up. Your mind drifts to a conversation you had three days ago. Meanwhile, the actual world—the one made of trees and light and texture and the sound of wind through leaves—continues on, largely unobserved.

And I don't say this as someone perched above it all. I say it as someone who checks their phone constantly, who plans tomorrow while existing in today, who has a thousand browser tabs open in their mind at all times. I'm describing my own life. I'm describing the condition I think many of us live in without quite realizing it.

But here's what I wonder: what if the solution isn't digital detox or meditation apps or any of the productivity-culture solutions we're constantly being sold? What if the solution is simpler and harder—to just deliberately look at things?

I read once about a painter who spent weeks painting a single barn. Not because the barn required weeks of work, but because to paint something truly, you have to see it. Really see it. You have to notice how light falls differently on the north side than the south. You have to observe the way shadows shift across its surface with the passing hours. You have to become intimate with the thing you're depicting.

I think that's what I was doing with the tree. I was learning to see it the way a painter would. Not seeing it as "a tree"—that generic category—but seeing *this* particular tree, in all its specific, unrepeatable particularity.

The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote about how language often prevents us from noticing things. We use the same word—"leaf"—for millions of different leaves, and in doing so, we flatten them into a kind of generic sameness. But every leaf is singular. Every one. I find this strangely beautiful and also slightly unsettling.

It makes me wonder what else I'm missing by categorizing too quickly, by naming something and then thinking I've understood it.

There's something else attention does, beyond just seeing more clearly. It seems to change the quality of your experience. When I really looked at that tree, I didn't just see it more accurately. The experience itself became more vivid, more present, more real in a way that's hard to explain but easy to feel. 

This might be what people mean when they talk about "being in the moment"—not some mystical state, but simply the experience of actually paying attention to what's in front of you, rather than treating it as background scenery to your mental narrative.

I think about my childhood and realize that I didn't have the ability to divide my attention the way I do now. If I was outside, I was outside—fully, completely. I wasn't wondering what was happening online. I wasn't thinking about what I should be doing. There was just... what was happening. The texture of bark under my hand. The taste of a specific apple from a specific tree. The particular quality of afternoon light.

We often frame growing up as gaining new abilities—and it is that. But it's also losing something. The capacity for simple, undivided attention. We trade it for abstract thinking, for the ability to plan and anticipate, for the consciousness of self that lets us imagine futures and pasts. These are valuable things. But maybe we didn't have to lose as much as we did.

I don't think you can ever fully go back. Consciousness, once fractured, doesn't easily return to wholeness. But I do think you can practice. You can choose, deliberately and repeatedly, to give your full attention to small things. Not as a exercise in mindfulness—I've never been able to sustain that kind of practice—but just as a choice. As a priority.

Notice the tree. Taste the coffee. Feel the texture of the sweater. Hear the actual words the person is saying instead of planning your response.

These feel like small things, almost trivial. And perhaps they are trivial. But maybe that's the point. Maybe the real action of living happens in these small moments of attention. Maybe that's where life actually is—not in the big narrative moments we're always anticipating, but in the texture of experience itself.

The tree doesn't care whether I look at it or not. It grows and stands and sheds its leaves and grows them again, indifferent to my observation. But I care. It changes something in me, the act of seeing. It makes the world feel less like a generic backdrop and more like a specific place, densely populated with particular things worthy of attention.

So that's what I've been thinking about. The gift of noticing. The strange power in paying attention. The way that boredom and disconnection might sometimes just be a failure of vision—a failure to really look at the impossible specificity of the world we live in.

The tree is still there. I'll probably walk past it a thousand more times. And I'll probably miss it most of those times. But now and then, I might actually see it. And that seems like enough.

# On the Strange Privilege of Being Uncertain

I want to write about uncertainty, because it's been on my mind lately—or rather, it's something I find myself returning to with a kind of fascination that feels almost involuntary. There's something curious about the modern world's relationship with not knowing. We've built systems, algorithms, and institutions all designed to minimize uncertainty, to replace the uncomfortable space of "I don't know" with confident predictions and definitive answers. And yet, despite all this infrastructure of certainty, uncertainty remains perhaps the most honest experience available to us.

When I think about uncertainty, I don't mean it in a negative sense. It's not simply about fear or the anxiety of not knowing what comes next. Rather, it's something closer to intellectual humility—the recognition that the world is genuinely complex, that our models of it are always incomplete, and that there's a kind of honesty in admitting the limits of what we can know.

Consider how much of life is spent pretending to certainties we don't actually possess. We're taught to speak with confidence, to project assurance, to avoid the appearance of doubt. A doctor who says "I'm not entirely sure" might inspire less confidence than one who speaks with authority, even if the uncertain doctor is being more honest. A politician who admits "we don't have all the answers" will likely lose the election to one who promises definitive solutions. Parents are supposed to seem like they know what they're doing, even in those moments at 3 AM when a child is sick and all the advice contradicts itself.

There's something I find both tragic and beautiful about this. Tragic because we lose access to collective wisdom that could come from honest acknowledgment of complexity. Beautiful because it speaks to something fundamentally human—our desire to provide comfort, stability, and guidance to others, even when we're uncertain ourselves.

I've noticed that some of the most interesting people I encounter seem to have made peace with uncertainty in a way that others haven't. They ask more questions. They're more curious. They don't rush to judgment. And paradoxically, they often seem more grounded, more capable, not less. It's as if admitting what you don't know somehow frees up mental space to actually learn things.

There's a concept from physics—the uncertainty principle—that I think has broader application. At the quantum level, you cannot simultaneously know both the exact position and the exact velocity of a particle. The more precisely you measure one, the less you know about the other. It's not a limitation of our instruments or our cleverness; it's written into the fabric of reality itself. I wonder if something similar applies to knowledge more broadly. The more we pretend to certain knowledge in one domain, the less we truly understand in another. The more our institutions commit to a single narrative, the more important truths we become blind to.

What would change if we took uncertainty seriously? Not in a paralyzed way, where nothing can be done without absolute certainty—that's impossible—but as a fundamental feature of how we approach problems. Scientific method, at its best, is already built on this principle. You make your best hypothesis, you test it, you accept that it might be wrong, and you remain open to evidence that contradicts you. But we rarely extend this intellectual humility beyond science. In politics, morality, relationships, personal identity, we tend to be much more dogmatic.

I think about the people who change their minds in meaningful ways. It's not usually because someone presented them with a single crushing argument. It's usually because they encountered something in their lived experience that didn't fit their model of reality. They noticed a contradiction. They asked a question they hadn't thought to ask before. They allowed themselves to be uncertain about something they thought they'd settled. And then, gradually, their thinking evolved.

There's also something valuable about uncertainty in the creative sense. All art exists in a state of uncertainty. When you're writing a story, painting a picture, composing music, you're genuinely unsure how it will turn out. You can't know in advance exactly what the work will become. Some of the best creative work happens in that space where you're following something you don't fully understand—a feeling, an image, a pattern—and allowing it to emerge. The moment you become too certain about what you're making, you often lose something essential.

I'm also thinking about uncertainty in relationships. We often want to be certain about other people—certain that we understand them, that we know what they'll do, that we've figured them out. But people are endlessly complicated and surprising. There's something perhaps more loving about accepting that you can never fully know another person, that they'll surprise you, that they remain, in some fundamental way, mysterious. This uncertainty could be paralyzing or it could be liberating. It could make us anxious or it could make us curious.

The question for me becomes: what does it mean to live well with uncertainty? Not to seek it out for its own sake, not to become paralyzed by it, but to accept it as a natural feature of existence and perhaps even to value it. To make decisions and commitments while holding our assumptions lightly. To build structures and systems while remaining aware that we might be wrong about fundamental things. To love people while accepting that we can never fully know them.

I suspect the answer has something to do with what I might call "committed tentativeness." You take action, you make choices, you build beliefs and systems and relationships—but you do so with the understanding that these are your best current efforts, subject to revision. You're willing to change course. You're curious about evidence that contradicts you. You don't demand absolute certainty before acting, but you also don't pretend to certainties you don't have.

This feels like the only honest way to live, actually. The world is uncertain. The future is uncertain. Other people are uncertain. Our own minds are uncertain to ourselves. Accepting this, rather than fighting it, might be the beginning of genuine wisdom.

# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the margins—in the spaces between the big moments we're supposedly supposed to be paying attention to. There's something almost subversive about noticing the small things. It feels like a quiet rebellion against the pressure to always be aiming somewhere, always becoming someone better, always moving forward toward the next checkpoint.

Last week I watched someone at a coffee shop stir their drink for what must have been thirty seconds, just round and round, staring at the coffee swirling. I wondered what they were thinking about. Were they lost in thought, or was stirring just something their hands needed to do while their mind was elsewhere? That moment probably meant nothing to them. They'll never think about it again. But I kept it, somehow. It's still with me.

I think this is what writers and artists mean when they talk about paying attention. Not the kind of attention that's strategic—noticing what will help you get ahead, what will make you more interesting or successful. But the kind that's almost useless. The kind that notices a particular way light falls across someone's face, or the specific rhythm of a stranger's footsteps, or how a particular word sounds funny if you say it five times in a row. The kind of attention that serves no purpose except to make you feel alive.

There's a peculiar comfort in this. In a world that constantly demands we be productive, optimized, always scaling, there's something radical about noticing things that have zero practical value. My observation of the coffee stirrer will never increase my productivity or help me achieve my goals. It won't make me money or improve my relationships or help me live longer. It's just there, a small strange gem I picked up and put in my mental pocket.

I wonder if this is why people keep journals, or take photographs of their breakfast, or write long emails about nothing in particular. We're trying to catch something. We're trying to preserve these moments that don't matter in any rational sense but matter desperately in some other way. We're trying to say: I was here, I noticed this, it was real.

The older I get, the more I understand that most of life is not the major events. It's not the graduation or the wedding or the promotion or the breakup. Those moments get the attention—they're underlined, bolded, marked as Important. But the texture of life, the actual substance of what it feels like to be alive, that's in the other stuff. It's in the Tuesday afternoon when nothing happens. It's in the conversation that wanders without getting anywhere. It's in the way someone laughs at a dumb joke. It's in the particular temperature of the light in winter.

I've also been thinking about how much we're trained not to notice. How we're encouraged to develop tunnel vision, to focus on goals and metrics and outcomes. How the culture of productivity and self-improvement almost necessarily requires us to treat most of experience as irrelevant background noise. You can't simultaneously be constantly optimizing yourself and be genuinely present with what's in front of you. Those two things are fundamentally incompatible.

Maybe that's why people complain about their lives feeling hollow, even when everything on paper looks good. Maybe it's because they haven't genuinely noticed anything in months. They've been too busy becoming the person they thought they needed to be to actually experience the life they're living.

I'm not saying we should all quit our jobs and become wandering monks of observation (though I admit the fantasy appeals to me). I'm just thinking about what happens if we give ourselves permission to notice more. What if noticing was enough? What if it was okay to sit with something beautiful or strange without immediately figuring out how to use it?

There's a Japanese concept called "ma"—the space between things. It's often translated as emptiness or void, but more accurately it refers to the meaningful space, the negative space that gives shape to positive space. I think that's what noticing is. It's the ability to see the ma in life, the spaces between events, the context that gives meaning to the foreground. And paradoxically, learning to see those spaces clearly might be the most meaningful thing we can do.

I read somewhere that the writer Ocean Vuong said something like: beauty is not a luxury, it's a necessity. And I think noticing is similar. The ability to pause and really look at something—really see it—that's not a luxury either. That's how we remember we're human. That's how we make meaning.

There's also something deeply connecting about noticing, I think. When I really observe another person, when I'm genuinely present with their existence, something shifts. The distance between self and other collapses a little bit. I can't hate someone I've really noticed. I can't dismiss them or treat them as invisible when I've actually seen them.

So maybe the project is this: to practice noticing. Not as a way to self-improve or become more interesting or more present (though maybe those would be side effects). But just as an end in itself. To collect small moments. To let your mind wander. To notice the coffee stirrer. To see the light. To hear the actual sound of your own breathing.

In a world that's increasingly virtual, abstract, removed from sensory reality, there's something almost revolutionary about insisting on paying attention to the actual texture of being alive. Not for a purpose. Not to get anywhere. Just to be more alive while you're alive.

That seems important, somehow. Even if I can't quite explain why.

# On the Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

There's something I've been thinking about lately—something that catches me off guard every time it happens, which is more often than you'd think. It's that moment when you realize you have absolutely no idea where you are, and instead of panic, something closer to delight floods through you.

I don't mean the dangerous kind of lost, the kind that ends with a frantic call to roadside assistance or your spouse giving you that particular look of resignation. I mean the gentle lost, the kind where you took a turn you weren't sure about, and now you're on a street you've never seen before, and your phone's battery is low enough that you're conserving it like it's a precious resource, and somehow that constraint feels liberating rather than limiting.

This happens to me most when I'm walking. There's something about walking that makes getting lost feel like discovery instead of failure. A car zooms you past everything in your rush to reach a predetermined destination. But walking—walking lets you notice. You notice the way light falls through an awning. You notice the smell of someone's dinner through an open window. You notice that there's a bookstore you never knew existed, or a park bench facing something worth facing, or that an alley has been transformed into a small garden by someone with more time or hope or both than most people seem to have.

I think we're supposed to feel ashamed of being lost. Our culture has built this entire infrastructure—maps, GPS, street signs, appointment apps—around the premise that we should always know where we are and where we're going. Uncertainty is inefficiency. Wandering is wasting time. The shortest distance between two points is a straight line, and we've become so obsessed with that line that we've forgotten to look at what exists just beyond it.

But there's a kind of wisdom in the lost moment, or maybe it's just honesty. When you're genuinely lost, you can't pretend to be somewhere you're not. You can't be going somewhere with purpose when you don't actually know the way. There's a vulnerability in it that's oddly clarifying. You have to admit: I don't know. I was wrong. I need to figure something out. These are not statements we make easily in normal life.

The pandemic did something to me—I suspect it did something to most of us—that made the idea of purposefulness feel more fragile. For months, we were all stripped of our destination. There was nowhere to go, nothing to do, no trajectory to maintain. It was terrible and strange and sometimes surprisingly peaceful. And afterward, when we emerged and got back to the business of going places and accomplishing things, I found I couldn't quite muster the same faith in the importance of always knowing exactly where I was headed.

This doesn't mean I've become irresponsible. I still show up to things. I still honor my commitments. But I've become suspicious of the assumption that being lost is something to be corrected as quickly as possible. Sometimes the correction takes longer than the detour.

There's a particular kind of person who plans everything down to the minute. I used to be more like this than I am now. I had systems. I had backup plans for my backup plans. And yes, that meant I rarely missed anything or disappointed anyone, but it also meant I was living according to a script I'd written in advance, and I missed the chance to be surprised by anything, including myself.

The novelist Anne Lamott has this concept about "shitty first drafts." The idea is that you have to write badly first to write well eventually. You have to be willing to make mistakes, to go places that don't end up in the final version, to waste time and energy on dead ends. The alternative is paralysis—waiting until you're perfect to begin, which means never beginning.

I think the same is true of life. We need more shitty first drafts. We need more wrong turns and strange detours and moments where we stop being the protagonist of our own movie and just become a person in the world, genuinely uncertain about what comes next.

There's also something about being lost that makes you more present. Your body is here, your attention is here, because you're actually paying attention to where you are rather than where you're supposed to be. You're looking at street names and storefronts and people. You're noticing. You're actually in your life instead of moving through it like you're driving somewhere on autopilot.

Some of my best days have happened because I was lost. A conversation with a stranger I met while asking for directions. A restaurant I found by accident and still think about years later. A street that had light in a particular way that made me understand something about beauty I hadn't grasped before. These weren't on the itinerary. They were bonuses, gifts, accidents.

I suppose what I'm really thinking about is the difference between existing and living. It's possible to exist while knowing exactly where you're going, while executing the plan, while staying on the mapped route. And it's possible to live while being utterly lost, while following a thread of curiosity into unknown streets, while being willing to not know what comes next.

Neither is wrong. We need both—we need the structure and the plans, the knowledge of where we're headed. But we also need the margin, the space off the map, the permission to be lost.

I don't know where this thought is headed, if I'm being honest. I started writing it knowing something was there but not quite what. And that's okay. That's maybe the whole point. Not everything needs a destination. Sometimes the walking is the point. Sometimes getting lost is how you find the thing you didn't know you were looking for.

# The Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that peculiar state we spend so much energy trying to escape. We treat it like a disease—something to be cured immediately with a notification, a video, a snack, anything to restore the stimulation we believe we're owed. But I wonder if we've misunderstood boredom entirely. What if it's not a failure state, but a feature?

When I was a kid, boredom felt infinite. A summer afternoon could stretch for years. My parents would send me outside with vague instructions to "go play," and I'd spend hours doing absolutely nothing remarkable. I'd lie in the grass watching clouds. I'd build complicated systems for organizing rocks. I'd sit by the window for no reason at all. There was no objective—no goal to achieve, no skill to master, no endpoint in sight. Just me, present, waiting for something to happen or, more often, waiting for nothing in particular.

The curious thing about those experiences is that they didn't feel empty. They felt full in a way I can barely access now. There was an aliveness to boredom, a kind of openness. My mind wasn't chasing anything. It wasn't performing or producing. It was just... available.

Modern life has made boredom seem obsolete. We've engineered it out of existence. Why be bored for five minutes in line at the grocery store when you can scroll through the infinite scroll? Why sit with restlessness when you can dispatch it instantly with entertainment? We've become very efficient at making boredom disappear. And in doing so, I suspect we've lost access to something important.

There's mounting evidence that understimulation is necessary for creativity. The brain, when given space to wander, makes novel connections. Ideas appear seemingly from nowhere because the unconscious mind is actually working—making associations, solving problems, generating possibilities—when the conscious mind is occupied with nothing. The shower thought, the solution that comes while driving, the creative breakthrough in the middle of the night: these emerge from a particular state of relaxed attention that's the opposite of focused productivity.

But I think the benefits of boredom go deeper than creative productivity. Boredom might be essential to knowing yourself.

When you're perpetually stimulated, you never have to face yourself. You never have to sit with your own thoughts, your own fears, your own smallness in the universe. There's always something demanding your attention—a notification, a video, a conversation thread. This constant external stimulation might be a form of escape more total than any drug. It's an escape from the fundamental human experience of existing as a small, uncertain creature in an incomprehensibly large world.

Boredom forces you to confront this. When nothing external is calling to you, you're left with your own mind. You notice things: the quality of your thoughts, the texture of your emotions, the things you're afraid of, the things you actually want (not the things you think you should want). You become conscious of your own consciousness, which is a strange and unavoidable experience.

I wonder if part of the epidemic of anxiety and depression in developed countries isn't actually caused by lack of stimulation but by lack of boredom—by the inability to be still enough to process our own existence. We're running so fast to escape ourselves that we never realize that's what we're doing.

There's also something to be said for boredom as a form of rebellion. When you choose boredom—when you sit and do nothing while the world screams at you to be productive, to optimize, to monetize every moment—you're making a quiet declaration. You're saying: I have intrinsic worth that doesn't depend on my output. My existence is valuable even when I'm not producing anything. I don't have to earn my place in the world through constant achievement and engagement.

This is radical in a culture built on productivity culture. We're told that we are what we do, that rest is laziness, that free time should be spent on "self-improvement." But what if the self doesn't need improvement? What if it just needs to exist?

The other thing I've noticed about boredom is that it teaches patience. In a world of instant gratification, patience has become an almost extinct virtue. But patience is what allows you to build real skills, develop deep relationships, see long-term projects through to completion. Patience is what separates shallow lives from meaningful ones. And boredom is where patience is born. It's the experience of time passing without immediate reward, and learning that this is survivable, even okay.

When you can sit with boredom for fifteen minutes without reaching for your phone, you've accomplished something. You've proven that you can tolerate the absence of stimulation. That you can be present without entertainment. That your mind won't collapse if it's left alone. This might sound simple, but it's increasingly rare.

I'm not arguing for a return to some imagined past. I'm not saying technology is evil or that we should all go live in cabins. But I do think we should reconsider our reflexive rush to eliminate boredom. Maybe we should schedule some. Maybe we should sit in a park for an hour with nothing to do. Maybe we should have dinner without checking our phones. Maybe we should sleep without the glow of a screen.

Not because it makes us more productive or creative (though it might), but because boredom might be where we actually become ourselves. It's where we find out what we think, what we feel, what we want. It's where we remember that we're alive and that life, despite its difficulties and uncertainties, has a basic texture to it that can be deeply satisfying if we're still enough to notice.

The gift of boredom is the gift of time to just exist. In a world that wants to consume every moment of our attention, this is a radical gift indeed.

# On the Quiet Art of Paying Attention

I've been thinking lately about how rarely we truly look at things. I don't mean glancing—that happens constantly, reflexive and automatic. I mean the kind of looking that requires you to actually stop, to let your eyes rest on something long enough that it begins to reveal itself to you in layers. The kind of attention that transforms the ordinary into something worth knowing.

It started when I watched someone sketch a coffee cup the other day. Not a fancy cup, just a ceramic mug sitting on a table. The sketcher spent what must have been twenty minutes on it—far longer than I would have imagined necessary. I expected them to finish in two or three minutes, just a quick outline. But they kept going, adjusting the curve of the handle, shading the interior darkness, considering the slight asymmetry of the rim. When they finally set down their pencil, I could see it. Not just a representation of a cup, but that cup, in all its particular existence. The drawing had caught something true about it.

This is what attention does. It doesn't transform things into something they're not—it reveals what was already there, waiting to be noticed.

We're living through an era that could be called the age of distraction, though that phrase has probably already been clichéd into uselessness. But it's true in ways both obvious and subtle. Yes, our phones ping constantly, demanding our focus, fragmenting our thoughts into smaller and smaller pieces. Yes, we're all half-present at dinner tables and conversations, part of our consciousness always elsewhere. But there's something deeper than that technological distraction, I think. There's a kind of cultural assumption that attention is an investment you make in things that matter—in big moments, important events, people you love. The everyday stuff gets the leftover scraps of our awareness.

What if that's backwards?

What if the capacity to pay attention to ordinary things is actually one of the most valuable and rare skills we can develop? Not in a practical sense—it won't help you advance your career or optimize your productivity. But in a human sense, in how it shapes the texture of your actual life.

I've noticed this in people who seem to move through the world differently. They're not necessarily happier (though sometimes they are), but they seem more present in their own existence. They notice the light hitting a wall at a particular time of day. They taste their food. They listen to what people are actually saying instead of thinking about their response. They see the people around them.

What strikes me is how much of their difference comes not from having better experiences, but from paying better attention to experiences they're already having.

There's something almost subversive about this, especially right now. In a world optimized for constant motion and upgrade and novelty, the decision to slow down and really look at what's in front of you feels like a small act of resistance. You could be doom-scrolling or shopping or working, but instead you're watching how the steam rises from a cup of tea. You're noticing how a friend's expression changes when they talk about something they care about. You're really tasting an apple instead of eating it while thinking about something else.

This is harder than it sounds, at least for me. My default mode is to be somewhere else mentally—replaying conversations, planning the future, following some thread of thought that's more interesting than the present moment. And the cultural machinery is designed to support this tendency. We're told to multitask, to optimize, to always be building toward the next thing. Sitting quietly with a cup of tea and really paying attention to how it tastes feels almost irresponsible by comparison.

But here's what I've been realizing: it might actually be one of the most responsible things you can do. Because attention is how you honor the reality of other people and things. It's how you resist reducing the world to your own internal narratives. It's how you live in the actual world instead of the one you're imagining.

There's an intimacy to real attention that's easy to miss. When you really look at someone—not staring in an uncomfortable way, but actually seeing them, noticing the particular architecture of their face, the way they move—something shifts. You can't hate people you've looked at carefully. You can't ignore them. You start to understand that they're as complex and real and full of inner life as you are, which is obvious in theory but revolutionary in practice.

The same goes for places and objects. Pay real attention to a tree and it stops being "a tree" and becomes a specific entity with its own particular way of existing in the world. Look closely at the patterns on a leaf. Notice the birds that visit it. See how it casts shadows. Suddenly you're in relationship with it in a way you weren't before.

I think this is what artists and poets are doing when they work—they're paying attention and then translating that attention into their medium so that others can see through their eyes. When a poem stops you mid-sentence with its rightness, that's because the poet looked carefully at something and found the exact words to make you look at it too. That's a gift.

We don't all need to be artists, but we could all be more attentive to our own lives. We could look more carefully at the people we love, the places we live, the small moments that make up days. We could taste our food. We could watch the sky change. We could listen to silence.

The strange thing is that this doesn't make life slower or quieter. It makes it bigger. There's more there than you realized. More complexity in a face you see every day. More variation in a street you walk down constantly. More depth in a person whose words you finally listen to completely.

I think about that sketcher again, spending all that time on one coffee cup. To someone rushing past, it would look like they were wasting time. But they were actually the opposite of wasteful. They were engaged in an act of profound respect—really seeing something, really knowing it. And in doing so, they'd created something that helped other people see it too.

Maybe that's the point. Not to accomplish more or be more productive, but to be more present in the one life we actually have. To pay attention to it. To let it be as full and complex and real as it actually is.

That's worth thinking about.
