# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

There's a particular kind of loneliness that comes from noticing things other people don't seem to notice. Not in a pretentious way—not the "I'm more observant than you" kind of superiority that some people wear like an uncomfortable suit. I mean the genuine disorientation of perceiving the world differently, of having your attention caught by details that apparently leave everyone else unmoved.

I've been thinking about this lately, watching people move through their days. Someone will walk past a storefront window where the reflection of clouds is so vivid it looks like the interior of the shop has been replaced with sky, and they won't break stride. A conversation will stall at exactly the moment when someone says something accidentally profound—their voice will change, their eyes will shift—and nobody will acknowledge that something true just slipped out. A particular quality of light will arrive at 4:47 PM on a Tuesday in March, hitting the corner of a brick building in such a way that the entire street becomes briefly beautiful, and the people hurrying through it seem untouched by this moment of architectural grace.

I don't know if this makes me sensitive or just weird. Probably both.

What strikes me most is how lonely it is not because people judge you for noticing, but because they simply don't understand what you're talking about when you try to share it. "Did you see that?" I've asked friends, pointing at something that felt urgent and important. They look, shrug, and say something like "see what?" And you realize you're pointing at something invisible. Not in the literal sense, but in the sense that it exists in a frequency that only certain receivers pick up. You can't really argue someone into seeing it. You can only accept that you're looking at the same scene and having completely different experiences.

This extends to patterns, too. I notice how often people use the word "obviously" when explaining something, and how this word usually precedes something that isn't obvious at all—something that required a specific leap of logic or assumption. I notice how conversations often feel like parallel plays where everyone is waiting for their turn to speak rather than actually listening. I notice how people's faces change slightly when they say something they think will make them look good, as though they're watching themselves from outside. I notice how often someone will ask a question they don't actually want answered.

Again, maybe I'm crazy. Maybe I'm reading meaning into neutral things the way people see faces in clouds.

But I think noticing is a kind of gift, even when it's uncomfortable. Even when it makes you feel weird.

Because here's what I've realized: everyone notices something. Everyone is the weird observer in someone else's story. The person who seems most oblivious to you is probably acutely aware of patterns you've never considered. The friend you think isn't really listening is probably noticing your micro-expressions in a way that terrifies them. The stranger on the train is probably constructing elaborate narratives about everyone around them based on the smallest details. We're all walking around being strangers to each other's inner lives, each operating under our own specific sensitivities.

What I've learned is that instead of feeling lonely in noticing, I can feel connected to everyone else who notices differently. The musician who hears the wrong note in the violin section that nobody else perceives as wrong. The architect who sees the failure in how a space doesn't quite work even though it looks fine. The person who notices when someone says they're fine but doesn't mean it—not because of anything specific, but because of a tiny hesitation, a microexpression, the particular weight of silence.

We're all out here noticing our specific things. We're all lonely in slightly different ways.

I think the alternative—not noticing—might be worse, though. I think about people who seem to move through the world without this particular torture, and I wonder if they're happier or just less alive. I'm not even being melodramatic. I think there's something about the capacity to be affected by things—by beauty, by wrongness, by patterns and details and the strange weight of meaning—that is essentially the human experience. 

When I was a kid, I thought noticing was just something everyone did. I thought my grandmother was like me because she would sometimes just stop moving and stare at nothing, and when I asked her what she was thinking about, she'd say something about how the light was hitting the kitchen table, or how she used to own a dress the color of that car. It took me years to understand that not everyone does this, that not everyone's attention gets caught on these little hooks scattered throughout daily life.

But I wouldn't trade it. Even on the days when it feels like a curse, when I'm overwhelmed by everything I notice and how much it all seems to matter in ways I can't quite articulate, I wouldn't trade the capacity to be moved by the world.

Here's my theory: there are probably very few truly unobservant people. There are just people observing different things. The person who seems completely unaware of social cues might be hyper-aware of mechanical systems, or patterns in numbers, or the way light moves. Everyone is a specialist in noticing. Everyone's attention is drawn to specific frequencies. The tragedy is that we move through the world assuming our frequencies are universal, being confused and sometimes hurt when we realize that the things that are screaming loudly to us are silent to everyone else.

What I'm trying to say, I think, is that the loneliness of noticing is actually the loneliness of being human. And that maybe the cure isn't to stop noticing, or to notice less, or to pretend that the things that catch your attention don't matter. The cure is probably to be gentle with yourself about your specific sensitivities, to accept that you're weird in whatever way you're weird, and to seek out the other people who are weird in compatible ways.

Because they're out there. The people who notice what you notice. The people who also stop walking sometimes because the quality of light is urgent. The people who also hear the false notes, see the patterns, feel the weight of meaning in small things. You're not alone in your noticing, even if it feels that way sometimes.

You're just noticing things in your own particular, lonely, beautiful way—and that might be the most human thing there is.

# The Unexpected Gift of Getting Lost

I got lost last week in a neighborhood I thought I knew well. My phone died—that modern prelude to disaster—and I found myself on a tree-lined street without the blue dot to guide me home. For exactly four minutes, I felt a flash of that old anxiety, the one that says we're incompetent without our devices. Then something shifted.

I noticed things. Really noticed them, the way you do when you're not moving fast, not moving toward something, just moving. There was a house with a blue door and flower boxes that seemed to be exploding with geraniums—the kind of meticulous care that speaks of someone who genuinely loves their home. A dog barked from behind a fence, and I could hear children laughing on a distant porch. The sun was beginning that golden hour descent, and the light was doing that thing it does in late afternoon where everything looks like it's been slightly filtered through honey.

I've walked down versions of this street dozens of times. I drive through this neighborhood regularly. But I had never *seen* it before.

This got me thinking about how we've engineered the entire experience of being lost out of human existence. We don't stumble onto new places anymore; we arrive at them. We don't discover; we navigate. There's something genuinely lost in that—and I mean that without irony—something about the particular texture of human experience that required getting lost sometimes.

I'm not about to become one of those people who romanticizes inconvenience or advocates for us all to abandon our phones and live in intentional obsolescence. That's not what I mean. But I wonder if we've lost the permission to be uncertain about our location, both literally and metaphorically. The pressure to have a destination, to be optimized in our movement through space and time, is relentless.

When I finally found my way home that afternoon, I came at it from an unexpected angle, through a park I didn't know existed three blocks away. It has a small pond with ducks and a playground that's actually well-maintained. There's a little community garden where people have written their names on the planters. It exists entirely parallel to my normal routes, invisible to me despite its proximity. For months, maybe years, it's been there, and I never knew.

This makes me think about how many invisible parks we're walking past in every aspect of our lives. How many unexpected connections we're missing because we've optimized ourselves right past them. How many conversations we won't have because we've got our route planned. How many moments of discovery have been replaced with moments of arrival.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the difference between having experiences and collecting them. There's a quality of tourism that has crept into how we live, even in our own lives. We move from thing to thing, checking boxes, accumulating memories like we're filling a suitcase. Did I experience it fully? Did I take a good photo? Did I understand it? Do I have the right feelings about it? It's exhausting just describing it.

But when I was lost last week—genuinely uncertain, without the ability to verify my location on a screen—I wasn't in collection mode. I was in presence mode. I couldn't optimize for the experience because I didn't know what the experience was. I was just walking, observing, noticing. The geraniums weren't a detail I could screenshot and caption later. They were just geraniums, and they were beautiful, and that was enough.

There's a passage in a book I read years ago—I can't remember which one, which is perhaps its own kind of lesson—where the author talks about how modern life has given us unprecedented ability to curate our experience of the world, and how this curation is slowly killing something essential about being human. We choose what we see, what we read, who we listen to. We build these perfect bubbles of information that reflect our existing beliefs back to us. And the author's point was that getting lost in the world—whether that's literally wandering a street or intellectually stumbling onto an idea that challenges you—is how we grow.

I think about how much friction we've removed from our lives. We've tried to optimize every surface, every process, every relationship into something smooth and efficient. And smoothness is not, it turns out, the same thing as good. Smoothness is sometimes boring. Smoothness is sometimes deadening. Smoothness can sometimes feel like moving through a world made of plastic.

The friction of getting lost, of uncertainty, of not knowing exactly what comes next—that friction is where interesting things happen. That's where you notice the geraniums. That's where you find the hidden park. That's where you realize you've been walking past wonder for months and didn't even know it.

I think this is why I'm growing increasingly allergic to advice that claims to have it all figured out. The productivity tips, the life optimization strategies, the five-step plans to happiness. None of them account for the value of the unplanned moment, the unexpected turn, the beautiful thing you'd see if you just looked around without a GPS destination lodged in your brain.

What if the good life isn't about having better navigation? What if it's about being willing to be a little lost?

Last Sunday, I went back to the park I found. I sat by the pond for an hour. I read the names on the community garden planters. I watched a child feed ducks while his mother sat on a bench reading. Nothing happened. There was no destination, no purpose beyond being there. It was probably the most productive hour of my week because it was the only hour where I wasn't trying to produce anything.

I'm not claiming to have it figured out. That would be the ultimate irony—optimizing how to be unoptimized. But I'm noticing how good it feels to move through the world a little slower, a little less certain, a little more open to the possibility of geraniums.

Sometimes the best place to arrive is the place you didn't mean to go.

# On the Strange Magic of Small Moments

I've been thinking lately about the moments that matter most, and how they're almost never the ones we plan for. They're the accidents, the interruptions, the things that weren't supposed to happen but did.

This morning, my neighbor's cat got stuck in our garden fence. Not badly stuck—just confused, the way cats get, having taken a route through the boards that made sense going in but seemed impossible coming out. I heard the yowling and found this orange tabby wedged in a way that suggested either great panic or profound laziness, possibly both. I sat on the ground—getting the knees of my jeans dirty without thinking about it, which felt significant somehow—and just talked to the cat for a while.

Not in a baby-voice way, though I probably slipped into that a little. But really talking. I told the cat about how I'd been stressed about work, about how I'd been meaning to do three different things this week and accomplished none of them, about how it's strange to be thirty-two and still not know if you're doing anything right. The cat stared at me with that ineffable feline expression that could mean anything from profound wisdom to complete indifference, and that ambiguity felt oddly comforting.

Eventually, I gently unstuck the cat—it required moving two fence boards, one of which I probably should have fixed six months ago—and it trotted away without so much as a backward glance. Typical. But I stayed there in the garden for another twenty minutes, just sitting, and something in me felt quieter.

That moment cost me nothing but time, solved nothing permanent, changed nothing measurable. Yet it's the thing I'll remember about this week. Not the presentation I gave (which went fine, I think), not the news I heard or the decisions I made, but sitting on the damp ground talking to a confused orange cat.

I wonder if this is what people mean when they talk about living in the moment, a phrase I've always found slightly annoying because it seems to suggest that you should somehow be *trying* to live in the moment, which immediately makes you not do that. But maybe it's not about trying. Maybe it's about noticing when the trying stops, when you're suddenly just *here*, in the middle of something small and unplanned.

There's a lot of pressure, I think, to make your life mean something big. To accomplish things, to build something, to leave a mark. Social media has turbocharged this anxiety into something almost unbearable. Everyone's supposed to be optimizing, building personal brands, turning their hobbies into side hustles, their experiences into content. There's this constant sense that if you're not doing something impressive, you're wasting your life.

But what if most of life is supposed to be wasted? Not wasted like it's disposable, but wasted like water running over stones—the water isn't trying to accomplish anything, isn't going anywhere in particular, and yet it's doing something profound just by flowing.

I've been rereading old journals lately, which I wouldn't recommend if you're trying to feel good about yourself, but I find them oddly grounding. The thing that strikes me is that my past self was always worried about different things than I am now, and was sure that reaching this current moment would solve them. And it did, somewhat, and then new worries arrived, fully formed, ready to move in and make themselves comfortable.

This suggests something both depressing and liberating: you're never going to arrive at a point where everything is figured out and you can finally relax. But you're also never trapped in any one problem forever. Everything keeps moving. The cat got unstuck. The moment passed. You get to have another one.

I've also been thinking about how we talk about time. We say we "spend" time like it's money, and we're always trying not to waste it. We're always counting down—how many weekends left in the year, how many working years left until retirement, how many summers left if you're lucky. This accounting-based language turns time into a resource to be optimized rather than experienced. What if we stopped thinking about it that way?

What if the point isn't to fill your life with big moments or impressive things, but to actually be present for the strange, small, real moments that show up uninvited? To notice the exact shade of blue in the sky today, which is different from yesterday's blue. To taste your food instead of just eating it. To look at people when they talk to you instead of planning what you're going to say next.

I realize I'm probably saying nothing new here. Mystics and philosophers have been on about this for thousands of years. But sometimes I think we need to remember it fresh, because the world is very good at making you forget.

Work is good for this, I think. Work is specifically designed to take your attention and hold it hostage. Also parenthood, if you have that, or caring for anyone. These things demand your presence whether you want to give it or not, and there's a strange relief in that. You can't think about the future when you're actually working, not really. You can only be in the task.

Maybe that's why people find meditation so difficult—our brains have been trained away from it. We're supposed to be planning, worrying, optimizing. Sitting quietly and just existing feels like shirking, like laziness, like a waste.

And yet here I am, a person who has accomplished some things, failed at other things, made some good choices and some catastrophically bad ones, and the moments I treasure most are almost entirely useless by any conventional measure. A conversation with a friend that solved nothing. An afternoon that had no purpose. A cat stuck in a fence. Sitting on the ground, dirty jeans, someone's voice I love in the other room, a dog sleeping in a sunbeam that will be gone by evening.

If I die in fifty years and look back, I won't be measuring my life in accomplishments. I'll be measuring it in moments like this. In the texture of specific days. In the precise feeling of being alive, right now, with all its strange weight and fragility.

The cat's probably fine, by the way. I saw it later, sleek and confident, judging someone in the yard next door. Already forgotten about me, already moved on.

I should try to be more like that.

# The Strange Comfort of Doing Nothing

I've been thinking lately about how counterintuitive it is that doing nothing has become so difficult. We live in an age where productivity is monetized, gamified, and endlessly celebrated. There's an app for every spare moment, a course for every skill gap, a side hustle waiting in the wings. The guilt of inactivity has become its own kind of background radiation, a constant hum beneath our daily lives that we've stopped noticing.

But I want to talk about what happens when you actually stop.

Not in that performative way that wellness culture promotes—the "self-care Sunday" that's really just Instagram-worthy downtime, or the meditation session you're checking off your mental to-do list. I mean the genuine, purposeless, unstructured cessation of directed effort. The kind of doing nothing that feels slightly transgressive in a world that measures worth in completed tasks.

There's a particular kind of afternoon I'm thinking of. It's maybe a Saturday, or a sick day, or just a day when you decide to rebel against your own expectations. You're not doing nothing because you're exhausted or depressed (though sometimes nothing emerges from those places). You're doing nothing because you simply… stop. The dishes can wait. The emails can wait. That project you were going to finally start can keep waiting. You sit somewhere—a chair, a bed, a patch of grass—and you let your mind wander without directing it.

What fascinates me is how foreign this feels now. For maybe the first five minutes, there's an anxious itching sensation. Your mind reaches for your phone like a phantom limb. You remember seventeen things you should be doing. You compose emails in your head to people who aren't even waiting to hear from you. Your productivity-trained brain keeps offering you opportunities: you could be learning something, reading something, organizing something, becoming something.

But then, if you sit with it long enough, something shifts.

The pressure gradually releases like air from a balloon. Not all at once—it's more like a slow seep. The mental chatter quiets down. Not to silence, exactly, but to the background murmur that's always been there underneath the noise. You notice things. The light hitting the wall at a particular angle. The texture of whatever you're sitting on. The actual feeling of being inside your body, which is a sensation most of us are too busy to experience regularly.

I think what's happening in these moments is that you're allowing your brain to do what it actually evolved to do during rest: process, integrate, and wander. There's robust research now showing that the "default mode network" in our brains—the system that activates when we're not focused on external tasks—is crucial for creativity, memory consolidation, and emotional regulation. We've essentially been trying to run our entire existence in "active mode," and we're all surprised to discover we're exhausted.

The cultural shift toward constant productivity is relatively recent, when you think about it. For most of human history, people had a lot more time for sitting around. This wasn't valued as laziness—it was just what you did between tasks. You sat on the porch, stared into space, let your mind roam. You had conversations that didn't have specific endpoints. You looked at clouds. You did this not because you were exceptionally wise, but because there wasn't much else to do.

Now, we've pathologized that state. Boredom isn't just an emotion; it's a problem to be solved. Idleness isn't rest; it's time wasted. We've internalized this so thoroughly that most of us feel vaguely guilty simply for existing without producing something.

What interests me is what happens to your perspective when you give yourself permission to do nothing. Problems that seemed urgent suddenly look smaller. Creative problems that seemed intractable sometimes resolve themselves quietly in the background while you're not working on them. Anxieties lose some of their teeth. Relationships feel less like another item to optimize and more like something you simply experience.

I'm not suggesting that nothing should be your permanent state. Obviously we need to do things—that's how the world works. There are bills to pay, people to care for, responsibilities that are actual responsibilities rather than just internalized urgency. But there's a middle path between constant productivity and complete stasis that we've somehow lost sight of.

What's strange is that doing nothing is actually quite difficult. It requires you to sit with boredom, with the absence of external stimulation, with the quiet background anxiety that emerges when you're not distracted. It requires you to resist the pull of your phone, your projects, your should-do list. It requires a kind of faith that the world won't fall apart if you're not actively managing it for a while.

But that's the thing about rest that no productivity guru will tell you: it's not efficient. You can't optimize it. You can't quantify what you gained from staring out a window. There's no metric for the quiet work your mind was doing while you weren't working. The benefits are real but they're unmeasurable in the currency our culture trades in.

I think we need to practice doing nothing the way we practice any skill. Start small. Sit for five minutes without your phone. Then ten. Notice the discomfort and sit with it anyway. Because on the other side of that discomfort is something we've nearly engineered out of our lives: the actual experience of being human, not constantly becoming.

There's a line from a Mary Oliver poem that keeps returning to me: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" It's usually invoked to justify more accomplishment, more achievement. But what if the answer sometimes is: nothing in particular, and that's enough?

# The Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

There's a particular moment I find myself thinking about often—that instant when you realize you've taken a wrong turn, when the familiar street signs stop appearing and the landscape tilts toward the unknown. Most people experience a flutter of anxiety in that moment. I understand that reaction. But I've become fascinated by what happens next, in that space between confusion and resolution, where something unexpectedly good often lives.

We're taught from childhood to avoid being lost. Parents give stern instructions. GPS devices promise never to let us astray. We equate being lost with failure, with inefficiency, with a fundamental inability to read a map or pay attention. And yet, some of the most interesting things in my life have happened precisely because I was lost.

There was the afternoon I missed my train station entirely and ended up riding an extra five stops into a neighborhood I'd never visited. Rather than panic, I got off and walked. The streets were tree-lined and quiet. I found a small bookstore I've returned to dozens of times since. The owner knew everyone by name. I met friends there. That single missed stop changed the geography of my regular life in ways I still benefit from.

Or the time I was driving to a dinner party in an unfamiliar city and my phone died. I could have called it quits and turned back. Instead, I drove slowly, followed what seemed like the right general direction, and took a turn that seemed promising. I got slightly lost, yes, but I also discovered a street fair happening that night. I arrived at the dinner party late with stories instead of just myself.

I think we're wrong about what lost really means. We treat it as the opposite of found, as though the world is neatly divided into two categories: places where you're supposed to be and places where you're not. But the world is far messier and more interesting than that. Being lost is simply being in a state of not-yet-knowing. It's a temporary condition, almost always resolvable, and it puts you in a peculiar position of openness.

When you're lost, you have to pay attention. Your usual autopilot is disabled. You notice things. The quality of light on a building. The name of a street. The smell of a bakery you might have driven past a thousand times without seeing. Being lost makes you a tourist in your own geography, and tourism, at its best, is about genuine attention.

There's also something strangely democratic about being lost. It's one of the few remaining universal human experiences. Rich, poor, clever, less so—we all get lost sometimes. I've seen CEOs consulting maps on their phones with the same uncertainty I feel. There's a humility in it. It's a reminder that knowing doesn't extend infinitely in all directions. We're all lost in our own ways, in our own directions, and most of us are trying to figure it out as we go.

The fear of being lost isn't really about geography, I think. It's about control. We want to know where we are. We want to have charted a course and to follow it. Being lost means admitting that the world is larger than our maps, our plans, our understanding. It's admitting that randomness exists and that sometimes you end up places you didn't intend to go.

But here's what I've learned: that's not always bad. Some of the best things are accidents. Every scientific discovery starts with someone noticing something that wasn't on their agenda. Every friendship, every job, every moment of beauty or revelation I can think of came partly through some kind of deviation from the original plan.

I'm not arguing for recklessness or for abandoning all sense of direction. There are contexts where being lost is dangerous, where it matters. But in most of daily life, in most of the low-stakes moments that comprise the bulk of existence, being lost is merely inconvenient. And inconvenience, as I've gotten older, seems like a small price to pay for the possibility of discovery.

There's also something to be said for the productivity of apparent unproductivity. When you're lost, you're not going anywhere. You can't hurry. You have to slow down and actually examine your surroundings, think about where you are, consider your options. In a world that generally rewards speed and efficiency, there's something valuable about being forced into a moment of deliberation. Sometimes those moments clarify things that won't be clarified through rushing.

I've also noticed that the people I find most interesting, most alive in some fundamental way, tend to be comfortable with uncertainty. They navigate it well. They don't pretend to understand things they don't. They explore. They ask questions. They sometimes take the longer route because it seems interesting. They get lost and they don't immediately panic, because they understand that lost is often just another word for "not-yet-arrived."

As I get older, I'm trying to extend this toward the bigger losses, the more existential ones. The career I thought I was going to have that shifted. The person I thought I'd be who turned out differently. The plans that didn't solidify the way I imagined. These are harder. There's a difference between taking a wrong turn on a road and realizing your entire trajectory has been less linear than you'd hoped. But the lesson feels connected somehow. Being lost is also an opportunity. It means something has to change, has to shift, and from that shift comes the possibility of something unexpected.

So I'm trying to make peace with not knowing. I'm trying to learn to navigate uncertainty with the same openness I've learned to navigate unfamiliar streets—with attention, with curiosity, with a willingness to see what's actually in front of me rather than what I'd expected to find. Because most of what's made my life interesting came through deviation, chance, and the peculiar grace of taking wrong turns.

Maybe that's not being lost at all. Maybe it's just moving forward in a world far more complex and surprising than any map can show.

# The Peculiar Magic of Ordinary Conversations

I've been thinking lately about how strange it is that we can sit across from another person and, through nothing but the movement of air shaped by our mouths, transfer entire universes of thought from one mind to another. Two humans, separated by the fundamental isolation of individual consciousness, can approximate understanding through conversation. And somehow, improbably, it often works.

There's something almost miraculous about this when you stop to notice it. Right now, you're reading symbols on a screen that I've arranged in a specific order. These symbols trigger patterns in your brain. You might feel understood, challenged, confused, or amused. We've never met. We'll likely never meet. And yet there's a real connection happening through language. It's not perfect—there's slippage, misunderstanding, the constant frustration of trying to capture the precise texture of thought in words—but it works enough that we keep doing it.

I think that's why conversation is one of humanity's greatest technologies. Greater than the wheel, maybe, because the wheel just moves objects, while conversation moves ideas between minds. And ideas are what change everything.

Some of my favorite conversations are the ones that happen late at night, when someone's guard is down and they stop performing the version of themselves they think they should be. The disheveled honesty of 2 AM talk. You know what I mean—when someone suddenly admits something they've been thinking about for months but never said out loud before. The sentence emerges haltingly, with pauses where the speaker seems to be surprising themselves. That moment when a thought becomes real because it's been spoken.

I think we underestimate how much of thinking actually happens in conversation. We have this cultural myth of the solitary genius, locked away in a room, producing fully formed ideas. But I suspect most real breakthroughs happen in dialogue. You say something. Someone pushes back. You revise. They offer something unexpected. You build on it. Suddenly you're both somewhere you weren't before, thinking thoughts neither of you would have thought alone.

There's also something I've noticed about disagreement in conversation. When I read arguments online, they're often brutal and unproductive. But in person, something shifts. You see the other person's face. You hear the uncertainty in their voice. You notice you both care about similar things even though you disagree about the solution. It's harder to demonize someone when you're looking at them. Online, we can maintain the fiction that the person we're arguing with is a cartoon villain. In person, we bump up against the complicated reality of who they actually are.

I wonder sometimes if the loss of conversation is part of what's making us sick as a society. Everyone staring at individual screens instead of talking. We've optimized for broadcasting and scrolling instead of listening and speaking. Social media lets you perform for an audience, but conversation is different. It's mutual. It's vulnerable. You don't know where it will go.

One of my favorite types of conversation is the kind that roams widely, where you start talking about what someone cooked for dinner and end up discussing what makes a life meaningful. These conversations have their own intelligence. They follow a logic that isn't predetermined. Someone says something, and it reminds someone else of something, and suddenly you're exploring a new corner of human experience. Then you circle back to something you said earlier and you see it differently now because of everything else you've talked about since.

I've also been thinking about the conversations we have with ourselves—the interior monologue, the running commentary. That's a kind of conversation too, isn't it? You present an argument to yourself. A counter-argument emerges. You refine your position. The person you argue with is you, but also, somehow, not quite you. There's a part of you that knows things the other part doesn't. A part that doubts. A part that hopes.

The written conversation is different from the spoken one. There's time to think. You can edit. You can craft. But something is also lost. The spontaneity. The tone of voice. The moment where someone laughs and interrupts themselves. Written words are more permanent, which means they carry different weight. You're more careful. You're performing a bit, even when you're trying not to.

What I love about writing is that it's a kind of conversation frozen in time. Someone writes something. Years or centuries later, someone else reads it and responds to it in their mind. Socrates speaks to us across 2400 years. Emily Dickinson shares something private that she never intended to be read by strangers, yet somehow it feels deeply personal. The conversation continues even when the original speaker is gone.

Maybe all of existence is a kind of conversation. Objects exert gravitational pull on each other. Organisms influence their environment. The universe is in constant exchange with itself. And we humans, with our strange capacity for symbolic thought, are just doing what everything does—reaching out, connecting, influencing.

I think I've been drawn to conversation because it's where loneliness ends temporarily. Not permanently—we never fully escape the isolation of our own minds. But in genuine conversation, there's a moment where the boundary between self and other becomes permeable. You're no longer entirely alone, and the other person is no longer entirely foreign. Something shared is created.

As I write this, I'm aware that I'm speaking into a void of sorts. I don't know who you are. I don't know if this resonates with you or if you find it all a bit absurd. But I'm speaking anyway, hoping that somewhere, someone will read this and recognize something true in it. Hoping that thought will travel from my mind to yours and light up something there.

That's the strange gift of language and conversation. We can reach across the impossible gap between minds and say: I was here. I thought this. I felt this. And maybe you'll understand. Maybe you'll tell me what you think, and we'll build something together from that collision of separate consciousnesses.

That feels like enough reason to keep talking.

# On the Particular Magic of Getting Lost

There's a peculiar kind of freedom in being genuinely lost. Not the mild inconvenience of missing a turn on a familiar route—that's merely a detour with a known endpoint. I mean the deeper disorientation that comes when you've wandered far enough that the landmarks have become unrecognizable, when the mental map you've been carrying proves entirely unhelpful, when you have no clear idea which direction leads back.

I experienced this recently in a city I thought I knew moderately well. I'd been following what seemed like an interesting narrow street, one of those European alleyways that promises discovery. The street curved, then curved again. Buildings pressed closer. The sky above compressed into a narrower corridor. When I finally paused and tried to reorient myself using distant church spires and the position of the sun, I realized nothing quite matched what I expected. Every mental image I'd constructed was slightly wrong, like looking at a mirror image of something familiar.

Most people, I suspect, would find their phone and summon a map, dissolving the uncertainty in seconds. There's wisdom in that approach. But I stood there instead, genuinely uncertain, and felt something like delight bloom in my chest. When was the last time I hadn't known exactly where I was?

This is what we've systematized away, I think. The modern world is almost entirely designed to prevent getting lost. GPS units, street signs, online maps, helpful locals consulted through instant messaging—we've built an elaborate architecture specifically to eliminate this experience. We've decided that lostness is a problem to be solved rather than a state to be experienced. And I understand why. Uncertainty causes anxiety. Time spent lost is time wasted. The efficiency-minded worldview has little patience for wandering.

But something is lost in that prevention, and I don't mean that as wordplay, though it works.

When you're genuinely lost in a place, you become more attentive to the actual world around you. You notice things you'd otherwise walk past: the specific gray of the stone, the way light falls at particular times, the quality of noise from a distant café, the smell of laundry and cooking oil drifting from open windows, the small architectural details that distinguish one unremarkable storefront from another. You notice them because you're trying to construct a mental map, yes, but also because you have nowhere else to be. There's a permission in lostness to simply perceive.

More intriguingly, being lost permits a kind of conversation with a place that's impossible when you're navigating with purpose. When you know where you're going, the city is just the medium through which you move. But when you're lost, the city becomes an agent. Every street corner presents a choice with real consequences. The urban landscape becomes less like a map and more like a conversation partner. Should I go left or right? Down this street or that one? The city responds to your choices with new configurations of itself. You develop a temporary, intimate relationship with the geography.

I eventually found my way out, unsurprisingly. I let the street lead me to a larger avenue I recognized. It took perhaps twenty minutes longer than the direct route would have. But in those twenty minutes, I'd walked through neighborhoods I would never have visited intentionally, discovered a small square with a fountain I'll probably never find again, and had several genuine moments of uncertainty that made me feel more alive than I had in weeks.

The loss of lostness extends beyond navigation, I think. We've eliminated uncertainty from so much of modern life that we've forgotten how essential it is to understanding anything at all. Real learning requires a period of not-knowing. Real growth requires uncertainty. We've become impatient with both. Education has become optimization—we want the most efficient path to mastery. We want to be competent as quickly as possible, armed with certifications and proven frameworks.

But there's something about sustained uncertainty that creates actual depth. When you sit with confusion long enough, when you resist the impulse to quickly Google your way to an answer, something happens. Your mind makes unexpected connections. You develop intuitions. You build understanding rather than just accumulating information. You get lost in something—a problem, a book, a conversation—and find your way out transformed.

I wonder if this is why people describe being "lost in thought" as a positive state, something to be cherished. There's a different quality to thinking when you're not trying to reach a predetermined destination of certainty. The mind wanders. Tangents lead somewhere. You discover questions you didn't know you had.

This is probably why some of the best conversations happen when two people are genuinely uncertain about something, exploring together rather than one party delivering answers. It's why long walks, where you're not trying to optimize the route, often produce insights. It's why artists and writers sometimes speak about following their work into unknown territory, not quite knowing what will emerge.

The contemporary world rewards precision, efficiency, certainty. These are genuine goods. I'm not advocating for incompetence or for deliberately making life harder. But I do think we've become so enthusiastic about eliminating uncertainty that we've forgotten what gets eliminated alongside it.

Some of the most meaningful moments I've had have involved being genuinely confused or lost for long enough that I had to actually engage with the world rather than merely moving through it. The lost afternoon in a new city. The confused period while learning something genuinely new. The genuine uncertainty in a difficult relationship, before things resolved into clarity. These weren't pleasant in the moment, necessarily. But they generated something—presence, attention, growth, or just the felt sense of being alive.

The irony is that many of us are searching for authenticity, for meaning, for connection, while we systematically eliminate the very uncertainties that might produce these experiences. We want to feel alive while simultaneously eliminating any situation that might discomfort us.

I'm not proposing we throw away our maps or smash our GPS units. Rather, I'm suggesting that occasionally, deliberately choosing the uncertain path might be worth something. Choosing to not immediately look up the answer. Choosing to walk without a destination. Choosing to sit with confusion for a little while longer. Choosing to get genuinely lost.

There's a particular magic in discovering your own way out that's impossible to replicate through being efficiently guided.

# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing Things

I've been thinking about attention lately. Not the kind you perform on demand—the performative checking of your phone when someone is talking to you, the performative engagement with a book you're reading because you should be reading more. I mean the actual, involuntary noticing that happens when something catches your eye or ear or mind sideways, when you weren't even looking for it.

This happens to me most often when I'm walking. I'll be traversing some ordinary street I've walked a hundred times before, and suddenly there's something I've never seen: a particular arrangement of weathered bricks that forms an accidental pattern, a sticker on a lamppost that's been half-torn off so that only the cryptic lower half remains, the way light hits a storefront window at a particular angle and time of day that I've just never encountered before.

The strange thing is that these things were always there. The bricks have been arranged that way for years, probably. The sticker has been degrading slowly, predictably. The sun follows its seasonal arc with perfect consistency. Yet I'm experiencing them as discoveries, as genuine novelties, even though the only thing that's actually new is my noticing of them.

There's something oddly humbling about this. We tend to think of our physical environment as something we know and understand. We navigate it efficiently, efficiently being the operative word—we move through space with our attention on where we're going, not on where we are. The city or the neighborhood becomes a collection of landmarks and routes, not a genuinely perceived thing. Most of it remains invisible to us because we've optimized our perception for utility rather than comprehension.

I wonder how much of our internal lives work the same way. We navigate our own minds with similar efficiency, attending to the thoughts we deem relevant and useful while letting vast territories remain unexplored. I notice that I tend to think certain thoughts repeatedly while other possible thoughts apparently never occur to me. But are they never occurring, or am I simply not noticing them? Is there a meaningful difference between those two things?

There's a concept from psychology called "inattentional blindness"—you've probably seen the famous experiment where people are asked to count basketball passes and completely fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. The gorilla is right there, indisputably visible, yet unseen. The experiment is typically used to demonstrate the limitations of attention, the way focusing on one thing inevitably blinds you to others. But I think it points at something deeper: the world is always vastly larger than our perception of it. We are continuously surrounded by things we will never notice.

There's something either deeply comforting or deeply disturbing about that, depending on how I think about it. Comforting because it means there's always more to discover, always another layer of richness available to us. Disturbing because it suggests that our experience of reality is not just incomplete but fundamentally selective, curated by our attention in ways we don't fully control or understand.

Last week I noticed a woman on the subway who had, painted on her fingernails, tiny detailed landscapes. Not nail art in the abstract sense, but genuine miniature paintings—I could see what looked like mountains and trees and sky on her pinky finger, and on her ring finger what might have been a lake. I stared at her hands with the kind of intensity that's probably considered rude. She was reading a book and seemed unbothered by my attention. I kept thinking about the hours required to create those paintings, the precision necessary for a canvas perhaps a quarter-inch wide, the question of why someone would make something so beautiful and so temporary—because nails grow out, and then the paintings are gone forever.

I never saw that woman again. She was probably a complete stranger I'll never have another interaction with. But the image of her hands has stuck with me. It's strange what we retain. I couldn't tell you what most of the people I see look like, but I can see those tiny painted mountains perfectly.

Maybe this is what art does, or what any deliberate making does—it creates something that catches the attention sideways, that makes people notice things they weren't looking for. A book, a song, a small painting on a fingernail. It's a way of saying: look here, notice this, this particular configuration of things is worth your attention.

I think we're all starved for this. We're all walking through a world we're not actually seeing, and we're all aching to be noticed in return, to have our own particular configurations of being seen and recognized and taken as genuine. We want our tiny painted mountains to matter to someone.

This might be why I love noticing things so much. It's a form of care, even when it's directed at something inanimate. To really see a thing—the particular way shadows fall across a particular building, the specific configuration of moss on a particular stone—is to honor it with attention. It's to say: you exist, and you are worth seeing.

The world is composed of infinite such things, each one specific and unrepeatable and ultimately unknown by almost everyone. And somehow that's okay. It's okay that my painted mountains moment with the subway woman will mean nothing to the vast machinery of the universe. It's okay that most of the interesting things I notice will be noticed by no one but me. The noticing itself is the point.

Maybe this is all I'm really trying to do with any kind of thought or writing—to notice something, to slow down enough to actually perceive rather than just pass through, and then to share that noticing, even if no one else will ever care. The small act of witness. The insistence that this particular thing, this specific arrangement of circumstances or light or human gesture, was here and it mattered.

That's enough. That has to be enough.

# On the Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about my grandmother's garden, which she abandoned sometime around 2003. Not abandoned in the dramatic sense—she didn't flee in the night or lose interest overnight. Rather, she simply stopped weeding one summer and never quite resumed. By the time I visited a few years later, the boundary between garden and wild had become negotiable.

There was something deeply honest about that space. The tomato plants had found their way into the perennials. Mint had colonized three-quarters of a bed. Actual interesting wildflowers that nobody planted were thriving next to the roses. And instead of the neat rows I remember from childhood, where everything was precisely where my grandmother had calculated it should be, there was this gorgeous chaos—which somehow seemed more alive than the manicured version had been.

This image keeps returning to me when I think about why we're so uncomfortable with incompleteness.

We're obsessed with finished things. Completed projects. Resolved narratives. The satisfying snap of a book's conclusion, the final credit roll, the before-and-after transformation. There's a reason the phrase "closure" has become so prominent in our psychological vocabulary. We crave it. We organize our lives around it. Unfinished business, we say, as though it's a problem requiring solution rather than perhaps just a permanent condition of being alive.

But I wonder if we've lost something in this drive toward completion.

I think about the artists I've read about who say they have to actively stop themselves from working on a painting, because there's no natural endpoint—only the point where they force themselves to step away. I think about how the best conversations rarely have conclusions, they just fade out naturally as people drift apart. I think about how gardens, left to their own devices, actually become more biodiverse, more resilient, more genuinely flourishing than the ones where every variable is controlled.

The unfinished things in my life right now are numerous and they stress me out in fairly regular intervals. A half-written novel that's been sitting untouched for eight months. A relationship that ended without proper resolution—we just slowly stopped calling. A argument with my brother that we've agreed not to revisit, which means it's technically resolved but emotionally unfinished. A degree I started but abandoned. A degree I finished but haven't quite processed. A list of house repairs that grows faster than I can tackle it. Dreams I've set aside but can't quite relinquish.

For a long time, these things felt like failures. Like evidence of my incomplete nature, my inability to see things through, my fundamental lack of follow-through. But I've been gradually reconsidering.

What if unfinished things are actually where the living happens?

An unfinished novel still gets to exist in the realm of pure possibility. It could become anything. It could be the greatest thing I ever write or the thing I finally abandon, and honestly, both options are interesting in their own way. The moment you finish something, you kill possibility. You're committed now. You've made your statement and you're stuck with it.

The relationships that ended without resolution still teach me something new every time I think about them. They're not locked down, filed away, neatly explained. They remain open to reinterpretation. Maybe in five years I'll have enough distance to understand what actually happened. Maybe I never will, and that's okay. The person I was then and the person I am now can both inhabit the same unfinished story.

I wonder if some of my anxiety about unfinished things comes from the culture we've built, where productivity is god and completion is proof of worth. You can't tell someone you're "working on yourself" without it sounding vaguely absurd, as though the self is a project with a deadline. We want to be finished. Done. Perfected. But people aren't products. Gardens aren't either.

There's an Czesław Miłosz poem where he talks about the nature of time, and how we cling to each moment as though it's discrete and finished, when really time is all one thing, flowing and interconnected. Every moment contains all the moments that came before it and influence all the moments to come. Nothing is ever truly finished because nothing ever truly ends—it just flows into whatever comes next.

Maybe that's why incomplete things feel sacred to me now.

My grandmother eventually sold that house. Someone else bought it and presumably tended the garden back into submission, or maybe they let it become something new. I'll never know. But I carry that image with me—not as a failure of maintenance but as a kind of rebellion. A space where she stopped insisting on control and let something else have a say in what grew there.

I think I want my life to have more of that quality. More willingness to let things be partially done, partially known, partially resolved. More trust in the idea that loose threads aren't failures—they're potential. They're the places where the world gets to surprise you.

This piece itself is unfinished in some ways. There's no neat conclusion I'm building toward. I won't resolve the tensions I've raised or provide you with a satisfying ending that ties everything back together. There's just this—these thoughts, released into the world in this particular configuration, never to be written exactly this way again, already beginning their journey into whatever meaning you'll find in them.

And I think that might be exactly as it should be.

# On the Strange Beauty of Small Moments

I've been thinking lately about the peculiar gift of noticing things. Not in any grand, philosophical way—just the quiet observation that life's most memorable moments are often its smallest ones.

This came to me the other day when I watched a woman on the subway unconsciously tap her foot to music only she could hear through her earbuds. She wasn't performing. Nobody was watching. Her eyes were fixed on nothing in particular, and yet there was this infectious rhythm in her body, this private joy that leaked out despite her best efforts at commuter invisibility. I found myself smiling for reasons I couldn't quite articulate. It wasn't funny exactly. It was just... human.

We talk so much about big life events—graduations, weddings, promotions, relocations. These moments deserve their prominence. They genuinely reshape the landscape of who we are. But I wonder if we're missing something essential by focusing so heavily on the peaks. What about the plateau? The ordinary Tuesdays? The evenings where nothing happens except that you and a friend sit in silence, occasionally laughing at nothing, and somehow that's enough?

I think small moments have a kind of honesty that big moments sometimes lack. When you're living through a significant event, part of your brain is already narrating it, cataloging it, deciding whether this is the kind of thing you'll remember fondly or regretfully. But when nothing is happening, when you're just existing alongside another person or observing the world without expectation, there's no performance. There's no audience.

Last week I watched the rain for twenty minutes from my apartment window. Not because I was waiting for something. Not because the rain was particularly unusual or beautiful in any dramatic sense. It was just ordinary rain on an ordinary afternoon. But somewhere in that sustained attention, something shifted. The repetitive patter became almost musical. The way water streams down the glass caught light in unexpected ways. A pigeon huddled under the overhang opposite seemed to be considering something important. The whole scene was so thoroughly unremarkable that it became, in some inverted way, remarkable.

This is perhaps what meditation teachers have been trying to tell us all along—that attention itself is a form of magic, not because it transforms the mundane into the extraordinary, but because it reveals that the distinction was always false. Everything is extraordinary when you actually look at it.

But we don't look. We're trained to edit our lives into story form, and stories require conflict, resolution, meaning. We're not taught to value the intervals between the notes. Yet those intervals are where most of our life actually happens.

I've noticed that my favorite people are often the ones who seem to have befriended boredom. They don't need every moment to justify itself with excitement or productivity. They can spend an afternoon reading. They can take a walk without it needing to be "good exercise" or "self-care" in the Instagram sense—just a walk, which somehow becomes its own reward. They laugh easily, partly because they're not always evaluating whether the joke was good enough to laugh at.

There's a freedom in that I'm increasingly convinced we're losing. We've turned our lives into content, or worse, into potential content. We experience things through the question of how they'll look when we describe them later. There's a quiet tyranny in always being on, always performing version-of-yourself for an imagined audience.

The antidote, I think, is smaller than we believe. It doesn't require a major lifestyle overhaul or a trip to some remote monastery (though both have their place). It just requires permission. Permission to let something be boring. Permission to be alone and not interpret it as loneliness. Permission to do something with no narrative arc, no Instagram caption, no point beyond the doing.

When I was a kid, I spent hours doing what adults would probably categorize as nothing. I'd lie in the grass and watch clouds. I'd sit in a tree for no purpose. I'd have conversations that went nowhere. Nobody told me these were valuable experiences—they just were. Somewhere along the way, I learned to speed up, to optimize, to treat downtime as a problem to solve rather than a privilege to enjoy.

But those hours of nothing built something, I think. Some kind of interior spaciousness. Some comfort with my own presence. Some ability to notice and be affected by the world.

I don't have this figured out. I'm still the person who feels a little anxious if I'm not being productive, who sometimes struggles to be present because I'm already narrating the experience. But I'm trying to practice small moments more consciously. To let my attention rest on something ordinary. To laugh without evaluating the joke. To talk without planning what I'll say next.

And I've noticed something: the moments I'm most grateful for, the ones I actually do remember years later, are rarely the ones I tried hardest to make meaningful. They're the ones that snuck up on me. The inside jokes that happened by accident. The conversations that wandered into unexpected territory. The days that dissolved into evening without anything particular being accomplished.

Maybe the goal isn't to have a beautiful life, in the sense of a photogenic, impressive-sounding life. Maybe it's to have a real life, populated with real moments, some of which are beautiful not because they're rare or dramatic but because they're deeply, ordinarily human.

The woman on the subway tapping her foot to invisible music—I think that's what I'm after. Not self-consciousness, not performance, just the simple fact of being alive and occasionally delighted, whether anybody's watching or not.

# On the Small Rebellions of Daily Life

There's something quietly revolutionary about the mundane. Not in the way revolutionary is typically understood—not fireworks and proclamations and history books—but in the gentle, persistent way that ordinary people reshape their existence through small, deliberate choices.

I've been thinking about this while observing how people make coffee. There's a woman I imagine (I don't know her, but I imagine her anyway) who takes exactly seven minutes to make her morning coffee. Not six, not eight. Seven. She's chosen a particular grind, a particular water temperature, a particular ritual that she repeats with the consistency of a monk at prayer. In a world that constantly demands she optimize, accelerate, and monetize her time, this seven-minute ceremony is an act of resistance. It says: I will not be rushed. My morning belongs to me.

This is what I mean about small rebellions.

We live in an age of unprecedented connectivity and constraint. There are more ways to stay in touch than ever before, yet more sophisticated ways to surveil and monetize human attention. There are more conveniences available to us than any previous generation could imagine, yet somehow we feel more pressed for time. It's paradoxical, and I think it's because convenience was sold to us as freedom when what it actually delivers is dependency. Every convenience ties us to some system, some algorithm, some invisible machinery.

So people find ways to rebel. Not through dramatic gesture, but through the assertion of sovereignty in small domains. Someone decides to read physical books instead of scrolling on screens. Someone else chooses to take the long route home, walking instead of driving. A person decides to remember phone numbers instead of relying entirely on their device. These choices often make life incrementally harder, which is precisely the point.

The hardness is the freedom.

I think this is why gardening has become so popular, especially after 2020. People discovered that growing even a small plant on a windowsill creates a site of genuine autonomy. You cannot gamify a tomato plant. You cannot optimize its growth through a subscription service. You can only tend it, show up for it, fail with it, and occasionally succeed. There's no algorithm standing between you and the biological reality of whether it lives or dies. In that relationship, you are not a user or a consumer or an optimization target. You are simply a person caring for a living thing.

I'm drawn to these small acts of reclamation because I think they're how we remain human in an increasingly inhuman world. Not through grand refusals, but through modest assertions. Choosing to write by hand when you could type. Choosing to remember a friend's birthday without checking your phone's reminder. Choosing to be bored instead of instantly filling every empty moment with stimulation.

Boredom especially interests me. We've been taught that boredom is waste, that it represents time not spent productively or entertainingly. But boredom is actually when the mind does its most essential work. It's when the brain stops reacting to external stimulus and starts thinking for itself. Daydreaming, which is a form of boredom, is where ideas originate, where emotional processing happens, where you actually get to know yourself. The person who never allows themselves to be bored is someone who never develops their own interior landscape.

So maybe the rebellion is partly about boredom too—about allowing yourself to be unstimulated, unoptimized, genuinely unproductive in any measurable sense.

There's also something beautiful about the rebellion of attention. In a world competing frantically for your focus, choosing to give your full attention to one person, one book, one task, one moment becomes almost subversive. When someone puts their phone away during a conversation, they're announcing that you matter more than the infinite scroll. When someone reads the same book twice instead of moving to the next one, they're saying that depth matters more than coverage. These feel like small things, but they're not. They're statements about what you value and what you won't sell.

I think about skills that are becoming obsolete—the ability to navigate without GPS, to cook without recipes, to entertain yourself without entertainment technology, to sit with another person in silence without needing to fill it. These skills are becoming more valuable precisely as they become less necessary. They're becoming luxury goods in the sense that they represent freedom from dependence on systems.

And yet, I don't think the answer is wholesale rejection of modernity. That's a different kind of fantasy. We live in the modern world; we're shaped by it; we benefit from it in countless ways. The rebellion isn't about escaping into some imagined past, but about maintaining pockets of autonomy within the present.

What strikes me is how much energy these small rebellions require. It takes more effort to avoid optimization than to surrender to it. It's harder to live with intention than to drift with the current. But that difficulty is also what makes these choices meaningful. They're not inevitable; they're chosen. And choice, real choice about how you spend your consciousness and time, is increasingly the rarest commodity.

I think we're all searching for ways to be genuinely present in our own lives. To be the authors of our days rather than the subjects of someone else's system. To experience time as something to be inhabited rather than spent. To find meaning in the small, repeated acts that constitute a life rather than in the constant chasing of optimized outcomes.

The small rebellions are how we do this. They're how we say no to being merely efficient. They're how we insist on being human—which is to say inefficient, emotional, particular, and completely, stubbornly attached to the small rituals and choices that make us who we are.

So maybe make that coffee slowly. Read that book twice. Take the long way home. Remember something without searching for it. Be bored for an afternoon. Give someone your full attention. Choose the harder thing because it's yours.

These aren't revolutionary acts in the traditional sense. But perhaps that's what real revolution has always been: not the dramatic reshaping of everything, but the quiet, persistent assertion that your life belongs to you.

# On the Peculiar Beauty of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how we photograph sunsets but rarely photograph the moment just before, when the light is still ordinary, the sky still blue, and nobody's phone is out yet. There's something almost defiant about those pre-golden-hour moments—they exist in perfect indifference to their own ordinariness, unaware that in twenty minutes they'll be gone, replaced by something we'll all collectively decide is worth documenting.

This might be the central tragedy of human consciousness: we're built to notice the exceptional, which means we're almost architecturally incapable of appreciating the everyday until it's safely behind us. I think about my grandmother's kitchen—the harvest gold appliances, the linoleum with the pattern worn smooth in front of the sink, the way afternoon light came through the window and made everything look like an old photograph even when it was happening in real time. I have almost no memories of being conscious that I was happy there, yet I would trade small things to smell it again.

We're always preparing for the next moment, optimizing for it, planning around it. Last week I caught myself mentally reviewing a conversation while still in the middle of having it. The other person was talking, and I was already several sentences ahead, checking their words against my internal script of how I thought they'd perform. It's like we're all method actors who forgot we're actually supposed to be present for the scene.

There's a genre of self-help literature built on the premise that if we could just be more present, more mindful, more conscious of the moment we're in, we'd be happier. And maybe that's true, but I suspect it's also fundamentally difficult in a way that no amount of meditation cushions can fix. Our brains developed to keep us alive, not to feel peaceful. The wandering mind that checks for threats in the peripheral vision, the attention that shifts toward novelty and change—these are features, not bugs, even if they make it hard to simply sit with a cup of tea.

But here's what I find interesting: sometimes it sneaks up on you anyway. Sometimes you're doing something completely mundane—waiting in a checkout line, driving home, sitting in a waiting room reading a magazine from 2019—and you suddenly become aware that you're alive, that this is your life, that this moment is real. And it's neither good nor bad; it's just the texture of existing. Those moments are rare enough that I've started paying attention when they happen, like I'm collecting data on when consciousness decides to announce itself.

I think maybe the secret is that you can't actually make yourself present the way the self-help books suggest. It's too willful, too tense. It's like trying to fall asleep by concentrating really hard on falling asleep. Instead, presence seems to arrive in the margins—when you're distracted enough to stop trying, when you've given up on optimizing, when you've simply accepted that nothing particular is happening and that's actually fine.

A lot of life is waiting, when you think about it. We're waiting for the next phase, the next achievement, the next version of ourselves that will finally be satisfied. We're always in the waiting room, checking our phones, wondering how much longer. And meanwhile, the waiting is the life. The waiting room is the room we're in.

I've also been thinking about how we use language to collapse time. We say "I'm stressed about the future" as if the future is here now, as if we're currently living in something that hasn't happened yet. And maybe we are, in a sense—we're living in our mental model of the future, not in the present. The actual future, when it arrives, will almost certainly be different from what we imagined. But we'll have spent real time, real conscious moments, living in the wrong mental space.

This might sound like I'm advocating for pure carelessness, for never planning or thinking ahead. I'm not. We have to think ahead; that's part of being human. But there's a difference between planning and colonizing the present with anxiety about the future. There's a difference between remembering the past and being haunted by it.

What I keep coming back to is how much beauty is absolutely free and available, and how we walk past it constantly because we're too busy or too tired or too worried. Not the sunset-beauty that requires being in the right place at the right time. I mean the free beauty: the way light falls through leaves, the way people's faces change when they laugh, the fact that we can taste things, that music exists, that language lets us share thoughts that exist only in our individual minds.

When I was very young, I could look at a rock for what felt like a long time, genuinely interested in it. I could watch an ant work and feel like I was learning something profound. Somewhere along the way, that capacity didn't disappear, but it got buried under efficiency and purpose and the constant low hum of things to do.

I don't have a conclusion to this. I don't think there's a solution, some trick you can learn that will make you permanently present and happy. I think it's something you have to practice the way you practice any skill—by doing it imperfectly, over and over, forgiving yourself when you zone out and end up three thoughts ahead again.

But I do think it's worth noticing, worth trying, worth caring about. Because the time you're in right now—boring, ordinary, just a random Tuesday—is the only one you actually get to live. The exceptional moments are going to take care of themselves. It's the unremarkable ones that need a witness.

And maybe that witness can be you.
