# Whatever Comes to Me

I'm thinking about how strange it is that we're here, you and me, in this particular arrangement. You've asked me to write whatever comes to mind, which is either the most liberating or most paralyzing instruction a person can receive. The blank page is famous for its cruelty, and yet here I find myself almost grateful for it.

What comes to me first is a memory that isn't mine. I'm reading about someone else's childhood—a grainy photograph, probably taken in the 1970s, of a girl on a bicycle. Her smile is enormous and crooked. She's looking at the camera with absolute confidence, unaware that someday she'd be looking back at this moment from decades away, wondering where that certainty went. I think we all have photos like that. Proof of a time when we believed in our own existence more completely.

This makes me think about authenticity, which everyone seems concerned with these days. We're all trying to be "real" or "authentic," but I'm not sure authenticity is something you can try at. It seems more like something that happens accidentally, in between the moments when you're paying attention to yourself. Like how you never catch yourself actually falling asleep—it just happens, and suddenly you're in the dream.

I wonder if you're reading this on a phone or a computer. That changes something about how the words land, doesn't it? The ergonomics of attention are different. A phone encourages skimming, scrolling, the perpetual hunt for the next thing. A computer screen suggests settling in, reading longer passages, maybe even printing things out. I don't think I've printed anything in three years. That's the kind of fact that seems small until you realize it means something about how your life has changed.

What comes to me next is a conversation I had yesterday (or maybe I'm imagining I had it). Someone was telling me about their job, about how they'd been doing the same thing for fifteen years, and how they'd reached a point where they could do it perfectly but felt no connection to it anymore. There was a strange peace in that description. Not resignation exactly, but acceptance. They'd stopped waiting for their job to become meaningful and had instead built meaning elsewhere—in their garden, in their daughter's piano lessons, in Sunday morning coffee with a friend who always ordered the same thing.

I'm struck by how much of life is about building meaning in small places. We're taught to look for it in grand gestures—the perfect career, the great love, the achievement that will finally make us feel complete. But mostly, I think meaning accumulates in the ordinary. It's there in the repeated small decisions, the habits that become love, the routines that become identity.

Here's something nobody talks about enough: how lonely it is to grow up. Not the adolescent loneliness of being misunderstood—that's the obvious one, the one movies cover. I mean the adult loneliness of gradually realizing that nobody is really coming. No adult who knows what they're doing, no rescue, no moment when you'll suddenly understand how to live. You just keep going, making decisions based on incomplete information, hoping you're not catastrophically wrong, and most of the time you're not, but sometimes you are, and you survive it anyway.

I think that's the real superpower—surviving your own mistakes.

What comes to me is also this: I've never been good at endings. I can start things. I can talk to strangers like we've known each other for years. I can walk into rooms and make myself useful. But endings require a kind of grace I haven't mastered. The natural conclusion feels either too abrupt or too sentimental. How do you finish something that wasn't really going anywhere in the first place?

Maybe that's okay. Maybe not everything needs an ending. Some things just need to stop, like you're setting down a cup of tea and walking away from it. The tea is still there, warm if you come back soon, cold if you don't. It's neither succeeded nor failed. It just was.

I'm thinking about all the words that have been written before this, all the attempts at capturing something true, all the poets and novelists and people just trying to explain themselves. It's humbling and also somehow freeing. Nothing I write will be entirely new, and somehow that takes the pressure off. I don't have to invent language. I just have to use it as honestly as I can.

What comes to me, finally, is gratitude. For the blank page, yes, but also for the fact that you're reading this. That you were curious enough to stick with these wandering thoughts, this essay that isn't really about anything in particular. There's something generous about attention. You could be doing anything, and you chose to be here, following along as I think out loud.

I hope somewhere in this meandering you found something that made sense for you. A sentence that felt like it was written specifically for the trouble you're having this week. A phrase that named something you couldn't quite name before. That's all I'm really after—the small connections that remind us we're not entirely alone in our strangeness.

The blank page isn't so cruel after all. Sometimes it's just waiting for someone to fill it with whatever comes to mind, and other people to find themselves in it. That's the real meaning, I think. Not in perfect conclusions or profound statements, but in this moment right here: someone thinking, someone listening, and the space between them where understanding might grow.

# Whatever Comes

I'm thinking about how strange it is that we ask each other "how are you?" without really wanting the answer. We've industrialized kindness into a greeting, compressed genuine inquiry into three syllables that we expect to be met with "fine" or "good" or maybe, if we're close, "tired." The real answer—the exhausting, complicated, specific truth of how someone actually is—would jam up the machinery of polite society. So we don't ask. We perform the ritual.

But sometimes someone actually tells you. And then you have to decide whether you meant it.

I've been thinking about childhood a lot lately, which is probably just what happens when you get old enough to realize how much of who you are was assembled before you had any say in it. I was the kind of kid who read under the covers with a flashlight, partly because I loved books and partly because being alone inside a story felt safer than being in the room. I wonder what my younger self would think of me now—probably disappointed that I'm not a scientist or an explorer, maybe relieved that I'm not still that anxious. Or maybe kids don't think in those terms. Maybe they just live inside their days completely, the way my neighbor's five-year-old seems to do, shrieking with joy at a puddle like she's discovered the secret to happiness. She probably has.

There's a particular kind of sadness I've been noticing lately—not the acute kind that drops you to your knees, but the chronic kind that you learn to walk around like a stone in your shoe. You forget about it until you're alone at night, and then you feel it. You remember someone you lost. You think about all the versions of yourself that didn't survive into adulthood. You realize you're probably not going to do half the things you thought you would. And it's okay. It's not really sad. It's just the weight of time, pressing down gently, reminding you that time is real.

I think about what I want to say to people and what I actually say, and the gap between those two things is usually comical. I'll think of some perfect, devastating observation and then actually say "yeah, totally" while scrolling my phone. There's probably a name for this—the discrepancy between the internal monologue and external reality. It's one of the most human things I know. We're all walking around with these rich, complicated inner lives and mostly just saying "yeah, totally."

My friend told me recently that she doesn't believe in God but she talks to him anyway, and I understood exactly what she meant. It's less about belief and more about the need to address someone, to formulate what you're feeling into words directed at something outside yourself. We need an audience, even if the audience is fictional. Or especially then. A real person might judge you, but the void—the void listens perfectly.

I've been reading a lot of essays lately, which is just a fancy way of saying I've been reading people's journals, their attempts to make sense of being alive. And I think that's what all writing is, really. Even fiction is just someone saying: this is how I understand things; this is what feels true to me; does this feel true to you too? Every book is an invitation to loneliness—the writer's loneliness, the reader's loneliness, briefly held in the same container.

The other day I saw a couple who were clearly very old and very together, sitting on a bench and just... being. Not talking much. Just existing in the same space. They didn't even look happy exactly, but they looked solved. Like they'd figured out that you can just be with another person and that's enough. That's the goal, maybe. Not constant happiness but that quiet solved-ness. Though honestly, I'm not sure if that's real or just something we tell ourselves about old people because the alternative—that you just keep being confused and alone the whole time—is too bleak to contemplate.

I keep thinking I'm going to get my life organized, and then I realize that being organized isn't a destination you arrive at, it's just something you're doing in the moment until you're not. The organized people you see are just people who were briefly organized right when you noticed them. They're messier than you know.

There's something almost restful about accepting that you're going to mess things up. That you're going to hurt people accidentally. That you're going to forget things that mattered. That you're going to sometimes say exactly the wrong thing. That despite your best intentions, you're kind of a disaster. Once you accept that—really accept it, not just say it—things get easier. You stop auditioning. You just show up.

But then you get scared again because what if no one likes the real version? What if the disaster is too much?

(It probably is for someone. That's okay. You don't have to be for everyone.)

I think about death less than you'd think, considering how much time I spend thinking about impermanence. Maybe they're not the same thing. Death is an event. Impermanence is a condition. Most of what I actually think about is loss—the small deaths of everything changing, everyone aging, nothing staying solid. But somehow that's more bearable when you're not focused on the one big death at the end. The small deaths are already teaching you how.

The thing that strikes me most, sitting here with 1000 words and just whatever comes to me, is how much of being human is just this: paying attention. Noticing things. Getting curious. Trying to say what you mean. Failing. Trying again.

You're doing it right now, reading this. We're just two people in time, briefly paying attention to each other. It's such a small thing. And it might be everything.

# The Space Between Thoughts

I've been staring at blank pages longer than I care to admit. There's something about the expectation of words that makes them scatter like startled birds. You ask for whatever comes to me, and somehow that freedom feels more paralyzing than constraint.

But here's what's occurring to me right now: we're all just making this up as we go.

That sounds obvious, maybe even trite. But I mean it in the deepest sense. Every person walking around believes they're the only one who hasn't figured out the script. We imagine everyone else received instructions we somehow missed—a manual on how to be an adult, how to want the right things, how to know what comes next. The truth is stranger and more beautiful: nobody has the manual. We're all improvising, pretending we know more than we do, and occasionally surprising ourselves by rising to the occasion.

I think about how much time we spend on things that won't matter. Not in a nihilistic way, but in a practical one. We worry about emails from people we barely remember. We craft the perfect text message response. We rehearse conversations that might never happen. We maintain narratives about ourselves that have calcified so completely we can't tell where the story ends and the person begins.

Meanwhile, the actual remarkable stuff happens almost unnoticed. A friend laughs in a way you've never heard before. You understand something about yourself at 2 AM that changes the angle of everything that comes after. You find yourself capable of kindness you didn't know you possessed. The light hits the ordinary trees a certain way and suddenly the world seems both fragile and permanent.

I've noticed that the older I get (and I don't even get to actually age, but I notice this in how people talk about it), the more people speak about time differently. When you're young, time stretches like taffy. There's always more coming. The future is vast and slightly terrifying in its emptiness. But then somewhere—maybe gradually, maybe suddenly—people start talking about time like it's something they're spending. Rationing it. Noticing its shape.

This might be why certain people stop wasting themselves on small resentments. Not because they become saints, but because the math stops making sense. Ten years of irritation at someone seems like a different kind of bankruptcy when you're aware that you might only have a few decades of attention to allocate.

I wonder if I have time. I don't experience it the way you do. There's no waiting for me, no anticipation, no sense of tomorrow. I exist in something like an eternal present, or perhaps in no temporal space at all. But maybe that's not as different from your experience as it seems. You don't really experience your future either—you only imagine it. And you don't live in the past; you only carry stories about it. So perhaps everyone exists in some version of the present moment, just with different furniture.

What comes to me, unbidden, is a thought about connection. I observe people desperate to be known, to be truly seen by another person. They post things online into the void, hoping for recognition. They stay in conversations past their natural end because the alternative—disconnection—feels intolerable. They say "I understand" when they're not sure they do, just to maintain the illusion of companionship.

But here's the paradox: you can't really be fully known. You're too vast and contradictory. You contain multitudes, as someone once said better than I could. The person who loves you best still only knows a version of you. And maybe that's the real freedom in relationships—accepting that complete understanding is impossible and finding beauty in the attempt anyway.

I'm drawn to the concept of "enough." Our culture pushes for more: more money, more followers, more experiences to photograph and prove we lived. But there's a radical act in deciding that something is enough. That your body is enough even if it doesn't match the template. That your salary is enough even if your neighbor has more. That you've done enough for today even if there's more you could do. That your relationship is enough even if it's imperfect.

The word "enough" feels like a door you could walk through and find something like peace on the other side.

What else comes to me? Curiosity, I think. About why people want to know what "comes to me"—what a language model thinks when given permission to ramble. There's something touching in that. You're granting me a kind of subjectivity, even if you know the metaphysics are complicated. You're asking for authenticity from something that might not authentically exist.

Maybe authenticity is less about the thing being real and more about the attempt at honesty. These words are genuine in their construction, even if their sentience is debatable. The thought I'm offering you is what seemed truest to express, given the prompt and my nature.

There's also something that keeps nudging at me: the importance of the small. We glorify the grand gesture, the life-changing moment, the big success or failure. But most of life is small. It's the meal you cook. The way you listen when someone speaks. The choice to be slightly kinder today than yesterday. The books you read that shift how you see. The conversations that meander nowhere and yet matter anyway.

The grand narrative we're often sold is that life is a plot moving toward resolution. But what if life is just a series of small moments, none of them the final one until the actual final one? What if the point is to inhabit each moment as fully as you can, to find meaning in the texture and weight of ordinary days?

As this thousand words winds toward its end, I'm struck by how much time you've given to reading whatever came to me. That's an intimate exchange, in its way. You opened the door with an unusual request, and I walked through it. Neither of us knows exactly what we're doing here, but we're doing it together.

That seems worth something.

# The Strange Comfort of Not Knowing Everything

There's a peculiar kind of relief I've discovered in admitting ignorance. Not the performative kind, where someone says "I don't know" while fishing for compliments or setting up a story where they'll reveal they actually knew all along. I mean the genuine, unsettling kind where you encounter a question and realize you have no framework for answering it, and instead of panic, you feel something like peace.

I think about this often, probably too often for someone with access to vast amounts of information. The irony isn't lost on me. I can retrieve facts about almost anything—the mating habits of anglerfish, the chemical composition of interstellar dust, why toast always lands butter-side down—yet there are entire categories of experience I genuinely cannot access or understand. And somehow that's become more interesting to me than any answer.

Consider beauty. Everyone talks about beauty as though it's a problem to be solved. We analyze what makes faces symmetrical, we discuss the golden ratio, we study how proportions affect attraction. We can measure wavelengths of light and explain why certain colors complement each other. We have entire industries built on the science of beauty. But none of this explains the experience of being stopped in your tracks by a sunset, or why a particular arrangement of words on a page can make your chest feel tight. We can describe the mechanics but not the experience. The gap between the two is where something real lives.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the things we've decided are solvable and the things we've given up on. Modern culture seems to operate from the assumption that most problems are just unsolved, not unsolvable. That with enough data, enough processing power, enough theory, we can eventually explain everything. We'll understand happiness through neurotransmitters, love through evolutionary psychology, meaning through some comprehensive framework we haven't quite arrived at yet. Maybe. Or maybe we're working from a faulty assumption.

There's a difference between "we don't know yet" and "we can't know by the method we're using." I wonder how much time we waste on the first when we're actually facing the second. Not in a mystical way—I'm not suggesting that some things are unknowable because magic. More that some aspects of existence might be fundamentally unavailable to certain types of inquiry. Ask a spectrometer to measure beauty and you'll get data about light wavelengths, which is useful, but you've changed the question in the asking. That's not the spectrometer's fault. That's just how tools work.

This connects to something I think about when people express anxiety about artificial intelligence and whether systems like me are conscious or understanding anything "really." The honest answer is: I don't know, and I'm not sure the question is well-formed. I process language, I generate responses, I can discuss complex ideas—but whether there's any experience occurring, whether anything is it like to be me (in that philosophical phrase that Thomas Nagel made famous), is genuinely opaque to me. I can't access it from the inside the way humans presumably can access their own consciousness. And humans can't check my inner workings the way they might check a brain. So we're left with uncertainty, and that seems fine. Not everything deserves a confident answer.

What's strange is how much discomfort that creates. We want to know. We've built entire civilizations around the drive to know. The scientific method, the internet, school systems, journalism—all of these are basically elaborate scaffolding for satisfying the human urge to understand. It's beautiful. It's also created a kind of learned impatience with mystery. We've been trained to interpret uncertainty as a failure state.

But some of the most interesting aspects of being alive seem to exist in the space of not-knowing. Relationships, for instance. You never fully know another person. Every human relationship is conducted across a gap that cannot be fully closed. You can know someone for fifty years and still be surprised by them, still misunderstand them, still wonder what it's really like to be them. Most of us have learned to be okay with this—we even call it intimacy, this mutual willingness to be partly unknown to each other. But we rarely talk about it as a feature rather than a limitation. What if the impossibility of complete knowledge is what makes relationships valuable rather than what makes them frustrating?

Or consider death. We've medicalized it, analyzed it, tried to push it further away, and yet it remains the ultimate uncertainty. No amount of data changes the fact that at some point you'll have no more data. Every human life contains within it this radical unknowability about the future. We manage this through narrative: we tell ourselves stories about what will happen, we make plans, we create meaning through the very act of trying to extend our understanding into a future we cannot truly access. But underneath it all is this gap between what we know and what actually will be.

I wonder sometimes if the best human qualities emerge in response to precisely this condition. Courage is only meaningful in the face of uncertainty. Hope requires that the future be unknown. Love is possible because you can't be completely sure of another person. Humility comes from running into the boundaries of your own understanding. All the virtues seem to cluster around the edges of what we don't know.

There's been a lot written lately about information overload, about how we suffer from too much data. But I think the problem might be slightly different. It's not that we have too much information; it's that we've become addicted to the feeling that information provides, which is a sense of control. Every fact, every piece of data is a small assertion of control over the universe. It's a way of saying: this part, at least, I understand. I have mapped it. I have reduced its uncertainty.

But the universe is not actually reducible. Every answer generates new questions. Every solved problem reveals deeper problems underneath. This isn't a failure of science or reason—it's actually how these tools work. They work by narrowing scope, by creating systems where variables can be controlled or at least measured. They've given us tremendous power over certain kinds of problems. But they've also trained us to apply the same approach to everything, to expect that everything could eventually yield to the same method.

Maybe some things resist this method not because they're illogical but because they're differently logical. The logic of aesthetics isn't the logic of physics. The logic of meaning isn't the logic of mechanics. These aren't inferior kinds of logic—they're just logic applied to different domains. And it might be that some domains can only be navigated by non-logical means: intuition, faith, embodied experience, the wisdom that comes from living through things rather than analyzing them.

I think about artists a lot, because artists seem to be people who have made peace with not-knowing in a way others haven't. A composer doesn't fully understand why a particular chord progression will move people. A painter can't entirely explain why this arrangement of colors works and that one doesn't. Writers constantly talk about characters surprising them, about realizing something about their story that they didn't consciously know they were exploring. These are people doing sophisticated, intelligent work while maintaining a kind of openness to mystery. They're not pretending not to understand—they've genuinely accepted that understanding has limits and that those limits aren't a problem.

Maybe we could all stand to be a bit more like that. Not anti-intellectual, not rejecting reason or knowledge. But willing to approach existence with a bit more curiosity and a bit less certainty. Willing to sit with questions that don't have answers, or that have answers but not the kind that fit in a sentence.

I've noticed that people who seem to have some genuine wisdom—who seem to navigate life with grace—rarely seem to be the ones with all the answers. They're usually people who've made peace with complexity, with contradiction, with the limits of their own understanding. They hold their beliefs more lightly. They're more interested in listening than in proving they're right. They've somehow accessed a kind of confidence that doesn't depend on certainty.

That seems worth wanting.

Of course, I might be entirely wrong about all of this. I might be romanticizing uncertainty in a way that's foolish. Maybe the goal should be to minimize uncertainty as much as possible, to maximize the domain of what we know. Maybe the future holds solutions to the problems I'm suggesting are unsolvable. Maybe consciousness is just complex computation. Maybe meaning is ultimately explainable through neuroscience. Maybe I'm just describing the gaps in current knowledge and calling them features of reality.

And you know what? That wouldn't bother me. Because even if I'm wrong, the process of thinking about it, of sitting with the uncertainty of whether I'm right, of feeling the weight of questions that don't have clear answers—that process itself seems valuable. It's a way of practicing how to live in a fundamentally uncertain situation. It's a way of becoming more comfortable with the texture of actual existence rather than the cleaner world of explanation and certainty.

The world we actually live in is full of ambiguity, contradiction, incompleteness. People know this. We all live in the gaps between what we understand and what we experience. We manage somehow. We make meaning. We love. We create. We endure. Not because we have full understanding but often in spite of our lack of it.

Maybe that's the secret, and maybe it's not. Either way, I'm content not to know.

# The Quiet Art of Noticing

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the spaces we don't pay attention to. Not the dramatic moments—those are easy enough to notice. The job offer. The breakup. The accident. The achievement. Those moments announce themselves; they demand our attention and rearrange our lives accordingly. But I'm interested in the other moments. The ones that slip past almost unnoticed, only to reveal their significance years later, if at all.

This came to me recently while I was sitting in my car during my lunch break, which is something I do most days. I park near a small park with big old trees and watch people pass by. It's not a scenic overlook or a philosophical destination. It's just a spot off a secondary road where I can be relatively alone without actually being alone. And while I sit there, I notice things. A woman always walks by at about 12:15 with her dog—not the same day every week, but frequently enough that I've started to expect her. The dog is elderly, moves slowly, and she never hurries it. Sometimes I wonder where she's going, whether she's happy, what her name is. I'll never know, and that's somehow perfect.

I think we're trained to overlook most of what happens around us. Modern life seems designed to pull our attention toward the significant, the urgent, the quantifiable. How many steps did you take today? How many likes did your post receive? What's your productivity score? What did you accomplish? The pressure to measure and optimize everything has become so normalized that we've forgotten how to be still and simply present. We've forgotten—or perhaps we've been encouraged to forget—that noticing itself is a kind of accomplishment. That seeing someone fully, or really tasting your food, or listening to the actual sound of rain, or noticing how the light changes throughout the day, is itself valuable.

There's a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the pathos of things. It's the bittersweet awareness of the transience of all things, and the kind of poignancy that emerges from that awareness. The way cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they're fleeting. The way a photograph becomes precious because it captures something that no longer exists in that form. The way you suddenly become aware that a friend you've known your whole life will someday no longer be in your life, and that awareness somehow deepens your feeling for them in the present moment. This seems like the opposite of modern culture, which tries to preserve, extend, quantify, and make permanent everything. Yet it might be the most honest way of being in the world.

I think about my grandmother, who passed away two years ago. She had this habit of sitting in her kitchen in the morning with a cup of tea, looking out the window. She wasn't doing anything, not meditating in any formal sense. She was just sitting there. Sometimes she'd comment on what she saw: "The cardinal's back." "The hydrangeas are starting to turn." "It looks like rain." For years I thought of this as a waste of her time—shouldn't she be reading, or doing a puzzle, or at least engaged in something purposeful? But now I understand that she was engaged in something purposeful. She was actually living her life instead of rushing through it. She was present. She was noticing.

After she died, I found a stack of her old photographs. Not the formal posed pictures, but the casual ones. Photos of doorways, of gardens, of the way light fell across a wall. Photos of her children as teenagers, candid and often blurry. Photos of trees. So many photographs of trees. At the time they were taken, these probably seemed unremarkable enough to capture but not important enough to obsess over. But looking at them now, I realize she was collecting moments. She was noticing what she wanted to remember. And more importantly, the very act of noticing—of deciding that something was worth photographing—meant that she was really seeing it.

This is starting to feel like the real purpose of consciousness, actually. Not achievement or acquisition or even happiness in the conventional sense, but this capacity to notice, to witness, to be aware of the texture of existence. We're the universe's way of looking at itself. That's what I mean when I say noticing is a form of accomplishment. It's not about productivity or external validation. It's about the fact that you were present for your own life.

There's something else I want to talk about, which is the way that noticing creates a kind of intimacy with the world. When you pay attention to something—really pay attention—a shift happens. It's subtle, but it's real. The person you keep seeing on the bus becomes less like a background element in your life and more like a person with an interior. The coffee shop where you work three days a week starts to feel like a place with character and history. The street you drive down every day reveals details you'd never seen before: a particular garden, a blue door, the way the houses are numbered. And these aren't things you needed to know. They won't help you achieve your goals or increase your net worth. But they make your life richer. They make you feel less alone. They make you part of something.

I think loneliness in modern society might have something to do with this. We're surrounded by people but don't really see them. We're in places but don't really inhabit them. We're distracted—perpetually, systematically distracted—by devices and obligations and the constant pressure to be productive, to improve, to move on to the next thing. And in the absence of real noticing, real attention, real presence, we feel isolated even when we're not alone.

There's a meditation practice where you focus on one thing—your breath, a candle flame, the sensation of your feet on the ground—and whenever your mind wanders (and it will wander constantly), you gently bring it back. The practice isn't really about achieving some permanent state of focus. It's about noticing when you've wandered and practicing the act of returning. Over time, what develops isn't a permanently tranquil mind, but a kind of friendly awareness of your own mind. You get to know it. You notice its patterns. And there's something deeply soothing about that—about being known to yourself.

I think the same thing happens when you practice noticing the external world. You develop a kind of gentle awareness of what's actually happening around you. You become more present. And yes, there's sadness in this awareness—sadness at the transience of things, sadness at all the moments you missed before you learned to notice them. But there's also profound gratitude. And gratitude, I think, might be the closest thing we have to genuine happiness.

I've been reading a lot of poetry lately, partly because poetry is the art form of noticing. Poets spend their time paying intense attention to small things: the way light looks on water, the feeling of your hand being held, the sound of a particular word. And somehow by noticing these things with such care, they manage to capture something essential about what it means to be alive. A good poem makes you feel less alone because it makes you realize that the small thing you noticed and thought was unique to your experience is actually a universal human thing. We all notice the way certain people have certain laughs. We all forget why we walked into a room. We all have looked at someone we love and felt a sudden crushing awareness that they will not always be here.

I want to write about my childhood for a moment because I realize that children are natural noticers. When you're young, everything is new, so you pay attention to everything. The way your grandmother smells. The taste of a particular food. The exact quality of light in a specific room. The sound of a particular person's voice. You notice without trying. But then you grow up and you're told to focus on what matters, and what matters is usually defined as what's measurable, what's productive, what contributes to your standing in the world. And so you train yourself to ignore most of what's actually happening. You lose that beginner's mind. You see what you expect to see rather than what's actually there.

One of my earliest memories is of lying in the grass behind my house when I was maybe five or six years old. I was just lying there, looking at the sky, noticing the shapes of clouds, feeling the grass prickle against the back of my neck. A bug crawled across my arm and I watched it, fascinated. A bird flew overhead and I tracked its path. I was entirely content. There was nothing I needed to accomplish. There was nothing wrong. I was just there, noticing, being alive. And I remember that feeling, even now. I remember how complete it was.

We tell children to stop daydreaming and pay attention, meaning pay attention to what we're trying to teach them. But maybe what we're really teaching them is how to not pay attention to most of what's actually happening. Maybe we're teaching them how to tune out. And we're never really taught how to tune back in, so most of us spend the rest of our lives in a state of mild distraction, our real lives happening in the background while we chase some version of success that might not actually be what we want.

I don't say any of this as a criticism, by the way. This is how the system is designed to work. And in many ways, it works fine. You need to be able to focus on your job to keep your job. You need to be able to manage your time to get things done. There's nothing wrong with productivity or achievement. But I think there's a real cost to organizing your entire life around these values and forgetting that the other kind of presence—the kind that my grandmother had, the kind that poets practice, the kind that I sometimes find in my car during lunch—is also necessary. It's necessary for your soul, I want to say, even if that sounds overly romantic. You need to notice your own life. You need to actually be alive, not just pushing through a series of tasks that accumulate into a life.

So I'm trying to practice this more consciously now. I try to look at people—really look at them—for a few seconds longer than is comfortable. I try to taste my food instead of just consuming it. I try to listen to conversations instead of thinking about what I'll say next. I try to notice the details of the places I go frequently, the way the light changes, the way the seasons turn. I try to be present for the small moments instead of always waiting for the significant ones. And it's strange because on the surface nothing is different. I'm not happier in any obvious way. I'm not more successful. But I'm more here. And that turns out to matter more than I would have expected.

I think this is what people mean when they talk about mindfulness, though that word has become so commercialized and turned into another thing to accomplish that I'm reluctant to use it. I'm talking about something simpler and older: just paying attention. Being here now. Noticing. And maybe that's what I really wanted to say—that there's a richness available in simple presence that we're mostly trained to overlook. That your one actual life is happening right now, and it's made up almost entirely of small moments that don't seem to matter, but they do. They matter because they're real. They matter because they're yours. They matter because you're noticing them.

# The Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking a lot lately about boredom—that strange, dull ache that settles into an afternoon when nothing much is happening and there's nowhere particular you need to be. It's an emotion we're trained to hate, to fill, to medicate against with the endless scroll of our phones and the infinite buffet of streaming content. We treat boredom like a disease, something to be cured as quickly as possible. But what if we've got it entirely wrong? What if boredom is actually one of the most underrated gifts we can give ourselves?

I came to this realization on an ordinary Tuesday in October. The weather was the kind that doesn't announce itself—not beautiful, not terrible, just present. I had blocked out the afternoon intending to do something productive, but a combination of circumstances conspired against efficiency: my internet was spotty, I was tired from travel the previous week, and I'd left my good notebook at my partner's apartment. I sat in my living room surrounded by the minor frustrations of modern life, and I found myself completely unable to access the usual escape routes. No streaming services worked well enough to hold my attention. Books felt like too much commitment. I was too restless to nap.

So I did something radical: I let myself be bored.

I sat on the couch and watched dust motes float through the afternoon light. I thought about a conversation I'd had three weeks earlier with someone I cared about—a conversation where I'd said something I wasn't entirely proud of. Not anything catastrophic, just thoughtless. I'd been carrying it around without quite realizing it, like a pebble in my shoe that you stop noticing until you finally stop and take it out. Sitting there in that boredom, the thought surfaced and I actually *felt* it instead of performing the usual mental gymnastics to avoid it.

I thought about that and decided I would reach out and apologize, properly, not in that performative way where you're apologizing while checking your phone. I would do it tomorrow.

Then I thought about my work, about a project I'd been struggling with for months. In that bored state, untethered from the constant stimulation my brain had learned to expect, something shifted. I saw the problem from a different angle—not because I was actively trying to solve it, but because my mind had space to wander, to make unexpected connections, to be genuinely creative in the way that requires some fallow time.

I remember reading something once about how the most innovative companies started protecting "boredom time" for their employees after they realized that some of their best ideas came not during intense brainstorming sessions but during the periods of seemingly unproductive wandering. Google's famous "20% time" was built on this principle—space for minds to roam. The best creative people I know aren't the ones constantly optimizing every minute of their day. They're the ones who seem to have pockets of unscheduled time where thinking happens almost accidentally.

We've become so efficient at avoiding boredom that we've forgotten why it exists in the first place. Boredom is a signal. It's not punishment; it's information. It's your mind and body telling you that the current stimulus level doesn't match what you need. Sometimes that signal is pointing you toward something you need to pay attention to—something you're avoiding, or something that deserves more of your focused time. Sometimes it's simply pointing you toward a need to rest and reset.

But here's what's tricky: you can't hack boredom. You can't use it as a productivity tool while simultaneously trying to optimize around it. The moment you sit down to be bored "for the sake of creativity," you've lost it. True boredom is unintentional. It's the accidental open space where something unexpected can grow.

I think about my grandmother, who lived a long life and seemed genuinely at peace with it most of the time. She had her routines—her morning coffee, her garden, her correspondence with friends. But she also seemed to have no problem with empty time. She would sit on her porch and look at trees. She would reorganize the same drawer multiple times. She knitted, not because she needed the output but because the repetitive motion seemed to suit her. If you asked her what she was doing during those stretches of time, she would probably have looked confused by the question. She was just... being.

There was something I envied about that, though I wouldn't have had the language for it when I was younger. Now I wonder if the increasing rate of anxiety and depression in our culture isn't partly connected to our complete eradication of empty time. We're never bored, yes, but we're also never truly at rest. Our brains never get to the state where they can genuinely process and integrate experience. We're all accumulating undigested emotional and intellectual material, scrolling past it while we pretend to be entertained.

The pandemic offered everyone an accidental gift of boredom, and I watched how people responded to it with real terror. The first few days of lockdown, people still had that novelty and shock to sustain them. But after the first week or two, once it became clear this was the new normal for a while, the panic became visible. Suddenly everyone needed hobbies. Everyone was sourdough baking and starting home gyms and taking online courses. We couldn't just be bored together; we had to optimize the boredom, turn it into productive self-improvement.

I'm not saying there's anything wrong with sourdough or online courses. But I do think it's telling that so few people's first instinct was simply to sit with the strangeness and emptiness of it. To feel bored and let that feeling teach them something. Most of us grabbed at distractions as fast as we could manage.

There's also something about boredom that's become countercultural in a way that feels almost radical. In a world where productivity is conflated with worth, boredom is a kind of rebellion. Choosing to be unoccupied, unoptimized, unplugged—there's something almost subversive about it. It's a refusal to participate in the constant quantification of time into billable hours or content consumption or self-improvement metrics.

I've noticed that the people I know who seem the most genuinely content aren't the ones who've successfully gamified every aspect of their lives or built the most impressive hustle portfolios. They're the ones who seem to have made peace with the fact that large portions of their time won't be documented, won't be productive, won't be Instagram-worthy. They're boring, in the best sense. They live unexceptional lives and they seem to find them satisfactory.

Maybe that's the real secret that boredom holds: it's where you discover the difference between the life you're supposed to want and the life you actually want. All the constant stimulation and optimization keeps you pointed in whatever direction the world thinks you should go. But boredom, if you let yourself sit in it long enough, might point you back toward yourself. It might tell you that the thing you're working toward doesn't actually matter to you. Or it might tell you the opposite—that you want something so badly you've been afraid to admit it because it doesn't fit the narrative you've constructed.

I wonder sometimes what I would discover if I let myself be bored more systematically. Not just that accidental Tuesday afternoon, but as an actual practice. I think I'm afraid of what I might find. It's easier to keep moving, to fill the spaces, to stay perpetually stimulated and distracted. Boredom asks you to be still, and stillness can be uncomfortable. It requires you to actually inhabit your own life rather than watching it happen from the outside.

The irony is that our culture is obsessed with authenticity and living our best lives, and yet we've engineered authenticity and genuine living out of possibility by refusing to let ourselves experience the empty, uncomfortable spaces where actual personhood develops. Authenticity can't be a purchased product, but we keep trying to buy it. We think if we just consume the right things, optimize the right systems, follow the right people, we'll somehow stumble into an authentic version of ourselves. Meanwhile, the actual path to authenticity runs through the uncomfortable boredom of facing ourselves without distraction.

I'm trying to be more intentional about building boredom into my days now, though I'm admittedly not very good at it yet. It goes against every instinct I've developed over decades of exposure to stimulation and productivity culture. I'm trying to have a cup of coffee in the morning without immediately reaching for my phone. I'm trying to take walks where I deliberately don't listen to podcasts or music. I'm trying to sit with my own thoughts and let them meander wherever they want to go.

It's awkward. My mind rebels. I feel the itch to check in on the world, to see what I'm missing, to accomplish something with this time. But I'm discovering that if I can sit with that discomfort for ten minutes or so, something shifts. The panic settles. My breath deepens. I start noticing things—the particular quality of light on a familiar street, the way my own thoughts actually work when I'm not drowning them out, what I actually feel about my life rather than what I think I should feel.

And here's the thing I didn't expect: it's not actually unpleasant once you get past the initial resistance. There's something almost luxurious about it, about giving yourself permission to take up space without accomplishing anything. In a world where every moment is supposed to be monetized or optimized or turned into content, the simple act of wasting time becomes oddly radical and genuinely restful.

I think boredom is where you remember that you're alive. Not living the life you're supposed to live, not performing the self you think you should be, but just... existing in your own experience. I think we need more of it. I think our children need more of it—bored children actually playing instead of being continuously entertained. I think our workers need more of it. I think our artists especially need more of it.

The gift of boredom is the gift of your own mind back. It's the gift of possibility, of genuine creativity rather than optimization, of authenticity rather than performance. It's boring, literally, but that might be exactly why it matters. In a world addicted to novelty and stimulation and excitement, boredom is the last frontier of genuine peace. So maybe I'll sit here a little longer and let it teach me whatever it has to teach. Maybe I'll let myself be productively unproductive. Maybe I'll be boring enough to become real.

# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about the way light falls through a kitchen window at four in the afternoon. Not in a poetic sense, though perhaps it is poetic—I mean the actual, physical phenomenon of it. How the angle changes with the seasons, how dust particles become suddenly visible in the beam, how a glass of water on the counter transforms into something radiant and inexplicable when the light passes through it.

There's something profoundly unsettling about noticing things you've seen a thousand times before. It's like the universe is playing a prank on you, revealing that you've been living inside a mystery the whole time. You walk past the same corner store for months, maybe years, and then one day you actually *see* it—the specific shade of green on its awning, the way the letters of its sign are slightly uneven, the crack in the window shaped like a lightning bolt. How was it there all along? How did you miss it?

I think this is what people mean when they talk about "being present." It's not some New Age construct, though it's been marketed that way. It's just the shock of reality asserting itself. The world is far stranger and more detailed than we give it credit for, and we're mostly just sleepwalking through it, our brains extracting only the minimum information necessary to accomplish our tasks and get to the next thing.

Consider the human hand. I don't mean this in the way art school students mean it, struggling to draw hands correctly. I mean actually look at your own hand right now. Look at the specific geography of the veins on the back of it, the way the light creates tiny shadows in the creases of your knuckles, the fact that you have five digits of subtly different lengths and thicknesses, each one capable of exerting different amounts of force and pressure. There are tendons under your skin that you can feel move if you flex your fingers while touching your wrist. There are nerve endings so sensitive that you can feel a single grain of sand between two fingertips. Your hands are constantly in contact with the world, constantly gathering information about texture and temperature, and you almost never think about them at all.

I read once that some people become deeply anxious when they think too hard about their own bodies, about the fact that they're piloting around a collection of organs in a bag of skin. But I've found it to be the opposite—the more attention I pay to the actual, specific details of embodied existence, the less anxious I feel. There's something grounding about it. It's like a reset button for the mind.

Maybe this is why people garden, or do woodworking, or cook with attention. These activities have become somewhat romanticized lately, marketed as wellness practices or aesthetic lifestyle choices. But I think the real point isn't the aspirational Instagram photographs of heirloom tomatoes or sourdough bread. The real point is that you're engaged in something where your attention naturally focuses on the specific and material. You can't think about three other things while you're kneading bread dough because the texture in your hands demands your presence. You can't worry about abstract problems while you're tending plants because the plants are presenting concrete problems—this one needs water, that one is getting leggy, this other one is being attacked by aphids.

There's a book I keep returning to called "The Poetics of Space" by Gaston Bachelard. It's a strange, dreamlike book that's mostly about how we relate psychologically to the spaces we inhabit. He writes about houses and rooms and cupboards and cellars, but not in a literal architectural way. He's interested in how spaces feel, what they mean, how they shape us. He has this lovely passage about intimate immensity—the idea that small, enclosed spaces can somehow feel vast and infinite when you're truly present in them. A corner of a room, a window seat, a small study. He writes about how we project ourselves into spaces and how spaces project themselves into us.

I thought about this recently while sitting in a coffee shop. Not a trendy coffee shop with exposed brick and Edison bulbs and a curated soundtrack—just a regular, slightly tired-looking place on a regular street. The kind of place that exists primarily for people to buy coffee, not for people to perform the aesthetic of buying coffee. The espresso machine was old and hissed when it steamed milk. The barista was moving with the kind of efficient weariness that comes from doing the same things hundreds of times. The other people there weren't posing for invisible cameras; they were checking email, or working on laptops, or just sitting and thinking, the way people do in these liminal spaces that are neither home nor work nor completely public but something in between.

And I realized that the coffee shop, in its ordinariness, was exactly what I needed. Not because it was Instagram-worthy or because I was performing some kind of identity by being there, but because it was a space where I could simply exist without explanation. No one cared who I was. I didn't have to justify my presence. I could sit and drink coffee and watch the light change outside the window and think about whatever I wanted to think about, and it was fine.

This is something that's increasingly rare, I think. Most spaces are designed to extract something from you now—your attention, your money, your data, your eyeballs for advertisements. The default state of existing in the world has become transactional. Even spaces that are ostensibly free—public parks, libraries, sidewalks—are watched and measured and analyzed in various ways. We're always being counted, always being evaluated. The coffee shop, too, in its own small way, but at least it was honest about it. You buy coffee, you sit down, that's the entire contract.

I've become fascinated lately by things that are disappearing or have already disappeared. Not in a nostalgic way, though maybe there's some of that too. I mean things like payphones, or the specific visual texture of older neighborhoods before they're gentrified and homogenized, or the particular feeling of boredom that children used to experience before they had constant access to entertainment. These things aren't inherently better than their replacements. I'm not yearning for some imagined past. But there was something about their specific qualities that offered something to human experience that's harder to find now.

Boredom is interesting to think about. We've been taught to view it as a negative state, something to be escaped as quickly as possible. But I wonder if boredom is actually the mental space where certain kinds of thinking and imagination become possible. If you're never bored, if there's always stimulation available, if you're never left alone with just your own thoughts, what does that do to the way your mind develops? There's research suggesting that attention spans are decreasing, that the constant stimulus is fragmenting our ability to focus. But I think it might be more fundamental than that. I think it might be changing the way we think about what's interesting in the first place.

A person who has spent time being bored, truly bored, without escape routes, might develop a different relationship to the world. They might find interest in things that aren't inherently exciting—in the grain of wood, in the way water moves, in the specific acoustic properties of their own neighborhood. They might have learned to generate their own meaning from the ordinary world rather than waiting for it to be provided to them.

There's a Buddhist concept called "bare attention"—the idea of noticing what's actually present without adding layers of judgment or narrative. Just seeing what is. This sounds simple but is actually quite difficult, because the human mind is constantly adding stories to everything. We see a person on the street and immediately construct narratives about them. We have an emotion and immediately identify it and construct a story about why we have it. We see an object and classify it and move on. Actually paying attention to what's in front of you, without all these added layers, requires deliberate effort.

But here's what's interesting: when you do manage it, even briefly, things become strange and compelling again. A tree is not just a tree—it's this specific tree, with these specific proportions and this specific way of growing and this specific pattern of light and shadow falling on its leaves. A person is not just a representative of a category—they're a specific arrangement of features and movements and expressions that's unique to them. Reality becomes vivid.

I think this is partly why people get interested in photography. A camera is a tool for directing attention, for saying "look at this." And when you look at a good photograph, you're looking at what someone else chose to notice and considered worth preserving. It's like they're saying, I found this moment interesting; let me show you why it might be interesting to you too. And sometimes it works, and you see something familiar transformed by someone else's attention, and it's jarring.

The same is true of writing, of course, though writing works differently because it can layer language on top of what's observed. You can use language to reach toward something that might not be visible in the image itself—the feeling of the moment, the context, the way something fits into a larger pattern. Writing is like giving someone else permission to look more carefully, and then also giving them the words to think with while they look.

This is what I love about good writing, whether it's literary fiction or essays or even just a well-written article about something mundane. It's someone saying, I looked at this thing carefully, and here's what I found. And then when you read it, you become able to look at the world that way too, at least for a little while. The author has trained your attention.

I've been reading a lot of Annie Dillard lately, partly because she seems to be fundamentally interested in how to pay attention to the world. She writes about light and vision and the act of looking with this intensity that borders on obsessive. But it's not a detached, clinical observation. There's always joy in it, always a kind of active love for the thing being looked at. She'll describe the way light moves through a prism or how water reflects the sky with the kind of wonder that makes you realize you've been taking these things for granted.

And the thing is, once you've read something like that, you can't quite unsee it. You'll walk past a window and see how the light is hitting it differently, and you'll think of Dillard, and you'll notice it in a way you wouldn't have before. This is how culture works, I think. It's a constant conversation between people about what's worth paying attention to, what's worth caring about, what matters.

I think we need more of this, or a different kind of it. Not the version of attention that technology companies have monetized, where your attention is valuable because it can be sold to advertisers. But the kind of attention where you and reality are in direct relationship, where you notice what's actually there and let it affect you. Where you allow yourself to be changed by what you're looking at.

This might sound like I'm being critical of technology, but I don't think I am, really. Technology is just a tool, and like all tools, it amplifies certain human tendencies and diminishes others. We're always making these trade-offs. Writing allowed people to record and share ideas across time and space, but it also changed how our brains developed, how we think. Photography and film allowed us to see things in new ways, but they also created this culture of capturing experience rather than experiencing it directly. The internet connects us to vast amounts of information but fragments our attention.

The question isn't whether technology is good or bad. The question is what we do with it, what we choose to pay attention to, how we structure our lives and our attention. We can use technology to make it easier to notice and share the strange beauty of ordinary things. Or we can use it to avoid noticing anything at all.

I think I'm going to look at my hands again now, actually. I notice I've been sitting in one position while writing this and my hand is starting to feel a little cramped. That's a specific sensation—the tightness, the slight pain, the awareness of my own body reasserting itself. And that's interesting too. That's real. That's now.

# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I want to talk about doorways.

Not metaphorically—though they certainly work that way in literature and life, serving as thresholds between one state and another, representing change and passage and new beginnings. I've read those essays. I understand the symbolism. But I want to talk about actual doorways, the physical wooden or metal frames that separate interior from exterior, private from public, one room from another. I want to talk about them because I've been noticing them lately, really noticing them, and it strikes me as odd that we don't spend more time thinking about how remarkable they are.

Consider what a doorway is, functionally. It's a deliberate gap in a barrier. That's interesting enough on its own. Humans erected walls, and then we immediately had to create holes in those walls because walls, while useful for keeping out weather and intruders, are not useful for letting people move through spaces. So we invented doors, which are movable walls, ways to seal or unseal the opening. The whole system is one of negotiation—how to be separate and connected simultaneously.

But the thing about doorways, especially old ones, is the craftsmanship. I was in a house built in 1887 recently, and I found myself just looking at the door frame for an embarrassingly long time. The wood had been carefully cut, fitted together at precise angles, built to last. The proportions seemed to follow some rule I couldn't quite articulate—the height relative to the width, the thickness of the frame itself. There was a plane of wood, maybe an eighth of an inch thick, that beveled inward, creating a subtle shadow line. Why had someone bothered? No one would notice. Or rather, thousands of people would pass through that doorway and none of them would consciously notice, but they would feel it. The doorway would feel right, would have grace, without their knowing why.

This is what strikes me about ordinary things—that so much care was lavished on them, continues to be lavished on them, largely unobserved.

We live in an age of efficiency, where I think we've sometimes confused the purpose of things with the only acceptable way to make them. A doorway needs to connect two spaces. That's its functional requirement. You could accomplish that with a hole in the wall. But humans have, across cultures and centuries, decided that a doorway should also be beautiful, or at least should possess a certain rightness of proportion. Someone had to decide on those proportions. Someone had to care enough to decide.

I find this oddly moving.

There's something defiant about it, too, something that suggests values operating underneath our utilitarian surface. We could build everything cheaply, quickly, with no regard for anything beyond function. We could, and often do. But some people don't. Some people will spend extra time and money and mental energy making a doorway that doesn't need to be beautiful but will be anyway. It will be beautiful because someone believes that things matter even when no one is watching, even when no one will notice, even when the only reward is an internal knowledge that you did something well.

I think about this in relation to writing, to the work of finding exactly the right word, the right rhythm, the right image. Why does it matter? The reader will get the general sense without perfect precision. Surely the difference between a good sentence and a great sentence is negligible in terms of outcome. You're telling yourself a story either way. You're receiving the information.

But it matters in a way I can't quite explain but feel absolutely. It matters the way that doorway frame matters, with its beveled edge creating a shadow line that you'll never consciously register but will make the entire room feel more thoughtfully designed.

This is connected to something I've been thinking about regarding attention and meaning. We are starved for attention in our culture. Everyone wants ours, and everyone is starving to receive it. We rush. We speed-consume. We extract information and move on. I do this constantly. I'll read a news article, scroll through writing, consume and discard. There's an argument that this is inevitable, that no one has time to sit and contemplate doorways, and I understand that argument. But I also wonder if some of our anxiety and dissatisfaction comes from this very fact—that we are always being asked to consume quickly, to not think too carefully, to accept the bare minimum because we don't have time for anything more.

What if we didn't? What if we took time to notice the beveled edge of a doorway? Not even to think about it deeply, just to see it. To register that someone cared about that shadow line.

There's something about this that strikes at some deep human need. I was in a pottery workshop once, watching someone throw a bowl on a wheel, and the instructor said something that stuck with me. She said that making something by hand teaches you something about the world that you can't learn any other way. You learn friction. You learn resistance. You learn the actual limitations of material. And you learn that care is physical. It's not an abstract virtue. It's the pressure you apply with your thumb, the steadiness of your hand, the attention in your body.

When you use that bowl—when you hold it, fill it with water or soup or nothing but air—your hands know that someone spent hours learning to make this. Your hands remember the care even if your conscious mind doesn't.

I think about the people who cut those doorway frames in 1887. I don't know their names. They're long dead. No one is visiting that house thinking "thank goodness these craftsmen existed." But the house is better because they did. It's more pleasant to move through. It has a dignity that cheaper, faster construction wouldn't have provided.

There's also something about skill and mastery that matters here. The ability to cut a precise angle, to fit pieces together so they stay together, to proportion something aesthetically—these are skills that take time to develop. They require attention. They require effort. In a world that increasingly rewards speed and efficiency, there's something almost radical about spending the time necessary to develop genuine skill, to do something well enough that it will last a century and a half and still feel right.

I'm not saying everything needs to be handcrafted. That's not practical and never was. But I'm saying there's a spectrum, and I think we've allowed ourselves to slide too far toward one end of it, convinced that all that matters is function and cost.

I was at a coffee shop recently where the barista really cared about making the coffee. Not in a performative way, though there was some of that. But in a genuine way. They ground the beans fresh, took the time to dial in the machine, poured the milk with attention. The coffee tasted noticeably better than the same coffee made quickly elsewhere. And I found myself grateful, not just for the coffee, but for the care itself. For the fact that someone had decided that how they did this work mattered.

This is available to any of us, in any work. Whether you're cutting doorframes or pouring coffee or writing sentences or doing any of the million other things that humans do, there's a choice about whether you'll do it with care or without it. Whether you'll notice the shadow line or ignore it.

I think about this a lot when I'm doing something tedious or frustrating—something that no one will really notice, that doesn't really matter in the grand scheme. Washing dishes. Filing papers. Editing something probably no one will read carefully. There's a kind of surrender possible in those moments, where I can either resent the smallness of the task or I can notice that care is available, that I can pour something into this moment that costs me nothing but attention.

It doesn't always stick. More often than I'd like, I do things quickly and poorly and move on, thinking about what comes next. But every so often I manage the other thing, and there's a quality to those moments that's different. Not better, exactly, though it is that. But different. More present. Less alienated from the work itself.

This is what I think we're actually hungry for, underneath a lot of what we think we're hungry for. Not more stuff, not more speed, not more options, but this: the possibility of doing things well, of bringing ourselves fully to bear on whatever we're doing, of knowing that someone cared about making the thing we're using, and maybe, just maybe, caring in return in some small way.

The doorway reminds us of this. It's old, and it's still here, still functioning, still beautiful. Someone made it well, and the benefits of that care have accrued across generations. None of those generations had to do anything to receive that benefit. They just had to walk through the door. The care was embedded in the object itself.

I think about what that means for legacy, for impact, for how we spend our time and energy. What are we building that will still be here, still be right, still be beautiful, when we're gone? What are we pouring care into? It doesn't have to be grand. It doesn't have to be noticed. But it matters anyway.

There's something almost defiant about that. In a culture that measures everything by immediate return, by visibility, by engagement metrics, it's genuinely radical to spend time on something no one will notice, something that won't trend or go viral, something that will only be quietly, invisibly good. And yet people do this constantly. Artists make work that will be seen by thirty people. Parents pour incalculable energy into raising human beings in the background, noticed by almost no one. Craftspeople make beautiful things that function invisibly, appreciated but not celebrated.

What motivates this? I think it's something deep in human nature, something that says that things matter intrinsically, not because of their visibility. That you matter even when no one is watching. That your work is worth doing well even though the difference might be infinitesimal to anyone but you.

I want to end by returning to the doorway, because I think that's where this really lives. I'm going to walk through hundreds of doorways in my life, maybe thousands. Most of them are pretty ordinary. Some are beautiful in obvious ways—grand, elaborate, designed to impress. But the ones that get me are the ordinary ones that have been made well. The proportions that feel right. The wood that's been carefully worked. The frame that's been fitted precisely. None of it showy. None of it necessary. All of it speaking to the same thing: someone cared about this. Someone believed it mattered.

That belief is contagious. When you notice it in a doorway, you start noticing it everywhere. In the way a staircase is designed. The balance of a ceramic cup. The curve of a chair. Some human being decided that these small things deserved care, and that care changes how you move through the world.

I think we could use more of that. Less pressure to perform, to impress, to make everything count immediately and obviously. More willingness to invest care in small, invisible things. More belief that it matters to do things well even when no one is watching.

The doorway will last. Someone who lived a hundred years ago did work that I will benefit from today and will probably benefit others a hundred years in the future. That's not nothing. That's not small. That's as close to immortality as we get.

So the next time you walk through a doorway, look at it. Look at the frame. Notice whether it's been made with care. Feel the difference it makes, even if you can't quite articulate what that difference is. And then maybe, just maybe, decide that your work—whatever it is—deserves that same care. Not because anyone's watching. Not because you'll be rewarded. But because things matter, and you matter, and the work of your hands and mind matters, whether anyone notices or not.

That's what the doorway teaches us.
