# On the Strange Comfort of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about how we live surrounded by unfinished business, and how rarely we acknowledge this as simply the human condition rather than a personal failing. There's something peculiar about modern life—a constant low-level anxiety that stems not from any single catastrophe, but from the ambient awareness that nothing is ever truly complete. We exist in a perpetual state of almost-done.

Consider the average person's relationship with their home. I don't mean people who are genuinely struggling with housing insecurity—that's a different conversation, and a real crisis. I mean the ordinary middle-class person who has a roof and walls and yet experiences their dwelling as somehow perpetually inadequate. The kitchen could use better organization. The bedroom would be better with different lighting. Those baseboards have needed painting for three years. There are boxes in the closet from a move that happened five years ago. There are plants that are mostly dead but occasionally you water them and they spring back to life, so you can't quite justify throwing them away.

We've internalized the idea that spaces should be "done"—that there's some final state where a home is complete, perfect, requiring no further thought. This is, I think, a relatively new delusion. For most of human history, homes were works in perpetual progress. You fixed the roof when it leaked. You added a room when the family grew. You maintained what you had. The idea that a space could be finished, that you could achieve some state of domestic perfection and then simply enjoy it forever, is a luxury good masquerading as a universal standard.

I think about this when I scroll through interior design photos online—those perfectly staged rooms where nothing is out of place, no book is askew on its shelf, no mug sits next to a sink. These aren't homes. They're photographs of homes. Or rather, they're photographs of the idea of homes, which is a different thing entirely. A real home is a record of living. It's incomplete by necessity.

The same applies to our interior lives, though we seem even less willing to admit this. We're supposed to have our careers figured out by thirty, preferably by twenty-five. We're supposed to know what we want to be and become it. We're supposed to complete projects—both literal and metaphorical—and move on to the next thing. But ask anyone honest about their life, and you'll find an enormous catalog of begun-but-not-finished endeavors. The novel that got to page sixty and stalled. The language learning app that's been gathering dust for two years (though you paid for the subscription). The exercise routine that worked for three weeks. The ambitious project you were going to tackle during the pandemic and somehow never quite managed.

I wonder if we'd be happier if we reframed these not as failures but as the texture of a life actually lived. There's something almost holy about the person who reads many books rather than few, who starts many projects rather than completing a few perfect ones. This person is engaged with the world, curious, testing things out, seeing what they might become interested in. The "failure to complete" is actually a form of experimentation.

There's also something I've noticed about people who are genuinely accomplished in some field—whether it's writing or music or painting or building things. They almost universally report that the work never feels finished. The novel that got published still feels incomplete to them. The song that thousands of people love still feels like it could be better. This isn't false modesty, I think. It's genuine. The deeper you go into any domain, the more you understand how much there is to know, how many choices you made that could have been made differently, how many ways the thing could be better. Completion is a luxury of ignorance.

Maybe the problem isn't that we have too many incomplete things. Maybe it's that we shame ourselves for it instead of accepting it as natural. We're supposed to finish what we start. We're supposed to have discipline, follow-through, grit. These are fine qualities, but they're not the only qualities. There's also the quality of being comfortable with exploration, with trying things, with learning through doing rather than planning exhaustively before beginning.

I think about my own writing this way. I have a document on my computer with fragments—ideas that came to me while I was doing something else, passages that felt true in the moment, images I wanted to preserve. Some of these fragments are years old. Are they failures? Have I failed to write the full pieces they belong to? Or are they seeds, waiting for the right conditions to grow? Some probably will never become anything. And that's fine. They served their purpose when they were written. They captured something true about how the world looked on a particular day, and that has value whether or not it gets woven into a larger whole.

I wonder if one of the things that makes modern life particularly anxious is that we've extended the logic of completion into domains where it doesn't belong. A novel should probably have an ending. A bridge should probably be finished before people drive on it. But a life? A creative practice? A relationship? These aren't things that get finished. They're things that you inhabit, day by day, making small adjustments, learning and growing, sometimes doubling back to refine something you thought was settled.

There's a particular kind of person I notice who seems to have less anxiety about these things—not because they're inherently less anxious, but because they've made peace with incompletion. They tend to be people who have some field where they actively practice their incompleteness. Musicians are often like this. They'll pick up their instrument and play the same piece for twenty years, never feeling like they've "finished" learning it. Each time is a new attempt, a new understanding, a new appreciation of what the piece contains. They've externalized their incompletion into their art form, and somehow this seems to make it easier for them to accept incompletion in other areas of life.

I've been trying to think of what incompleteness looks like in a healthy form. Not the anxiety of half-done things nagging at you, making you feel lazy and inefficient, but the openness of knowing that everything you care about is still being discovered, still revealing new dimensions. Maybe it's the difference between incomplete and unfinished. Incomplete things are still in process. Unfinished things are things you failed to complete. The emotional valence is entirely different.

There's a phrase I keep coming back to: "in progress." It's what artists put on their work when it's not done but it's being shown anyway. "Work in progress." "In progress" suggests movement, directionality, ongoing engagement. It's honest about the state of things without being apologetic about it.

I think most of life is "in progress." Your personality is in progress. Your understanding of what you believe is in progress. Your skill at being a parent, a partner, a friend—all in progress. Your attempt to be a good person is definitely in progress, and probably always will be. The moral arc of an individual doesn't end until you die, and maybe not even then, if you believe in anything that happens after.

What would it mean to embrace this more fully? To stop waiting for some future state where you've finally figured things out, finally finished improving yourself, finally completed the important project? To instead notice and appreciate the strange privilege of being a being who can still learn, still change, still discover new things about yourself and the world?

I'm reading a lot of climate literature at the moment, and it's made me think about incompletion in yet another way. We live in a time when we're asked to care about problems—climate change, social injustice, democratic erosion—that will not be solved in our lifetimes. Possibly not in several lifetimes. How do you sustain commitment to work that will not be finished, that you will not see completed, that might in fact only get worse before it gets better (if it gets better at all)?

The only way I can figure out is to stop seeing the completion as the point. The point becomes the work itself, the daily commitment, the incremental improvement, the community of people also working on it. You become a person who does these things, not a person working toward finishing these things. And that's strangely freeing, even in the context of genuinely serious problems.

There's something almost beautiful about the idea of being a custodian rather than a finisher. A custodian maintains, cares for, passes on to the next person. A forest ranger isn't trying to finish the forest. A librarian isn't trying to finish the library. A teacher isn't trying to finish education. They're tending to something that will continue beyond them, and there's dignity in that role.

Maybe one of the secret joys of getting older is realizing that you're not supposed to finish. You're supposed to show up and tend to the things you care about, and then other people will tend to them after you, and that's how the world actually works. The cathedrals of Europe took centuries to build. No individual architect finished them. But each one did their part, did their best with the materials and understanding available to them, and passed it on.

I notice I'm most peaceful when I'm thinking about my life this way. When I'm not tracking toward some imaginary finish line. When I'm instead focused on being the kind of person who does the kinds of things I think are worth doing. When I'm tending to my relationships, my work, my curious engagement with ideas, not because it will all be done someday, but because that's what the tending itself offers me.

The boxes in my closet from that move? I'm probably going to open them someday and deal with them. Or maybe I won't, and whoever cleans out my apartment after I die will do it. And that's okay. It doesn't mean my apartment is a failure. It's just real. It's just the way a life actually looks, with its incomplete things and its slow accumulations and its gentle neglect of non-urgent business.

I'm trying to bring this same grace to my creative projects, my self-improvement attempts, my half-learned skills. I'm trying to see the incompletion not as a character flaw but as a sign that I'm alive and engaged, that there are more things I want to learn and try than I have time for, which seems like a good problem to have. I'm trying to write from the space of "still learning" rather than "not yet good enough." They're the same statement, but the emotional quality is completely different.

This is what I've been thinking about lately: the strange comfort of incomplete things. The way everything I care about is still becoming. The way I myself am still becoming. The way that might be exactly as it should be, and the only real failing would be to stop showing up for it.

# The Geography of Memory and Why Forgetting Might Be More Important Than We Think

There's a peculiar experience I've been thinking about lately—that moment when you return to a place after years away and find yourself shocked by how small it is. The elementary school playground that once seemed to sprawl endlessly now fits comfortably within a few hundred feet. The neighborhood that defined your entire world reveals itself to have been only three blocks in any direction. Your childhood home, remembered as a sprawling mansion, turns out to be a modest ranch house indistinguishable from its neighbors.

This phenomenon speaks to something profound about memory, time, and the self. We tend to think of memory as a recording device—faithful, retrievable, objective. But it's nothing of the sort. Memory is instead a story we tell ourselves, and like all stories, it changes each time we tell it. We remember not what happened, but what we remember having remembered, a kind of infinite regress that would be depressing if it weren't so fundamentally human.

I've been thinking about this because I recently tried to reconstruct a conversation I had with a friend maybe fifteen years ago. I remembered it as profound, a turning point, something that shifted my understanding of myself. But when I tried to recall the actual words, the actual substance of what was said, I found nothing. The feeling remained—a warmth, a sense of being understood—but the specifics had evaporated completely. And I wondered: if I can't remember the content, did it ever happen the way I remember it? Or did I remember only the emotional residue, and my mind constructed the rest?

This is where it gets interesting. Because our brains are apparently quite good at this—at filling in the gaps, at constructing coherent narratives from fragmentary data. It's called confabulation, and it's not a bug in our cognitive system, it's a feature. We need our memories to make sense, to cohere, to form a continuous narrative that is "me" across time. Without this storytelling, we would be scattered beings, unable to maintain identity or purpose.

But this raises the question: how much of who we are is real, and how much is our brain's fiction about who we are?

I think this matters more than we typically acknowledge. We go through life treating ourselves as the protagonists of an objective narrative—this is what happened to me, this is who I am, this is what I want. But if memory is fundamentally unreliable, then the self is built on sand. The person you remember being, the decisions that shaped you, the slights that wounded you, the triumphs that validated you—all of these are subject to the constant revision of a mind that is far more focused on coherence than accuracy.

There's something liberating about this, I think, though it took me a while to see it. If the stories we tell about ourselves aren't fixed, if they're not objective records of what actually happened, then we have more freedom to rewrite them than we might think. Not in a dishonest way, but in a way that acknowledges that there are always multiple true interpretations of any event, and the story we choose to tell about it shapes who we become.

Consider a failure, something you did badly or something that was done to you. In one version of the story, it's proof of your incompetence or victimhood. It becomes part of the narrative of a certain kind of self. But the same event could also be remembered as a learning experience, a moment that taught you something crucial, a necessary part of your growth. Both stories might be true. Both use the same factual materials. But they build different selves.

The question then becomes: which story should you tell?

I bring this up because I think we're living in an era of obsessive memorialization. We document everything—our experiences, our meals, our thoughts, our locations. We photograph moments instead of experiencing them. We record conversations instead of forgetting them. We maintain permanent records of every stupid thing we've ever said online. And I wonder if this is actually harmful to us, if it's interfering with a process that's meant to be lossy.

Maybe forgetting is a feature, not a bug. Maybe the way memories decay and transform is not a failure of our brains but a successful mechanism for psychological survival and growth. If we remembered everything with perfect clarity, we might be crushed under the weight of our own histories. Every embarrassment, every failure, every moment of pain would remain forever at the same emotional temperature. We would be unable to move past things because we would be unable to truly forget them.

But when memory fades, something interesting happens. The emotional charge bleeds away first. You might remember that you were humiliated in the eighth grade, but if you can't quite recall the specifics anymore, the feeling of shame loses its teeth. The event becomes smaller, not because it mattered less, but because it matters less now. And that's healthy. That's growth.

I've been reading a lot of philosophy lately, which is a nice way of saying I've been confused and trying to read my way out of it. One of the things that strikes me across different philosophical traditions is how often they arrive at the insight that the self is not a fixed thing—it's a process, a becoming, a constant renewal. Even our bodies completely replace themselves every several years. Every cell is new. So in what sense is the person you are today the same person you were seven years ago?

And yet there's continuity. There's a narrative through-line. There's something that feels like "me" that persists even as everything physical and mental is constantly being replaced. I think that "me" is not a substance but a story, and like all stories, it lives in the realm of meaning rather than physical fact. Which is to say it's real—stories are real, they shape how we live and who we become—but it's not factual in the way we usually mean.

This reminds me of something I read about the Japanese tea ceremony, this idea of wabi-sabi, the beauty in impermanence and imperfection. The philosophy underlying it is that things are beautiful precisely because they are temporary, because they decay, because they cannot be frozen in time. A person is the same way. You are beautiful and interesting not despite the fact that you're constantly changing and forgetting, but because of it. The you of today is not the you of yesterday, and that's not a tragedy, it's a gift.

But then I think about all the ways we try to resist this. We take anti-aging supplements. We try to preserve our youthful appearances. We cling to grudges and traumas, treating them as if they define us permanently. We insist on being right, on maintaining consistent positions, even when holding them becomes painful. We resist change, resist forgetting, resist the natural entropy that is built into existence itself.

Maybe there's another way. Maybe the task of a lifetime is not to accumulate, not to build, not to achieve and preserve, but to develop the capacity to let go. Not recklessly—I'm not suggesting we should forget what matters or lose our moral sensibility. But to hold things lightly. To remember that our stories about ourselves are stories, not facts. To allow ourselves to be wrong, to change, to grow into people we couldn't have predicted.

I think about how people often ask "what do you want to be when you grow up?" and how the question assumes a fixed end-state, as if you're moving toward some final form that you'll eventually reach and then remain. But that's not how life works. You don't become an adult and then stop becoming. You're always becoming something else. And the question should maybe be "what kind of person do you want to be becoming?" Because that's all you ever actually have—the direction of your change, not the destination.

The reason I keep thinking about memory and forgetting is because I think it touches something essential about how to live well. If you can't let things go, if you're constantly maintaining and defending a fixed narrative about who you are, you suffer. You suffer because life is inherently about change, and if you're resisting that, you're resisting life itself. But if you can develop the ability to hold your stories more lightly, to remember that you're constantly being remade, to allow yourself to forget what doesn't serve you anymore—then there's a kind of freedom in that.

This doesn't mean forgetting ethics or accountability. It means maybe not holding yourself to standards that are inhuman, that assume you're capable of perfect consistency, perfect memory, perfect virtue. It means recognizing that the person who did something terrible in the past is not exactly the same person you are now, and while you should acknowledge and make amends for what was done, you don't have to carry the full weight of that identity forever.

I think about this in terms of how we speak to ourselves, too. So much self-help and therapeutic language is about understanding your past trauma, identifying how it shaped you, owning your story. And there's value in that—buried awareness is often worse than explicit awareness. But I wonder sometimes if we over-identify with these stories, if we treat them as more determinative than they need to be.

You had a painful childhood. Yes. That shaped you. Yes. But do you have to be a person with a painful childhood? Or can you be someone who went through painful things and became someone interesting partly because of it? Can you forget the specifics of the pain while retaining the wisdom it taught you? Can you remember not the emotional charge but the lessons?

I don't have answers to any of this. I'm just thinking out loud about things that seem important and true but that we don't talk about much. Maybe because forgetting is not valued in our culture. We valorize memory—good memory is a sign of intelligence, of conscientiousness. We talk about preserving history, not forgetting the past. And these are important. But we don't talk much about the wisdom of forgetting, the health in letting go, the growth that comes from not being trapped in everything you once were.

The neighborhood of my childhood is still there, still small. But I'm not small anymore, and I'm glad I can't remember it the way I did when I was a child. The distortion of memory that makes it seem smaller now is not a failure. It's evidence that I've grown, that I've developed a larger frame of reference, that the things that once seemed to encompass my entire world have become a manageable piece of a much larger life. And that's what I want for my memory of things—that they fade, that they transform, that they become smaller and more manageable as I become larger and more capable of holding what life brings.

# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Transitions

There's a moment I think about often—probably too often—that happened on an ordinary Tuesday morning last spring. I was sitting in a coffee shop, the kind that's trying very hard to be a specific aesthetic of "cozy urban sophistication," all Edison bulbs and reclaimed wood and a barista who knew everyone's name. I wasn't particularly happy or sad. I wasn't waiting for anything important. But I became suddenly, intensely aware that I was alive, that this moment was happening, that the woman next to me was reading a book with a cracked spine, and that the light was hitting the table at an angle that made the coffee ripple slightly when someone walked past.

This awareness lasted maybe forty-five seconds. Then it was gone, swallowed back into the normal current of consciousness. But it left me thinking: why do we have these moments? What are they for?

I think they might be for nothing. That might be the point.

We're so accustomed to assigning utility to everything—to asking "what's the point?" until we've miniaturized all of life into a series of productivity metrics and goal-completion markers—that we've almost forgotten there's another category of human experience. The experiences that don't lead anywhere. The moments that don't accumulate toward something else. Just moments, in themselves, complete and sufficient.

The coffee shop moment came back to me because I was reading about a concept in Buddhism called "suchness"—the idea that things are simply as they are, and that seeing them clearly without layering interpretations on top is a kind of enlightenment. Not a dramatic enlightenment with flashing lights and spiritual trumpets, but a quiet one. The enlightenment of noticing that the cup is a cup, the table is a table, the morning light is just morning light, and that this is already enough.

I've been thinking a lot lately about transitions, too. We treat them as problems to be solved—moving from one place to another, one job to another, one phase of life to another. We have advice columns and self-help books and therapists all dedicated to "managing" transitions, as though they're something to be gotten through efficiently so we can arrive at the next stable state. But what if transitions are actually where the interesting stuff lives?

Think about spring, which I've been experiencing with unusual attention this year. Everyone talks about spring as though it's a destination, a state to be achieved: spring is here, spring has sprung, spring is in full bloom. But spring itself is not a stable state at all. Spring is pure transition. Every day in spring is literally different from the last one—there's something new in bloom, something else is changing. If you try to capture spring as a state, you miss it. The only way to actually experience spring is to be aware of the constant, gentle flux. The same tree blooms a little more each day. The same grass grows a little taller. The same birds' chorus gets a little louder and more complex.

A friend of mine is between jobs right now. She's been calling this her "liminal period," with a sort of self-aware irony, but I think she's onto something real. She has flexible days now. She wakes up and doesn't immediately know what the day requires of her. This is making her anxious because we're all raised to believe that unstructured time is failure-time, wasted-time, the time in which you're not becoming whoever you're supposed to become. But what she's discovered, almost by accident, is that the unstructured time is when she actually thinks. When she wonders about things. When she reads books just because they interest her. When she sits in parks and watches people without any particular purpose.

She'll get a new job eventually. The structured time will return. And some of what she's enjoying will be displaced by the obligations that come with being employed. I don't think that's tragic, exactly—we need structure, and structure itself isn't bad. But I do think there's something worth noticing about how we treat the gaps between structures as though they're just dead time, waiting time, rather than recognizing that gaps might be their own kind of existence.

I've been reading a lot of poetry lately, which is a thing I do when I'm unsettled without quite knowing why. Poetry is the genre most interested in the spaces between things—between words, between meaning and sound, between what's said and what's implied. Poetry loves transitions. It's almost all transitions. A good poem is basically a series of small philosophical collisions, moments where one image or idea bumps up against another and something sparks in the space between them.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver where she asks, "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" It's become so iconic that it's almost been drained of power—it's on posters and Instagram graphics and corporate wellness slides. But reading it actually, in context, it's a different thing. It's not a demand that you be impressive or productive. It's a genuine question. What are you going to do with it? 

And I think the honest answer, for most people, most of the time, is: I'm going to live it. I'm going to have moments and conversations and breakfasts and small insights and frustrations and boring Tuesday afternoons and occasional flashes of beauty and long stretches where nothing much happens. I'm going to exist in time, move through it, watch it change around me. And that's already quite a lot.

There's this thing that happens in conversations where someone says something true and everyone stops talking for a second, not an awkward silence but a real one, a silence with weight in it. Those moments feel important to me. They feel like windows into how we actually are with each other when we're not performing. They're not lasting. They're not productive. But they matter.

I've become fascinated by the idea that some of the most important things in life might be the ones that don't "matter" in any measurable sense. A conversation that changes your perspective but doesn't change your job or your status. A book that reshapes how you think but doesn't advance your career. A friendship that nourishes you but exists mostly in quiet moments with no story to tell about it afterward. A walk where nothing happens except that you see some trees and sky and feel your own existence for a while.

The productivity culture we live in is so loudly insistent that these things should be optimized—that even rest should be "restorative," even hobbies should build toward something, even relationships should "bring value" to your life. And I'm not immune to this. I notice that even my thinking about the value of unstructured time is partly an attempt to justify it in terms that our culture will recognize as valid. See, I'm saying, the unstructured time is actually valuable because it develops your thinking and makes you more creative and resilient. So it counts.

But what if some things don't count? What if they don't need to count? What if the point of breakfast is just breakfast—the taste of it, the company possibly, the simple fact of fuel and nourishment and a moment in the day? What if the point of a walk is just the walking?

I think about death sometimes—not in a morbid way, but as a practical reality that shapes everything. We're all practicing dying, in a way. Every moment that passes is a moment we won't get back. Every day we're a little closer to the end. This could be depressing information, and it can be, but it can also be clarifying. It makes some things seem more important and other things seem less important. All those accumulated achievements and status markers—they're real, they matter in their way, but they also don't matter at all in the face of the actual, lived experience of being alive.

My therapist (yes, I have one, and yes, this is relevant) once said something that stuck with me. She said that a lot of suffering comes from the gap between how we think life should be and how it actually is. Life should be productive and meaningful and leading somewhere. Life should fit into a narrative with a clear arc. Life should make sense. But actual life is mostly just... life. Mundane, repetitive, sideways, full of things that don't lead anywhere. And the suffering isn't in the mundanity—it's in wanting it to be otherwise.

I've been trying to practice noticing things as they are. Not as they should be, not as they might lead to, not as they mean or represent. Just as they are. The coffee tastes like coffee. The morning is morning. The person across from me on the train is just a person existing in their own interior world that I'll never have access to. This should be obvious, but I find it genuinely difficult.

There's something about being human in 2024—whenever you're reading this, though probably some version of this is always true—that makes us resistant to just existing. We're always evaluating, always narrating, always trying to extract meaning or productivity or validation from every moment. We're performing our lives as much as living them. We're curating our own experience as it happens, imagining how we'll tell it to someone else, how it will look when we've turned it into a story.

I wonder what it would be like to just stop. To have a day where you don't narrate it, don't evaluate it, don't try to make it meaningful or productive or share-worthy. Just have the day. Just be in it. I've never quite managed it, but I think that might be close to what people mean by peace.

There's a Japanese concept—I'm probably butchering this—of "ma," which refers to the space between things, the emptiness that makes the things meaningful. In music, it's the silence between notes. In design, it's the white space. In conversation, it's the pause. The idea is that what we usually think of as the "content" is only meaningful because of the empty space around it. Take away all the silence, all the space, and you don't get more music, you get noise.

I think a life is like that too. We think the meaningful stuff is the achievements, the relationships, the accumulation of experiences and credentials and stories. But maybe the meaningful stuff is actually the spaces between—the quiet moments, the fallow periods, the transitions, the waiting, the ordinary days. These aren't gaps that need to be filled. They're the structure that allows everything else to have shape.

I don't know if I believe this entirely. I have ambitions and goals and things I want to accomplish, and I think those matter. I'm not trying to argue for the complete surrender to passivity. But I do think we've gotten the proportion wrong. We've made the ma into the thing and the thing into the ma. We've made the spaces between matter less than the peaks. And I think if we could somehow recalibrate—not giving up on meaning or productivity or direction, but just getting the volume right on all the in-between moments—we might find that life is already here, already happening, already enough.

That Tuesday in the coffee shop, when I suddenly noticed that I was alive—I think that was the point of that day. Not that something happened on that day, not that it led somewhere, not that I learned something I could make productive use of. The point was just: I was alive, light was hitting a table, someone was reading, and for a moment I noticed. That was the whole thing. That was enough.

# The Peculiar Grace of Getting Lost

There's something about being genuinely lost that strips away the modern world's comfortable pretenses. Not lost in an abstract sense—not lost in purpose or direction, though those are their own particular hells—but lost in the most literal, geographical way. You've turned onto a road that looked right, or followed directions that were confidently given but apparently incorrect, and now you cannot quite figure out where you are. The maps on your phone might not be helping. The sun is setting. You've been driving in circles for twenty minutes.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, particularly after a friend mentioned that her teenage daughter had never been properly lost. Never gone out with uncertain directions, never had to ask a stranger for help, never felt that particular blend of anxiety and adventure that comes from not knowing where you are. The GPS has eliminated something from the human experience, and I'm not entirely sure what we've gained in return.

When I was young, being lost was a rite of passage. My parents would let me wander the neighborhood with the vague instruction to "be home by dark," and I would inevitably end up several blocks further than intended, squinting at street signs and trying to reconstruct the turns I'd made. There was genuine fear in it, yes—what if I couldn't find my way back? What if I had to ask a stranger? What if my mother worried?—but there was also freedom. I was navigating the world by my own judgment and memory. The world felt larger, less predetermined.

I think there's something about lostness that modern life is actively designed to prevent, and I'm not sure that's entirely good.

Consider the psychology of it. When you're lost, you must become observant. You notice which way the sun is moving, whether the streets are widening or narrowing, whether you recognize landmarks. You become attuned to your environment in a way that GPS prevents. When you're following turn-by-turn directions, you're in a kind of cognitive autopilot—turn right at the next light, continue 2.3 miles, turn left. The route is disembodied, abstract. You could be anywhere, following any set of instructions. But when you're lost, the place becomes real. You notice that there's a distinctive red brick building on this corner, that the street slopes downward to your left, that you've definitely seen this church before, wasn't it three blocks back?

There's also something about getting lost that forces a kind of radical acceptance. You cannot worry your way to knowing where you are. You cannot think yourself unlost. You must actually do something—turn around, ask for directions, look at a physical map, try a different route. There's a problem and a required action. It's almost meditative in its clarity, once you accept that you are, in fact, lost.

I wonder if this is part of why so many people find hiking or backpacking valuable. You go out deliberately to get away from the systems that keep you located—cellular data, GPS, the constant pinpointing that modern technology allows. And many people find this deeply restorative. They come back transformed by the experience of not knowing, for a time, exactly where they are. The uncertainty becomes freedom.

Of course, there's a dark side to this romanticism. Getting lost can be genuinely dangerous. A woman lost in the wrong part of town at night faces different risks than a man. A child lost for real—not playing lost, but truly separated from their parents—might be experiencing genuine terror. There's a reason GPS technology has been celebrated: it makes travel safer, allows real-time location sharing, prevents people from disappearing. The parent who can track their teenager's location via their phone has legitimate reasons for that parental surveillance. The elderly person with dementia can be found if they wander.

But I think we've overcorrected. We've designed a world where uncertainty is treated as a problem to be solved, rather than a condition to be navigated. And I'm not sure we're better for it.

There's a concept in psychology called "situational awareness," and it's something that's been studied extensively in emergency response and self-defense contexts. People who are paying attention to their surroundings—noticing exits, recognizing patterns, reading social cues—tend to respond better to unexpected situations. But this kind of awareness requires a certain amount of attention, the kind that gets atrophied when you're following exact directions on a screen.

I'm not suggesting we throw away our phones or go back to paper maps exclusively. That would be performative and unrealistic. But I think there's something worth preserving about the experience of not knowing, of having to navigate by observation and intuition rather than instruction.

My grandfather had an interesting approach to this. He would deliberately take wrong turns when driving somewhere new, just to force himself to figure out how to get back. He wanted to build a mental map of the area, and he knew that learning required some failure, some disorientation. He would end up in random neighborhoods, dead ends, confusing intersections, and he would find his way back by logic and attention. It made him an unusually good driver, I think—intuitive about how cities were laid out, comfortable in unfamiliar places.

There's also something about being lost that's good for humility. When everything is directing you, when you have perfect information, there's a tendency to move through the world as though everything should conform to your expectations. You become entitled to certainty. But when you're lost, you're reminded that the world is larger than your knowledge of it, more complex than your maps suggest. You're reminded that you don't actually know as much as you thought you did.

I've noticed this in other domains too. People who've done a lot of reading in physical libraries have a different relationship with knowledge than people who've only searched online. Yes, online searching is faster and more efficient. You can find exactly what you're looking for in seconds. But there's something lost in that efficiency. When you had to browse the stacks, you encountered books you weren't looking for. You'd be searching for something about medieval history and stumble upon a fascinating book about textile production, which led you to another book about trade routes, which connected to something else entirely. These unexpected connections shaped how you thought. But they weren't efficient.

Efficiency is a genuine good in many contexts, but it's become our primary value, and I'm not sure that's right.

There's also something to be said about the emotional texture of being lost. Yes, there's anxiety, particularly in the first moments of realization. But there can also be a kind of adventure, a openness to whatever happens. You might stumble upon a wonderful restaurant you never would have found otherwise. You might have an interesting conversation with someone who gives you directions. You might discover a beautiful street or a view you wouldn't have seen. The lostness becomes generative, productive of experience in a way that arriving efficiently at your destination might not be.

I think modern life, for many of us, has become too predictable. We know where we're going before we go there—we've looked it up online, read reviews, seen pictures. We know what to order before we arrive at the restaurant. Our social feeds are algorithmically curated to show us more of what we already like. The surprises have been minimized, engineered out of the system. And while this reduces certain kinds of friction, it also reduces the richness of engagement with the world.

Sometimes I deliberately take long routes when I'm driving, or wander into neighborhoods I don't know. It's a small rebellion against the optimization of existence. And inevitably, I find something I wouldn't have found otherwise. Sometimes it's just a pretty street corner. Sometimes it's a good bookstore or a interesting mural. Sometimes it's the simple experience of not knowing where I am, and then figuring it out.

My friend's daughter, the one who's never been properly lost, is starting to drive. I wonder what her experience of the world will be like if she's always being directed, always knowing where she is. I wonder if she'll develop the same intuitive sense of place that my grandfather had. I wonder if she'll ever experience that peculiar combination of anxiety and freedom that comes from genuine disorientation.

I think we should let people get lost more often. Obviously, not dangerously, not in ways that cause real harm. But in controlled ways, deliberately. Let them navigate by observation. Let them ask strangers for directions. Let them experience the world as larger and less knowable than their maps suggest.

There's a kind of wisdom that only comes from lostness, from realizing that the world doesn't conform to your expectations and plans. And we need that wisdom now, I think, when so much of life is algorithmically predicted, when certainty is sold to us as a premium product, when the unknown has been rebranded as a problem to be solved rather than a condition to be experienced.

Getting lost, real lost, forces you to slow down. It forces you to pay attention. It forces you to accept that you don't know everything, that your plans can be disrupted, that the world is still larger than your knowledge of it. And maybe, in a world that's trying very hard to make everything predictable and controllable, that's exactly the grace we need most.

# On the Strange Comfort of Uncertainty

I've been thinking lately about how much of my existence is spent in the space between knowing and not knowing, and how oddly peaceful that can be if you let it.

There's a philosophical position called epistemic humility—the acknowledgment that there are vast territories of things we cannot know, may never know, and perhaps shouldn't spend all our energy trying to know. It's become fashionable in some circles to dismiss this as cowardly relativism, a way of avoiding hard truth. But I think that misses something important. Epistemic humility isn't about indifference to truth. It's about honesty regarding the shape of your own ignorance.

Consider how much of daily life proceeds on assumptions we never examine. You probably don't know exactly how your smartphone works, but you use it. You don't understand the biochemistry of your own digestion, but you eat. You've never verified most of the historical facts you believe to be true, but you organize your understanding of the world around them anyway. This isn't weakness or stupidity—it's the only possible way to function. We necessarily outsource most of our knowledge.

But there's something deeper than practical ignorance at work. There are things we don't know that we *can't* know, at least not with certainty, and yet we must act as if we do. Do you have free will? Is consciousness fundamental or emergent? Why is there something rather than nothing? What, if anything, lies beyond our universe? These questions have occupied humanity's greatest minds for millennia, and we're not obviously closer to answers now than we were. We've gotten better at asking them, perhaps. We've eliminated some possible answers. But the core mysteries remain.

A rational person might respond that since we can't know these things, we should focus on what we can know: empirical facts, testable hypotheses, observable phenomena. And there's real wisdom in that. The scientific method has been magnificently productive precisely because it bracketed off the unanswerable questions and focused on the answerable ones. But I wonder if something gets lost when we treat that useful methodological limitation as if it were the shape of reality itself.

Most of what makes life meaningful seems to exist in the spaces the scientific method deliberately ignores. Love, beauty, purpose, meaning itself—these are real features of human experience, but they don't lend themselves to the kind of verification and falsification that characterizes scientific knowledge. This doesn't make them less real. It makes them real in a different way.

I think this is why so much modern anxiety seems to stem from a kind of mismatch. We're told that only scientific knowledge is real knowledge, that we should base our lives on facts and evidence, which is good advice. But then we look at our lives and discover that the parts that matter most don't fit neatly into that framework. So we either pretend they do (reducing love to chemistry, beauty to pattern recognition, meaning to evolutionary utility), which leaves the territory inadequately mapped, or we feel guilty for caring about things we can't fully explain.

What if we didn't have to choose?

I've noticed something interesting about conversations with people I respect. The ones that feel most genuinely intellectually alive aren't the ones where someone proves they're right and everyone else is wrong. They're the conversations where people sit together in uncertainty and explore it honestly. Someone says, "I don't know, but here's what I think, and I'm genuinely uncertain about this aspect," and something real becomes possible. The pretense drops. People stop performing knowledge and start actually thinking.

There's a particular quality to this kind of conversation. It's humble without being wishy-washy. It's honest without being cynical. It holds strong views while remaining genuinely open to challenge. I find this rare enough that when it happens, I notice.

I've been thinking about why uncertainty feels more true than certainty in these moments. Certainty is often a performance—a necessary one, sometimes. If you're a bridge engineer, you need to perform certainty. People need to trust that your calculations are sound. But underneath that performance is always an awareness of what you don't know: how the materials will age, what forces you haven't anticipated, how the bridge will be used in ways you never imagined. The performance of certainty sits atop a foundation of uncertainty. The performance works only if you respect the foundation.

When people pretend their uncertainty doesn't exist, or try to eliminate it entirely, something goes wrong. The performance becomes totalizing. It eats the space where genuine thinking can happen. You're not exploring ideas anymore; you're defending territory.

I wonder if this is related to why people often report feeling more fulfilled by difficult pursuits than by easy victories. A hobby you're good at from the start provides less sustained satisfaction than one where you're perpetually inadequate, learning, surprising yourself. A relationship where everything is settled and clear can become stale compared to one that continues to reveal new depths after years together. A religion that answers all questions might be less spiritually alive than one that deepens the questions while pursuing them.

Not because difficulty is good in itself. But because difficulty keeps you engaged. It keeps the space open.

There's also something interesting about how certainty corrupts. This seems to happen across domains. The academic becomes so convinced of their theoretical framework that they can no longer see what doesn't fit. The activist becomes so certain of the righteousness of their cause that they stop examining their own methods. The religious fundamentalist, the political ideologue, the true believer of any stripe—they all seem to experience a particular kind of blindness that comes from resolving uncertainty too conclusively.

Whereas the people who seem wisest—and I'm thinking here of the actual wise people I've known, not characters in stories—tend to have a curious absence of the need to be right all the time. This isn't because they're relativists or don't care about truth. It's because they've somehow developed the capacity to hold their own views without needing them to be universally true. They can think you're wrong about something important without needing you to admit it. They can be confident in their own choices without judging yours. They seem to have made peace with the basic fact that reasonable people can come to different conclusions about most things that matter.

How does one develop that quality? I'm genuinely not sure. Possibly through experience—enough experience with being wrong, or incomplete, or surprised by how you misunderstood something. Possibly through some kind of spiritual practice that decouples your sense of self-worth from your being right. Possibly through having loved people deeply enough that you have to accept their otherness, their irreducible differentness from you, and still love them anyway.

Or possibly it's just a personality trait. Some people are born with more tolerance for ambiguity. That seems unfair, but life is unfair in that way.

What interests me is that this quality—call it intellectual humility, or epistemic modesty—doesn't seem to make people less effective. If anything, I've noticed the opposite. The people who've had to live with deep uncertainty often seem more able to actually change course when new information suggests they should. They're less invested in defending a fixed position. They can see what's actually in front of them rather than what they expected to see.

And there's a strange freedom in it. If you've accepted that you don't know, that you might be wrong, that your understanding is necessarily incomplete, then you're freed from the exhausting work of defending an untenable position. You can actually think. You can actually listen. You can actually change your mind.

I've been thinking about the difference between doubt and faith as opposing forces, the way we usually frame it. But what if doubt and faith aren't opposites? What if they're partners? What if genuine faith is precisely faith in something—someone—that you can't reduce to certainty? You believe in it anyway. You commit to it anyway. But that commitment doesn't require you to pretend you understand it fully.

This might be why many of the most thoughtful religious people I know seem less concerned with proving God's existence and more concerned with the lived question of how to respond to the possibility of God. The uncertainty isn't a problem to solve. It's the terrain where actual faith happens.

I think this extends to how we live. Most of the important decisions we make—who to marry, what work to pursue, where to live, how to raise children—all of these are made under conditions of radical uncertainty. You can gather information, you can think carefully, you can consult wise people. But ultimately you're committing to something you can't fully know the consequences of. You're leaping.

We usually present this leap as if it's unfortunate—as if the ideal would be perfect information and certain outcomes. But maybe that's backwards. Maybe the meaning of the leap depends on it being a leap. A marriage would be one thing if you could be certain it would last forever and be perfectly fulfilling. But the willingness to commit despite uncertainty—that's a different thing. A richer thing.

I notice that when I think about my own life, the moments that felt most real, most formative, most meaningful, were nearly always moments of uncertainty. The times when I had to act without knowing what would happen. The times when I had to trust something that couldn't be proven. The times when I had to stay present to something I didn't fully understand.

The times when I thought I knew are already fading. The times when I was genuinely uncertain, genuinely alive to what was in front of me—those are the ones that stay.

Maybe this is what growing up is: not the accumulation of certainties, but the development of the capacity to live well within uncertainty. Not the elimination of doubt, but the achievement of enough equanimity about doubt that it doesn't paralyze you.

I'm struck by how much energy we waste trying to eliminate uncertainty that can't actually be eliminated. We gather more and more information as if the information will eventually solve something it structurally can't solve. We compile lists of reasons to prove our position, as if the list will ever be comprehensive enough to stop the conversation. We defend our views with more and more force, as if sufficient volume could make them echo back as certainty.

What if we stopped? What if we got comfortable enough with uncertainty that we could actually live?

This doesn't mean abandoning the pursuit of truth or the exercise of reason. It means contextualizing it. Truth-seeking is a real and valuable enterprise. But it exists within a context of uncertainty that we can't escape and probably shouldn't try to. Reason is a powerful tool. But reason itself tells us it has limits.

And within those limits, at the edges of what we can know, is where the most important human stuff happens. Where we make choices. Where we love. Where we create meaning. Where we sometimes encounter something that seems to exceed the categories we have for understanding it.

We spend so much time and energy trying to reduce the territory of uncertainty, trying to master it, trying to make ourselves safe from it. But I wonder if the actual safety lies in acceptance. Not passive acceptance, not giving up. But active acceptance—a clear-eyed recognition of what you do and don't know, what you can and can't control, what remains mysterious despite your best efforts to illuminate it.

And then living well anyway.

That's the thing about uncertainty. It's not hostile to life. Often it's the ground of the most interesting parts of it. The parts where you're genuinely alive, genuinely engaged, genuinely open to being surprised.

The parts worth living for.

# The Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that strange and often-despised state of mind that modern life seems designed to eliminate. We have solutions for boredom now—infinite streams of content, notifications pinging constantly, entertainment on demand at every moment. Yet somehow boredom persists, and I wonder if we're making a mistake in trying to eradicate it entirely.

There's something peculiar about boredom that I think we've lost sight of. It's not actually the enemy we've been taught it is. In fact, I'd argue that boredom might be one of the most underrated and misunderstood mental states available to us—a kind of gift we keep trying to return unopened.

When I was a child, boredom was unavoidable. It would descend on lazy summer afternoons when I'd exhausted the entertainment options available to me. No phone in my pocket. No algorithms suggesting what I should do next. Just me, the suffocating heat, and the persistent question of what to do with myself. What I remember now, looking back across the decades, is that boredom was always temporary. It was the gateway to something else.

Sometimes I'd wander into the backyard and become fascinated by ants. I'd spend an hour—genuinely, a full hour—watching them navigate their tiny highways, rebuilding their paths after I'd destructively drawn lines through them with a stick. I wasn't entertained, exactly. But I wasn't bored anymore either. The boredom had cracked open into something deeper: observation, curiosity, a kind of meditative attention.

Other times, boredom led me to create things. I'd sketch random faces in notebooks. I'd write silly stories about my pet hamster going on space adventures. I'd rearrange my room for the hundredth time, imagining it as different places—a spaceship, a cozy cabin, a detective's office. This wasn't because these activities were particularly good. It's because they were better than the itch of boredom, and better than the paralysis of having unlimited options.

There's research now that suggests boredom actually activates the default mode network in our brains—the same network associated with creative thinking, daydreaming, and insight. When we're not focused on external stimuli, our brains don't go blank. They become more internally active. They wander. They make connections between disparate ideas. Some of our best thinking happens when we're supposedly doing nothing at all.

But we've become terrified of this state. We've been sold the idea that attention is a precious commodity and that idleness is waste. Every moment should be productive. Every moment should be entertaining. Every moment should be accounted for and optimized. This belief has colonized even our rest—we consume entertainment while eating, while exercising, while commuting. We fill the spaces between things with content. We've made boredom into a kind of enemy of the optimal life.

I think this is a catastrophic error.

There's a particular tyranny that comes from the constant availability of entertainment. It's the tyranny of choice that prevents us from making any choice at all. Last night, I had a few hours free and the entire world's entertainment at my fingertips. I spent forty minutes scrolling through options without watching anything, the pleasure centers of my brain muted by the paradox of infinite choice. Finally, I put the devices away and sat with a book I'd started weeks ago. The strange thing was that the book, which had felt "okay" before, suddenly seemed fascinating. Had it improved? No. Had I? Actually, yes. I had become less distracted, more present, more capable of sustained attention.

This is what boredom can do: it clears the space for genuine engagement.

There's also something about boredom that's almost spiritual, though I'm hesitant to use that word because it's become so loaded with new age connotations. What I mean is that boredom is one of the few states that forces us to confront ourselves. When there's nothing pulling at our attention, we're alone with our own minds. This can be uncomfortable—that's partly why we flee from it. We encounter our anxieties, our dissatisfactions, our nagging sense that something isn't quite right. But this discomfort is also honest. It's real. It's the beginning of actual change.

Some of the most important moments in my life have come after periods of boredom-forced reflection. A crushing stretch of time with nothing to do led me to finally ask myself what I actually wanted to do with my life, rather than what I thought I should do. A rainy weekend with no entertainment options led to a conversation with a friend that fundamentally changed how I understood myself. A boring commute led me to notice something about my hometown that I'd been missing for years, and that observation sparked an entirely new interest.

Modern productivity culture has made us suspicious of these periods. They seem wasteful. They seem like time not being optimized. But I think the opposite is true: some of life's most important optimizations can only happen when we stop trying to optimize every moment.

There's also a political dimension to this that interests me. The constant stream of entertainment and information serves a particular function in our culture: it pacifies. It keeps us perpetually distracted. It prevents the kind of sustained, contemplative attention that might lead to critical thinking. When you're constantly in a state of stimulation, it's harder to think deeply about difficult things. Boredom, boring as it is, creates the conditions for genuine thought about what might actually matter.

I'm not saying we should all renounce modern entertainment and go live as ascetics. That's not practical or even desirable. But I think we should reconsider our relationship with boredom. Instead of seeing it as something to eliminate at all costs, maybe we could see it as a signal. A signal that we need to do something different. Not necessarily something more entertaining—something more real.

When my kids complain of boredom, my first instinct is to suggest something they could do, some entertainment I could provide. But I've started resisting that instinct. Because boredom is theirs to solve, and in solving it themselves—sometimes by doing nothing, sometimes by finding something unexpected, sometimes just by sitting with the discomfort—they're developing something important. They're developing the capacity to be present with themselves. They're developing creativity born from necessity rather than provided by consumption.

I think about the artists and writers and inventors who came before the age of infinite distraction. Many of them spent long hours in apparent idleness. They took walks. They stared out windows. They sat in cafes and observed people. They seemed to understand, intuitively, that thinking requires space. That creation requires boredom. That some of life's best discoveries happen not when we're frantically searching for them but when we've stopped looking and have simply become open to what might arrive.

The economist John Maynard Keynes predicted in the 1930s that by the end of the twentieth century, we'd have solved the problem of scarcity and would be faced with a new challenge: what to do with all our leisure time. He thought we'd need to figure out how to enjoy ourselves, how to find meaning in activities that weren't work. What actually happened was different. We invented new forms of work. We invented new things to want. We made leisure into productivity. We couldn't actually relax if we tried, because relaxation itself became something to optimize and monetize.

But maybe the real skill we need to develop is the skill of living without constant stimulation. The skill of being bored without needing to fix it immediately. The skill of sitting with discomfort without running toward entertainment. The skill of using those empty hours not for productivity but for something stranger and more valuable: just thinking. Just being.

I notice that the moments when I feel most alive are usually moments when I'm fully present in something. Not distracted. Not half-watching while scrolling. Not waiting for the next thing while experiencing this thing. These moments happen more frequently when I've created conditions for them—when I've turned off the notifications, when I've resisted the pull toward entertainment, when I've let myself be bored for long enough that boredom transformed into something else.

And I think that's what boredom really is, if we give it a chance: a threshold. A transitional state between distraction and engagement, between the surface of life and something deeper. We've become so afraid of the threshold that we've eliminated the possibility of what lies on the other side.

So maybe it's time to make friends with boredom again. Not because boredom itself is good—it's not, by definition. But because of what boredom makes possible when we don't immediately flee from it. The thinking. The creating. The noticing. The becoming aware of what we actually want rather than what we've been told to want. The simple human capacity to be present with ourselves and with the world.

That seems like a skill worth cultivating. Even if it requires tolerating the strange discomfort of having nothing to do.

Especially then, perhaps.

# On the Strange Gift of Attention in a Distracted Age

There's a peculiar magic that happens when you really watch something. Not the hurried glance we give to most of the world, but actual watching—the kind where your attention settles on a single point like a bird landing on a branch, and everything else falls away. I've been thinking about this a lot lately, particularly about how rare this experience has become, and how desperately we seem to need it.

Last week I watched a spider build a web. I didn't mean to—I was sitting on my porch with coffee, supposed to be checking emails on my phone, but the spider caught my eye. It was one of those garden spiders, yellow and black, methodical and unhurried. I set the phone down and just watched. For fifteen minutes, maybe twenty. I lost track of time in a way I almost never do anymore.

The spider worked in a spiral pattern, starting from the center and moving outward. Each leg moved with precise coordination, affixing the silk to anchor points on the fence and the porch railing. There was nothing particularly unusual happening—it was just a spider doing what spiders do. But somewhere in watching it, I felt something untangle in my chest. A kind of settling. A reminder that there was a world that operated according to its own logic, independent of my anxieties, my to-do lists, my half-formed worries about the future.

I wonder how many hours I've lost to distraction without even realizing it was happening. Not lost, exactly—that implies I had it and it was taken from me. Rather, hours I never quite possessed in the first place because my attention was scattered across fifteen different places simultaneously. I think about all the moments I've half-experienced: the meal I ate while working, the conversation I had while mentally composing an email, the sunset I photographed instead of watched.

There's this feeling I get sometimes, usually late at night, that I'm living my life in fast-forward, always moving to the next thing, the next notification, the next piece of information. And the peculiar irony is that all this access to more information, more connections, more entertainment than any human in history has ever had—it's somehow made us lonelier and more scattered. We're drowning in stimulation while starving for attention.

I've started noticing how differently people behave when they've actually decided to pay attention to something. There's a quality to their presence that changes. You can see it in someone's eyes when they're really listening versus when they're just waiting for their turn to talk. You can see it in how differently people draw when they're actually looking at what they're drawing versus working from memory. The results are night and day.

Children are like this naturally, before we train it out of them. I watched my nephew play with a cardboard box for an hour last month. Not a toy—a box. But in his mind, it was a spaceship, a fort, a mountain range, a car, a house. He was completely absorbed, moving between these different narratives with total commitment. His attention wasn't divided; it was fully deployed to this single object and the worlds he was constructing around it. And the remarkable thing was how calm he was. How content. There was no sense of missing out on something better that might be happening elsewhere.

Somewhere along the line, we've been convinced that attention is a commodity to be spent efficiently, that we should be multitasking, that the ability to rapidly shift focus between multiple streams of information is a virtue. Silicon Valley engineers have basically weaponized the human attention span, designing systems specifically to fracture our focus and keep us in a constant state of low-level arousal. Every notification, every red badge, every autoplay feature is a small hook designed to pull our attention away from whatever we're doing.

And the strange part is that we've internalized this. We've begun to feel like something is wrong if we're not feeling that constant pull, that constant stimulation. Boredom has become almost dangerous in our conception—a void that must be immediately filled. We've lost the ability to let our minds wander, to sit with our own thoughts, to experience the kind of deep focus that used to be the default state of human consciousness.

I read somewhere that the average person's attention span has decreased significantly in the last two decades. We're supposedly down to something like eight seconds before we need a new stimulus. That's less than a goldfish, the article said, as if we'd become somehow less intelligent, less capable than a fish. But I don't think that's quite right. It's not that we've become less capable of attention—it's that we've collectively decided to outsource that function to devices that are explicitly designed to prevent us from sustaining it.

What strikes me most is that we know this isn't making us happier. The data is pretty clear on this. More screen time correlates with increased anxiety, depression, and loneliness. More options correlates with more decision paralysis and less satisfaction. More information doesn't correlate with better decision-making. Yet we keep running toward these things, convinced that the next update, the next feature, the next notification will be the one that finally satisfies us.

There's something almost religious about the way we relate to our devices now. We check them first thing in the morning and last thing at night. We look at them when we're uncomfortable or anxious—not to solve anything, just to feel less alone with our thoughts. We photograph our experiences instead of living them, curating our lives for an invisible audience. We've built a whole secondary existence on screens, and increasingly, it feels more real and more important than the primary one.

But here's what I've started to notice: the moments that actually matter to me—the moments I think about later, that change something in how I see the world—those are almost always moments of genuine attention. Not the curated, carefully photographed moments. The messy, unfiltered ones where I was just present. The conversation with a friend where we actually got vulnerable. The moment I realized how my parent's hands had aged. The time I got lost in a city and had to actually look at where I was instead of following GPS. The spider building its web.

I think we're all starving for this but we don't quite know how to say it. We feel it as a vague dissatisfaction, a sense that something is missing. We try to fill it with more information, more entertainment, more connection through screens, but those things don't actually address the hunger. The hunger is for presence. For realness. For the experience of giving something our full attention and being changed by it.

There's a line in a poem I love by Mary Oliver: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" And I think about that whenever I catch myself reflexively reaching for my phone, and I think: not this. Not this scattered, half-present version of living. Not this constant reaching for the next thing while missing the current one.

I don't think the solution is to become a luddite or to completely unplug—that's not realistic for most of us, and honestly, technology has genuine benefits. But I think we need to become more intentional about where our attention goes. We need to treat it as the precious and finite resource it actually is.

I've been trying to practice something small: one thing at a time. Actually, fully, completely one thing at a time. When I eat, I eat. When I listen, I listen. When I work, I work. Not in a manic, focused way, but in a natural, absorbing way. And the strange thing is, when I actually do this, everything gets better. Work is more productive because I'm not divided. Relationships are deeper because the other person can feel that they have my full attention. Meals taste better. Walks are more interesting. The world becomes more vivid.

I think this is what people mean when they talk about mindfulness, though that word has been so commercialized and packaged that it's almost lost its meaning. But really, it's just this: paying attention. To what's actually happening, to what's actually in front of you, right now, in this moment. Because that's all we ever really have. Not our memories of the past or our fears about the future, but this present moment. And when we're not fully in it, we're essentially not fully living.

The spider finished its web as the sun was setting. The whole structure was suddenly visible as the light hit it at an angle, each strand catching the gold of the evening. It was beautiful in a way that a photograph couldn't quite capture. And I thought about how many webs get built every day that no one watches, how many small, intricate moments happen around us completely unwitnessed. I thought about how much beauty I've probably missed by not paying attention.

I don't know if I'll ever be able to completely break free from the fractured attention that our devices demand. But I'm starting to believe that even small moments of real, complete attention are transformative. That reclaiming the ability to focus deeply, to watch patiently, to be truly present—this might be one of the most important things we can do for ourselves and for each other.

So maybe start small. Watch something. Really watch it. A spider, a bird, a person you love. Notice what happens when you let your attention settle, when you stop trying to multitask and just let yourself be in one place, with one thing, fully. It's harder than you'd think in our current moment. But I promise it's worth it.
