# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how we move through the world mostly asleep, our attention scattered like loose change between work emails, social media feeds, and the perpetual background hum of things we should be doing. We have this idea that meaning lives in the mountaintop moments—graduations, weddings, that promotion we've been working toward for three years. But I'm increasingly convinced that the real texture of life, the stuff that actually makes it worth living, happens in spaces so mundane we barely notice them at all.

Yesterday morning, I sat in my kitchen for what I thought would be five minutes while my coffee brewed. The light was coming in at that particular angle that only happens in autumn, when the sun is lower and more golden, and it was hitting the side of my favorite mug in a way that made the ceramic seem almost luminous. I wasn't doing anything special—just standing there, waiting. And somewhere in that waiting, something shifted.

There's a Japanese concept called *kintsugi*, where broken pottery is repaired using gold, making the breaks visible and, in a strange way, more beautiful than the original. I think about this a lot. We're trained to hide our cracks, to sand them down, to present a version of ourselves that looks whole and unblemished. But what if the cracks are where the light gets in? What if that's not just nice poetry but actually true?

I know a woman—I'll call her Margaret—who worked in marketing for most of her life. She was good at it, wore the right clothes, said the right things, climbed the appropriate ladders. But she told me once, in that honest way people sometimes do after a glass of wine, that she spent thirty years in a career that never once made her feel truly alive. The money was fine. The status was fine. Everything was fine, except for the fundamental wrongness of spending the bulk of her waking life on something that didn't matter to her.

When she turned sixty, she quit. Not to pursue some glamorous dream—she didn't become a painter or move to Costa Rica or anything that would make a good Instagram post. She started a little garden. She learned to bake bread. She spent time with her grandchildren, not in that scheduled, activity-based way that modern parenting demands, but in the slow, aimless way of simply being together. She told me that baking bread has taught her more about patience and imperfection than anything else in her life. You can't rush dough. You can't force it. You have to work with its nature, feel the shifts in humidity and temperature, adjust accordingly. It's meditative. It's honest.

This is what I find myself returning to: the idea that we've organized modern life in a way that's fundamentally at odds with how humans actually thrive. We valorize productivity and optimization and disruption. We treat our bodies like machines that should never need downtime, our minds like computers that should be operating at maximum capacity at all times. We've turned rest into something you have to earn, rather than something essential to the basic machinery of being alive.

I'm not arguing for total rejection of ambition or structure. That would be naive. But I do think we've overcorrected, swung the pendulum so far toward constant achievement that we've made ourselves stranger to the texture of actual living.

There's something I've noticed about children before they're fully socialized into achievement culture. They notice things. A three-year-old will stop walking to observe an ant carrying something. They'll spend twenty minutes watching clouds move across the sky. They're not trying to be productive; they're just awake to the world in a way that seems, from the other side of adulthood, almost unimaginably precious.

Somewhere between childhood and adulthood, we lose this. We're trained to look through things rather than at them, to move quickly from moment to moment, always with an eye on what's next. The present becomes just a means to an end, never valuable in itself.

I wonder what would happen if we started building more space for the aimless. Not in that aspirational wellness way where meditation becomes another achievement to check off your list ("I meditated for 40 days straight"), but in a real, radical way. Time that has no outcome attached to it. Attention that doesn't need to produce anything.

There's this moment in the morning, after I've finished my coffee but before I really have to be anywhere, where I sometimes just sit. Not meditating, which implies a goal or technique I'm trying to master. Just sitting. Noticing what's happening—the quality of light, the sounds from the street, the texture of the chair against my back. It's almost embarrassingly simple, and yet it's become something I guard fiercely. Because I've noticed that the days when I protect this time are different. They're slower. I'm gentler with myself. Things don't feel quite so urgent.

I've been reading about the Japanese concept of *ma*—the space between things. In architecture, it refers to negative space. In music, it's the silence between notes. In conversation, it's the pause that lets meaning settle. The whole point is that emptiness isn't absence; it's full of potential. It's where things can breathe.

We don't build *ma* into our lives anymore. Every moment is filled with content, with purpose, with something that's supposed to be improving us or making us more productive. We've forgotten that emptiness might be valuable in itself.

I've also been thinking about how we relate to our own stories. We're encouraged to curate, to present a narrative that's coherent and compelling and preferably shows some kind of upward trajectory. But actual life is messier than that. It's full of false starts and side roads and periods where nothing much seems to be happening. We have moments of meaning tangled up with boredom and confusion and the simple fact of being alive without anything particularly interesting occurring.

And I think we're being cheated by the demand that everything be extraordinary. The ordinary *is* extraordinary, if you actually pay attention to it. The way light falls on a face you love. The specific taste of coffee made exactly the way you like it. The sound of someone you care about laughing in another room. These aren't lesser experiences than skydiving or traveling to exotic countries. They're just different. They're the texture of actual life.

One of the most important conversations I ever had happened in a car, stuck in traffic on a highway neither of us wanted to be on. There was nowhere to be, nothing to accomplish, so we just talked. Not about anything particularly grand—mostly small stuff, observations about people we knew, memories from childhood, things we'd been thinking about lately. But because there was no goal to the conversation, because we weren't trying to achieve anything, it went places that conversations rarely go. We said things we didn't know we were thinking until we said them.

I think about how that's almost impossible now. We're so structured. We have to carve out time for deep talks, schedule them, make them intentional. And intention is good, but there's something about accident, about stumbling into connection and meaning rather than planning for it, that feels vital.

My neighbor grows tomatoes. Just tomatoes, nothing else, in a small garden beside his house. He's retired, and from what I can tell, he spends the majority of his time tending to these plants. He waters them, talks to them, covers them with netting against the birds, adjusts the stakes as they grow. And then, when they're ripe, he gives them away. He doesn't sell them. He just hands them to neighbors, offers them to people walking by.

There's something radical about that. Spending months of work on something that will never make you money, just so you can give it away. It's almost obscene in its lack of productivity. And yet there's something deeply satisfying about it too. He seems genuinely happy. More happy, I'd wager, than people making six figures doing work they hate.

I think happiness might be less complicated than we've been told. Not easy, necessarily, but less complicated. It might be more about having time to be in your own life, less about having an impressive life to show to others. It might be about knowing the people around you, really knowing them. About noticing things. About doing work that feels like it means something, even if it doesn't mean anything to the world.

We've been sold this story where significance only comes from scale. You have to change the world, impact millions, build an empire. But what if significance just lives in showing up fully for the people in front of you? In making a meal someone enjoys. In being present during hard times. In noticing and appreciating the small beautiful things that are happening all the time.

The truth is, I don't know what the answer is. I'm still mostly caught in the same systems, the same anxieties as everyone else. I still check my email compulsively. I still feel that itch to be productive, that sense that time is slipping away and I should be accomplishing something. But I'm trying. I'm trying to build in more *ma*. More sitting. More noticing.

And what I've found is that this doesn't require dramatic changes. You don't have to quit your job or move to the woods (though if you want to, go ahead). You just have to occasionally say no to one more thing, so you can say yes to nothing in particular. You have to protect a little space where you're not trying to optimize or improve or achieve. Where you're just alive, just here, just paying attention.

Because that's where it is, I think. Not in the spectacular moments we're waiting for, but in the quiet ones we're trained to overlook. In the morning light. In the taste of good coffee. In the feeling of being fully present in a conversation with someone you care about. In the strange pleasure of watching an ant carry a crumb. In the spaces between, where nothing is happening and everything is.

# On the Architecture of Wonder: Why We Build Cathedrals We'll Never See Completed

There's a particular kind of hope embedded in the act of planting a tree you'll never sit beneath, of beginning work that extends beyond your lifetime. This is different from faith—it's something quieter, more practical, yet somehow more audacious. It's the impulse that built Chartres Cathedral over nearly two centuries, that drove the Japanese to design gardens meant to mature 300 years after their designers' deaths, that makes a person renovate a house they're already planning to leave.

I've been thinking about this lately, especially in an age that prizes efficiency, immediate returns, and the quantifiable impact of individual effort. We live in a culture obsessed with disruption and innovation—the quick pivots, the exit strategies, the quarterly earnings calls. And yet something in us rebels against this velocity. Something in us wants to build slowly, to contribute to something larger than ourselves, to participate in projects whose full beauty we'll never witness.

My grandfather was a carpenter. Not a famous one—he built houses in a small Pennsylvania town, nothing that would ever make an architectural magazine. He died at seventy-two, and I inherited a small wooden box filled with his hand planes, their wooden handles worn smooth from decades of use. These tools are beautiful in a way that's hard to explain to someone who doesn't work with their hands. The patina isn't the result of stylistic choice; it's the honest record of use, of thousands of hours spent shaping wood.

When I hold these planes, I think about the houses he built, many of which still stand. I've walked past some of them over the years. They're ordinary houses—three bedrooms, maybe, simple pitched roofs, nothing extraordinary. But they're solid. They've weathered sixty years of Pennsylvania winters. They shelter families who had nothing to do with my grandfather's decision to join the carpenter's union, to learn his craft, to apply himself with integrity.

Did he expect to be remembered through his tools? Did he imagine someone—his grandson—holding his planes and wondering about the houses they built? I don't think he thought about it much. He was solving the problem in front of him: how to build a house that would last, that would shelter people, that would be worth the work it demanded. The immortality was incidental.

But that incidental quality is exactly what I want to explore. We've become so conscious of legacy, so aware of how every action might be "remembered" or "go viral," that we've lost track of what made the best work so durable in the first place: the fact that it wasn't built for remembrance. It was built because it needed to be built, because it was the right thing to make, because the work itself demanded excellence.

There's a medieval term I love: *ad maiorem Dei gloriam*—for the greater glory of God. It's what motivated the craftsmen who carved intricate details into the undersides of pews, places no one would ever see. The ornament was there not for human praise but for the integrity of the whole. The cathedral was being built for God, allegedly, but really it was being built for its own sake, so that whoever encountered it—a century later, three centuries later—would experience something true about human aspiration and capability.

I think about this in our current moment, when so much of what we make is designed to be consumed immediately and discarded. We're drowning in products engineered for obsolescence, in content designed to trigger engagement rather than understanding, in buildings that will be demolished before their mortgages are paid off. The speed is dizzying.

And yet there are pockets of resistance. I've noticed them everywhere, once you start looking. There are people who apprentice for years to learn how to make Japanese swords or hand-forge tools or restore medieval illuminated manuscripts. There are urban farmers who've planted perennial food forests knowing they'll take years to mature. There are programmers building open-source software that no one will pay them for, creating tools that will outlive them, benefit people they'll never meet.

What motivates these people? Not hope of fame, certainly. Not economic reward. It's something closer to love—love of the craft itself, love of making something true, love of being part of a conversation that stretches across centuries.

I read recently about the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona. Gaudí took over the project in 1883 and worked on it until his death in 1926. He famously didn't expect to see it completed. When asked about the slow pace, he reportedly said: "My client is not in a hurry." His client was God, and he meant it both literally (this was a religious man) and metaphorically (the work itself was the point, not its completion).

The cathedral still isn't finished, over a century after his death. And instead of being a failure, this has become part of its power. The ongoing construction is an act of humility, an acknowledgment that some things are bigger than any individual life. The scaffolding is part of the structure. The work continues, carried forward by people who knew neither Gaudí nor the original architects, but who understand that they're custodians of something that matters.

This is almost incomprehensible in a startup culture. The entire business model depends on completing the arc: found company, achieve growth, exit. The longer something takes, the less viable it becomes. We measure success in speed. Move fast and break things, as they say, and somehow the "breaking things" part has been gradually erased from the equation.

But I wonder if we've miscalculated what speed actually costs us. When everything is optimized for rapid iteration and quick returns, we lose the capacity for deep work—for understanding something so thoroughly that you can contribute to its improvement across decades. We lose the ability to plant trees for our grandchildren. We lose the very possibility of becoming masters, because mastery requires a kind of commitment that a career of disruption doesn't permit.

I have a friend who's spent the last fifteen years learning to repair old typewriters. Not because there's a market for it. The opposite—typewriters are supposedly obsolete. But she loves them, loves the mechanical ingenuity of them, loves the relationship that develops between a person and a particular machine. She has customers who came to her with their grandfather's typewriter, the one he typed his novel on in 1962, and she brings it back to life. It's beautiful work. It's utterly impractical. It's absolutely necessary.

There's a passage in a Robert Pirsig book about the concept of quality—the idea that if you're doing something, you might as well do it well, for its own sake. Not because anyone's watching, not because it will be monetized or celebrated, but because quality is inherently satisfying to the person performing the work. It's an answer to meaninglessness. If nothing else, I can make this well. I can contribute something true to the world, something it didn't have before.

The cathedrals of the Middle Ages were built by people who would never see them completed. The masons who laid the foundation stones knew they were working on behalf of people not yet born. It wasn't a sacrifice—it was an honor. To be part of something that would outlive you, to make something that would shelter generations you'd never meet: that was achievement.

We've lost access to that kind of meaning, I think. We've been told that meaning comes from individual achievement, from disruption, from being first or being famous. But these are shallow sources of meaning. They're exhausting to chase. The real satisfaction comes from participating in something larger than yourself, from doing work that matters regardless of whether you're recognized for it, from building things whose full impact you'll never witness.

I don't know what my grandfather would have made of all this—of my attempt to derive meaning from his hand planes, to fashion a narrative of quiet integrity from his ordinary professional life. He probably would have just suggested I fix something with one of the planes if I wanted to understand them. That's the kind of person he was—action over reflection, results over philosophy.

But maybe that's exactly the point. The philosophy that matters most isn't the kind you write or speak. It's the philosophy embedded in how you do your work, in the choices you make about quality when no one's watching, in the decision to contribute to something you won't see completed because it's the right contribution to make.

There's a cathedral being built in our age, even if we can't see it clearly. It's not made of stone. It's made of code written to solve real problems, of art created to change how we see, of relationships tended with care, of knowledge preserved and transmitted to those who come after. Every person who chooses to do their work well, who takes on the apprenticeship required to develop mastery, who plants something with faith that others will tend it—they're all adding to that cathedral.

And that, I think, is the architecture of hope: not confidence that you'll see the results, but willingness to contribute your part anyway. Not certainty of legacy, but commitment to excellence regardless. It's radical, in its quiet way. It's the opposite of the culture of speed. And it might be the only way back to work that actually means something.

# The Strange Comfort of Impermanence

I've been thinking lately about how we spend so much energy fighting against the nature of things. Not in some grand philosophical sense, though there's that too—I mean in the small, daily ways we resist what's actually happening in favor of what we wish were happening instead.

Last week, I watched a man at a coffee shop spend forty-five minutes trying to get the perfect photograph of his cappuccino. He'd take a shot, examine it on his phone, adjust the cup slightly, move it toward the light, then away from it, try a different angle. The cappuccino was getting cold. I'm certain it was getting cold because I could see the foam flattening, the latte art that had been precise and geometric becoming something softer and less defined. At some point, he seemed to accept this and took a drink, but his expression suggested he was disappointed—not with the taste, necessarily, but with the fact that the perfect moment had passed.

I recognized myself in him immediately.

There's something peculiar about living in an age of perfect preservation. My parents have a handful of photographs from their childhood, grainy things that captured moments but were ultimately irreplaceable. That limitation created a kind of acceptance. You took the photo, you hoped it turned out, and then you moved on. But now we can take hundreds of photos in a single afternoon. We can edit them, filter them, crop out the parts that don't serve the narrative we're constructing. We can take them again and again until we get it right. And somehow, this abundance of control has made us feel more out of control than ever, more anxious about capturing the "right" version of our lives.

The cappuccino foam was going to dissolve. That was its nature. It was literally designed to dissolve, to be temporary. And maybe—this is what I keep coming back to—maybe that was exactly what made it beautiful.

I think about impermanence a lot. Partly because I read too much Japanese philosophy, partly because I'm at an age where I'm suddenly noticing that things I took to be permanent fixtures are starting to disappear. My grandfather's bookshelf is being emptied. My childhood home is being renovated by its new owners. A restaurant I went to every other week for seven years closed last month without any warning. Friends have moved to new cities and the old rhythm of seeing them regularly just... stopped.

When you're younger, this kind of loss feels catastrophic. It feels like the world is ending. But there's something interesting that happens if you sit with it long enough: you start to see that the ending of one thing is always the condition for the beginning of another. The cappuccino's foam has to dissolve for you to actually drink the coffee. Your childhood home has to be left behind for you to have an adult life. That restaurant had to close to make room for whatever comes next.

This doesn't make loss painless. I'm not trying to write some motivational piece where I convince you that everything is fine because the universe recycles. Loss is real, and grief is appropriate, and sometimes things end that you wish had continued. But I think there's a difference between accepting that grief and believing that impermanence is a design flaw in the universe that we need to overcome.

We seem determined to overcome it, though. Look at how much of our technology and culture is bent toward preservation and permanence. We digitize everything. We archive. We back up. We have storage units full of things we haven't looked at in decades because we can't bear to throw them away. We post our lives on social media as if creating a permanent record of our days might somehow protect us against time. We talk about legacy and immortality and the fact that our digital presence might outlive our physical bodies.

Is that comforting or terrifying? I can't decide.

What strikes me is that in pursuing permanence, we seem to have made ourselves less present. If you're constantly documenting something, are you actually experiencing it? If you're trying to preserve a moment perfectly, are you allowing the moment to simply be what it is? There's a paradox in all this—we want to hold onto life, so we turn it into data, into records, into something static and safe. And in doing so, we miss the life that's actually happening, the one that's always moving, always changing, always dissolving like foam on cooling coffee.

I read somewhere that the Japanese have a concept called *mono no aware*—the pathos of things. The idea that there's a deep beauty and poignancy in transience itself. The cherry blossoms in spring are beautiful partly because they bloom briefly and then fall. If they bloomed year-round, they'd lose something essential. Their meaning is bound up with their impermanence. That's not a defect. That's the point.

I wonder what we'd appreciate differently if we really internalized this. Would we experience ordinary moments more vividly if we accepted that we couldn't preserve them? Would we be kinder to people if we acknowledged that our time with them is limited and unpredictable? Would we complain less about aging if we stopped seeing it as something to resist and started seeing it as the condition that makes life mean anything at all?

There's a Japanese practice called *shinrin-yoku*—forest bathing. It's not about exercise or accomplishing anything. You just walk through a forest slowly, taking it in. No photographs (or at least not as the primary goal), no hiking to a destination, just being present with the changing light through the trees, the smell of soil, the sound of things living and dying. People report that it's profoundly calming. I think part of why is that you can't preserve a forest bath. You can't capture it. You can only have it, and then it's gone, and then you have something else.

I've started trying to do this more. Not literally in forests (though I do that too), but in regular life. I'll sit at dinner with someone I care about and instead of pulling out my phone to take a photo, I'll just... sit there. I'll notice the way the light catches their face when they laugh. I'll notice details I would never have seen through a camera lens. And when the evening ends, I won't have documentation of it. I'll just have the memory, which is fragmented and imperfect and will probably fade over time. And somehow, knowing that makes it feel more real, not less.

It's hard to do this consistently. The impulse to preserve is strong, especially when you love something or someone. The thought of losing it terrifies us. So we reach for whatever tools we have to hold onto it—photographs, journals, social media posts, repeated conversations about the past. Sometimes these things help. Mostly, I think they're a way of trying to negotiate with time itself, trying to convince it not to take what we love.

Time doesn't negotiate.

But here's what I've noticed: the things I remember most vividly aren't the ones I tried hardest to preserve. They're often random moments I didn't try to capture at all. A conversation in a car on a cloudy afternoon. The way my friend laughed at a joke that probably wasn't even that funny. The smell of a specific season in a specific place. These memories feel more real to me than any photograph, and I think it's because I was actually present for them. I wasn't observing them from the remove of a recording device. I was in them, living them, while they were still alive and changing.

Maybe the reason we're so anxious is that we're not actually living many of our lives. We're curating them, editing them, trying to turn them into something more permanent and presentable than the raw, messy, temporary thing that actually is.

I think about this especially around milestones. We treat them like they should be permanently crystallized—the perfect wedding day, the perfect graduation, the perfect vacation. And we work so hard to make them perfect that we miss the actual experience of them. Perfection is static. Life is not. Life is a cappuccino where the foam dissolves whether you wanted it to or not. It's a moment that's already over the second it begins.

What if we stopped treating that as a problem?

What if we accepted that everything we love will eventually be lost, and that that's not a tragedy but a feature? That it's what makes love feel urgent and necessary? That it's what transforms an ordinary moment—coffee with a friend, a conversation with your child, a day at the beach—into something that matters?

I'm not saying we shouldn't preserve anything. Memory is valuable. Art is valuable. Records are valuable. But maybe we should preserve things differently than we're doing it now. Maybe we should preserve them less obsessively, more lightly. Maybe we should document some moments while allowing others to fade, as a way of practicing the acceptance we'll need anyway.

Because everything fades. Your childhood home will be renovated. The restaurant you love will close. Your favorite songs will start to sound dated. The friends you see every day will move away. Your own face will change in the mirror. The small aches will become bigger ones. People you love will die. You will die.

And you know what? That's okay. It's not okay like "everything works out and there's a happy ending." It's okay like "this is what life is, and the only way to feel less alien in it is to accept it rather than resist it."

The funny thing is, I think accepting impermanence might be what actually lets us enjoy things. Not constantly reaching for the camera, not performing our lives, not trying to make everything permanent and perfect. Just being in it. Just living it. Just knowing it will end and appreciating it anyway.

That cappuccino will be cold eventually. But right now, at this moment, it's warm. Right now, it's exactly what it is—temporary, specific, unrepeatable. The man at the coffee shop could have spent forty-five minutes taking pictures, or he could have spent forty-five minutes actually tasting it, noticing it, being present with it.

I wonder which choice he would have regretted less.

I wonder which choice any of us will regret less, when we're at the end, looking back at all the moments we didn't quite allow ourselves to have because we were too busy trying to preserve them.

# The Quiet Architecture of Everyday Wonder

There's something I've been thinking about lately, and it's the way we move through the world without truly seeing it. Not because we're incapable of seeing, but because we're trapped in the momentum of living. We wake, we shower, we navigate to wherever it is we need to be, and somewhere between the alarm and the arrival, the world becomes invisible. It's a kind of practiced blindness, almost necessary for survival in a world designed to overwhelm us with stimuli.

But every so often—and this is what I want to write about—something catches your eye. Not because it's loud or demanding, but because you happen to be present enough to notice it.

Yesterday, I watched a woman on the bus adjust her glasses while looking out the window. Just that simple gesture—fingers to bridge of nose, a slight tilt of her head—but in that moment, I saw someone who was fully alive to the experience of traveling through a city. She wasn't checking her phone. She wasn't staring blankly ahead. She was looking at something—perhaps nothing in particular, perhaps everything—with what seemed like genuine presence.

It made me think about presence, which is maybe the most discussed and least understood concept in contemporary life. We're told constantly that we need to be more present. Yoga instructors tell us this. Wellness gurus tell us this. Parents tell us this while they're checking their email. There's an almost cruel irony in how often the advice to be present is delivered in a way that makes you anxious about not being present enough.

But what if presence isn't something you can force or optimize? What if it's something that arrives unbidden, like that moment with the woman on the bus?

I think about my childhood—not in a sentimental way, but practically. I remember being bored frequently. And I don't mean the clinical boredom that modern parents worry about, the kind they believe leads to developmental problems. I mean the deep, absolute, world-without-stimulation boredom of a kid on a long car ride with nothing to do. My brain, desperate for input, would inventory everything. The texture of the car seat. The way light filtered through the windows at different angles as the sun moved. The rhythm of the road. The sound of my parent's conversation in the front seat—not the words, necessarily, but the cadence, the humor, the small intimacies of two people who had been together a long time.

In those moments, I wasn't trying to be present. I was just bored enough that presence was the only option.

Now, boredom has been thoroughly pathologized. We treat it as something to be immediately remedied with content, with stimulation, with something to do. I'm not arguing against the internet or against entertainment—I love these things, and I'd be a hypocrite to pretend otherwise. But I wonder what we've lost in the assumption that every moment needs to be filled, or at least made pleasant.

There's a kind of consciousness that emerges from boredom, a noticing that happens when your brain isn't being fed pre-packaged experiences. And I don't think we can force this state. You can't optimize boredom. You can't mindfulness-app your way into it.

What I think might matter more than presence itself is what I'll call "attentional generosity"—the occasional decision to let your mind linger on something small and ordinary. Not as an achievement. Not as something to post about. Just as a private act of attention.

When I was a teenager, I had a friend whose grandfather was a painter. Not famous. Not particularly successful in the economic sense. But someone who had spent fifty years really looking at light on water, at the way a particular corner of his garden looked in different seasons, at the color of rust on a fence post. One day, he showed us some of his paintings, and what struck me wasn't their technical skill—though they were technically accomplished—but that you could feel in them the hours of looking. The genuine, unhurried attention. It was like being let into someone's interior experience of the world.

I've been thinking about that lately because I notice that attention—real attention—is becoming scarce in a way that matters. Not just personally, but culturally. We've structured almost everything to be as frictionless as possible, which means we can move through more of life in less time, experiencing less of each moment.

This isn't a moral failing. It's not about being a better person if you're more attentive. But there's something precious we're losing, which is the feeling of having genuinely inhabited a moment rather than simply passed through it.

There's a Japanese concept called "ma"—it's usually translated as negative space or emptiness, but it's more specific than that. It's the space between things that gives them meaning. In architecture, it's the space in a room that makes the walls matter. In music, it's the silence between notes that makes the melody audible. In a conversation, it's the pause that lets something land.

We've been systematically filling in the "ma" of our lives. Every silence is now an opportunity for a notification. Every pause is a chance to check something. Every moment of blankness is a failure to be productive. And I think we're losing something important, which is the sense that meaning can emerge from emptiness rather than needing to be constantly supplied.

The other day I was waiting for a dentist appointment, and I noticed something I've never noticed before: how much visual chaos there is in a standard waiting room. There's the television mounted in the corner showing something nobody's actually watching. There are magazines from six months ago. There are posters about dental hygiene with pictures of people displaying teeth in a way no human ever does. There's the receptionist's area, all glass and metal and business-casual efficiency. And there are the chairs, arranged in a configuration that says "sit here but don't interact with anyone else."

And I realized that most of modern architecture is designed to fill space without filling time. It's created in a way that assumes people won't actually be present in it. The room doesn't expect your attention, so it doesn't reward it. It's designed to be passable, not inhabitable.

But sometimes you'll enter a space—a good coffee shop, a thoughtfully arranged apartment, a particular corner of a park—and you can feel that someone has paid attention to how a human actually exists in that space. The proportions feel right. The light falls in a way that makes you want to stay. There's nothing frantic about it. It just makes sense to your body.

I think this is what I'm really trying to articulate: there's a way of moving through the world that assumes you'll be present in it, and there's a way that assumes you won't. And most of modern life is designed with the latter assumption.

But here's the thing—and this is what gives me hope—the solution isn't to rage against the system or to move to a cabin in the woods. It's much quieter than that. It's just the occasional decision to actually look at something. To let your attention settle on a particular tree, or a particular person, or a particular moment, not because you're trying to be mindful or enlightened, but simply because it's there and you're here.

I've been reading a lot of poetry lately, not because I'm trying to improve myself, but because poetry seems to operate in the space I'm trying to describe. A good poem doesn't try to fill time with meaning; it assumes that time is full of meaning and its job is just to make you aware of it. Mary Oliver asks, "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" and the question works not because it's profound in a philosophical sense but because it's so achingly specific. It's not asking you to do something great. It's asking you to actually show up for the one life you have.

There's something in that—that shift from doing to being, from improving to noticing—that feels increasingly radical in a world structured around optimization.

I was at a bookstore recently—yes, they still exist, though they feel increasingly precious—and I watched an elderly man spend twenty minutes reading the back cover of different books in the poetry section. Not trying to decide what to buy. Just reading. Taking his time. The absolute luxuriousness of twenty minutes in a bookstore with no agenda. How many people in that store were scrolling through Goodreads reviews trying to optimize their reading? And here was this man just reading.

I've started trying to do this more—not because I'm good at it, but because I notice how good it makes me feel. Spending ten minutes really looking at a houseplant instead of just seeing it. Actually tasting my coffee instead of just caffeinating. Watching the way a particular person moves when they think no one's looking.

These are small things. They don't solve any problems. They don't make you more productive. They won't show up on any metric of self-improvement. But they seem to be where happiness actually lives—not in some far-off achievement, but in the precise quality of attention you bring to the ordinary moments that make up your actual life.

The paradox is that you can't optimize this. The moment you try to turn attention into a practice you're doing for self-improvement, it stops working. It has to be pointless. It has to be its own reward.

I think a lot about how much mental energy we use trying to figure out how to live, when sometimes the answer is just: be present for this moment. Not as a goal. Not as a means to some other end. Just as the practice of being alive.

Maybe this is all I'm really trying to say. That there's a kind of consciousness available to us that isn't about productivity or achievement or even wellness. It's just about showing up for your life with enough attention that you actually experience it. And that this might be one of the most radical and subversive acts possible in a world structured to prevent exactly that.

It's late as I'm writing this, and I'm aware that I'm rambling in the way you do when you're trying to articulate something that doesn't quite have language yet. But that feels right too. Not everything needs to be polished or perfect or delivered with certainty. Sometimes the act of reaching toward an idea is enough.

# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the margins, noticed by no one, significant to no one, yet somehow constituting the actual texture of existence. This thought came to me last Tuesday while watching a pigeon navigate a parking lot—not a dramatic observation, not something that would impress anyone at dinner, but the kind of small attention that seems increasingly rare.

We live in an age of curated significance. Everything worth noticing has already been noticed, packaged, and presented to us through screens. We consume these pre-digested observations and call ourselves informed. Meanwhile, the actual world—messy, redundant, ungainly—continues its work unobserved. I find something deeply moving about this. It suggests that beneath the layers of attention we've collectively decided to pay to major events and carefully crafted content, there exists an entire parallel universe of unremarkable things, simply existing, asking nothing of us.

That pigeon, for instance. I watched it for perhaps three minutes while waiting for someone at a coffee shop. It was engaged in what I can only describe as aggressive optimization—attempting to navigate around a puddle, reconsidering, trying another route, eventually just walking through the puddle with obvious irritation, as if the water had personally offended it. I found myself wondering whether pigeons have the capacity to be annoyed, whether what I was interpreting as annoyance was something else entirely, or whether, in fact, this particular pigeon was simply executing a series of mechanical responses and I was projecting an entire inner life onto a bird that probably didn't have one.

This is the fundamental problem with noticing: it immediately leads to interpretation, and interpretation leads to stories, and stories are where we lose the thing itself.

But I'm interested in stories anyway. I'm interested in the stories we tell ourselves about what we notice, because those stories might be more true, in some meaningful sense, than the raw facts. If I'm the only person who watched that pigeon, and I watched it with the genuine attention that most people reserve for their phones, didn't I create something real? Wasn't there a small event—a pigeon noticing, witnessed—that didn't exist before?

This connects to something I've been reading about attention as a moral act. The idea that there is something almost sacred about genuine attention—the kind where you're not performing attention for some audience, not scrolling while pretending to listen, but actually there, actually present with the thing in front of you. This kind of attention has become so rare that I wonder if we should coin a new word for it, something with more weight than "attention," which has been so depleted by overuse that it barely means anything anymore.

I've noticed that the people I most enjoy talking to are the ones who practice this kind of attention. Not in a performative way—they're not being "mindful" or "present" with the self-conscious intensity of someone trying to prove something. Rather, they simply seem to be genuinely interested in what's in front of them, including conversations. When you're talking to someone like this, you can feel it. It's a rare sensation, this experience of being fully attended to. We're so starved for it that when it happens, we often mistake it for romance or special connection, when sometimes it's just someone actually listening.

I've also noticed that attention is contagious. When you really look at something, other people start to look too. I remember once, years ago, stopping in the middle of a busy street because I'd seen something—I can't even remember what now, some configuration of light or color—and within thirty seconds, three other people had stopped beside me wondering what I was looking at. We all stood there staring at whatever it was, strangers united in curiosity, and I felt a genuine sense of community in that moment. The spell broke when someone asked "what are we looking at?" and we all realized we couldn't quite articulate it, so we laughed and moved on. But something real had happened.

There's a particular kind of boredom that I think is valuable, though it's almost extinct now. It's the boredom you experience when you're not allowed to use your phone, not in any social punishment sense, but just in normal daily life. Walking somewhere without music, waiting for someone without scrolling, sitting in a quiet room without entertainment. In these moments, boredom used to lead to observation. Your brain, desperate for stimulus, would start really noticing things. The cracks in the pavement. The way light falls through a window. The small social dramas unfolding around you.

I've been deliberately creating these moments lately, and I've found it surprisingly difficult. My instinct, trained by years of constant stimulus availability, is to reach for my phone the moment I'm not actively engaged with something. When I manage to resist this instinct, there's usually a grace period of acute discomfort—fifteen seconds, sometimes thirty—where I feel genuinely anxious. Then it passes, and I start to notice things again. It's like my attention apparatus has to be rebooted each time.

One thing I've noticed is how many small kindnesses happen invisibly. A person holding a door even though the person behind them is still far enough away that they're going to have to hold it for an awkward amount of time. Someone picking up a dropped glove and looking around to find the owner, with zero chance of recognition or thanks. A barista remembering how someone likes their coffee. These are not the kind of things that appear on social media, not because they're not good, but because they're not performed. There's something about the invisible kindness that makes it purer, less corrupted by the possibility of external reward.

I wonder if this is why so many people feel an emptiness even when everything in their lives appears, by reasonable metrics, to be going well. We're optimizing for visibility rather than quality. We're curating our lives for an imaginary audience that doesn't actually exist, or if it does, doesn't actually care as much as we think. The parts of life that are most meaningful—the small moments of genuine connection, the quiet satisfaction of doing something well with no one watching, the strange peace of being alone without being lonely—these aren't on our résumés. They don't show up in photos. They're the stuff that life is made of, and we're training ourselves to overlook them.

There's also something interesting about the specific ways that people develop their own noticing patterns. We don't all notice the same things. Some people are extremely attuned to others' emotional states, picking up on microexpressions and tone shifts that completely escape me. Other people notice architectural details or bird species or the mechanical consistency of a well-made object. I've found that I notice patterns of behavior, the way people handle small frustrations, the revealed preferences in how people talk about their days.

This might be why conversations are so valuable—because each person brings a different quality of attention to the world, and when you really listen to someone talk about what they've noticed, you get to borrow their attention apparatus for a while. You get to see the world through their particular filter. A friend who notices birds can take you on a walk and transform it into a completely different experience than you would have had alone. Another friend might make you acutely aware of the emotional dynamics at a party you might have thought was fine.

The problem, of course, is that we have less time for this kind of conversation now. We have more "connections" but less deep attention within those connections. We're all rushing toward the next thing, the next notification, the next stimulus. The paradox is that by trying to maximize experiences, we're minimizing the quality of attention we can bring to any given experience. We're trying to taste all the wines, and in doing so, we're not really tasting any of them.

I've started a small practice of what I'm calling "mandatory noticing." Once a day, usually while I'm out somewhere, I pick something and really look at it—not for any purpose, not to write about it or post about it or tell anyone about it, just to see it clearly. It's harder than it sounds. My mind keeps trying to turn the observation into something—a thought, a story, a photograph. I have to keep gently bringing it back to the simple act of looking.

Some of these observations are beautiful. A garden in someone's front yard where you can see exactly which plants are getting adequate light and which are struggling. The way a particular tree grows, all its limbs reaching toward one side because of how the surrounding buildings block the light. A storefront window display that's obviously been arranged by someone with specific aesthetics and taste.

But some of them are mundane in a way that's almost meditative. The texture of a wall. The pattern of cracks in concrete. A pile of leaves in a corner. The accumulated grime on a streetlight. These things are not beautiful, but they are real in a way that curated images are not. They are the actual world, unarranged, unfiltered, indifferent to whether anyone notices.

And I think that indifference might be important. In a world where everything is increasingly personalized, where algorithms learn our preferences and serve us more of the same, there's something grounding about things that simply exist without any reference to us. A tree doesn't know you're looking at it. A pigeon doesn't care whether you think it's annoyed. The world was here before you paid attention to it, and it will continue after you stop. There's something reassuring about this.

I don't have any grand conclusions here. I'm not suggesting that everyone should practice mandatory noticing or that attention is the solution to all modern malaise. But I do think there's something we're losing by outsourcing our noticing to algorithms and curators. We're losing touch with the irreplaceable experience of being a conscious creature in a world full of things worth paying attention to.

The pigeon probably never appears in anyone else's story. It navigated its parking lot, found what it was looking for or didn't, and moved on, completely indifferent to the fact that someone was watching. But for those three minutes, it was the entire world—the only thing happening that mattered. And I think we need more moments like that, moments where the entire world shrinks down to whatever is directly in front of us, and we're content to simply notice.

# The Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I want to talk about boredom, that strange state we spend so much energy trying to escape. Not the clinical kind of boredom that gets pathologized in medical literature, but the ordinary, everyday boredom that most of us experience regularly and yet rarely examine closely. We treat it like a malfunction, a sign that something has gone wrong with our entertainment system or our productivity machine. But I think boredom might be one of the more valuable experiences we can have, particularly in a world increasingly designed to eliminate it.

There's a peculiar contradiction in modern life. We have access to more forms of entertainment, information, and stimulation than any humans in history. I can open my phone and within seconds access thousands of hours of video, millions of articles, countless games, social feeds updating in real time. And yet, paradoxically, we seem to experience boredom more acutely than ever. People describe themselves as "bored" while scrolling through infinite content. The stimulation has become so constant, so readily available, that nothing quite satisfies anymore. We've created a kind of hedonic treadmill powered by algorithms.

I think part of what's happening is that we've confused boredom with emptiness. Boredom used to mean something specific: a situation where external stimulation was limited, where you had to sit with your own mind. Now, we use the word to describe a kind of frenetic dissatisfaction, the feeling that what we're currently consuming isn't engaging enough, that we should be doing something more stimulating. We swipe left, we change the channel, we refresh our feeds. The anxiety of potential boredom drives us to constantly seek novelty.

What I'm interested in is what happens when you actually let yourself be bored. Not deliberately torturing yourself, but allowing situations to unfold where boredom becomes unavoidable, and then observing what occurs in that space.

When I was a child, summer days were long and surprisingly boring. There were periods where there was genuinely nothing to do. No devices to check, no streaming services, limited television. My friends were inside or away. I found myself alone in my backyard or my room with very little external stimulation. And in that boredom, something remarkable would happen. My mind would begin generating its own content. I'd play elaborate imaginative games, create stories, rearrange my room, experiment with things, draw, think about problems that interested me. The boredom was the condition that forced my creativity to activate.

I notice this doesn't happen when I'm constantly stimulated. If I have my phone available, if there's always something new to engage with, that generative space simply doesn't open. My mind stays in consumption mode, reactive rather than creative. The external stimulation crowds out the internal voice that might have something to offer.

There's research suggesting this is real. Studies on mind-wandering and the default mode network of the brain show that when we're not focused on external tasks, our minds do something different—they make connections, integrate memories, explore possibilities. This default mode isn't a bug; it seems to be crucial for creativity, problem-solving, and psychological integration. Yet we've become increasingly hostile to the conditions that allow it. We treat idle time as wasted time. We optimize every moment for productivity or entertainment.

I wonder if what we call boredom is sometimes actually the sound of our internal systems trying to activate. It's an uncomfortable feeling because we've lost the tolerance for it. A mild version of that feeling—what I'd call understimulation—is necessary for that generative mode to engage. But instead of allowing ourselves to experience it, we immediately reach for our phones, turn on music, start planning something. We've made understimulation something to be avoided at all costs.

There's also something valuable about boredom in terms of perspective and values. When you're perpetually entertained, when you're always consuming content chosen by algorithms optimized to engage you, it's easy to lose touch with what actually matters to you. Entertainment is someone else's art, someone else's vision. Boredom creates space to notice your own desires, your own curiosities. It's quieter, less seductive than well-crafted entertainment, but it's more authentic to who you actually are.

I've noticed this with reading. I used to read books I didn't particularly like because I'd made a commitment to them, and I'd have to sit with them through moments of boredom. Now I have hundreds of entertainment options at hand, and the moment a book stops perfectly engaging me, I can switch to something else. This seems like freedom, and in some sense it is. But I think I also miss something from the experience of pushing through boredom in a book, of having to engage more deeply with something that doesn't immediately appeal. Sometimes that leads to unexpected appreciation. And the act of staying with something despite its difficulty, despite moments of disengagement, is itself valuable. It's a kind of discipline that affects how you approach other challenges.

There's also a social dimension to this. Boredom used to be something you experienced communally sometimes. You'd be stuck somewhere with other people, with limited options, and out of that boredom, conversation would emerge. Real, unscripted conversation. Not the curated versions we share online. I think about how much differently my extended family gatherings work now. Before, when there were limits on entertainment, people would actually sit and talk. Now everyone is checking their phones, escaping into individual content streams. The boredom that used to be a driver of connection has been eliminated.

I also want to acknowledge that boredom can be unpleasant. I'm not arguing that it's some pure good. Acute boredom, especially without hope of it ending, can be genuinely distressing. The boredom of a long car ride with nothing to do, no one to talk to, and no end in sight. The boredom of a boring job where you're trapped for eight hours. This kind of boredom can be alienating and painful. But I think the answer isn't to become incapable of experiencing any boredom—it's to preserve some capacity for it while recognizing situations where it's genuinely harmful.

What I'm suggesting is a more nuanced relationship with boredom than the current approach of total elimination. The goal shouldn't be to never be bored. The goal might be to be selectively bored, to preserve time and space where boredom is possible, while also having resources to escape it when it becomes genuinely harmful.

I think of boredom tolerance as a kind of resilience. If you've never experienced boredom, or only the mildest version of it, then any situation without perfect stimulation becomes unbearable. You become dependent on external entertainment for basic contentment. But if you develop tolerance for boredom, you become more resilient. You can manage situations that aren't perfectly optimized for engagement. You can be alone with your thoughts without it being torture. You can sit with difficulty.

There's also something I'd call the paradox of interesting boredom. Some of the most interesting moments of my life have come from periods of what I'd initially experience as boredom. A quiet morning with no plans, where I'm not engaging with anything external—in those spaces, thoughts surface that wouldn't otherwise. Insights emerge. Decisions become clearer. Creativity activates. The boredom is the price of entry to those spaces.

I think about how artists and writers often talk about the importance of boredom. They describe it as essential to their process. They need time that isn't stimulated, isn't "productive," to let their creative work germinate. They're not talking about entertainment boredom—the frustration of not having enough diversions. They're talking about the fertile boredom that opens creative possibility.

One of the things I've become aware of is how the war on boredom has commercialized it. Every moment of potential boredom is now a market opportunity. Bored on the toilet? Here's a game. Bored waiting in line? Here's social media. Bored before sleep? Here's a podcast. Every gap in stimulation is something to be filled with a product or service. This is profitable for the companies creating the entertainment, but I wonder what we lose in the process.

I wonder if part of the alienation and dissatisfaction so many people report might actually be connected to this inability to tolerate any boredom. If your internal rewards system has been trained by algorithms designed to hit dopamine targets, then ordinary life will seem less engaging. A conversation with a friend might seem boring compared to a perfectly edited entertainment product. Ordinary meals might seem less stimulating than a engineered snack. This seems like a recipe for perpetual dissatisfaction.

I'm not arguing for a return to some pre-digital past. Those earlier eras had their own problems, their own ways of being unsatisfying. But I think there's something worth preserving from that experience of boredom, something valuable about space that isn't optimized for engagement.

What would it look like to reclaim some tolerance for boredom? I think it might mean periodically choosing not to fill available time with stimulation. Taking walks without podcasts. Eating meals without devices. Sitting quietly without the radio. Not all the time—the modern world does offer genuine goods that entertainment provides. But regularly, deliberately, creating space where boredom becomes possible.

It might also mean being more intentional about what we do choose to engage with. Instead of consuming whatever algorithm presents next, actually selecting things we think are worth our attention. Finishing books we find challenging. Having conversations without the safety net of our phones. These aren't particularly novel suggestions, but they take on new meaning in the context of an environment actively hostile to boredom.

What strikes me about boredom is that it's honest. Entertainment lies to you—not maliciously, but by design. It's engineered to be more engaging than reality. It's a best-case version of stimulation. Boredom, by contrast, is just life as it actually is for many stretches—not terrible, but not dramatically engaging either. Learning to tolerate and even appreciate that might be one of the more mature adjustments we can make.

I think we need boredom. Not as a failure state to be corrected, but as a necessary part of being human. The capacity to be alone with your thoughts, to sit with understimulation, to let your mind wander where it will—these seem essential to developing as thoughtful, creative people. The alternative is perpetual reactivity, always responding to the next stimulus, never generating anything from within.

The irony is that boredom is free, and the alternatives are often quite expensive. The entertainment industry spends billions to create the most engaging possible content, to make boredom impossible to tolerate. Meanwhile, boredom just happens. It doesn't require monetization or infrastructure. It's just what's left when you're not being entertained.

So I'm interested in boredom not as a problem to solve, but as a resource we've been throwing away. A weird kind of gift hidden in something we've been trained to find unpleasant. The space where your own mind gets to speak, where you're not being sold anything, where creativity can germinate and genuine thoughts can emerge.

The challenge is to preserve some relationship with it, even in a world increasingly designed to make it impossible.

# On the Strange Beauty of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about unfinished sentences. You know the ones—they trail off mid-thought, suspended in white space, leaving the reader to fill in the gaps. There's something peculiarly honest about them. They suggest that not everything needs wrapping up, that ambiguity isn't always a failure of communication but sometimes its most perfect expression.

This thought came to me while I was looking at my bookshelves, at all the books I've started but never finished. I used to feel guilty about these half-read volumes, stacked horizontally atop the finished ones like a monument to my own incompetence. Why couldn't I just commit? Why did I start Moby Dick four separate times across four different decades? But recently I've made peace with it. Some books, I think, are meant to be kept incomplete. They exist in my life as perpetual possibilities rather than resolved narratives, and there's something beautiful in that.

We're obsessed with completion in ways that seem almost pathological. We finish what we start. We close the loops. We want narrative arcs that resolve, projects that conclude, conversations that reach understanding. I understand the impulse. There's a satisfaction to completion that's almost physiological—that sense of a task accomplished, a box checked, a weight set down. We are creatures who crave closure.

But I wonder if we've lost something in this relentless drive toward finished things. I think about medieval cathedrals, built across centuries, their architecture and ornamentation evolving with changing styles and sensibilities. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction since 1883. Most of the people who began it died never seeing it finished. Yet it stands as one of the most magnificent structures humanity has created, and perhaps it's magnificent partly *because* it remains incomplete, because it refuses the finality of conclusion.

Or consider scientific understanding. We talk about scientific facts as though they're finished products, perfect little boxes of knowledge. But that's a profound misunderstanding of how science works. Every answer opens new questions. Every solved mystery spawns a dozen new mysteries. The entire enterprise would collapse if we achieved total completion. Science is beautiful precisely because it's infinite in its incompleteness, because there will always be something else to discover, some new frontier pushing back the darkness.

I've been reading about Japanese aesthetics lately, and I keep coming back to the concept of *ma*—negative space, the space between things. In art, architecture, music, and design, there's this deep understanding that what you don't show is as important as what you do. That silence between musical notes is as much part of the composition as the notes themselves. The empty space in a painting is an active component, not a failure to fill the canvas.

There's also *wabi-sabi*, which encompasses an appreciation for impermanence, imperfection, and the incomplete. A cracked tea bowl, weathered by use and time. A poem that cuts off abruptly. A garden that's allowed to decay in beautiful ways. There's a tenderness in this aesthetic that Western perfectionism doesn't easily accommodate. It accepts that things break, that beauty doesn't require flawlessness, that incompleteness might be closer to truth than any finished product could be.

I think about my own life this way increasingly. I'm in my thirties now, and I don't know if that's more than halfway through or not even close. I certainly don't have life "figured out" in any comprehensive way. I'm still learning how to be a person. I still make mistakes I thought I'd graduated from making. I still wrestle with self-doubt and uncertainty. And increasingly, I'm okay with this. Not in the toxic-positivity way of "embrace the journey, man," but in a deeper sense: I'm okay with being an incomplete work.

There's a temptation to see one's thirties as a deadline—by this age you should have your career established, your relationships secured, your personality finalized. But what if that's the wrong framework entirely? What if the goal isn't to reach some finished state of "adulthood" but to remain perpetually in motion, perpetually growing, perpetually uncompleted?

I have a friend who's been working on the same novel for eight years. When I asked him when he'd finish it, he looked slightly offended. "I don't want to finish it," he said. "I like who I am as a person while I'm writing it. When I finish it, I'll be someone else, and I'm not sure I want to know who that person is." I thought he was joking, but I don't think he was. There's something wise in that resistance to completion.

The fear underneath productivity culture, I think, is the fear that once we've finished everything on our list, once we've achieved everything we've set out to achieve, we'll have to confront the fundamental emptiness of existence. So we keep adding to the list. We gamify our lives. We turn everything into a project to be managed. What if we stopped?

I've been thinking about habits this way too. We talk about building good habits and breaking bad ones, as though our behavioral lives are construction projects. But what if habits are more like gardens? You plant something, and it grows, and it spreads, and sometimes it thrives in unexpected ways and sometimes it withers. You don't build a garden and then finish with it. You're always tending it, always in relationship with it, always learning from it.

My mother has been doing the same crossword puzzle, on and off, for three years. It's a crossword in a hardcover book, not a newspaper, so it won't degrade or disappear. She works on it when she's waiting for coffee to brew or during a lunch break. She's maybe a third of the way through it. I asked her if she's trying to finish it, and she said, "Not particularly." She just likes the activity, the way it focuses her mind. Finishing would be beside the point.

There's something about incompleteness that preserves possibility. A finished meal becomes memory; a meal in the midst of being eaten is present experience. A finished conversation is history; an ongoing conversation is actual relationship. A finished life—well, we don't really know what that looks like, but we fear it.

Incompleteness is also more honest about the nature of meaning-making. We act as though meaning exists in the world waiting to be discovered, like facts about geology or biology. But meaning is something we create, something we generate through our engagement with things. A novel isn't finished when the author writes the final word; it's finished when a reader reads it, and then finished again when another reader reads it, differently, in the light of their own life. Meaning is infinitely incomplete.

I think about all the things I've wanted to learn and abandoned halfway through. Piano lessons from age seven to twelve. Spanish, which I attempted to learn in college and high school and casually and seriously. Drawing classes. Photography. Programming. At one time, I felt ashamed of this scattered incompleteness, this lack of mastery. Now I'm not sure. I can play a few songs on the piano. I can conduct basic conversations in Spanish. I can see the world partially through a photographer's eye. I can understand code well enough to read other people's and roughly understand what's happening.

Is this failure? Or is it a kind of literacy? A sampling of different ways of being in the world, different modes of perception? I don't regret any of them for being incomplete. I think they've all become part of how I think and see and move through the world.

There's an essay by Annie Dillard where she talks about how living is not something most people are good at. It's something people do, mostly badly, while thinking about other things. We're all fundamentally incomplete at this central task. We're all amateurs at being alive. There's a strange comfort in that—if we're all stumbling through this more or less incompetently, maybe the goal isn't to achieve some kind of mastery but just to show up, to pay attention, to be as present as we can manage in the midst of our confusion.

I've been rereading some David Foster Wallace essays, and he keeps returning to the idea that life is fundamentally about attention—about learning to direct your consciousness deliberately rather than having it directed for you by habit, fear, and desire. But notice what he doesn't claim: that you'll ever achieve perfect attention, complete clarity, full presence. You won't. You're always going to be partial, limited, incomplete in your awareness. The practice isn't about reaching a finished state of enlightenment but about the practice itself.

Incompleteness is also, I think, a prerequisite for compassion. When you're incomplete, when you don't have everything figured out, you extend grace to others who are similarly lost. When you admit your own brokenness, you can hold space for others' brokenness. Perfection is isolating. Completeness is lonely. We connect through our gaps.

I think of the kintsugi technique in Japanese pottery, where broken ceramics are repaired with gold seams. The breaks don't disappear; they're highlighted, integrated, made into part of the beauty. That seems like a good way to move through the world—not trying to hide the places where we've broken or failed or remained incomplete, but acknowledging them as part of our actual shape.

There's a line in Leonard Cohen's "Anthem" that keeps coming back to me: "There is a crack in everything / That's how the light gets in." Not: there shouldn't be cracks. Not: you should fix the cracks. The cracks are essential. They're how light penetrates the darkness. They're how growth happens. They're what keeps us open.

As I write this, I'm aware that I haven't said anything terribly original. The imperfection of things, the value of incompleteness, the problem with perfectionism—these are not new insights. But maybe that's the point. Maybe these truths need to be repeated endlessly because we keep forgetting them, keep slipping back into the pursuit of completion and closure and certainty.

Let me end this essay incompletely. Let me trail off without a neat conclusion, without having tied everything together or resolved all the tensions I've raised. Let me leave you with unfinished thoughts floating in white space.

Because maybe that's more honest. Maybe that's how we actually live—in fragments, in pieces, in ongoing becoming. Not working toward some finished version of ourselves or our understanding, but perpetually in the process of becoming, perpetually incomplete, perpetually open to what comes next.

And maybe that's not a failure or a tragedy. Maybe that's the only life worth living.
