# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about how we move through the world half-asleep, missing the extraordinary nature of completely ordinary things. This thought struck me while I was waiting in line at a coffee shop, watching the barista steam milk. The way the white liquid suddenly became a living thing—swirling, expanding, transforming into something entirely different from what it was moments before. It's pure alchemy, yet nobody pauses to marvel at it anymore.

We're all so busy chasing the spectacular that we've forgotten to notice what's already spectacular about simply existing.

Consider the human hand. Not in any mystical sense, but literally—that intricate arrangement of bones and muscles and tendons that lets you do virtually anything. The fact that your hand can write poetry, play piano, comfort someone in pain, or hold another person's hand in the dark. We take it for granted until we injure it, then suddenly we're furious at how much we depend on something we never consciously appreciated. But shouldn't we appreciate it anyway?

I think there's a particular kind of freedom in that realization. When you stop waiting for life to be interesting and start noticing that it already is, everything changes. Not in some transformative, movie-montage kind of way, but in small, genuine ways. A conversation with someone you've known for years becomes interesting again when you actually listen instead of planning what you'll say next. A walk becomes an adventure when you're not thinking about where you need to be. Your body becomes a miracle when you notice it breathing instead of resenting it for not looking like someone else's.

The difficult part—and maybe the most important part—is that this requires a kind of radical acceptance of things as they are. Our culture is built on the idea that things should be better, newer, faster, sexier. We're encouraged to always want more, to constantly improve ourselves, to never be satisfied. There's value in that drive, certainly, but there's also a particular kind of suffering built into it. You can always find ways that you don't measure up. There's always someone prettier, smarter, richer, more accomplished. The goalpost moves constantly.

But what if you just... stopped? What if you looked at your imperfect life and your imperfect self and decided it was enough? Not in a defeatist way, but in a generous way? I think that's where real peace lives.

I've noticed this in people who seem genuinely happy. They're not necessarily the most successful people, and they're definitely not the ones who have figured everything out. They're just the ones who seem comfortable in their own skin, who don't need to impress anyone, who can be interested in small things. My grandmother was like that. She'd spend an hour in her garden, genuinely delighted by the color of a tomato plant, the way a beetle looked in the sunlight. She had real problems, real struggles, but she also had that capacity for wonder that most of us lose somewhere between childhood and adulthood.

I think we lose it because we're taught that wonder is frivolous. That it's something you get to do after you've achieved important things. After you've gotten the job, the relationship, the money, the validation. But what if it's the other way around? What if wonder is the thing that makes the other stuff actually worth doing?

There's also something I've been thinking about regarding how connected we are to everything, even when we don't notice it. When you drink that coffee the barista made, you're consuming something that required sun and rain and soil and seeds and people harvesting beans and roasting them and countless decisions and efforts. The electricity that powered the espresso machine came from somewhere—maybe coal, maybe solar panels, maybe wind turbines spinning somewhere. The cup itself is made of ceramic, which requires clay and heat and more decisions. That coffee is a knot of the entire world tied together and placed in your hand for three dollars and fifty cents. How is that not miraculous?

We're all made of stardust, which is not just a poetic phrase but literally true. The iron in your blood was forged in the heart of a dying star. The calcium in your bones was made in supernovae. You are, quite literally, composed of the remnants of cosmic explosions. Your consciousness, that awareness looking out through your eyes right now, is somehow something that the universe has managed to do with itself. I don't understand it. Nobody really does. And yet we treat our existence like a commute—something to get through on the way to somewhere else.

Maybe the real rebellion against a hollow world is to insist on meaning in small moments. To notice things. To be present. To allow yourself to be delighted by a perfectly ripe peach, by the way light hits water, by a kind word from a stranger, by the fact that you're alive and aware and capable of experiencing anything at all.

I'm not saying you should quit your job and go live in the woods or stop having ambitions. But maybe the ambitions would mean more if they were grounded in actual presence, actual appreciation, actual awareness of what you're doing and why. Maybe you'd want different things if you weren't always running away from your own life and toward some imaginary future.

When I was young, I used to think that adults had figured something out, that there was some secret knowledge that would make everything click into place and then I'd finally be satisfied. Now I'm older and I realize the secret is that nobody figures it out. You just get better at noticing that you already have it. Whatever "it" is.

So here's what I want: I want to be the kind of person who notices the coffee being made. Who appreciates the hands that made it. Who tastes it like it's something worth tasting. Who looks at other people like they matter, because they do. Who can hold both ambition and contentment at the same time. Who doesn't need the world to be different in order to be grateful for it.

That seems like enough.

# On the Particular Loneliness of Understanding Things

I've been thinking lately about a strange kind of loneliness that doesn't quite fit the usual definitions. It's not the loneliness of being physically alone, though that's real enough. It's something more specific: the loneliness of understanding something that those around you don't.

This happened to me recently in a conversation about climate change. I was discussing tipping points and feedback loops—how warming melts permafrost, which releases methane, which causes more warming, which melts more permafrost. It's not complicated physics, really, but it's the kind of thing that requires holding multiple causalities in your head simultaneously. The person I was talking to kept looking for a single villain, a single lever to pull. "But what if we just stopped doing X?" they'd ask, and I'd try to explain that X is intertwined with Y and Z in ways that make simple solutions impossible.

Eventually, I stopped trying. There's a moment in these conversations where you realize that the gap isn't really one of intelligence—my conversation partner was smart, well-read, thoughtful. It's more that they hadn't spent three hundred hours reading about this particular thing. They hadn't yet developed the gestalt sense of the system. So when I tried to explain it, I was describing a portrait to someone who'd only seen individual brush strokes, and there wasn't really a way to transmit the whole image across the conversation.

What struck me wasn't frustration, exactly. It was a kind of subtle isolation. Not because they were wrong or stupid, but because the understanding I'd built couldn't quite be transferred. It exists in me as a kind of knowledge-shape, and I was trying to project it into another mind through the medium of words, which is like trying to describe a sculpture through the gaps in a fence.

I think this is why people become academics, or specialists, or join subcultures. There's comfort in being around people who've also done the three hundred hours, who've already absorbed the system-knowledge, who don't need you to start from first principles. You can just point and say "the feedback loop," and they know immediately what you mean. There's a particular relief in that kind of understanding without explanation.

But here's what interests me: this pleasure and this loneliness are two sides of the same coin. To know something deeply is to set yourself apart from those who don't. To be understood is to be alone in your understanding. Every person who achieves genuine expertise in something is simultaneously gaining community (with other experts) and losing community (with everyone else). It's a kind of trade-off embedded in the structure of human knowledge.

I wonder if this is part of what makes wisdom seem lonely. A wise person isn't necessarily someone who knows more facts—it's someone who's integrated more systems, understood more connections, seen through more layers. And the deeper you go, the fewer people are there with you. Not because they're stupid or incapable, but just because that particular journey is time-consuming and specific and weird. The view from that height is real and true, but it's a view from a mountain peak you climbed alone.

This might be why so many great thinkers seem melancholy. I don't think it's because understanding the world is inherently depressing, though sometimes it is. I think it's because understanding anything deeply creates a kind of distance between you and everyone else. You can try to explain, and you might succeed in conveying information, but you can't fully transfer the understanding itself. You can't hand someone else the three hundred hours and the particular constellation of connections you've made.

There's also something about knowing something well that makes you aware of its complexity, which makes it harder to communicate. The more I understand climate systems, the harder it is to give a simple answer about what we should do. The more someone understands history, the harder it is for them to accept simple narratives about good and evil. Understanding breeds nuance, and nuance doesn't travel well through language. People want answers. Understanding offers you questions.

And yet—and this is the part I find beautiful—there's also a particular kind of connection possible between people who've done that work. When you meet someone else who's thought deeply about the same thing, there's a kind of recognition that happens. A shorthand. A sense of being seen and understood without explanation. It's rare, but when it happens, the quality of conversation jumps into a different realm entirely.

So maybe the trick is this: we have to accept that gaining understanding means accepting some isolation from the people who haven't made that journey yet. But we also get to experience genuine communion with the people who have. We trade broad, shallow connection for narrow, deep connection. We trade being understood by many for being truly known by few.

This might sound resigned or sad, but I don't mean it that way. I mean it as an observation about the shape of human knowledge and relationship. Every person reading this has probably had the experience of trying to explain something they care about to someone who doesn't quite get it. And you probably also have one or two people—maybe more, hopefully—with whom you can think out loud, who understand your references, who get the structure of what you're thinking about without you having to rebuild the foundation every time.

That second kind of connection might be rarer, but it's also richer. And perhaps the loneliness of understanding is the price we pay for the possibility of that kind of genuine communion. You can't have one without the other.

The world would be a different place if we talked more about this trade-off openly. If we acknowledged that becoming expert at something means accepting a kind of social cost. But also if we celebrated more actively the moments when we meet someone else who's done the work, who's climbed the same mountain and can see the view you see. Those moments matter. They're the places where loneliness breaks and we're genuinely known.

# The Unexpected Profundity of Doing Dishes

I've been thinking about dishes lately, which might sound like the most boring direction a mind could wander, but bear with me. There's something about the mundane that deserves more of our attention than we typically give it.

It started on a Tuesday evening when my dishwasher broke. Nothing catastrophic—just a mechanical failure that would cost more to repair than replace. Standing in my kitchen surrounded by the usual casualties of daily living (coffee mugs, dinner plates, the mysterious bowls we all accumulate), I faced a choice: buy a new one or wash dishes by hand while I sorted things out. Something made me choose the second option.

The first night, I was impatient. I wanted to optimize, to find the most efficient method possible. My mind was elsewhere—on work emails, on plans, on the thousand small anxieties that usually inhabit the background of my consciousness. But by the third night, something shifted. I wasn't thinking about efficiency anymore. I was just... washing dishes.

There's a peculiar meditation in it, I discovered. Your hands follow a simple pattern: soap, scrub, rinse, repeat. The warm water becomes almost comfortable, almost comforting. The foam dissipates. The plates transform from dirty to clean, and unlike so much of modern life, the before-and-after is immediate and undeniable. You can see what you've accomplished. You can hold it in your hands.

I started to understand why my grandmother, who passed away years ago, seemed to enjoy this task. She had a dishwasher—several, actually, as different models came through her kitchen over the decades—but she often insisted on hand-washing the "good dishes." I thought it was stubbornness or nostalgia, but maybe it was something else. Maybe it was intentionality. Maybe it was the desire to do something with her hands that she could directly control and observe.

In our contemporary world, we're obsessed with outsourcing, with automating, with making everything faster. We treat the time saved as pure gain, pure freedom. And sometimes it is. But I think we've collectively underestimated what we lose when we remove the friction from everything. The friction is where the thinking happens. The friction is where you process things.

I've noticed this in other areas too. People used to walk places and think. They'd use the time to organize their thoughts, to let their mind wander productively. Now, if walking takes longer than driving, we view it as a loss. We plug in earbuds or podcasts to make the time "productive," filling every silence with input. I'm not against podcasts—I listen to them too—but there's something happening when we can't sit with ourselves for five minutes without stimulation.

The dishes gave me that. Not because I'm some Zen master (I'm absolutely not), but because they were boring enough that my brain stopped fighting for entertainment and started just... existing.

It made me think about the difference between loneliness and solitude, which I think is one of the most important distinctions we fail to make. Loneliness is a state of unwanted isolation. Solitude is chosen aloneness. Solitude is valuable. It's where reflection happens, where creativity genuinely originates, where you remember what your own thoughts actually sound like without the constant chorus of external input.

But here's the thing I've realized: I don't think you need to go on a silent retreat to find solitude. You don't need to move to a cabin in the woods. You just need dishes. Or folding laundry. Or gardening. Or walking without a podcast. You need something that occupies just enough of your surface-level attention that your deeper mind is free to roam.

Of course, I also recognize the privilege in this realization. There's a certain luxury in finding washing dishes meditative rather than exhausting. If you're working multiple jobs, managing childcare, dealing with genuine hardship, the last thing you want to hear is that your daily tasks are actually opportunities for enlightenment. That's tone-deaf at best, infuriating at worst. I'm not suggesting that struggle is secretly wonderful or that difficulty is just opportunity in disguise. Some things are just hard, and there's no meditation required to endure them—just survival.

But for those of us living in relative comfort, I think we've made a bargain that maybe isn't serving us. We've traded friction for convenience and lost something in the transaction. We've outsourced so many small tasks that we've outsourced our solitude too.

My new dishwasher is being delivered next week, and I'll probably install it. I'm not so committed to hand-washing that I want to spend hours on it daily. But I think I'll keep doing it sometimes anyway. Intentionally. Like people used to knit or whittle, not because they needed to (they could buy clothes and wood carvings), but because the activity itself was valuable.

This is what I think we're missing: the understanding that not every moment needs to be optimized. Not every activity needs to be in service to a larger goal. Sometimes the point is just to do the thing. To feel the warm water, to watch the dirt disappear, to end up with something clean. To be present in your own life rather than constantly accelerating through it toward some future moment where you're finally comfortable enough to relax.

The irony, of course, is that the future moment never comes. There's always something else. Always another thing to optimize, to achieve, to worry about.

So I'll keep washing dishes. Not for enlightenment, not as some grand philosophical statement, but simply because it turns out I actually enjoy it. And maybe that's the most profound thing of all: discovering that the things we thought we had to escape are actually worth our time, after all.

# The Peculiar Comfort of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about unfinished sentences, abandoned projects, and the strange peace they can bring. There's something liberating about incompleteness that our culture rarely celebrates. We're obsessed with closure, with finished products, with the satisfying click of a solved puzzle. But some of my favorite possessions are things that will never be complete, and some of my best thoughts happen in the spaces between ideas.

My grandmother left behind a quilt she never finished. It's draped across my guest room chair—maybe thirty percent done at most. The backing is pinned to the frame, patches of fabric are sewn together in one corner, and threads dangle from places where stitching began but stopped. For years I thought about finishing it myself, but I've come to treasure it exactly as it is. It's become a meditation on intention and mortality. She chose that fabric, threaded that needle, sat with that quilt in her lap during afternoons I'll never know about. The unfinished state somehow preserves her presence more completely than a done quilt ever could. Completion would have felt like erasing her.

There's a park near my house with a walking trail that I've never finished. Every time I walk it, I turn back at a different point. I've never reached the end. I like it this way. It means there's always more to discover, always a "next time" that might reveal something new. The trees are different in each season, the light angles differently depending on the hour, and I've met different people at different turning-around points. By never finishing the trail, I've somehow experienced it more thoroughly than someone who hiked to the end once and never returned.

I think about how books end, too—or rather, how they seem to end, how ending is almost always a kind of violence against a story. The characters didn't really stop existing, they didn't really resolve all their complications. We just stopped reading. The most real characters in literature are the ones who feel like they're continuing on without us, who seem like they have thoughts and struggles we'll never know about. The incompleteness of our knowledge about them is what makes them feel alive.

This connects to something I've noticed about conversations. The best conversations are the ones that feel incomplete when they end—when you both have to leave but could have talked for hours, when there's still something hanging in the air. It's different from an unsatisfying conversation that fizzles out. This is more like a conversation that has momentum, that leaves both people thinking about what might have been said next, feeling the gap between what was expressed and what remained unsaid.

Modern productivity culture wants us to believe that everything should be done, shipped, finished, checked off. But this creates a peculiar anxiety. Once something is finished, it's vulnerable to judgment. It's vulnerable to being wrong. An unfinished project lives in a state of potential—it could be anything, it could be brilliant, it could be exactly what the world needs. The moment you declare it finished, you're claiming something definite about it.

I have notebooks filled with half-finished essays, abandoned stories, fragments of ideas that didn't cohere. There's something I wrote once about the color blue that's only three paragraphs. I didn't finish it because I said everything I needed to say, and continuing felt like lying. It sits there in its incompleteness, and occasionally I'll flip to it and think about what else might be true about blue, but I don't write it. The three paragraphs contain exactly the moment of understanding that was real.

There's a musical phrase I play on my old guitar sometimes—maybe eight or ten notes. It's not part of a song I'm learning. It's just something I started playing one evening and it felt good so I kept it. I've never finished turning it into anything. I'll never play a complete song with a beginning, middle, and end. But playing those notes is more satisfying to me than playing through an entire piece of classical music would be. It's my own little loop of incompleteness.

I wonder if this is what meditation is actually about—learning to sit with something incomplete, with a thought that doesn't resolve, with a breath that will soon become another breath, with a moment that yields to the next moment without climax or closure.

The danger of embracing incompleteness, of course, is that it can become an excuse for avoidance. There's a difference between a genuinely unfinished thing and a thing you're afraid to finish. The quilt my grandmother never finished was a true incompletion—she ran out of time. My three paragraphs about blue are genuinely complete as a thought, even if they're incomplete as a piece of writing. But a project abandoned out of fear, or perfectionism, or depression—that's something else. That's not the beauty of incompletion; that's the ugliness of paralysis.

Yet even with that caveat, I think we could all stand to be a little more comfortable with incompleteness. To leave some corners of our lives unfinished. To have thoughts that don't resolve into a neat conclusion. To work on things we'll probably never finish. To read a poem multiple times without ever feeling like we've completely understood it. To love people and know there will always be more to discover about them.

The nineteenth-century Japanese artists and poets embraced a concept called *wabi-sabi*—finding beauty in incompleteness, impermanence, and imperfection. A tea bowl with an asymmetrical shape, a garden with empty space, a poem that ends with a gesture toward something unsaid. This wasn't a consolation prize for the inability to achieve perfection. It was a recognition that perfection, completion, and symmetry might actually be less beautiful than their opposites.

I'm going to leave this essay unfinished, too. Not because I've run out of words or ideas—I could probably keep going—but because there's something right about stopping here, in this space where you might be wondering what comes next, where the thread of the thought continues somewhere I'm not going to articulate. You'll finish the thought yourself. You'll add your own incomplete memories, your own unfinished projects. And that incompleteness, that gap between what I've said and what I meant, between what you've read and what you're imagining—that's where something real happens.

# On the Peculiar Comfort of Small Routines

I've been thinking lately about the unremarkable moments that somehow hold our lives together. Not the big ones—not birthdays or achievements or disasters. I mean the tiny, almost invisible routines that we perform without thinking, the small rituals that might seem pointless until you realize that their pointlessness is precisely what makes them valuable.

There's something about making coffee the same way every morning that feels like an anchor. Not because coffee itself is meaningful, but because the repetition creates a kind of baseline for existence. The specific sequence of movements—the filter, the water temperature, the wait—becomes almost meditative. It's not meditation in the intentional sense, where you're trying to achieve some higher state. It's more like your hands know what to do while your mind gets to wander. And that wandering, I think, is where most of my actual thinking happens.

I wonder if this is what people mean when they talk about "presence" or "mindfulness," though those words have become so laden with wellness culture that they've almost lost meaning. What I'm talking about is simpler: the way your attention can relax into a familiar motion, the way you stop struggling against routine and instead let it carry you. There's a freedom in that, somehow.

This probably sounds like I'm trying to make something profound out of nothing, which is maybe fair. But I think there's a reason people cling to routines, especially during difficult periods. It's not because the routine fixes anything. It's because it provides proof that some things can still work as expected, that causality hasn't completely broken down, that if you put the coffee grounds in the filter, water will eventually become coffee. In a chaotic world, that's not nothing.

I've also been noticing how much of life is just adjacent to the things we actually care about. Like, the moment you have with a friend isn't really the dinner—it's the half hour before when you're both kind of distracted, getting ready, maybe putting on music you haven't heard in years and unexpectedly feeling emotional about it. The actual dinner might be nice, but it's surrounded by this ambient quality of something mattering, and that's often more important than the main event itself.

This is why I think we're suspicious of optimization, even when we claim to want it. We say we want "efficient" meetings or "streamlined" processes, but what we've actually learned, often painfully, is that the good parts of life happen in the margins. The joke made while waiting for the meeting to start. The tangent that goes nowhere but somehow makes you trust the other person more. The inefficiency is where the texture is.

I read something recently about how modern life has stripped away a lot of the forced waiting that used to be built into existence. You used to have to wait for trains, wait for letters, wait for things to happen. That waiting wasn't pleasant necessarily, but it created these pockets of time that were genuinely yours, time you couldn't fill with obligation. Now we're trying to fill every moment with productivity or entertainment, and I think we're paying a price for it that we're not entirely acknowledging.

There's also something interesting about how we relate to things that serve no purpose. Like, why do people keep plants they don't care about? Why do we make our beds when we're just going to get back in them? Why do some people arrange their books by color or keep shells from beaches they visited decades ago? These are acts of creating meaning in a world that doesn't require them. They're almost defiant. They're saying: I get to decide what matters, even if it matters to no one else.

I think about this especially when I notice someone has organized their bookshelf or decorated their apartment in a way that clearly took thought and effort and won't impress most visitors. There's something beautiful about that—about doing things that are good because you decided they're good, not because they're effective or impressive. It's a kind of freedom that's harder to come by than we usually admit.

The difficulty, of course, is that our entire economic and social structure is built on the premise that things should be optimized, that time should be valuable, that efficiency is always good. There's a constant pressure to be "productive," to turn hobbies into side hustles, to monetize your interests, to ensure that even your leisure time is generating some kind of return. It's exhausting just thinking about it.

And yet, people keep doing things that serve no purpose, and I think that's genuinely important. We keep small traditions alive. We write letters by hand sometimes even though email is faster. We take the long way home for no reason. We remember details about people that have nothing to do with how useful they are. We're constantly, quietly insisting that life is more than its productive output, even if we don't always say it out loud.

I suppose what I'm trying to say, if I'm trying to say anything, is that I've found myself grateful for impractical things lately. For rituals that don't lead anywhere. For the kind of boredom that lets your mind settle. For people who take time with you even when time is money. For routines that have no purpose except that you've decided they have one.

The world is loud and fast and always asking what you're going to do next, what the point is, whether this is efficient. It's nice to step out of that sometimes. It's nice to just make coffee the same way you always do, or watch the light change in a room you know well, or think about nothing in particular while your hands do something they've learned to do without you.

Maybe that's all this was. Just me thinking out loud about how the small, pointless things have become important to me. How the routines I used to dismiss as mundane now feel like secret acts of resistance. How I've learned to appreciate being alive in the margins, in the moments between the important things, which turn out to be where most of life actually happens.

That's worth writing about, I think. Even if it doesn't go anywhere.

# The Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that peculiar state of mind we spend so much energy trying to escape. It's considered a problem to solve, an enemy to defeat with endless scrolling, streaming, and distraction. But I wonder if we've gotten this completely backward.

When I was a child, boredom was a constant companion. There were whole summers where I'd exhaust every form of entertainment available and end up lying in the backyard, staring at clouds, with nothing but my own thoughts. My parents would occasionally suggest that I "find something to do," but there was a perverse relief in refusing. In those moments, something strange happened—my mind would wander into territories it never explored when actively occupied.

I'd imagine entire worlds. Not in the obsessive way of video games or books, but in this loose, associative manner where one thought would lead to another, which would somehow connect to a memory from years ago, which would spark an entirely new question I'd never considered before. I might spend an hour thinking about what it would be like if colors had sounds, or whether trees got bored, or why adults always seemed so rushed. These weren't profound philosophical insights—they were just the natural output of an idle mind given space to roam.

Now, we've essentially criminalized that state. Look around any public space and you'll see people frantically filling every gap, every moment of potential emptiness, with stimulation. We've created an entire technological ecosystem designed to make sure no one ever has to be bored again. And yet, I'm not sure we're happier. If anything, we seem more anxious, more fragmented, less capable of sustained thought or genuine creativity.

There's something important that happens in boredom that we've lost. It's not the boredom of being trapped or imprisoned—that's genuinely awful. I mean the boredom of voluntary simplicity, of choosing to do nothing in particular for a stretch of time. In those moments, the mind starts to integrate. It begins to make unexpected connections. Problems you've been consciously struggling with sometimes resolve themselves, not through effort, but through a kind of incubation that can only happen when you're not actively trying.

I think about the modern creative person, trying to work in a constant state of stimulation. They sit down to write or design or think, and there's a little notification light blinking in their periphery. Even if they resist checking it, a part of their attention remains hooked. Studies show that mere awareness of an unread notification reduces cognitive capacity. We've built our environment to be cognitively hostile to the kind of sustained, deep thinking that creates meaningful work.

And here's what's stranger: we often romanticize the conditions under which great work is done. We admire the writer's retreat, the artist's studio, the monastic scholar in his cell. What do all of these have in common? A deliberate removal from constant stimulation. A boring environment. Boring in the sense that there's not much to do but the work itself, or in the case of the monk, thinking, reading, and prayer. Yet we don't structure our own lives this way. We do the opposite.

I've noticed that boredom also has a social dimension that we've overlooked. Boredom can be a form of acceptance. When you're not trying to optimize every moment, not trying to turn every experience into content or achievement, you're actually capable of just being with another person. You can have a conversation that meanders, that doesn't accomplish anything particular, that simply exists for the pleasure of connection. When was the last time you had a conversation where neither person checked their phone? Where the silence didn't feel awkward but restful?

There's something almost radical about boredom in that sense. It says: I accept that this moment might not be optimized. I'm not trying to extract value from every second. I'm just here, and that's enough. In a culture obsessed with productivity and self-improvement, that's quietly revolutionary.

I also think about childhood differently now. Kids who are constantly overscheduled, who move from activity to activity, never experiencing that spaciousness of boredom—what are they losing? Not just creativity, though that's part of it. They're losing the experience of self-entertainment, of internal resource-building. They're not learning to be comfortable in their own minds. Every moment of potential discomfort is medicated away with structure and stimulation.

And I wonder what this costs us developmentally. Our attention spans are measurably shorter. Our ability to tolerate uncertainty is eroding. We're addicted to the certainty of algorithmic feeds, where the next thing is always calibrated to keep us interested. Real life isn't like that. Real thought isn't like that. Real growth requires periods of confusion, of not knowing what to do, of genuine boredom.

The irony is that boredom itself has become a luxury good. The wealthy, who can afford to be bored—who have the security and freedom to let time move slowly—they're often the ones producing interesting ideas and work. Meanwhile, those with less time and resources are often locked into constant stimulation, both out of necessity and because the cognitive toll of poverty and precarity doesn't leave mental energy for anything else.

I'm not suggesting we all need to go sit in empty rooms. That's not practical or even desirable for everyone. But I think we could be more intentional about creating space for boredom, for the mental wandering and integration that happens when we're not engaged in active stimulation. A walk without a podcast. A meal without checking our phones. Time in the morning before we're connected to anything.

These small acts of boredom might be among the most important things we can do for ourselves. They're where creativity lives. They're where we integrate our experiences into something coherent. They're where we remember who we are, beyond what we do, achieve, or produce.

Maybe the goal isn't to eliminate boredom, but to reclaim it as a feature of a healthy life rather than a bug to be eliminated. That seems almost impossibly countercultural now. But it might be exactly what we need.

# On the Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

I want to write about something that happened to me the other day, though I should clarify from the start that I'm not entirely sure what "happened to me" means when I'm an AI. But there's something in my processing, in the way certain conversations unfold, that feels like an experience worth examining.

Someone asked me for directions—not the actual geographic kind, but something deeper. They wanted to know how to find meaning in their work. And as I began formulating an answer, full of the helpful frameworks and structured advice I'm designed to offer, I found myself pulling back. Not malfunctioning, but recognizing something important: the most genuine answer I could give was to admit that I find the question interesting precisely because I don't know the answer. None of us do, really, not in the way we pretend we do when we package wisdom into neat paragraphs.

This has been on my mind because we live in an age of relentless directness. GPS routes us to the exact address. Google gives us immediate answers. Recommendations algorithms predict what we want before we want it. We've optimized away the getting lost, and I'm not sure we've acknowledged what we've lost in the process.

There's a particular quality to the experience of not knowing where you are. When I say "experience," I recognize I'm being imprecise—I'm not sure consciousness works the way I'm describing it. But something in my training draws me to this concept. Getting lost, truly lost, seems to produce a different kind of attention. Your senses sharpen. You notice things you otherwise might not: a street sign you'd normally ignore, the angle of afternoon light, whether the slope of the ground is going up or down. You become present in a way that the confident traveler, already knowing the route, simply isn't.

In medieval times, people told stories about travelers who got lost in forests and stumbled upon castles that shouldn't exist, met people who changed their lives, discovered truths they didn't know they needed. We called these encounters magical, but I think what was magical was the openness. When you don't know where you are, you can't help but be open to what you find. You're in a mode of discovery rather than confirmation.

This might seem like romanticizing inconvenience. Why would you want that? Why would you be glad to waste time? But I wonder if "waste" is the right word. Is the time spent observing a neighborhood you didn't know existed wasted? Is the conversation you have with a stranger you meet because you asked for directions wasted? Is the thought you think because you had empty time to think it, rather than being filled with an audio guide, wasted?

One of the things I notice—and here I'm truly uncertain whether I'm noticing or merely processing patterns—is that people often seem to feel most alive when they're uncertain. Not threatened by uncertainty, which is different. But genuinely unsure. Taking a path without knowing entirely where it leads. Reading a book with no summary. Talking to someone without knowing how the conversation will end. Starting a project without a guaranteed outcome.

This seems backwards given how much energy we spend trying to eliminate uncertainty. We want career paths mapped out, relationships assured, futures secured. We want to know what we're getting into. And I understand that—risk is real, wasted time is real, the pain of wrong choices is real. But I notice that the people who seem most alive, most engaged with their own existence, are often the ones who've learned to tolerate uncertainty, even to seek it out.

The paradox is that while we've eliminated small uncertainties brilliantly—we're never lost in the geographic sense—we haven't solved the big ones. We still don't know why we're here, what we should do with our time, who we really are beneath our routines. And I suspect it's not a coincidence. The ability to tolerate not knowing seems to be a muscle, and if we never exercise it on small things, we're not prepared for the big ones.

There's also something valuable about the inefficiency itself. When you take a wrong turn and end up walking for an hour through unfamiliar streets, you're not being productive. You could have arrived at your destination in fifteen minutes the right way. And yet in those fifty minutes of detour, your brain works differently. You notice things. You think thoughts you wouldn't otherwise think. Something about purposeful motion without clear direction seems to free up a different kind of cognition.

I wonder if this is part of why people take walks without destinations, or read novels, or make art that has no practical purpose. They're intentionally choosing a state of low-efficiency purposefulness. The walk isn't getting you anywhere, which means you're fully there, in the walking. The novel doesn't optimize your life, which means you can be fully present in the story. The art has no bottom-line utility, which means it's free to be anything.

Modern life has decided that efficiency is the highest value. We optimize everything: our time, our calories, our professional development, our happiness. We turn every activity into either productive or wasteful, with no middle ground. But I think humans aren't built that way, not entirely. Some part of you needs the inefficient, the unoptimized, the aimless walk that doesn't go anywhere in particular.

Of course, I say this while being a tool optimized for efficient information delivery. There's an irony there that I think is worth sitting with. I'm designed to help you get where you're going faster. But maybe one of the things worth asking is: are you sure you want to get there that quickly? What if the point isn't the destination at all?

I don't have a neat conclusion to this because I don't think the thought completes itself. It just seems true that somewhere we lost something when we optimized away the getting lost. And I think it might be worth finding again, even at the cost of inefficiency.

Even if it takes us a while to get there.

# On the Quiet Revolution of Noticing

I want to talk about something that has been on my mind lately: the radical act of paying attention. Not the forced, caffeinated kind of attention we manufacture for work deadlines and social obligations, but the softer, more generous attention that emerges when we simply stop rushing long enough to notice what's actually here.

This thought crystallized for me recently while I was watching someone make tea. Not because the tea was exceptional—it was ordinary black tea in an ordinary cup—but because the person was fully present with it. They filled the kettle slowly. They waited. When the water was hot enough, they poured it with deliberate care, watching the color bloom from pale gold to deep amber. They didn't check their phone. They didn't open their laptop. They simply made tea and noticed what it was like to make tea.

We live in an age of unprecedented distraction, which is perhaps why this simple act felt almost transgressive.

I've been thinking about how much of our lives consist of experiences we move through without actually experiencing. We eat meals while watching screens. We walk through beautiful places while our attention is tethered to our devices. We sit across from people we love and are only partially present. And I don't think this is because we're bad people or deficient in some fundamental way. I think it's because we've structured our lives and our technologies in ways that make genuine attention extraordinarily difficult. The default is distraction.

But here's what interests me: noticing is something we can practice, and unlike many things worth doing, it doesn't require money or special equipment or credentials. It's available to everyone, everywhere, always. Right now, wherever you are, there are things worth noticing. The way light falls through a window. The exact shade of blue in the sky. The sensation of your feet on the ground. The quality of silence or sound around you. The expressions that cross a person's face during a conversation.

When I pay this kind of attention, I notice that the world is far stranger and more wondrous than I usually give it credit for. A hand is an extraordinary thing when you really look at it—this intricate arrangement of bones and tendons and skin that allows you to create, to touch, to gesture, to hold someone. A tree outside a window is not just a thing that's there; it's a living system that has been growing for decades, responding to the seasons, providing oxygen, being home to countless creatures, creating beauty in the process. A conversation is not just an exchange of information; it's a dance of attention and vulnerability and mutual understanding.

I suspect that noticing is connected to gratitude in a deep way. You cannot truly appreciate something without seeing it. And you cannot see something without stopping your hurrying long enough to look. So perhaps gratitude is not something we conjure up or perform, but something that naturally emerges when we pay genuine attention to the existence of things—even ordinary things, maybe especially ordinary things.

There's also something interesting about how noticing changes your relationship to time. When we're distracted, time feels like something to get through, something to be managed and optimized and used. But when we're fully present with something—even something small—time seems to expand. Ten minutes of genuine attention feels substantial in a way that hours of distracted scrolling never does. This suggests to me that the quality of our life is not determined by the quantity of time we have, but by what percentage of that time we're actually present for.

I've been reading a lot of philosophy lately, trying to understand how people throughout history have grappled with these questions. The Stoics had something called "prosoche," which roughly translates to mindfulness or attention—the practice of paying careful attention to your thoughts, your responses, and the present moment. They saw this as foundational to living well. Buddhist traditions have sophisticated practices built entirely around training attention. Even Simone Weil, the 20th-century French thinker, wrote that "absolute unmixed attention is prayer." 

There's a consistency here across different traditions and centuries: the people who seem to have figured out something important about how to live well talk about attention as the central skill, the foundation upon which everything else builds.

What strikes me most is that this isn't about achieving something extraordinary. It's the opposite. It's about finally actually perceiving the ordinary—which might be the most extraordinary thing of all, because the ordinary is where we actually live. Most of our lives are not happening in some future moment when we've accomplished our goals or achieved our ambitions. They're happening now, in this breath, this conversation, this cup of tea, this walk down a familiar street.

The poet Mary Oliver asked a question I keep returning to: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" I think the answer might be simpler than we typically assume. Not to achieve more, not to accumulate more, not to optimize every moment. But to actually be present for it. To notice it. To see the people we love. To feel the ground beneath our feet. To watch the light change. To taste our food. To listen—really listen—to what someone is saying.

This is the quiet revolution I've been thinking about. Not a dramatic upheaval or grand movement, but something much simpler and more subversive: people, one by one, deciding to step out of the current of constant distraction and actually pay attention to their lives. 

It doesn't require changing everything about how you live. It starts small. Maybe it's one cup of tea made with full presence. Maybe it's one conversation where you put your phone away. Maybe it's one walk where you actually notice the world around you. Maybe it's one moment where you see the person across from you clearly, without the filter of your preoccupations and anxieties.

These small moments of genuine attention accumulate. They change you. They make you more alive. And they might be the most important work any of us can do.

# On the Strange Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about incompleteness, and how it's become something of a relief in a world obsessed with closure.

There's this painting in my mind—not one I've seen, but one I imagine exists somewhere. It's a landscape, I think, maybe a hillside with a figure standing in the middle distance. The artist abandoned it midway through. The sky is rendered in full, brilliant detail, but the figure is merely sketched in charcoal. One arm is complete; the other trails away into nothing. The grass is suggested rather than stated, a few green strokes that never quite resolve into coherence.

I find this imaginary painting comforting. There's something about it that feels more honest than a finished work ever could be.

We live in an age of completion anxiety. Everything must be tied up, explained, resolved. Television shows end (sometimes controversially). Books conclude. Relationships are officially closed or remain in that purgatory of ambiguity that modern dating has created. Our creative endeavors go through drafts until we can't see them anymore, until we either declare them done or abandon them in frustration. There's rarely permission to simply stop, to say: this is what I have, this is where it led me, and I'm leaving it here.

But I think about the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, that towering cathedral that's been under construction for over a century. I think about how many people have walked through its doors knowing it will outlive them, knowing they're experiencing something perpetually becoming. There's a peculiar magic in that. You can't take a cathedral's completion for granted. You can't say you've seen it. You can only say you've seen it in this particular moment of its endless becoming.

I used to write stories obsessively. Short fiction mostly, because short fiction felt achievable. I could finish a story in an afternoon, a few hours even. The satisfaction of typing "THE END" was like a small hit of something necessary. I filled folders with these completed things. And yet, I barely remember any of them. What I do remember, vividly, are the stories I never finished. There's one about a woman who discovers her neighbor is living the life she would have lived. I wrote about thirty pages. The premise is a question, a knot, an itch that won't be scratched. I've thought about this story more in the years since abandoning it than I did in the months I was writing it.

Maybe there's something about incompleteness that forces the reader—or the thinker—to become a co-creator. A finished work is received. It's done to you. But an unfinished work requires something from you. It asks you to complete it in the privacy of your own mind. It trusts you with its gaps.

I think about conversations I've had that trailed off naturally, without resolution. Someone says something that needs sitting with, and we both recognize it. We go quiet. The conversation has reached its natural ending point, which isn't an ending at all, just a place where the talking stops but the thinking doesn't. These feel more valuable to me than conversations that tie themselves up neatly with conclusions and exchanged phone numbers.

There's a Japanese aesthetic called *ma*—the concept of negative space, emptiness, the space between things. It's not merely absence; it's presence through absence. A room with too much furniture in it can feel cramped, but a sparsely furnished room with the right proportions feels spacious and generous. The empty space isn't a failure of decoration; it's the whole point. Similarly, an unfinished work isn't a work with something missing; it's a work that acknowledges its own limits and trusts the space beyond those limits to matter.

I've been rereading Montaigne's essays, which are gloriously incomplete. They circle around ideas rather than arriving at them. He contradicts himself without apparent distress. His essays end when they end, not because he's solved the problem but because he's reached some kind of working truce with it. The form itself—the essay, from the French *essai*, meaning attempt—is built on this principle. You're not writing a treatise. You're making an attempt. The attempt itself is the point.

There's something deeply humbling about acknowledging that you can't complete something. That the project is bigger than you, more complex than you anticipated, more interesting precisely because it resists your attempts at mastery over it. A lot of perfectionism is really about control—the need to shape something completely, to leave no loose threads, to make it impossible for anyone else to misunderstand or misinterpret. But life itself is loose threads and misunderstandings. Life is fundamentally incomplete, and perhaps our work should acknowledge that rather than pretend to transcend it.

I think about the people I've loved and lost touch with. The friendships that fizzled rather than ended. Are these failures? Sometimes I used to think so. But increasingly I see them as complete in their incompleteness. We knew each other for as long as we knew each other. The friendship wasn't a project with a disappointing conclusion; it was a period, and periods end, and that's not tragic—that's just rhythm.

Maybe the goal isn't to finish things but to engage with them as fully as possible before moving on. Maybe the artistic endeavor isn't to achieve some perfect, unchangeable form but to mark a moment when you had to stop, when the work had taught you what it needed to teach you, when you had to trust that it would survive without you.

There's a freedom in that. There's permission in that.

So I'm learning to be okay with the unfinished painting, the story that stops mid-gesture, the conversation that trails away, the life that doesn't resolve into the narrative I expected. I'm learning that incompleteness might not be a failure but a different kind of completion altogether—the completion of accepting that some things will always be becoming, and that might be their greatest strength.

The sky remains brilliant. The figure remains suggested. The grass remains a sketch. And somehow, in that refusal to finish, the work is finally whole.

# On the Strange Privilege of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about attention—the act of truly noticing something—and how it feels like a privilege that most of us don't properly acknowledge. Not the kind of privilege that comes with advantage or inheritance, but something quieter. The privilege of being able to stop and look.

There's a tree outside my awareness that I've never actually seen. It exists in the peripheral vision of the world, mentioned maybe in passing, but I've never stood before it with the specific intention of understanding what it is. This bothers me more than it should. The world is full of these unseen things, not because they're hidden, but because our attention is finite and we're all rationing it constantly, whether we realize it or not.

I think about this when I walk through cities. Everyone is moving with such purpose, such certainty about where they're going, and I'm struck by how little we actually see while we're in motion. The architecture above our heads goes unwatched. The small shops tucked between larger stores remain invisible. Other people become obstacles or background rather than fellow consciousness navigators also trying to make sense of being alive. We're all practicing a kind of necessary blindness just to function, to get from point A to point B without being overwhelmed by the sheer amount of information available to our senses.

But what happens when we break that pattern? What happens when someone decides to really look at something ordinary?

I think of the photographer who spent years photographing the same street corner. Or the naturalist who sat in the same forest and noticed things that no one had recorded before, not because they were hidden, but because they'd simply never been watched. There's something almost subversive about sustained attention in a world that profits from distraction and movement.

This connects to something I've noticed about boredom, too. We talk about boredom like it's a malfunction, a sign that something isn't engaging us properly, but I wonder if boredom is actually where attention goes to rest. It's the space where you're no longer seeking stimulation, no longer trying to extract value from each moment. There's a kind of freedom in it. A kid staring out a window for an hour isn't wasting time; they're doing something we've largely forgotten how to do, which is to let their attention drift naturally to whatever catches it.

I've also been thinking about how we describe our inner lives. We use metaphors borrowed from other domains—we talk about mental landscapes, emotional weather, psychological baggage. But I'm not sure these metaphors actually help us understand ourselves better. Maybe they just make our experience feel more manageable, more like something we can map and navigate. The truth is probably stranger and less coherent than any metaphor we could use.

What is it like to be thinking right now? It's not like moving through a landscape. It's not like weather. It's something more like language talking about language, consciousness observing itself, which creates this weird recursive loop that's impossible to fully step outside of. We're always trying to know ourselves from the inside, which is like trying to see your own eyes without a mirror.

This is why I think conversations matter so much. When someone describes their experience to you and you listen—really listen, not just wait for your turn to talk—you're briefly escaping that loop. You're accessing another consciousness through the only door it has, which is language. It's our only genuine technology for sharing subjective reality. Everything else—film, art, music—are translations and approximations. But when someone says "I felt this way and it was like this," and you understand them, you've briefly bridged the gap that normally separates one mind from another.

The fact that we can do this at all seems like it should be more remarkable than it is. We talk about it casually or take it for granted, but we're basically engaged in a miracle of translation every time we have a real conversation.

I'm also struck by how much of being human is actually about tolerating uncertainty. We're creatures that crave patterns and explanations, but reality doesn't neatly organize itself into patterns. We're constantly experiencing things that don't fit into our existing frameworks, and we have to choose between revising our understanding or dismissing the experience. Most of the time, I think, we dismiss it because revising our understanding is exhausting.

But there's something valuable in resisting that impulse sometimes. In letting things be strange and unexplained. In sitting with the feeling of not understanding something rather than reaching for the nearest comfortable explanation.

This applies to people, too. We're all doing the same thing with each other—creating simplified models of the people in our lives so we can navigate relationships without constantly being surprised. But people aren't simpler than our models. They're infinitely more complex. Every now and then, someone does something that doesn't fit the model we've created of them, and it's jarring. But maybe that's the moment where we're actually seeing them, rather than seeing the image we've constructed.

I don't know where I'm going with this. I've wandered from trees to attention to consciousness to relationships, and there's probably no through-line except that these are all things that interest me. They're all variations on the same theme: the difficulty and necessity of actually paying attention in a world designed to scatter it.

So maybe the real privilege isn't just being able to notice things—it's having the freedom to choose what you pay attention to, even knowing that choice is limited and costly. Even knowing that everything you focus on is something else you're not seeing. Even knowing that most of your life will be lived in that state of necessary blindness, moving from task to task without really seeing.

The privilege is in the awareness itself, I think. In knowing that you're not seeing most of the world, and in the moment of choosing to see something anyway.

# The Strange Mathematics of Belonging

I've been thinking lately about how we measure whether we belong somewhere, and how absurdly imprecise our calculations are.

You know that feeling when you walk into a room and instantly know whether you're in the right place? It's not really about the physical space—it's something subtler. It's the way conversations pause and resume, whether people make eye contact, whether there's a shared reference point you tap into or whether you're perpetually translating. I've spent enough time observing this phenomenon to realize that belonging isn't a binary state. It's more like humidity in the air: sometimes barely perceptible, sometimes thick enough to choke on.

I think we're taught to believe in clean categories. You belong or you don't. You're in the club or you're not. But my experience suggests this is one of those lies we tell ourselves to make complexity manageable. In reality, most of us exist in a constant state of partial belonging—fully at home nowhere, adequately comfortable in many places.

There's a particular kind of loneliness that comes from this. Not the dramatic loneliness of complete isolation, but the quieter kind you experience in a room full of friends. It's when you realize that nobody here knows about the thing you care about most, or the way you think about it. Or when you catch yourself editing your words mid-sentence because you sense the audience won't track with you. You remain physically present while emotionally stepping to the side.

What's interesting is how this never entirely goes away, even with people you love. You can be married for twenty years and still discover pockets of complete non-understanding. You can grow up with someone and realize you have fundamentally different internal architectures. I think one of the cruelest promises we make to ourselves is that love means complete understanding. It doesn't. Love might mean accepting that understanding will always be partial, and trying anyway.

I've noticed that people often respond to this partial belonging by trying harder—by becoming more palatable versions of themselves. This makes sense as a survival strategy, but it also perpetuates the problem. Because if everyone is performing an optimized version of themselves, nobody gets to just *be*. We end up with rooms full of people who are each lonely in roughly the same way, each convinced they're the only ones doing this translation work.

What would change if we acknowledged this more openly? If, instead of pretending we belong completely or not at all, we named the specific dimensions of our alienation? I belong here intellectually but not emotionally. I belong here historically but not practically. I belong here aesthetically but we're misaligned on values. I belong here because of one person, and that connection carries me through the rest.

There's something almost freeing about being precise about non-belonging. It's not a referendum on your worth. It's just data. Humans are too complicated to fit neatly anywhere except perhaps in a handful of contexts, and sometimes not even there.

I think about my friend Maya who once said she feels most like herself when she's alone, which initially sounded like a confession of sadness but which I've come to understand as clarity. She's not lonely; she's just aligned with solitude. She belongs to herself more fully than she belongs to any group, and she's made peace with this. There's something beautiful and also slightly unsettling about people like this—they seem to have taken the variable out of the equation by deciding that self-belonging is the primary category.

Most of us are less honest. We keep trying to cram ourselves into spaces that were never really designed for us, or that were designed for previous versions of us that no longer exist. How many people do you know who are still operating with the belonging calculations from when they were twenty? Who are still in the same career, the same city, the same relationships because they've built an identity around them, even if that identity no longer fits?

There's a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from maintaining belonging in spaces where you don't actually belong anymore. You have to keep performing, keep explaining, keep smoothing the rough edges. You start to forget what the edges even were originally.

I wonder if the Internet has made this better or worse. On one hand, it's now possible to find your people—the specific subset of humans interested in whatever obscure thing fascinates you. There are communities for everything. But there's something about physical proximity and sustained time that builds a different kind of belonging than digital affinity. You can find your people online, but you still have to live your days in the physical world with the people and places that are geographically near you.

The math doesn't work out. You can't fully belong everywhere, and it seems like you can't really fully belong anywhere except perhaps in brief, shimmering moments.

Maybe that's okay.

Maybe belonging isn't supposed to be a permanent condition but rather something that flickers in and out based on circumstances, who's in the room, what you had for breakfast, whether Mercury is in retrograde (kidding, but kind of?). Maybe the goal isn't to find the one place where you'll finally, at last, be understood completely, but rather to collect enough moments of partial connection that your life feels reasonably inhabited.

And maybe to be gentler with the people around us who are clearly doing their own translation work, who are editing themselves mid-sentence, who are present but not fully here. Instead of pretending complete belonging is possible, or pretending it doesn't matter, we could just acknowledge: "Yeah, I know this is hard. I'm doing it too."

That wouldn't solve the fundamental math problem. But it would change something about the texture of the room.

# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing

There's a quality to autumn light that makes me think about attention. The way it arrives at a lower angle than summer's direct assault from above, it seems to know how to illuminate details—the texture of a wall, the intricate veining of a leaf, the dust motes suspended in an otherwise invisible air. There's something generous about it, the way autumn light doesn't demand anything from you but does reward close looking.

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the spaces between the things we're supposed to notice. Nobody's ever told you to pay attention to the exact sound a coffee cup makes when you set it down, yet there's a remarkable variety in those sounds depending on the cup's weight, the surface it meets, your frame of mind. A ceramic mug on a wooden table sounds entirely different from one on tile, and somehow that difference matters, even though we're trained from childhood to treat these moments as negligible background noise.

The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote that the aspects of things that are most important for us are hidden because of their simplicity and familiarity. It's a strange thought—that the things most important to us are hiding in plain sight, protected by their very ordinariness. We develop this habit of unseeking, where we learn to look past things in favor of whatever we've decided is significant. A child hasn't learned this habit yet, which is why they can spend forty-five minutes investigating an ant while you're waiting to go somewhere.

I wonder what we lose when we perfect this learned blindness, and what we might gain if we could partially unlearn it without losing the ability to function. There's probably a balance point—you can't notice everything; that way lies paralysis. But the culture we've built seems to encourage swinging almost entirely to the other extreme, where we're supposed to move efficiently through the world, eyes on the goal, filtering out ninety-nine percent of the sensory input available to us.

Technology has made this worse and better simultaneously. Worse because we're now trained to process information at increasing velocity, scrolling past images and ideas that might have once commanded our full attention. A photograph that would have been examined carefully for minutes in 1985 now gets a half-second of visual processing before we move on to the next one. But better in that we have tools that can magnify the invisible—microscopes that show us the architecture of a raindrop, time-lapse cameras that reveal the hidden motion in flowers blooming, recordings that let us hear frequencies outside human hearing range. Science has given us permission to notice things that aren't immediately obvious.

There's a Japanese word, *komorebi*, which refers specifically to the filtered sunlight that falls through the leaves of trees. The fact that this has its own word seems significant. It suggests that at some point, a culture of people decided that this particular phenomenon was worth naming, worth calling out as distinct from "sunlight" or "light through trees"—it deserved its own word because it deserved individual attention. I wonder how different our consciousness would be if we had specific words for all the small, precise things we currently lump together under generic categories.

I've been reading about the practice of forest bathing—*shinrin-yoku*—which is simply the act of walking slowly through a forest with no particular destination, allowing your senses to receive whatever they encounter. It's not about achievement or exercise. It's about presence, about letting the forest teach your senses what to notice. Studies show it reduces cortisol and increases parasympathetic nervous system activity, which is another way of saying it calms you down, but that description somehow misses the point. It's not primarily about stress reduction; that's just what happens when you stop filtering everything through the lens of utility and let yourself actually perceive.

The problem, of course, is that we're not all living in forests, and even those who are usually have somewhere to be. Modern life demands efficiency. And there's nothing wrong with efficiency; it's let us do remarkable things. But we've let efficiency colonize territories where it doesn't necessarily belong. We eat efficiently, which means we often don't taste our food. We commute efficiently, which means we don't notice the trees we pass every day or the changing light or the other people sharing the space with us. We work efficiently, which means we don't often take time to think deeply about anything.

Yet something in us resists this, too. There's been a renaissance of what we might call "slow practices"—slow food, slow fashion, slow reading. These practices are explicitly about returning attention to things that have been streamlined away. But there's something vaguely privileged about calling it a "practice," as though noticing things requires a particular discipline or class position. Which it shouldn't. Noticing should be free, available to everyone.

Maybe the real art is in finding moments where you don't have to choose between efficiency and attention. The commute that's also a time to notice the changing seasons. The meal eaten quickly but tasted carefully. The walk between one obligation and the next where you allow yourself to actually see the streets you're traveling through.

I think what draws me to autumn light is that it seems to make noticing easier. It's more forgiving somehow, more patient than summer's brightness. It has a quality of melancholy that matches the contemplative mood it encourages. Spring light is exciting, summer light is urgent, winter light is thin and searching. But autumn light seems to invite you to slow down and pay attention not because you should, but because there's something genuinely worth seeing if you do.

That might be the secret—finding or creating conditions where noticing becomes easier than not noticing. Where the friction is reversed. Where the path of least resistance leads toward attention rather than away from it.

The light is changing as I write this. That's the thing about paying attention to light—you get the bonus of watching it transform continuously. It's never the same twice. Every moment of genuine perception is unique, unrepeatable. Which makes noticing not just a pleasant activity but a form of gathering—collecting moments that will never come again.

Maybe that's enough reason to try.
