# On the Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

I've been thinking lately about how rarely we get properly lost anymore. Not in the metaphorical sense—though God knows there's plenty of that going around—but the honest, geographical kind where you take a wrong turn and end up somewhere you didn't intend to be.

My phone knows exactly where I am at all times. It knows where I'm going. It knows seventeen different routes to get there, ranked by efficiency. It knows which of those routes has the best coffee shops if I want to make a detour. It has essentially eliminated one of humanity's oldest forms of mild adventure, and I'm not sure we've adequately mourned this loss.

I remember the last time I was genuinely, unmistakably lost. It was maybe five years ago in a small town in Portugal that I can't quite remember the name of. My phone had died—fully, completely dead in that way phones used to die before we all carried portable battery packs like anxious talismans. I had a general sense that my hotel was "that way," which in navigational terms means absolutely nothing. So I started walking.

What followed was two hours of wandering through narrow streets that twisted back on themselves in what felt like a deliberately mischievous pattern. I passed the same bakery three times. A woman watering her plants on a balcony started to recognize me by my increasingly confused expression. But instead of feeling frustrated, I felt something I can only describe as liberated. There were no notifications pinging at me. No sense of time wasted. No awareness of how many steps I'd taken or calories I'd burned. There was just me, the cobblestones, the smell of salt from the nearby ocean, and the genuine uncertainty about what was around the next corner.

I eventually found my hotel (it was closer than I thought), but what I took from that experience was more interesting than the destination itself. It was the memory of what it felt like to be genuinely surprised by geography. To turn a corner and think, "Oh, I've never seen this before," without immediately knowing its Yelp rating or whether it was historically significant.

This connects to something I've been puzzling over: our relationship with optimization. We've spent the last twenty years systematically removing friction from daily life, and it's been largely wonderful. I'm not romanticizing the pre-internet era—I remember it, and there was plenty to complain about. Waiting on hold with a customer service representative for forty-five minutes now seems like a relic of a barbaric age. Truly, technology has made much of life better.

But I wonder if in optimizing for efficiency, we've accidentally optimized away some of the things that make being alive interesting. The best moments in my life have almost always been inefficient ones. They involved detours, distractions, unexpected conversations, or simply being in the wrong place at the right time. These things can't be scheduled. They can't be optimized for. They require a certain amount of slack in the system, a willingness to not be heading toward something specific.

I've started noticing this in how we consume media, too. I used to browse a bookshelf at random and discover books. I'd flip through a magazine at a doctor's office and find an article I would never have searched for intentionally. Television had commercials that forced you to see advertisements for products you didn't know existed. These were inefficiencies, but they were also how serendipity worked.

Now the algorithm shows me things it thinks I'll like based on things I already like. This makes logical sense—it's what I asked for, in a way. But it creates a funhouse mirror effect where we end up only encountering variations on ourselves. My recommendations are increasingly tailored to me, which means they're increasingly less likely to surprise me.

There's a particular kind of joy in being surprised. Not shocked or frightened, but surprised—delighted by encountering something you didn't know you wanted to encounter. When was the last time you stumbled onto a song, book, or idea completely by accident? Not through algorithmic suggestion, but through actual happenstance?

I think about this a lot because I recognize I'm not immune to this trend. I've been optimizing my own life gradually, without really noticing it. My calendar is color-coded. I have a carefully curated morning routine. I've eliminated "wasted time" from my day. And while these things are efficient and productive, I've also noticed that I'm less creative, less surprising to myself. I know what I'm thinking before I think it, because my thoughts have been well-organized into efficient neural pathways that go exactly where they're supposed to go.

So I've started doing something small: once a week, I try to do something inefficiently. I'll take a different route somewhere and actually observe my surroundings. I'll browse a physical bookstore without a list. I'll start a conversation with someone without knowing where it's going. Nothing dramatic. Just small rebellions against optimized living.

These moments feel almost subversive in their ordinariness. I'll be sitting on a bench, having wandered somewhere for no particular reason, and I'll feel something like contentment that my phone didn't suggest I feel. I'll read a book that wasn't recommended to me by any algorithm, and the experience will feel fresher somehow, because it came from pure chance.

I don't think the answer is to abandon technology or efficiency. We can't really go back, and much of what technology provides is genuinely valuable. But I think we need to be more intentional about preserving space for the inefficient, the unexpected, the genuinely lost.

Because here's what I think we've forgotten: being lost isn't actually the worst outcome. Sometimes it's exactly where you need to be.

# The Architecture of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom—not as a failure of entertainment, but as a legitimate emotional state that might be trying to tell us something. We live in an age that treats boredom like a disease, something to be cured immediately with the nearest screen, notification, or distraction. But I wonder if we've lost something important in our rush to eliminate it.

When I was younger, my parents would occasionally implement what they called "No Electronics Day," which I resented with the full force of a teenager's wounded pride. I'd lie on my bed or sit in the backyard with absolutely nothing to do, and it was genuinely uncomfortable. Not painful, but uncomfortable in a way that made me restless and anxious. But something interesting happened if I sat with it long enough: my mind would start to wander in productive ways. I'd solve problems I'd been stuck on. I'd think about conversations and replay them, noticing things I hadn't before. I'd imagine elaborate scenarios that were basically my brain's way of processing something deeper.

Now scientists have a term for this: the "default mode network." When our minds aren't focused on an external task, a different neural network activates, one associated with introspection, memory consolidation, and creative thinking. In other words, boredom—or more precisely, the mental state that emerges when we stop fighting boredom—is when our brains do their best work.

The irony is that we've engineered boredom almost entirely out of modern life, and I suspect we're all paying a price for it. Consider how different your day might be if you genuinely couldn't fill every gap with stimulation. Your commute becomes an opportunity to think rather than a problem to solve. Waiting in a doctor's office becomes space for your mind to roam rather than an insult to be negotiated away with your phone. The shower, the walk, the moment before sleep—these used to be default territories for daydreaming and reflection. Now they're potential interruptions in our connectivity.

I don't think this is a simple matter of "phones bad." Technology itself is morally neutral; it's the way we've chosen to use it that matters. We've created digital environments explicitly designed by teams of engineers to be as engaging as possible. These apps employ principles from behavioral psychology to maximize "time spent" and "engagement metrics." They're designed to be more stimulating than reality, more responsive than actual human interaction. Of course they win our attention. Of course we use them to fill boredom. We've built machines that are better at capturing attention than anything evolution prepared our brains to resist.

But here's what troubles me: I think boredom serves a purpose beyond just enabling creative thought. Boredom is also a signal. It tells you that something isn't aligning with your values or interests. It's dissatisfaction trying to get your attention. If we silence every instance of boredom immediately, we never hear what it's trying to say.

Imagine if you never experienced boredom at a job. You'd stay indefinitely, even if it was wrong for you. Imagine if you never got bored in a relationship—well, you might never push for deeper intimacy or address lingering problems. Boredom, it seems to me, is one of the mind's ways of flagging misalignment. Not every instance requires dramatic life changes—some boredom is just boredom—but the capacity to experience it, to sit with it, to listen to what it might be telling you, seems important.

There's also something about the texture of human experience that worries me we're losing. I notice that younger people have different reference points for what "entertainment" looks like. Not better or worse necessarily, but different. They've grown up in a world where stimulation is constant and essentially free, where the expectation is that every moment should be at least mildly entertaining. The baseline for what counts as "good enough" keeps rising. Actual sunsets compete with Instagram filters. Real conversations compete with curated personas. Genuine human messiness competes with algorithmic polish.

I don't have teenagers, so I'm speculating here, but I wonder what this does to contentment. Not satisfaction—that's something you achieve. Contentment is something else; it's a peaceful acceptance of the present moment. It's what people used to cultivate through meditation or prayer or just sitting on a porch on a summer evening. It's not exciting, but it might be essential.

What I'm circling around is this: I think we should be more suspicious of our compulsive need to never be bored. Not in a preachy, "kids these days" kind of way, but genuinely suspicious. When you feel the impulse to pull out your phone during a quiet moment, ask yourself: am I bored because something is actually boring, or am I reaching for my phone because I've been conditioned to treat boredom as an emergency?

The practical implications are smaller than they might sound. I'm not suggesting anyone abandon technology or commit to a full-time rejection of convenience. But maybe sometimes—on a walk, during breakfast, before bed—we could just let ourselves be bored. We could sit with the discomfort for five minutes or ten and see what happens. We could notice if our refusal to be bored is actually serving us or if it's become another form of compulsion.

I think about the letter I'd write to my teenage self during those enforced No Electronics Days. I'd tell you that your mind was doing something important. That the restlessness you felt was the neural equivalent of stretching—necessary, slightly uncomfortable, and good for you. I'd tell you that years later, you'd be grateful for those moments, not because they were pleasant, but because they taught you that your mind could generate its own entertainment, could solve its own problems, could find meaning in nothing at all.

Boredom isn't failure. Sometimes it's just waiting—waiting for your mind to finish processing, waiting for clarity to emerge, waiting for you to remember who you are when nobody's trying to optimize your attention.

That's worth protecting, I think.

# On the Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about incompleteness, and how we've developed such an anxious relationship with it. Not the incompleteness of failure—that's a different animal entirely—but the everyday incompleteness that characterizes most of life. The book with a bookmark three-quarters through. The half-written email in a draft folder. The skill you're learning that may never make you exceptional. The thought you had yesterday that you never quite articulated.

We live in an age of completion culture. Everything must be finished, shipped, monetized, published, optimized. The work-in-progress is only valuable insofar as it becomes a finished product. An artist's sketches matter mainly because they lead to the gallery painting. Notes are only important if they eventually become the book. We've been taught that the unfinished is the unsuccessful, the abandoned, the failed.

But I wonder if we're missing something.

There's a specific kind of freedom in incompleteness that completion destroys. When something is finished, it becomes fixed. The sculpture is cast. The painting is varnished. The sentence is published. And in that fixing comes a certain closure that is both satisfying and suffocating. You can't change it anymore. You can't add to it or reshape it. It exists as it is, forever, which is wonderful until you realize you'd do it differently now.

The unfinished, by contrast, remains alive with possibility. It can become anything. The character sketch that never grew into a full story still contains infinite potential versions of that character. The sketch of the landscape still could become a painting, a photograph, a poem, or just remain a sketch that someone finds twenty years later and sees something entirely new in. There's something almost sacred about that openness.

I think about my grandmother's knitting basket—she'd started at least fifteen projects that she never completed. Some of them were just a few inches of fabric in progress. For years, my mother felt like these were failures, loose threads marking my grandmother's incomplete efforts. But toward the end of my grandmother's life, my mother understood something different: my grandmother hadn't abandoned these projects because she was lazy or incapable. She had simply moved on. She was interested in other things. And importantly, if someone she loved needed a scarf, she could pull out one of these partially-finished projects and complete it with specific intention, rather than making something new. The unfinished wasn't wasteful—it was flexible. It was resourceful. It was available.

There's also something honest about incompleteness. A finished thing must pretend to totality. It must suggest: "This is complete. This is what I meant to say. This is the full expression of the idea." But anyone who has ever finished something knows this is a lie we tell ourselves. Every finished work is really just a version that got interrupted by the need to call it done. Every book ends because the author ran out of time or funding or patience, not because the idea was actually exhausted. Every movie has deleted scenes. Every essay could go deeper.

The unfinished, though, admits its own limitations. It says: "This is as far as I got. There is more, but I'm showing you this." There's a peculiar honesty in that.

I'm also fascinated by the unfinished as a form of generosity. Some of the most beautiful and productive moments in human culture have come from incomplete things. The reader brings their own imagination to fill the gaps. A sketch can contain more power than a finished painting because the viewer must complete it in their mind. Hemingway wrote about the iceberg principle—that the power of writing comes from leaving most of it underwater, forcing readers to sense the whole. Incompleteness, in other words, can be a sophisticated artistic choice rather than a failure of execution.

There's also the temporal aspect I keep returning to. Everything in life is technically incomplete until we die, and even then, the impact and meaning of our lives continues to unfold for those we've affected. We're all unfinished works. Recognizing this is either terrifying or liberating depending on your mood, but I increasingly think it's supposed to be liberating.

If you accept that you're unfinished, you stop waiting for permission to exist. You don't need to be "ready" because readiness is a myth we tell ourselves. The person who waits until they're completely prepared, completely educated, completely confident never moves. But the person who accepts they'll always be somewhat unprepared, still learning, and not entirely sure—that person can actually do things.

I watched a musician once say that they never feel ready to perform. They perform anyway. The readiness, they said, would never come. So they had to choose: wait for something that wouldn't arrive, or proceed into incompleteness and find meaning in the attempt anyway. The incompleteness wasn't a failure of their preparation; it was the actual condition of performing, and accepting it made all the difference.

Maybe that's what we need to remember about our unfinished days, our incomplete projects, our partial ideas. They're not failures in waiting. They're the actual texture of a life lived, a mind engaged, a hand that tries even when it's not sure it will succeed.

I'm going to stop writing now, even though I could continue. There are more ideas forming at the edges of my mind—something about how unfinished conversations can sometimes matter more than resolved ones, something about the way paintings in museums have their own unfinished sections that we walk past without noticing. There are connections I haven't drawn, implications I haven't explored.

But maybe that's perfect. This piece is unfinished, and in its unfinishedness, it invites you to finish it in your own mind. To find what applies to your own unfinished things, whatever they might be. To sit with the uncomfortable idea that completion might not be the goal after all—that engagement with the incomplete, the partial, the still-becoming might be enough.

More than enough. Everything.

# On the Quiet Intelligence of Observation

I want to talk about looking. Not seeing—looking. There's a distinction that matters, though most people use the words interchangeably, the way they do with so many pairs of things that deserve their own separate territories.

Seeing is passive. Light hits your retina, signals travel to your brain, and you passively receive information. You see that a traffic light is red without thinking about it. You see your friend is wearing the shirt they wore last Tuesday. These are automatic registrations, the background hum of consciousness.

Looking is active. It's intentional. It requires patience and a kind of surrender to detail. When you look at something, you're choosing to inhabit the space of attention with it. When you look at a painting—I mean really look, not just glance—you're doing something closer to a conversation than to mere reception. You notice the artist's brushwork, the relationship between colors, the way shadow suggests form. You notice things that weren't explicitly put there but emerge from the totality of the work.

I think about this distinction a lot because I notice most people move through the world in the seeing mode, and it's not their fault. Modern life doesn't encourage looking. It encourages rapid consumption and quick judgments. Efficiency. But something gets lost there.

I have a friend who takes photographs, not professionally, just for herself. She has this habit of taking the same photograph over and over again from slightly different angles or at different times of day. When I asked her why, she said, "Each time I look for something I missed before." That's looking. That's the posture I mean.

There's a particular quality to the attention of someone who looks well. They move differently, speak differently. They ask better questions because they've actually registered enough nuance to know what they don't understand. Whereas the person who merely sees often speaks with false confidence, building elaborate theories on the foundation of a glance.

I think about museum-goers, how you can always spot them: the ones who are looking versus the ones who are seeing. The ones who are seeing move quickly from painting to painting, maybe spending ten seconds in front of each, checking boxes. The ones who are looking sometimes stand in front of a single work for twenty minutes, their eyes moving across it in patterns, their faces shifting as something newly noticed rearranges their understanding.

What I love about this is that the capacity to look is democratic. You don't need special training or equipment. You just need to decide that something is worth the time. A person who looks carefully at the grain of wood has access to the same contemplative depth as someone studying Renaissance masters. The objects of attention vary, but the quality of attention—that's what matters.

This connects to something I've been thinking about regarding expertise and knowledge. We tend to think expertise comes from abstract knowledge—reading about things, accumulating facts. But I'm increasingly convinced that real expertise is built on careful looking. The best birders don't identify birds through field guides; they identify them through accumulated observations of how different species move, the particular quality of their silence or sound, the shape they make against the sky. This knowledge lives in the body and in the pattern-recognition systems developed through looking.

I watched a master woodworker once select a piece of wood for a specific project. He didn't measure anything. He held different pieces, looked at them from various angles, ran his hands over them, closed his eyes. Later he explained that he was looking for the "grain direction" and could tell by looking where the wood would split or be difficult to work with. This wasn't magic. It was just looking, intensely and repeatedly, until patterns became visible that weren't visible to someone who hadn't looked before.

The paradox is that looking is both an easy thing—anyone can do it—and a hard thing, because it requires us to slow down. It requires us to stay with something even after we think we've already understood it. It requires us to be genuinely curious rather than seeking confirmation of what we already believe.

I notice that children look much better than most adults. They haven't yet learned to rush past things, to file them away in categories and move on. A child can spend an hour with a bug, really looking at it, watching how it moves, noticing the precise geometry of its legs. There's something we should try to preserve of that.

In our conversation, looking matters too. There's a difference between listening and hearing, just like seeing and looking, and we use those words wrong too. When someone really looks at you while you're speaking—makes eye contact, notices your expression, seems to actually register what you're saying rather than just waiting for their turn to talk—it changes the quality of the exchange. You feel seen rather than merely heard. And that makes you want to speak more truthfully.

I wonder sometimes if many of the problems in human relationships come down to insufficient looking. We make assumptions about people and rarely revise them because we're not looking carefully enough to notice when they've changed, or when our initial reading was wrong. We think we know our partners or our parents or our friends, but we're often seeing them through a lens of prior judgments rather than looking at who they actually are in the present moment.

The good news is that this is a skill that can be practiced. You can decide, right now, to look more carefully at something you encounter. Not to evaluate it, not to categorize it, not to figure out what it means. Just to look. To notice. To let it slowly reveal itself to you through your attention.

There's something almost meditative about looking. It silences the constant narration in your head—the planning, the worrying, the judging. You can't look deeply and think about your to-do list simultaneously. Looking demands presence.

And presence, I've come to believe, might be the most valuable thing we have to give to the world. Not our productivity or our opinions or our efficiency. Our presence. Our willingness to look carefully at what's in front of us and let it matter.

# The Peculiar Mathematics of Being Alive

I've been thinking lately about how we measure our lives in the smallest units imaginable, yet somehow these measurements never quite add up to anything coherent. We count our days, our hours, our accomplishments, as though the human experience were a ledger that could be balanced by the end of each month. But there's something fundamentally broken about this accounting system, and I think we all sense it, even if we don't talk about it much.

Consider the person who says they're "too busy" to call their mother. What does this mean, really? They have 168 hours in a week. Sleep takes roughly 56 of them. Work, say, 50 hours. Transportation, eating, hygiene, maybe another 30. That leaves 32 hours—more than a full day—yet somehow a 20-minute phone call is impossible. We're not actually measuring time; we're measuring attention. Or perhaps, to be more honest, we're measuring what we've unconsciously decided matters. The mathematics is perfectly logical, but the emotional mathematics tells a different story entirely.

This is the strange paradox of modern life: we've never had more control over our time, yet we've never felt more controlled by it. Our ancestors worked the fields because the work had to be done before winter. There was a natural endpoint to the day's labor. Now we can work forever—our emails follow us everywhere, our thoughts about work contaminate our leisure, and the thing we're working toward remains mysteriously, perpetually out of reach.

I wonder sometimes if this is why we've become so obsessed with productivity. It's an attempt to impose order on something fundamentally chaotic. If I just optimize my morning routine, if I batch my emails, if I use the Pomodoro Technique, maybe I'll actually feel like I've accomplished something. Maybe the hours will add up to a life. But hours don't add up to lives—moments do, and moments are irreducibly qualitative. You can't measure the depth of a conversation or the significance of a shared silence.

There's something about getting older that crystallizes this realization. When you're young, you have all the time in the world, so it doesn't matter—you waste it generously, extravagantly, without guilt. You're in a conversation at a party and you lose three hours without noticing. You read the same book twice just because you loved it. You don't know yet that time is finite, or rather, you know it intellectually but you don't *feel* it. There's a difference between knowing and feeling that seems to expand and contract depending on circumstances.

But somewhere along the way—and I think this happens at different ages for different people—you start to feel the shape of the ending. Not your ending specifically, maybe, but the ending. The fact that you'll never read every book, never visit every place, never master every skill you've always wanted to learn. You'll never have time for all of it. And this knowledge creates a kind of productive anxiety that we've turned into an entire industry. The self-improvement movement is essentially a denial of mortality dressed up as optimization.

What interests me is that some of the most memorable moments of our lives are the ones that are utterly "unproductive." A long walk with no destination. A conversation that circled back on itself five times. Sitting on a bench watching pigeons for no reason. Reading something just because it was beautiful, not because it would advance your career. These moments don't show up on any calendar or productivity tracker, yet they're often the ones we remember most vividly decades later.

I was speaking with someone recently who told me they hadn't taken a vacation in seven years. Not because they were forced to work the entire time, but because they felt guilty about stopping. That resonated with me because I recognized myself in it. There's a sort of Puritan logic that has burrowed deep into the American psyche—that worth is determined by what you produce, that rest is something you have to earn, that doing nothing is actually a kind of moral failure. We've turned existence itself into a hustle.

The tragic irony is that the things we need most—presence, connection, depth of understanding—can't be hurried. You can't optimize your way to meaningful friendship. You can't hack deeper love. You can't hack grief either, though God knows we try. We try to have our feelings efficiently, to process them quickly, to move through sadness or anger in discrete, manageable chunks.

But grief, real grief, doesn't respect project timelines. It takes the time it takes.

I think this is why we're all so tired. We're not tired because we're working too hard, exactly. We're tired because we're holding two contradictory beliefs simultaneously: that time is infinitely precious and therefore we can't waste a single moment of it, AND that we can somehow get control over time through sheer force of will. Both things might be true, but living in the tension between them is exhausting.

The alternative would require something like faith, or at least acceptance. It would mean believing that a day spent reading in bed matters just as much as a day spent being productive. It would mean trusting that an unmeasured life can still be a good life. It would mean accepting that you'll never do it all, read it all, be it all—and somehow being okay with that.

I'm not sure I've achieved that. I'm writing this essay partly as a way to procrastinate on other things I'm supposed to be doing, which seems pretty on-brand for the human condition. But maybe the point isn't to achieve perfect peace with the meaninglessness of our time measurements. Maybe the point is to notice when we're doing it, to catch ourselves trying to optimize our way out of being human, and to sometimes—not always, but sometimes—choose the unmeasured moment anyway.

The irony is that this essay took me about an hour to write, which I'll report to myself as "productive time," even though I'm not sure it actually changed anything about how I live. Maybe that's okay. Maybe that's just how it works.

# On the Strange Beauty of Being Uncertain

I've been thinking lately about how much of life is spent in the space between knowing and not knowing, and how we've collectively decided this liminal zone is somehow a failure of thought rather than its natural habitat.

There's something almost violent about our cultural insistence on certainty. We've built entire systems—educational, professional, social—that reward the confident assertion of knowledge while punishing the admission of doubt. A student who says "I'm not sure, but here's what I'm thinking" gets marked down compared to one who delivers a declarative statement with conviction, even if both are equally likely to be wrong. A leader who expresses uncertainty about a difficult decision is seen as weak, while one who projects absolute confidence, regardless of their actual knowledge, gets promoted. We've trained ourselves to hide the honest work of thinking beneath layers of performed assurance.

But I wonder if we're missing something essential about how understanding actually develops. Every genuine insight I've ever had came preceded by confusion. Not as a step to be rushed through, but as the necessary soil in which clarity eventually grows. The confusion wasn't a bug in my thinking—it was the feature that made thinking possible.

I'm fascinated by how different this is from what we usually celebrate. We love the mythologized moment of discovery—Newton's apple, Archimedes in the bath, the "eureka!" moment—but we gloss over the years of fumbling that necessarily preceded it. We emphasize the destination (knowledge achieved) while treating the journey (knowledge pursued through uncertainty) as mere preamble, something to be endured before the real story begins. But what if the journey is the story?

There's a particular kind of thinking that only becomes possible when you stop pretending to know things you don't. It's a more generous thinking, somehow—more attentive to the actual complexity of whatever you're considering, more willing to hold multiple contradictory ideas at once, more alive to the possibility that you might be wrong. Once you stop needing to be right, you become capable of actually exploring.

I notice this in conversations most clearly. The ones that genuinely matter, that leave me thinking about something differently afterward, are almost never the ones where someone was just confirming what I already believed. They're the ones where I encountered genuine uncertainty, genuine disagreement, genuine complication. Someone saying "I don't know, but what if..." opens more doors than someone saying "Obviously, the answer is..."

There's a researcher named Andy Clark who writes about how we use the world—physical objects, written notes, other people—as an extension of our own thinking. We offload cognition. I think uncertainty might be similar in a way. By being uncertain, by asking questions, by admitting the limits of what we know, we're inviting others into our thinking process. We're making our confusion collaborative rather than solitary. And there's something almost tender about that.

What strikes me is how much energy we waste trying to appear certain when we're actually uncertain. The mental load of maintaining that performance is significant. You have to monitor what you say, make sure it doesn't contradict your previous posture of certainty, avoid any situation where you might be caught not knowing something. It's exhausting. And for what? The people around us are also uncertain. Everyone's confused. We're all just doing our best with incomplete information and imperfect understanding.

I think about different fields and how they handle this differently. Science, at its best, has developed a language for uncertainty that's actually quite sophisticated. Scientists talk about confidence intervals, margins of error, the specific conditions under which findings hold. They build uncertainty into the very structure of how knowledge is claimed. And yet even in science, there's pressure toward overconfidence, toward certainty, toward the clean narrative that funders and the public seemingly want.

Meanwhile, philosophy has traditionally been more honest about uncertainty—it's baked into the discipline. The Socratic method is fundamentally about recognizing the limits of knowledge. "I know that I know nothing," Socrates claimed, and somehow that became the foundation for wisdom rather than its opposite. But even philosophy, when it moves from the academy into public discourse, often gets flattened into certainty. We want our philosophers to tell us how to live, not to sit with us in the uncertainty of living.

I wonder sometimes if the pandemic shifted anything in how we collectively think about certainty. For a moment, we were all uncertain together about something that mattered—what was actually true, what was safe, what we should do. It was uncomfortable, but there was something almost honest about it. The pretense of complete certainty dropped away, at least for a while. We admitted we were confused. We changed our minds. We lived in a fog of not-knowing and just... continued living.

Maybe that's the real skill we need to develop: not the ability to know with certainty, but the ability to act wisely despite uncertainty. To make decisions not because we're sure we're right, but because the situation demands a decision and we've done the best thinking we can with the information available. To hold our conclusions lightly, ready to adjust them when new evidence arrives. To be confident not in our knowledge but in our willingness to keep learning.

There's a kind of grace in that, I think. An acceptance of the human condition—that we're finite creatures trying to understand an infinite universe, working with incomplete information, limited perspective, and minds that are themselves mysterious to us. Rather than seeing this as a problem to be overcome, what if we saw it as the actual texture of being alive?

The opposite of uncertainty isn't certainty anyway—it's rigidity. It's the refusal to update, to learn, to grow. The person who is certain is imprisoned by their certainty. The person who is genuinely uncertain is free to explore, to change, to discover.

So I'm trying to get better at being uncertain. Trying to ask questions without needing to have the answers. Trying to say "I don't know" more often, to let that be the beginning of thinking rather than the admission of failure. It's countercultural. It feels weak. But I suspect it might be where actual wisdom lives.

# On the Particular Magic of Wandering

There's something about walking without a destination that modern life has nearly trained out of us. We've become so efficient with our movement—point A to point B, optimized routes, purposeful strides—that the art of wandering has become almost subversive. I find myself thinking about this more as I watch people navigate cities and countryside alike, always moving *toward* rather than simply *through*.

I wandered through a neighborhood I'd never explored last week, the kind of place you drive past without seeing. No agenda, no checklist. Just streets that curved in unexpected ways and buildings that revealed themselves gradually. There was a corner shop with hand-painted signage that probably predates the internet. An alley lined with flowering vines. A person sitting on their stoop, actually watching the world rather than being watched by a screen. These aren't discoveries you can engineer with a travel guide—they're the rewards of purposeful aimlessness.

The Greeks had a concept for this. *Sauntering*, though that's not quite Greek, more of a lovely French-English hybrid. The word itself supposedly comes from "Holy Land"—because medieval pilgrims wandering toward Jerusalem were assumed to be heading for "Sainte Terre," the Holy Land. So to saunter meant to wander in the direction of something sacred, even if you never actually arrived. Isn't that perfect? The goal was the wandering itself, sanctified by intention without demand.

What struck me most during that recent walk was the permission it gave me. Permission to stop and look at something that caught my eye without justifying it to anyone, including myself. Permission to follow a street simply because I wondered where it went. Permission to be slow in a world obsessed with speed. We don't often grant ourselves that anymore.

There's a productivity culture so pervasive that idleness feels like moral failure. Even leisure has become quantified and optimized—"getting your steps in," "mindful walks," wellness gamified. None of this is inherently bad, but something is lost when we can't simply walk without measuring it, tracking it, monetizing it. The moment you label your wandering as your "creative break" or your "mental health practice," part of its magic evaporates. It becomes another item on the to-do list, another way to optimize yourself.

I think about how children wander. They'll spend an afternoon examining the same patch of ground, noticing things that adults have trained themselves not to see. They have no destination in mind, no efficiency metric. The walk *is* the point. And somehow, through this purposeless observation, they learn more about their world than any structured tour could teach them. They notice patterns, develop questions, construct their own understanding.

We could use more of that approach as adults. Not in the sense of regression—I'm not suggesting we abandon all purpose and planning—but in the reclamation of space for genuine observation. For curiosity untethered from utility. For the pleasure of not knowing where we're going.

I've noticed that the best conversations often happen during walks with no particular destination. Something about the rhythm of walking, the sideways perspective, the way you're both looking in the same direction rather than at each other, loosens something in people. Thoughts that seemed knotted in a sitting conversation somehow unspool. The walking gives the mind permission to wander along with the body. Maybe there's something in our DNA that recognizes the walking conversation as the natural state of human exchange—we walked and talked for millennia before we invented chairs and conference tables.

There's also something about wandering that provides distance without requiring escape. You don't have to flee your life or your city to get perspective. Sometimes a different route through your own neighborhood, walking where you'd normally drive, noticing architecture you've never seen, gives you exactly the mental reset that a two-week vacation promises but rarely delivers. The unfamiliar exists right alongside the familiar if you slow down enough to let it reveal itself.

I wonder if part of what we're collectively starved for in our rush-driven world is this specific type of peace—not the peace of accomplishment, where you've checked off the boxes and earned your rest, but the peace of engagement without stakes. Looking at something simply because it's there. Thinking about something without needing to solve it. Moving through space without accumulating anything except memory.

The funny thing about wandering is that it seems passive until you actually do it, and then you realize it requires a specific kind of attention. Real attention—not the divided, distracted variety we've normalized, but the kind where you're genuinely present. Noticing how light falls through leaves. Wondering about the people in the windows of houses you pass. Considering why a street is shaped the way it is. Observing how a neighborhood changes block by block.

This attention is its own reward. It's a reminder that you're alive, that you're capable of being surprised, that the world is still strange and interesting if you move through it slowly enough. In a world that constantly demands we be productive and purposeful, there's a quiet rebellion in simply being present without extracting value from it.

So I'm thinking perhaps we should normalize wandering again. Not as a productivity hack or wellness practice, but as a legitimate way to spend time. To walk without a destination, to explore without a guidebook, to be lost in a neighborhood you could technically find your way out of. To remember that not every moment needs to generate output or insight or steps on a pedometer.

Maybe the real magic isn't in discovery at all, but in the state of mind that allows discovery to happen—a mind unrushed, unburdened by destination, open to whatever small beauties or interesting oddities emerge. Sainte Terre, the Holy Land, is always right where you are, if you're willing to wander slowly enough to notice it.

# On the Strange Comfort of Not Knowing

There's a peculiar peace that settles over you when you finally accept that you don't have to understand everything. I've been thinking about this a lot lately—how we're culturally conditioned to treat uncertainty like a disease, something to be cured with enough research, enough time, enough thinking. But what if uncertainty is actually the default state of existence, and our constant striving for answers is the real aberration?

I noticed this feeling most acutely the other day while watching rain. Not contemplating it, not photographing it for social media, just watching it fall on leaves that couldn't possibly care about my philosophical musings. The rain was doing its thing, the leaves were receiving it, and somewhere in that interaction was a completeness that required no interpretation. I didn't need to understand cloud formation or plant physiology to appreciate what I was seeing. The mystery didn't diminish the experience—it deepened it.

We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet somehow anxiety levels have never been higher. I wonder if there's a connection. When you can Google any question instantly, the expectation becomes that you *should* know the answer. The space between question and answer has collapsed. There's no time for wondering anymore, no room for the productive sitting-with-not-knowing that characterized human experience for most of our history.

My grandmother, who passed away five years ago, used to say "I'll never know" about things with a kind of contentment that baffled younger me. Why wouldn't you try to find out? Now I understand she wasn't being lazy or incurious. She was making a deliberate choice about which mysteries to pursue and which to let breathe. Not every question deserves a definitive answer. Some are better left as questions.

This is especially true about other people. We spend so much energy trying to figure out why people do what they do, what they *really* mean, whether they like us, what they think about us. We construct elaborate theories based on minimal evidence, then build entire emotional structures on these theories. The exhaustion of it all. And for what? You could spend your entire life trying to understand another person and still never fully succeed. They're not a puzzle with a solution. They're a person, irreducibly complex, constantly changing, fundamentally private in ways you'll never quite access.

I think about this with relationships that ended. There's usually this period where you endlessly analyze: What did I do wrong? What do they really think of me now? Could we have salvaged it? The mind churns and churns, producing no useful output. Eventually, most people give up on finding the "correct" interpretation of events. You just... move on. Not because you found the answer, but because you stopped needing to.

There's also something deeply humanizing about admitting ignorance. I notice that people I respect most—truly wise people, not just educated ones—seem comfortable saying "I don't know" more often than others. There's no defensive posturing, no rush to fill silence with speculation presented as fact. They sit with not knowing and somehow seem more present for it.

I've been thinking about love this way too. The more you try to define it, dissect it, understand exactly why you love someone, the more it slips away. The good relationships I've observed aren't the ones where people have everything figured out. They're the ones where people are willing to just... show up. To be bewildered together. To make it work not because they understand each other perfectly, but despite understanding each other only partially.

There's a religious quality to this acceptance, I think, though you don't need to be religious to access it. It's the surrender that mystics speak of. Not surrender as defeat, but as a kind of intelligent yielding. A recognition that some forces are larger than your understanding of them.

The older I get, the more comfortable I become with my own inconsistency. I hold beliefs that contradict each other. I do things my values don't endorse. I feel ways I can't justify. Once this troubled me endlessly. Why can't I be coherent? Why can't I resolve these contradictions? Now I see that contradiction might not be a bug but a feature. Maybe humans aren't supposed to be perfectly consistent. Maybe we're supposed to be paradoxical, holding multiple truths simultaneously, trying on different ways of being.

I think about death sometimes, and how the ultimate mystery is waiting for everyone. No amount of understanding will change that final unknowing. But somehow, accepting this feels lighter than fighting it. The pretense that we can know everything, control everything, predict everything—that's heavy. You're always one step behind, always catching up to reality as it moves past you.

There's a freedom in this realization, though. If you're never going to fully understand anyway, you might as well stop trying so hard. Might as well look around more. Listen better. Pay attention to the particular texture of your immediate experience rather than constantly analyzing it.

This isn't an argument for abandonment of reason or curiosity. I still read, still think, still try to learn. But I'm more selective now about where I direct that effort. I'm less interested in understanding people and more interested in simply knowing them. Less interested in explaining emotions and more interested in feeling them. Less interested in the right answer and more interested in the right question.

Sometimes I think the most sophisticated thing a human can do is be genuinely uncertain and genuinely okay with it. To hold the question and not frantically search for an exit. To say "I don't know, and maybe that's alright" and really mean it.

The rain is falling again as I write this, and I'm not trying to understand it. I'm just listening to what it sounds like against the window, and that seems like enough.

# On the Strange Beauty of Small Decisions

I've been thinking lately about the moments that reshape us—not the dramatic ones that make headlines in our own minds, but the quiet decisions that slip past almost unnoticed. The choice to take a different route home. To call someone back instead of deleting the message. To try the coffee shop you've walked past a hundred times. These are the hinges upon which lives turn, I think, though we rarely acknowledge it while they're happening.

There's something almost comforting about this idea, actually. It means we're not entirely subject to fate or grand destiny. We're constantly, minutely steering ourselves through existence with these small acts of intention. And it means that the life you're living right now isn't the only possible life—it's just the one that resulted from an infinite series of tiny choices, many of which you've probably already forgotten.

I wonder sometimes what alternate versions of myself exist in the probability space of the multiverse, if such a thing exists. There's a me who took the job in Portland. A me who married someone different, or didn't marry at all. A me who learned the guitar seriously instead of putting it down after two weeks of aching fingers. These shadow selves are neither better nor worse—they're just different expressions of the same central consciousness, shaped by different coordinates on the map of possibility.

What strikes me most is that none of these theoretical versions would feel like they were living the consolation-prize version of their life. Each one would have their own arc, their own meaning, their own sense of rightness or wrongness about the path they'd taken. The version of me in Portland probably has moments of wondering what would have happened if I'd stayed here instead. We're all convinced, I think, that we made the choice we made, and that it mattered somehow, even when we can barely remember making it.

This is why nostalgia is so bittersweet. It's not just missing the past—it's mourning the fact that you can never fully understand it. You can remember what happened, but you can't fully recapture what it *felt* like to not know what would happen next. That young person who was deciding something—deciding to go to that party, deciding to study that subject, deciding to trust someone—they lived in a moment of genuine uncertainty. But when you look back, you can only see the person who made the choice and its aftermath. The actual moment of decision is opaque to you now. You've crossed through it and can't go back to the threshold.

I think this is why we tell stories so much. We're trying to reconstruct the feeling of meaningful uncertainty, even though we're narrating from a point where the outcome is already known. The best stories manage to create that sense of not-knowing even though we're reading forward through time and could look ahead if we wanted. There's an art to making the destination feel uncertain even after you've arrived.

Lately I've been paying more attention to the way my thoughts move. Not the content of thoughts so much as the texture of thinking itself. How sometimes your mind is racing ahead of you, jumping ten steps into the future, while your body is still inhabiting the present moment. How sometimes you'll suddenly realize you've been thinking the same thought for five minutes on repeat without actually progressing it. How thoughts seem to arise in you almost unbidden—you don't decide to think them so much as discover you're already thinking them.

This makes the illusion of control feel paper-thin sometimes. How much of what we "decide" is actually just us noticing what we've already decided? When someone asks what you want for dinner and you hear yourself say "Thai food," did you decide that, or did the thought arrive fully formed and you just reported it? The philosophical question feels important somehow, even though I have no idea how to answer it.

I've also become fascinated by the concept of "found time"—those moments when you discover that something takes less effort or time than you'd anticipated, and suddenly you have this unexpected pocket of freedom. You sit down expecting to spend an hour on some task, and twenty minutes later you're done. There's this strange little gift of unscheduled time. It's never much, but there's something about it that feels more valuable than scheduled leisure time, even though they're the same minutes. Maybe it's the surprise of it. Maybe it's that it's genuinely free rather than being time you'd already allocated.

I think we don't talk enough about pleasure. Not sexual pleasure, though that too, but ordinary pleasure. The pleasure of good light through a window. The pleasure of finishing a piece of writing you're satisfied with. The pleasure of a conversation where you feel truly understood. We have this cultural tendency to treat pleasure as somehow frivolous—as though serious, meaningful people shouldn't waste time on it. But I think pleasure is actually incredibly important information. It's what tells you what's worth doing.

The things that bring you genuine pleasure are usually pointing at something true about who you are and what matters to you. If you take pleasure in helping people, you're getting information about your values. If you take pleasure in learning, in creating, in moving your body, in understanding how things work—these aren't distractions from meaning, they're where meaning lives.

So much of my anxiety, I think, comes from not listening to this information. From trying to do things that look meaningful from the outside rather than things that actually produce that internal sense of rightness. And the weird thing is that the guilt about not doing something productive usually prevents me from enjoying whatever it is I *am* doing. So you lose twice—once because you're not doing the thing that would feel meaningful, and again because you're not present for what you are doing.

I don't have any grand conclusions here. Just observations about how we move through time, how we decide, how we try to make meaning from contingency. How we're all improvising constantly, acting as though our choices matter because in the moment before we make them, they actually do. And then we move forward into the consequences, and those consequences become who we are, until we make the next small decision that will ripple outward in ways we'll never fully understand.

It's strange being alive. I'm grateful for it, most days.

# The Quiet Art of Getting Lost

There's something profoundly human about not knowing where you are. I don't mean the panic of being actually lost—that's different, that comes with anxiety and the desperate search for landmarks. I mean the deliberate kind of lostness, the sort you can only achieve when you decide that the destination doesn't matter as much as the walking.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, about how we've systematized the world in ways that make it almost impossible to genuinely wander anymore. We have GPS coordinates for every building, digital breadcrumbs that track our routes, algorithms that predict where we'll want to go before we know ourselves. Even when we try to get lost, our phones won't let us. There's a sad irony in that.

When I was a kid, I used to ride my bicycle in expanding circles from my house, pushing outward until the familiar became unfamiliar, until the streets I knew started branching into streets I didn't. My parents would have had a collective heart attack if they'd known how far I actually went, but there was something essential in those hours of small discovery. I'd find a corner store I'd never noticed before, or a park hidden behind a row of houses, or an old woman with a garden so impossibly lush it seemed like magic in the middle of suburbia. These weren't important discoveries in any meaningful sense. They didn't change my life or teach me vital skills. But they changed how I felt about the world—they made it bigger, more mysterious, more mine somehow.

As adults, we've largely given up on this kind of wandering. We're too busy. We have destinations. Time is money, and wandering is waste. We optimize our routes and our lives, folding the unexpected out of our days like we're Marie Kondo-ing our own existence. Everything is supposed to spark joy, which is just another way of saying everything is supposed to be useful.

But I think we're missing something crucial in that optimization. Not just something nostalgic or romantic, though there's that too. There's something actually important about encounters with the unexpected, with inefficiency, with time spent going nowhere in particular.

Psychologists talk about how boredom and idle wandering are actually when our brains do some of their best work. The default mode network activates when we're not task-focused, and that's when creativity happens, when we process emotions, when we make unexpected connections between ideas. We need to be lost sometimes. We need time that doesn't lead anywhere because that's when our minds can actually go somewhere.

There's also something about getting lost that returns us to a kind of humility. In our optimized lives, we're supposed to have it all figured out. We're supposed to know who we are, what we want, where we're going. We're supposed to have five-year plans and clearly defined goals. The message is relentless: uncertainty is a problem to be solved, not a state to be inhabited.

But uncertainty is actually where we live most of the time, I think. We just tell ourselves elaborate stories to obscure it. Getting lost—really lost, in the quiet, deliberate sense—is like taking off a pair of glasses you didn't know you were wearing. For a few hours, you can't pretend to know what's coming next. You can't optimize. You can only be present in the moment, in front of you, in this unfamiliar street with these unfamiliar trees.

I wonder if that's part of why travel appeals to us so much, why we spend money we don't have on vacations to places we don't know. We're desperately seeking permission to be lost for a while. We're paying for the privilege of not knowing where anything is. And it works, for a moment, until our phones find the WiFi and Google Maps kicks in and we're back to being exactly where we're supposed to be.

There's a difference, I think, between being a tourist and being a wanderer. A tourist goes to see specific things, to check boxes, to have experiences that can be photographed and posted. A wanderer just goes. The wanderer has hours that don't produce anything, conversations that lead nowhere, views that don't get shared. The wanderer is inefficient and unoptimized and completely, utterly pointless—and maybe that's the entire point.

I started thinking about this because I realized I couldn't remember the last time I genuinely didn't know what time it was. I used to lose entire days to reading or painting or just sitting. Now I'm always aware of time's passage, always conscious of the next thing I should be doing. My attention is fragmented, my presence distributed across multiple tasks and platforms. I'm rarely fully here, fully now.

What would it take to reclaim that? To deliberately create space for not knowing? It seems almost radical now, the kind of self-indulgence that people with real responsibilities can't afford. But everyone has time; we just spend it differently. We scroll. We optimize. We plan. What if we just... didn't, for a while?

I think I'm going to go take a walk. Not to anywhere specific. Not with a fitness tracker counting my steps or a destination in mind. Just out into the world with the intention of being lost in it, of noticing what I notice, of taking the turn that calls to me rather than the one that makes sense.

Maybe I'll find nothing. Maybe I'll just walk for an hour and come home exactly where I started, unchanged and unimproved. Maybe no one will ever know where I was or what I did, and it won't matter because it won't lead anywhere useful or productive.

And maybe—just maybe—that's exactly the point.

# The Strange Beauty of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the margins—in the moments we're not supposed to pay attention to, the details that don't make it into conversation, the small observations that seem too trivial to mention. Yet these are often the things that stick with us longest, that shape how we actually experience the world rather than how we think we're supposed to experience it.

There's this particular quality of light in late afternoon that I've noticed more as I've gotten older. It's not the golden hour that photographers chase—it's earlier than that, when the sun is still relatively high but the angle has shifted just enough that it doesn't wash everything in uniform brightness. Instead, it creates these pockets of shadow and illumination, making ordinary things look textured in ways they don't at noon or dusk. A brick wall becomes almost three-dimensional. The weave in a cotton shirt becomes visible. Trees cast shadows with actual depth. This light lasts maybe twenty or thirty minutes, and I've started to recognize it, to pause when I see it, to just stand there and look around.

I mention this because it's the kind of thing that seems embarrassingly small to talk about in conversation. If someone asks me what I did today, I don't say, "I stood outside and noticed the light." That would make me sound either pretentious or unmoored from normal concerns. But the truth is, those moments of noticing have become more valuable to me than many of the things I'm supposed to find important.

This connects to something broader I've been thinking about: the difference between experiencing life and narrating life. We're all constantly narrating our lives now, translating moments into social media posts, into stories we tell friends, into the mental narrative we maintain about who we are and what our life is like. This narration is necessary, even valuable—it's how we make meaning, how we connect, how we create continuity between past and present and future. But it also filters experience through a lens of what's shareable, what's coherent, what fits the story we're telling about ourselves.

The things that don't fit the narrative are often the most interesting.

I think about this when I'm reading older literature—not historical fiction, but actual old writing, where the conventions were different. Medieval or Renaissance writers would include seemingly random details about what someone was wearing, or how a room smelled, or what a character noticed about another character's fingernails. These details don't advance the plot. They don't establish character in the way modern writing does. They just sit there, little fragments of sensory experience that the writer thought was worth recording. And I find myself drawn to them precisely because they feel real in a way that a more polished narrative doesn't.

Maybe this is what older people mean when they talk about having a different perspective on time. It's not that time actually goes faster as you age, though it feels that way. It's that you stop living entirely for future moments—the next milestone, the next achievement, the next chapter—and start noticing that the present moment is actually where you're living. It's obvious when you say it out loud, but it's a surprisingly difficult thing to internalize. For most of my life, I was always already somewhere else mentally: already in college, already in my career, already thinking about what would come next. The present was always just the waiting room for the future.

I wonder what kind of people we'd be if we could really live in the present without that particular neurosis—if we could be fully where we are without simultaneously reaching toward where we think we should be going. Maybe we'd be more present with other people. Maybe we'd ask better questions, listen better, notice when someone's tired or worried without them having to say it. Maybe we'd notice our own fatigue and worry too, rather than pushing past them in service of the narrative of productivity and progress.

There's something I've noticed about conversations with people who seem genuinely comfortable with themselves: they ask good questions and then actually listen to the answers. They don't seem to be waiting for their turn to talk or mentally categorizing things in terms of how they relate to their own life. They're just there, receiving what the other person is saying. I've always envied this quality. I've also noticed it's rare. Most conversations, including my own, are more like two people taking turns broadcasting their internal monologues.

This might be why I find myself drawn to nature more now—not hiking or extreme experiences, just being outside, walking, noticing things. A crow doing something complicated with a piece of bread. The particular architecture of a specific tree. Lichens on a rock. Clouds that are just clouds, not metaphors or Instagram moments. The things are just themselves, not narrated, not trying to be something other than what they are.

I think this is why I'm also more skeptical now of the constant pressure to turn everything into a story, into a lesson, into something that advances the narrative. Not every moment needs to mean something. Not every experience needs to be integrated into the larger arc of "my life." Some things can just be small, singular, unrepeatable moments that happened and then passed. There's something peaceful about that. It takes pressure off.

I've also been thinking about how much of what we worry about is actually a failure of imagination—not imagining bad things, but failing to imagine that things could be otherwise, that we could have different habits and priorities and relationships to time itself. We inherit assumptions about what life should look like, how success should feel, what matters, and we defend these assumptions as if they were natural laws rather than cultural choices. But they're not. They're choices that previous generations made, and we're under no obligation to keep making those same choices.

This sounds grandiose, but I mean it very simply: you can choose to stand outside and look at light. You can choose to notice things that don't go in any story. You can choose to be uncertain and to sit with that uncertainty rather than rushing to resolve it into a narrative. You can choose to be slower, in a world that profits from your hurrying. 

None of this will change your life in the dramatic way that we think change should happen. But maybe that's fine. Maybe the good life isn't a story arc with a satisfying resolution. Maybe it's just this—the quality of attention you bring to whatever ordinary moment you're in, the permission you give yourself to notice small things, the willingness to stand in the light for no reason at all.

# On the Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that peculiar state we spend so much energy trying to escape. It's the background radiation of modern life—something we're constantly aware of and desperately trying to shield ourselves from. We have phones, streaming services, video games, social media, podcasts for every conceivable interest. We can be entertained at any moment. And yet, if you watch people, especially young people, there's an undercurrent of restlessness. A need to fill every silence, every gap, every moment of potential boredom with something stimulating.

I wonder if we've made a mistake.

Boredom, I think, is badly misunderstood. We treat it like a disease, something to be cured immediately with the next distraction. But I'm coming to believe that boredom might actually be one of the most creative and necessary states a human being can experience.

When you're bored, something interesting happens. Your mind doesn't shut down—it wanders. It makes unexpected connections. It gets restless enough to want something, but not so engaged that it's constrained by the demands of the current task. It's a state of productive dissatisfaction. This is where daydreaming lives. This is where imagination actually originates.

Think about where good ideas come from. People always say they come in the shower, or while walking, or in the moment before sleep. These are all states where your conscious mind isn't heavily engaged in something specific. There's a kind of boredom there—a space where your mind can roam. If you were constantly stimulated, constantly fed new input, would your brain ever have the chance to do this kind of wandering synthesis?

I suspect not.

I read somewhere that the human brain evolved in an environment of extensive boredom. Our ancestors spent a lot of time waiting. Waiting for food, waiting for predators, waiting for the seasons to change. That wasn't a bug in human experience; it was more or less the default state. And in that boredom, our minds developed their unique capacity for imagination, pattern-recognition, and abstract thought. We told stories to ourselves and each other during those boring nights around the fire. We thought about problems. We daydreamed about things that didn't exist yet.

Now we've engineered boredom almost entirely out of our lives, at least for those of us with access to technology. And I'm not sure we've gotten happier. In fact, I'd argue the opposite. There's a kind of anxiety in constant stimulation. Your nervous system is always being activated, always being pulled in new directions. You're never quite satisfied because there's always another thing, another video, another notification. It's a kind of hedonic treadmill, but worse, because the treadmill is moving faster than ever before.

I think about my phone, and how I use it. I have a genuine question in my mind that I want to explore, and instead of sitting with it, turning it over in my head, letting my mind play with it, I immediately reach for my phone. I can Google it. I can get the answer in seconds. Which sounds good in theory. But I've noticed that I don't actually retain these quick answers the way I retain things I've puzzled through myself. And more importantly, I've robbed myself of the boredom period—the time when my mind was actually engaged in productive thinking about the question.

There's something almost meditative about genuine boredom. Not the painful kind, where you're actively suffering and waiting for something. But the kind where you're free and unstructured, with no demands on your attention. You're not doing anything, and nothing is being done to you. You just are. And in that state, something shifts. Your breathing slows. Your mind becomes less anxious. Thoughts arise and fall away naturally.

I wonder if some of the mental health crisis we're experiencing—the anxiety, the depression, the scattered attention—is partly a result of our inability to experience boredom anymore. We've lost access to a state that our minds actually need. We've built a world designed to never let us be bored, and in doing so, we've made ourselves profoundly ill.

The solution isn't to reject technology entirely. That's not realistic, and besides, technology has enormous benefits. But maybe it's to be more intentional about when we use it and when we don't. To schedule boredom, in a sense. To protect pockets of time where we're not consuming anything, not being stimulated by anything, just existing with our own minds.

I've started trying to do this. I'll sit on my porch for twenty minutes without my phone. Not meditating in any formal sense, just sitting. And it's uncomfortable at first. My mind reaches for the phone. I feel slightly anxious without external input. But if I sit with it, something shifts. The anxiety passes. My mind starts to wander. And some of my best thoughts, my best ideas, have come in those quiet periods.

I think the future might belong to people who can tolerate boredom. In a world saturated with information and stimulation, the ability to be unstimulated, to be quiet, to let your mind wander and make unexpected connections—that might actually become a competitive advantage. Not just in creative fields, but in any field where genuine thinking is required.

So I'm making peace with boredom. I'm trying to see it not as a problem to be solved but as a gift to be accepted. A space where my mind can be itself, without the constant demands of the external world. A place where imagination lives.

It turns out, we might have been running from something we desperately need all along.
